title: Pay Only for Disagreement: Certified No-Regression Verdicts for Model Updates with Matching Label-Complexity Bounds
summary: Every production model is updated, by retraining, fine-tuning, quantization, or a silent vendor swap, and each update risks being worse than what it replaced. We formalize update promotion as certified paired risk-difference auditing. Our starting point is a support identity: the risk difference between two models lives on the inputs where they disagree, observable without labels. We build DISCERN, a sequential two-tier protocol. A zero-label tier certifies benign updates whose disagreement rate is below tolerance from unlabeled traffic alone. An audited tier labels only sampled disagreements through an anytime-valid confidence sequence, valid at every stopping time and under any label-routing rule, even an adversarial judge. We prove finite-sample validity and matching label-complexity bounds of order rho^2/eps^2 at the rate level, so exploiting free disagreement provably saves a factor 1/rho over any pairing-blind auditor, and the guarantee composes across an unbounded sequence of promotions from one error budget. Across 14,000+ replayed audit streams over 785 update pairs, including LoRA fine-tunes of language models up to 1.4B parameters, miscoverage is 0.0002 (nominal 5%), power 0.986 with zero false alarms, and 56% of benign updates certify with zero labels. Each audit emits a machine-checkable evidence record for post-market monitoring.

AI.tldr: DISCERN is a two-tier protocol for certifying machine learning model updates through certified paired risk-difference auditing. It uses a "support identity" concept where risk difference between two models lives on inputs where they disagree, observable without labels. The protocol has a zero-label tier for benign updates and an audited tier that uses anytime-valid confidence sequences for sampled disagreements.
AI.motivation: Production ML models are regularly updated (retraining, fine-tuning, quantization, vendor swaps), and each update risks being worse than the previous version. The authors formalize "update promotion" as a certified paired risk-difference auditing problem to ensure updates don't degrade model quality before deployment.
AI.method: The method uses a support identity: the risk difference between two models lives on inputs where they disagree, observable without labels. DISCERN is a sequential two-tier protocol: (1) A zero-label tier certifies benign updates whose disagreement rate is below tolerance from unlabeled traffic alone. (2) An audited tier labels only sampled disagreements through an anytime-valid confidence sequence, valid at every stopping time and under any label-routing rule, even an adversarial judge. The method provides finite-sample validity and matching label-complexity bounds of order rho^2/eps^2.
AI.result: Across 14,000+ replayed audit streams over 785 update pairs, including LoRA fine-tunes of language models up to 1.4B parameters: miscoverage is 0.0002 (nominal 5%), power 0.986 with zero false alarms, and 56% of benign updates certify with zero labels.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting free disagreement (via the support identity) provably saves a factor of 1/rho over any pairing-blind auditor. The guarantee composes across an unbounded sequence of promotions from one error budget. Each audit emits a machine-checkable evidence record for post-market monitoring.

title: Beyond Static RAG: An Adaptive, Tri-Metric Routing Framework for Efficient Long-Context Inference on Commodity GPUs
comment: This Paper is accepted and presented at ICML Scale Workshop 2026. https://scale-icml-2026.github.io/accepted_papers.html (Paper ID :72)
summary: Deploying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on commodity GPUs such as the NVIDIA T4 (16 GB VRAM) exposes a practical failure mode we call the Compression Paradox: neural prompt compression can add key-value (KV) cache contention and preprocessing latency that outweigh generation-time savings, while skipping compression can cause out-of-memory (OOM) failures on long contexts. We identify two distinct failure mechanisms when a vLLM-served LLM and a PyTorch-based compressor are co-deployed under tight memory budgets, and introduce the Tri-Metric Router, a deterministic, training-free policy that selects among Raw, Neural (LLMLingua-2), and Lexical (BM25) pipelines. The router uses three CPU-side signals: spatial complexity ($L$), syntactic density ($ρ_{key}$), and type-token ratio (TTR). Unlike prior semantic-only adaptation, our dispatch signal is hardware-physical, based on VRAM headroom and a latency crossover point. Thresholds are calibrated from profiling on LongBench qasper, yielding an operating crossover near 4,332 words on T4; our contribution is this calibration methodology rather than a hardware-specific constant. On out-of-distribution holdouts, the method achieves 0% OOM failures, 88.5 $\pm$ 4.4% oracle alignment, and 49.3% Combined F1, improving over always-on lexical compression by 5.2 points without additional VRAM or training cost.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the "Compression Paradox" in deploying RAG on commodity GPUs (NVIDIA T4), where neural prompt compression can cause KV cache contention and preprocessing latency issues, while skipping compression leads to OOM failures. The authors propose the Tri-Metric Router, a training-free policy that dynamically selects between Raw, Neural (LLMLingua-2), and Lexical (BM25) compression pipelines based on three CPU-side signals: spatial complexity, syntactic density, and type-token ratio.
AI.motivation: Deploying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on commodity GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA T4 with 16GB VRAM) reveals a practical failure mode: neural prompt compression can add KV cache contention and preprocessing latency that outweigh generation-time savings, while skipping compression causes OOM failures on long contexts. Existing semantic-only adaptation methods fail to address this hardware-physical constraint.
AI.method: The authors identify two distinct failure mechanisms when vLLM-served LLM and PyTorch-based compressor are co-deployed under tight memory budgets. They introduce the Tri-Metric Router, a deterministic, training-free policy that selects among Raw, Neural (LLMLingua-2), and Lexical (BM25) pipelines. The router uses three CPU-side signals: spatial complexity (L), syntactic density (ρ_key), and type-token ratio (TTR). Thresholds are calibrated from profiling on LongBench qasper, yielding an operating crossover near 4,332 words on T4.
AI.result: The method achieves 0% OOM failures, 88.5 ± 4.4% oracle alignment, and 49.3% Combined F1 on out-of-distribution holdouts, improving over always-on lexical compression by 5.2 points without additional VRAM or training cost.
AI.conclusion: The Tri-Metric Router effectively resolves the Compression Paradox by dynamically selecting compression strategies based on hardware-physical signals (VRAM headroom and latency crossover point). The key contribution is the calibration methodology (not hardware-specific constants), which enables 0% OOM failures while maintaining high oracle alignment and improving F1 scores over baseline approaches.

title: Where Grokking Happens: Distributed Utility and Fourier Recoding Without a Module Switch
summary: Where in a Transformer is the change from memorization to generalization functionally expressed? We introduce Transition Games--behavior-aligned exact activation games with paired non-generalizing controls--and find distributed utility gain with a prospective block-0 attention bias; selected degree-two modes account for 67--92% of its addition contrast across replacement games, and a disjoint exact path study confirms that block-1 MLP mediates more of their effect than all other tested downstream paths in 12/12 pairs. The sharper "MLP memorizes, attention generalizes" prediction instead reverses (-.331 bits/example at the memory anchor; 0/12 in the predicted direction), while routing onset, global rank collapse, and a prime-invariant architecture ridge also fail, identifying grokking here as spectral recoding of an existing distributed circuit rather than a module switch.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates where in a Transformer the transition from memorization to generalization occurs. Through "Transition Games" - controlled activation games with paired non-generalizing controls - the authors find that contrary to the common belief that "MLP memorizes, attention generalizes," block-0 attention bias and block-1 MLP are actually the key components involved. The study shows that grokking (sudden generalization after prolonged memorization) represents spectral recoding of an existing distributed circuit rather than a module switch.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a fundamental question in understanding Transformers: where exactly does the model transition from memorization to generalization? This is crucial for understanding interpretability and mechanistic reasoning in neural networks.
AI.method: The authors introduce "Transition Games" - behavior-aligned exact activation games with paired non-generalizing controls. They use degree-two modes analysis (accounting for 67-92% of addition contrast) and exact path studies to trace information flow through different Transformer components.
AI.result: The key findings challenge conventional wisdom: the "MLP memorizes, attention generalizes" prediction is reversed (-.331 bits/example at memory anchor; 0/12 in predicted direction). Block-1 MLP mediates more effect than all other downstream paths in 12/12 pairs. Grokking is identified as spectral recoding of an existing distributed circuit rather than a module switch.
AI.conclusion: The transition from memorization to generalization is functionally expressed through distributed utility gain with block-0 attention bias and block-1 MLP mediation, rather than through module switching or the previously hypothesized attention/MLP division of labor. Grokking represents spectral recoding of existing circuits.

title: SemABR: Measuring Video Semantic Fidelity with Multimodal LLMs for Adaptive Bitrate Streaming
summary: Conventional video metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and VMAF measure visual distortion or perceptual quality, but they do not directly capture semantic preservation: whether compression retains a video's objects, actions, and temporal narrative. Existing Quality-of-Experience (QoE)-driven bitrate-selection and resource-allocation methods primarily aim to minimize rebuffering and bitrate switching while maximizing perceptual video quality, without explicitly considering semantic preservation. To address this gap, we introduce video semantic fidelity (SF), a metric that quantifies how well a compressed video preserves the semantic content of its source. An offline multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates structured descriptions of the reference and compressed versions of the video, and a separate text-only large language model (LLM) evaluates their semantic correspondence. The resulting content-dependent SF--bitrate profiles are cached and queried by the online bitrate selector without invoking MLLMs at runtime. Evaluations on three subjective QoE benchmarks show a consistent positive association between SF and mean opinion scores (MOS). A separate human semantic-rating study evaluates semantic preservation and shows that SF correlates more strongly with human judgments than conventional video metrics. We then embed these profiles into a 5G MEC-assisted video-on-demand (VoD) resource-allocation framework at the base station. When wireless resources cannot support high bitrate levels for all users, the framework uses the SF--bitrate profiles to select bitrate levels jointly across users and reduce the semantic loss caused by the required bitrate reductions. NS-3 simulations with the 5G NR module show that the proposed framework achieves higher average and worst-user SF than the evaluated baselines, with a widening advantage as the wireless resources available to each user decrease.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces video semantic fidelity (SF), a novel metric that quantifies semantic preservation in compressed video using multimodal and text-only LLMs. The SF-bitrate profiles are integrated into a 5G MEC-assisted VoD resource-allocation framework, achieving superior semantic quality over conventional metrics in both subjective evaluations and NS-3 simulations.
AI.motivation: Conventional video metrics (PSNR, SSIM, VMAF) measure visual distortion or perceptual quality but fail to capture semantic preservation—whether compression retains a video's objects, actions, and temporal narrative. Existing QoE-driven bitrate-selection methods focus on minimizing rebuffering and bitrate switching without explicitly considering semantic content.
AI.method: The paper proposes video semantic fidelity (SF) using: (1) An offline multimodal LLM (MLLM) to generate structured descriptions of reference and compressed videos; (2) A separate text-only LLM to evaluate semantic correspondence between descriptions; (3) SF-bitrate profiles cached for online bitrate selection without runtime MLLM invocation. This is embedded into a 5G MEC-assisted VoD resource-allocation framework at the base station to jointly select bitrate levels across users when wireless resources are constrained.
AI.result: Evaluations on three subjective QoE benchmarks show consistent positive association between SF and mean opinion scores (MOS). A human semantic-rating study demonstrates SF correlates more strongly with human judgments than conventional video metrics. NS-3 simulations with 5G NR module show the framework achieves higher average and worst-user SF than baselines, with widening advantage as wireless resources decrease.
AI.conclusion: Semantic fidelity (SF) is a more human-aligned metric for video compression quality assessment than traditional perceptual metrics. Integrating SF-bitrate profiles into 5G MEC-assisted resource allocation effectively reduces semantic loss during bitrate reductions, providing superior QoE especially under constrained wireless resources.

title: Disentangling Algorithmic Bias from Archival Artifacts: A Controlled Audit of Vision-Language Model Valuation in Metropolitan Museum Archives
summary:
Auditing vision-language models (VLMs) for societal bias requires distinguishing direct algorithmic valuation disparities from confounders embedded within archival metadata. In this study, we audit Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models using historical artwork metadata from the Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access collection (N = 1,500 total objects; N = 743 attributed works: Male n = 534, Female n = 209; n = 618 anonymous).
  We establish a quantitative audit framework evaluating zero-shot CLIP logit differential scores across three semantic prompt pairs (masterpiece, quality, and influence). Unadjusted evaluations demonstrate high score convergence without a statistically significant main gender effect under OpenAI CLIP (mu_F = -0.0067 vs mu_M = -0.0035, p = 0.1829) or OpenCLIP (mu_F = 0.0171 vs mu_M = 0.0237, p = 0.1224). Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) confirm statistical equivalence across Cohen's d >= 0.25 bounds (pTOST < 0.005).
  Multivariate OLS regression controlling for artwork medium, creation era, and aspect ratio (R^2 < 0.02) confirms that artist gender has no statistically significant conditional effect (p > 0.20). High residual embedding variance (R^2 < 2%) indicates that global zero-shot valuation metrics operate near an embedding noise floor, showing that broad zero-shot prompt logit differentials are a coarse measurement instrument rather than proving absolute model fairness.
  We highlight two key caveats: (i) macro-level score equivalence reflects metric insensitivity to fine-grained visual-semantic features and does not preclude localized micro-level visual biases, and (ii) excluding 41.2% unattributed holdings reflects institutional survival bias. These results demonstrate the necessity of multivariate confound control, equivalence testing, and archival provenance auditing when assessing AI fairness in cultural heritage collections.

AI.tldr: This paper audits CLIP vision-language models for gender bias using Metropolitan Museum artwork, finding statistical equivalence in how models evaluate works by male vs. female artists at the macro level. However, this equivalence likely reflects measurement insensitivity rather than true fairness, as high residual variance indicates the metrics operate near noise floor.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to distinguish direct algorithmic valuation disparities from confounders embedded within archival metadata when auditing vision-language models for societal bias. The researchers aim to determine whether CLIP models exhibit gender bias in evaluating artwork, while properly accounting for confounding variables in historical datasets.
AI.method: The study audits CLIP models (both OpenAI and OpenCLIP variants) using historical artwork metadata from the Metropolitan Museum of Art (N = 1,500 objects; 743 attributed works with 534 male and 209 female artists, plus 618 anonymous). They employ a quantitative audit framework evaluating zero-shot CLIP logit differential scores across three semantic prompt pairs (masterpiece, quality, and influence). They use Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) for equivalence testing and multivariate OLS regression controlling for artwork medium, creation era, and aspect ratio to assess conditional effects.
AI.result: Unadjusted evaluations showed high score convergence without statistically significant gender effects for both OpenAI CLIP (μ_F = -0.0067 vs μ_M = -0.0035, p = 0.1829) and OpenCLIP (μ_F = 0.0171 vs μ_M = 0.0237, p = 0.1224). TOST confirmed statistical equivalence across Cohen's d ≥ 0.25 bounds (pTOST < 0.005). Multivariate OLS regression (R² < 0.02) confirmed no significant conditional effect of artist gender (p > 0.20). High residual embedding variance (R² < 2%) indicates the metrics operate near an embedding noise floor.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that CLIP models show statistical equivalence in evaluating artwork by male vs. female artists at the macro level, but this equivalence likely reflects metric insensitivity rather than true fairness. The authors argue that zero-shot logit differentials are too coarse a measurement instrument, and they highlight the importance of multivariate confound control, equivalence testing, and archival provenance auditing when assessing AI fairness in cultural heritage contexts. Key limitations include the coarse-grained nature of global metrics and institutional survival bias from excluding unattributed works.

title: Multimodal Aspect-Level Sentiment Analysis Based on Gated Noise Filtering and Emotion-Relevance Interaction
summary: Multimodal Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (MABSA) infers fine-grained sentiment polarity toward specific aspects by jointly modeling text and images. Despite progress in cross-modal fusion, two challenges remain in multi-aspect settings: (1) multimodal noise, where aspect-irrelevant content distracts sentiment learning; and (2) weak cross-modal sentiment alignment, as visual evidence can be ambiguous and textual--visual sentiments may conflict, limiting multimodal complementarity. To address these issues, we propose a Gated Noise-filtered Sentiment-Relevance Interaction (GNSRI) framework. It employs a gated noise-filtering module to suppress sentiment-irrelevant features and enhance aspect-aware sentiment cues, and a sentiment-relevance interaction module to capture consistent and conflicting cross-modal signals at micro and macro levels. Finally, a learnable decision fusion mechanism adaptively combines predictions from textual, visual, and cross-modal branches at the aspect level. Experiments on public MABSA benchmarks show that GNSRI outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving accuracy by 1.94\% and 2.06\% on Twitter-2015 and Twitter-2017, respectively.

AI.tldr: GNSRI is a novel framework for Multimodal Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis that addresses multimodal noise and weak cross-modal sentiment alignment through gated noise-filtering, sentiment-relevance interaction, and learnable decision fusion mechanisms.
AI.motivation: MABSA faces two key challenges in multi-aspect settings: (1) multimodal noise from aspect-irrelevant content, and (2) weak cross-modal sentiment alignment due to ambiguous visual evidence and conflicting textual-visual sentiments, limiting multimodal complementarity.
AI.method: The GNSRI framework consists of three components: (1) a gated noise-filtering module to suppress sentiment-irrelevant features and enhance aspect-aware sentiment cues; (2) a sentiment-relevance interaction module to capture consistent and conflicting cross-modal signals at micro and macro levels; (3) a learnable decision fusion mechanism that adaptively combines predictions from textual, visual, and cross-modal branches at the aspect level.
AI.result: GNSRI outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Twitter-2015 and Twitter-2017 benchmarks, achieving accuracy improvements of 1.94% and 2.06% respectively.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GNSRI framework effectively addresses multimodal noise and cross-modal sentiment alignment challenges in MABSA, demonstrating superior performance through its gated filtering and adaptive fusion mechanisms.

title: Not All Agents Are Equal: Code Quality and Post-Merge Maintenance Across Five Autonomous Coding Agents in the Wild
summary: Autonomous coding agents now open pull requests in public repositories at a scale that was out of reach two years ago, yet little is known about what happens to that code after it lands. This paper studies 37,623 provenance-labeled pull requests (PRs) from five commercial agents (OpenAI Codex, Devin, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code) and a matched human baseline, drawn from 2,807 GitHub repositories between December 2024 and July 2025. We combine the AIDev dataset with 58,792 cached GitHub API responses to measure security smells in added code, structural maintainability, post-merge churn, revert rates, and human review behavior. Three results stand out. First, quality differences are vendor-specific rather than uniform: Codex-authored PRs were reverted about half as often as human PRs (6.1% vs. 11.5%, odds ratio 0.50), while Devin PRs were reverted more often (14.5%, odds ratio 1.31). Second, agent code pooled across vendors was less likely than human code to contain a security smell (odds ratio 0.63), driven by fewer hardcoded credentials and eval-style constructs. Third, review effort concentrates unevenly: Copilot PRs drew the most human reviews and change requests, and Claude Code PRs waited the longest for a first human review (median 12.6 hours). All pipeline code, statistical reports, and figures are released for replication.

AI.tldr: This paper studies what happens to code from autonomous coding agents (OpenAI Codex, Devin, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code) after it is merged into public GitHub repositories. Analyzing 37,623 pull requests from 2,807 repositories between December 2024 and July 2025, researchers found vendor-specific quality differences, with agent code generally having fewer security smells but varying revert rates compared to human-written code.
AI.motivation: Autonomous coding agents now open pull requests at scale, but there is limited knowledge about the quality and long-term outcomes of their code after merging. This study addresses the gap by examining security, maintainability, and review patterns of agent-authored code in real-world repositories.
AI.method: The researchers combined the AIDev dataset with 58,792 cached GitHub API responses to analyze 37,623 provenance-labeled pull requests from five commercial agents and a matched human baseline across 2,807 GitHub repositories. They measured security smells, structural maintainability, post-merge churn, revert rates, and human review behavior.
AI.result: Three key findings emerged: (1) Quality differences are vendor-specific—Codex PRs reverted half as often as human PRs (6.1% vs 11.5%, OR 0.50), while Devin PRs reverted more often (14.5%, OR 1.31); (2) Agent code was less likely to contain security smells overall (OR 0.63), with fewer hardcoded credentials and eval-style constructs; (3) Review effort was unevenly distributed—Copilot PRs received the most human reviews and change requests, while Claude Code PRs had the longest wait for first review (median 12.6 hours).
AI.conclusion: The quality of autonomous agent code varies significantly by vendor, with no uniform pattern across agents. While agent code generally has fewer security issues, revert rates and review patterns differ substantially. These findings highlight the need for vendor-specific evaluation and monitoring of AI-generated code in production environments.

title: Selective Prediction and Uncertainty-Aware Referral for Pap Smear Classification
summary: Deep learning models for cervical cytology are almost always evaluated as if every prediction must be acted upon, yet a screening system deployed alongside a cytopathologist need not classify every slide: it can defer the cases it is least certain about. Evaluating such a system requires asking not only how often it is correct, but whether its confidence ranks its errors to the bottom. This paper studies selective prediction and uncertainty-aware referral on the Herlev Pap smear dataset under a binary Normal-versus-Abnormal formulation. Two lightweight transformer backbones (Swin-Tiny, TinyViT-5M) are fine-tuned on Herlev from ImageNet-pretrained weights with weighted random sampling, calibrated by post-hoc temperature scaling fit on a held-out calibration subset, and compared against a soft-voting ensemble of both models. Discrimination is reported alongside expected calibration error (ECE) and, as the primary endpoint, the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC). No statistically significant difference was detected between the two configurations in accuracy or macro-F1, yet the ensemble halves AURC (0.0022 vs. 0.0045, a 51.8% reduction, lower in all five folds) and extends the coverage at which zero errors are made from 18.3% to 72.8% of the pooled test predictions. The same ensemble is nonetheless worse calibrated in absolute terms (ECE 0.0339 vs. 0.0247) and produces more false negatives (14 vs. 10). These results separate two properties that are frequently conflated: the ability to rank predictions by trustworthiness, and the accuracy of the confidence values themselves. Ensembling improves the former while degrading the latter, and the former directly governs the observed risk-coverage tradeoff, whereas the latter governs the interpretation of the reported confidence values.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical gap in medical AI evaluation: rather than requiring every prediction to be acted upon, a screening system can defer uncertain cases to human experts. The study evaluates selective prediction on the Herlev Pap smear dataset using lightweight transformer ensembles, demonstrating that ensembling improves the ability to rank predictions by trustworthiness (halving AURC) but degrades the absolute calibration of confidence values.
AI.motivation: Current deep learning evaluations for cervical cytology assume every prediction must be acted upon. However, in practical deployment alongside a cytopathologist, the system can defer uncertain cases. This requires evaluating not just accuracy, but whether the model's confidence correctly ranks errors to the bottom (i.e., uncertain predictions are actually more likely to be wrong).
AI.method: Two lightweight transformer backbones (Swin-Tiny, TinyViT-5M) were fine-tuned on the Herlev Pap smear dataset (binary Normal vs Abnormal) from ImageNet-pretrained weights using weighted random sampling. Post-hoc temperature scaling was applied using a held-out calibration subset. The single models were compared against a soft-voting ensemble of both models. Evaluation metrics included discrimination, Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and the primary endpoint: Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve (AURC).
AI.result: No statistically significant difference was found between configurations in accuracy or macro-F1. However, the ensemble halved AURC (0.0022 vs 0.0045, a 51.8% reduction, lower in all five folds) and extended coverage at zero errors from 18.3% to 72.8% of pooled test predictions. Paradoxically, the ensemble was worse calibrated in absolute terms (ECE 0.0339 vs 0.0247) and produced more false negatives (14 vs 10).
AI.conclusion: The study disentangles two frequently conflated properties: (1) the ability to rank predictions by trustworthiness, and (2) the accuracy of confidence values themselves. Ensembling improves the former while degrading the latter. The risk-coverage tradeoff is governed by ranking ability, while confidence value interpretation depends on calibration. This has important implications for clinical deployment: a system can reliably defer low-confidence cases even if its confidence scores are not perfectly calibrated.

title: Making AI-Assisted Claims Independently Challengeable: Publication Authority and a Protocol for Falsifiable Publication Records
comment: Main article: 24 pages, 4 figures; supplementary material: 13 pages. Preprint; not peer-reviewed. Yifei Dong is the corresponding author
summary: AI-assisted claims can appear authoritative when evidence, analysis, human authorization, presentation, and correction history refer to different states. Provenance, attestation, and transparency expose history but alone do not specify the publication transition examined here. We develop Publication Authority as an exact-state, non-transferable, single-use publication capability and instantiate it in PAC-2026 (Publication-Accountability Calculus), a machine-readable AIJIM Protocol candidate. We evaluate its fourth bounded semantic freeze (SF-4), a fixed-profile specification designed for replaceable bindings. Six obligations govern evidence, runs and artifacts, measurement disclosure, authorization, surface correspondence, and lifecycle continuity. Each yields a target-bound witness, localized counterexample, or localized unverifiability; none can compensate for another. Only a fresh, complete all-pass record derives the permit consumed by one atomic publication transition. We use identity vectors, adversarial cases, finite models, and historical implementations. Ten models explored 110,764 safe reachable states; 76 unsafe configurations produced the expected violation or observer countermodel. A reader surface passing its correspondence check cannot authorize publication unless the accepted record admits that surface. SF-4 separates evidence horizon from verification time and rejects an authentic but causally invalid authorization. A historical predecessor path reproduced 17 frozen authorization-successor outcomes. A later in-house, instance-blind test of known case classes matched all 183 scored expectations; same-host package execution reproduced its 240 archived observations. Results support internal coherence, bounded safety, fault sensitivity, and limited constructibility, but not factual truth, general refinement, blind interoperability, field efficacy, or standards status.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Publication Authority as a novel, exact-state, non-transferable, single-use publication capability for AI-assisted claims. It is instantiated in PAC-2026 (Publication-Accountability Calculus), a machine-readable protocol with bounded semantic freeze (SF-4). The system uses six obligations governing evidence, artifacts, measurement, authorization, correspondence, and lifecycle continuity. Evaluation through ten models explored 110,764 safe states and 76 unsafe configurations, with subsequent testing matching 183 expectations and reproducing 240 observations. Results support internal coherence and bounded safety but not factual truth or general applicability.
AI.motivation: The motivation addresses a critical gap in AI-assisted publication: existing provenance, attestation, and transparency mechanisms expose history but fail to specify the publication transition itself. AI-assisted claims can appear authoritative even when evidence, analysis, authorization, presentation, and correction history refer to different states. The paper seeks to create a mechanism that ensures publication transitions are controlled, accountable, and not transferable.
AI.method: The paper develops PAC-2026 (Publication-Accountability Calculus) as a machine-readable AIJIM Protocol candidate. Key methods include: (1) defining Publication Authority as an exact-state, non-transferable, single-use capability; (2) implementing SF-4 (fourth bounded semantic freeze) as a fixed-profile specification for replaceable bindings; (3) establishing six obligations governing evidence, runs/artifacts, measurement disclosure, authorization, surface correspondence, and lifecycle continuity; (4) using identity vectors, adversarial cases, finite models, and historical implementations; (5) evaluating through ten models exploring 110,764 safe reachable states and 76 unsafe configurations; (6) conducting later instance-blind testing of known case classes matching 183 expectations.
AI.result: The evaluation produced: (1) 110,764 safe reachable states explored across ten models; (2) 76 unsafe configurations producing expected violations or observer countermodels; (3) a reader surface passing correspondence check cannot authorize publication unless the accepted record admits that surface; (4) SF-4 separates evidence horizon from verification time and rejects authentic but causally invalid authorization; (5) a historical predecessor path reproduced 17 frozen authorization-successor outcomes; (6) later in-house testing matched all 183 scored expectations; (7) same-host package execution reproduced 240 archived observations.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that PAC-2026 supports internal coherence, bounded safety, fault sensitivity, and limited constructibility. However, it explicitly does NOT support factual truth, general refinement, blind interoperability, field efficacy, or standards status. The system ensures publication transitions require fresh, complete all-pass records and that no single obligation can compensate for another. The approach is novel in specifying publication transition itself, not merely exposing history.

title: Human-aware Design Generation: Adding 3D Humans into Graphic Designs
summary: Graphic designs nowadays predominantly contain human images, where people are posed and framed in a delicate way to guide viewers' visual exploration and evoke desired feelings. Despite recent progress in automatic graphic design generation, there has been no work on investigating the role of the human representations in design creation. In this paper, we seek to emphasize the importance of visual human representations in graphic design generation, by studying a novel task, dubbed as design-conditioned 3D human adding. To solve this task, we propose a model that adds 3D human representations into an existing partial design, by predicting their 3D poses, their 2D composition in the image containing them, as well as the spatial arrangement of the image in the input design, to generate a complete design. Our experiments show that our model outperforms baselines by predicting the 3D human poses, 2D framing and human image layout that better harmonize with the other existing design elements, and generating higher-quality holistic designs. Our work is the first to explore connections between 3D human generation and 2D graphic design generation, which would inspire future research in leveraging 3D information to build more powerful generative models for graphic designs in the 2D domain. The code is available at https://github.com/GreyNails/Human-aware-Design-Generation-Adding-3D-Humans-into-Graphic-Designs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel task called "design-conditioned 3D human adding," which aims to add 3D human representations into existing partial graphic designs. The proposed model predicts 3D poses, 2D composition/framing, and spatial arrangement to generate harmonized complete designs.
AI.motivation: Graphic designs predominantly contain human images posed and framed to guide viewers' visual exploration. Despite progress in automatic graphic design generation, no prior work has investigated the role of human representations in design creation. This work seeks to emphasize the importance of visual human representations in graphic design generation.
AI.method: The proposed model adds 3D human representations into existing partial designs by predicting: (1) 3D poses of humans, (2) 2D composition/framing in the image, and (3) spatial arrangement of the image in the input design, to generate a complete design.
AI.result: The model outperforms baselines by predicting 3D human poses, 2D framing, and human image layout that better harmonize with other existing design elements, and generates higher-quality holistic designs.
AI.conclusion: This work is the first to explore connections between 3D human generation and 2D graphic design generation. It inspires future research in leveraging 3D information to build more powerful generative models for graphic designs in the 2D domain. Code is available at GitHub.

title: Timbre Analysis of the Hulusi, a Southwestern Chinese Free-Reed Instrument, using Machine Learning
summary: The hulusi is a wind instrument that was invented in Yunnan Province, China, and has become tremendously popular in recent years. It consists of a mouthpiece, a gourd, and three bamboo tubes, all with free reeds made of copper. The main bamboo tube in the middle has seven finger holes. In this instrument, the pipe length, not the free reed's eigenfrequency, determines the instrument's pitch, unlike, for example, with the Western accordion or the blues harp. In this study, a machine learning model implemented in the COMSAR framework (https://github.com/ifsm) was used to investigate the timbre characteristics of the \emph{hulusi} to cluster different instruments and pitches. The measured \emph{hulusi} pitches C, B, A, G, and F were analyzed according to seven psychoacoustic features, among which only the spectral centroid, sharpness, and fractal correlation dimension are shown to form pitch clusters. These timbre features were used to train Kohonen self-organizing maps (SOMs) for clustering. Brightness and sharpness analysis revealed that the highest pitches were less bright and less sharp than mid- and low-range pitches were. Furthermore, the fractal correlation dimension, which mainly determines the chaoticity of the initial transients, was the best-clustering timbre feature for the hulusi, with the highest pitches showing the least chaoticity. This result is supported by defining a cluster quality index for the SOMs.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the timbre characteristics of the hulusi (a Chinese wind instrument) using machine learning to cluster different instruments and pitches. The analysis focuses on psychoacoustic features including spectral centroid, sharpness, and fractal correlation dimension, which were found to form pitch clusters. Kohonen self-organizing maps (SOMs) were used for clustering analysis.
AI.motivation: The hulusi is a unique wind instrument where pipe length determines pitch rather than the free reed's eigenfrequency (unlike Western accordions or harmonicas). Despite its growing popularity, its timbre characteristics have not been thoroughly studied. This research aims to understand how psychoacoustic features can cluster different hulusi pitches and instruments.
AI.method: A machine learning model implemented in the COMSAR framework was used to analyze measured hulusi pitches (C, B, A, G, and F). Seven psychoacoustic features were evaluated, and three (spectral centroid, sharpness, and fractal correlation dimension) were identified as forming pitch clusters. Kohonen self-organizing maps (SOMs) were trained for clustering, with a cluster quality index defined to evaluate the results.
AI.result: Only three psychoacoustic features (spectral centroid, sharpness, and fractal correlation dimension) formed pitch clusters. The highest pitches were found to be less bright and less sharp than mid- and low-range pitches. The fractal correlation dimension (which determines chaoticity of initial transients) was the best clustering feature, with highest pitches showing the least chaoticity.
AI.conclusion: The fractal correlation dimension is the most effective timbre feature for clustering hulusi pitches. The inverse relationship between pitch and brightness/sharpness contradicts typical expectations, suggesting unique acoustic properties of the hulusi. This research demonstrates the potential of machine learning and psychoacoustic features for analyzing traditional musical instruments.

title: Temperon: Full-Time SAM Quality at a Third Less Wall-Clock
summary: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) doubles the cost of every training step, yet its benefit concentrates where training ends. We study where an expensive training mode should be spent and propose Temperon: a plain-SGD explorer for the first 43% of the epoch budget, then one scheduled hand-off that gives the entire final cosine anneal to a SAM-wrapped Muon refiner. On CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet (five seeds, times reported as epochs-to-target times an idle-GPU-calibrated epoch cost), Temperon matches the best full-time-SAM recipe on accuracy everywhere while reaching the hardest common target 35%, 34% and 32% sooner on three of the four, and sits a tier above the published SAM+SGD recipe at level cost. Ablations make the attribution exact: the Muon refiner is worth +0.85pp with everything else fixed; the explorer's shape and its restarts are worth nothing, and we withdraw them as contributions. Re-running the closest rival, late-phase SAM, at matched budget shows the frontier: it is fastest to every mid-level target, but the tier the Muon refiner buys (0.83 on CIFAR-100, 0.97 on CIFAR-10) is reached by no SGD-refined method in any seed, and on Tiny ImageNet, where Muon buys no tier, the rival simply wins -- the measured boundary of the method. The allocation law transfers to GPT-2 pretraining (full-SAM quality at -29% wall-clock) and GLUE fine-tuning (never worse than full-time SAM at a third of its SAM cost). Two constants organize the economics: skipping SAM early buys a fixed credit, and a Muon epoch costs 1.50x a SAM+SGD epoch on all four datasets. Finally, the hand-off cannot be timed from the trajectory: under cosine schedules the accuracy curve is plateau-then-surge, so the information lives in the schedule, making the scheduled switch principled rather than convenient. Code and a pip-installable implementation are released.

AI.tldr: Temperon is a training schedule that uses plain SGD for the first 43% of training, then switches to SAM-wrapped Muon optimizer for the remaining epochs with cosine annealing. This approach achieves full-SAM quality at significantly reduced computational cost by exploiting the observation that SAM's benefits concentrate near the end of training.
AI.motivation: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) doubles training cost but its benefits concentrate at the end of training. This creates inefficiency - most training steps don't need SAM's regularization. The authors sought to determine where expensive training modes should be spent to maximize efficiency.
AI.method: Temperon uses a scheduled hand-off approach: (1) Plain SGD for first 43% of epoch budget as an "explorer", then (2) One scheduled switch to SAM-wrapped Muon refiner with full cosine annealing for the remaining epochs. The 43% threshold and scheduling principle are key - the hand-off cannot be detected from the accuracy trajectory (which shows plateau-then-surge under cosine schedules), so the schedule itself encodes the timing information.
AI.result: Matches full-time SAM accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet. Reaches hardest common targets 35%, 34%, and 32% sooner on three of four datasets. At matched budget, late-phase SAM is fastest to mid-level targets, but Muon refiner achieves accuracy tiers (0.83 on CIFAR-100, 0.97 on CIFAR-10) unreachable by any SGD-refined method. Transfers to GPT-2 pretraining (full-SAM quality at -29% wall-clock) and GLUE fine-tuning (never worse than full-time SAM at 1/3 SAM cost).
AI.conclusion: The key insight is that computational budget allocation should follow a schedule rather than trajectory-based triggers. Two constants organize the economics: skipping SAM early buys a fixed credit, and a Muon epoch costs 1.50× a SAM+SGD epoch. The Muon refiner contributes +0.85pp accuracy while the explorer's shape and restarts contribute nothing. The method achieves full-SAM quality at substantially reduced computational cost, with the scheduled switch being principled rather than convenient.

title: Divide and Conquer: Mixture-of-Bottleneck Experts in Informative Ordinal Space for Video-based Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
summary: Video-based Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) must handle information from text, audio, and image sequence in human speaking videos, yet current methods often fail to integrate modalities with task awareness. Most models treat video sentiment prediction as a single task, overlooking its ordinal nature, and their fusion strategies struggle to capture diverse unique and synergic cues across modalities. To address these limitations, we adopt a divide-and-conquer perspective by reformulating MSA as an ordinal regression problem and decoupling it into polarity recognition and intensity prediction. Driven by information theory, we introduce a Mixture-of-Bottleneck (MoB) framework that assigns different latents to polarity- and intensity-specific experts for different modalities. With the learning of information bottleneck, each expert learns compact and task-relevant representations while filtering out redundancy and noise. A multimodal bottleneck routing fusion module then fuses these expert latents with hard mining strategy, guiding the prediction in the ordinal sentiment space. Extensive experiments on 4 MSA datasets and 4 language models show that MoB effectively leverages informative latents from diverse modalities and captures general sentiment structure. Beyond stronger performance, MoB comprehensively captures fine-grained intra- and inter-modal dynamics, enabling more trustworthy localization of nuanced video sentiment signals.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Mixture-of-Bottleneck (MoB) framework for video-based multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) that addresses limitations in task awareness and modality integration by reformulating sentiment prediction as an ordinal regression problem with separate polarity recognition and intensity prediction components.
AI.motivation: Current MSA methods fail to integrate modalities with task awareness, treat video sentiment prediction as a single task (ignoring its ordinal nature), and struggle to capture diverse unique and synergic cues across modalities through their fusion strategies.
AI.method: The paper adopts a divide-and-conquer perspective by: (1) Reformulating MSA as ordinal regression decoupled into polarity recognition and intensity prediction; (2) Introducing a Mixture-of-Bottleneck (MoB) framework that assigns different latents to polarity- and intensity-specific experts for different modalities; (3) Using information bottleneck learning to learn compact, task-relevant representations while filtering redundancy and noise; (4) Developing a multimodal bottleneck routing fusion module with hard mining strategy to guide prediction in ordinal sentiment space.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 4 MSA datasets and 4 language models demonstrate that MoB effectively leverages informative latents from diverse modalities, captures general sentiment structure, and achieves stronger performance while enabling more trustworthy localization of nuanced video sentiment signals.
AI.conclusion: The MoB framework provides a novel approach to video-based MSA by addressing the ordinal nature of sentiment and effectively fusing multimodal information through specialized experts and information bottleneck principles, enabling fine-grained intra- and inter-modal dynamics capture.

title: Quiescence in Concert: Composing Multi-Channel Time-Outs for IOCO
summary: In Model-Based Testing (MBT), test suites are generated automatically from a formal specification. The theory of testing real-time systems is rich, but often underused in practice, partly because applying the timed machinery demands expertise practitioners should not need. In prior work we addressed this for timed testing with a canonic lifting operator, which lets a modeller specify behaviour as plain labelled transition systems while implicitly obtaining the timed automata that express their quiescent behaviour (the explicit absence of outputs) with timers. This paper takes the next step: we show that our lifting still works when each component carries its own time-out on its own channel. This way, we introduce a multi-channel lifting. We show that it commutes with parallel composition, i.e. composing and lifting is the same as lifting first and then composing. We show that the MBT apparatus survives: conformance, test generation and verdicts are preserved by the lifting, on the testable traces that a time-out based tester can observe.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a prior canonic lifting operator for timed testing to support multi-channel timeouts where each component has its own timeout per channel. The key contributions are proving that this multi-channel lifting commutes with parallel composition and preserves the full MBT apparatus (conformance, test generation, verdicts) for testable traces observable by timeout-based testers.
AI.motivation: The theory of testing real-time systems is well-developed but underused in practice because applying timed machinery requires significant expertise that practitioners should not need. Prior work attempted to address this by introducing a canonic lifting operator allowing behavior specification as plain labelled transition systems (LTS) with implicit conversion to timed automata expressing quiescent behavior with timers. This paper extends that approach to handle multiple channels with individual timeouts.
AI.method: The paper extends the canonic lifting operator to a multi-channel setting where each component can have its own timeout on individual communication channels. The key theoretical work involves proving that this multi-channel lifting commutes with parallel composition (lifting after composition equals composition after lifting), and that the MBT apparatus (conformance relations, test generation algorithms, and verdict determination) remains preserved for testable traces observable by timeout-based testers.
AI.result: The paper establishes two main results: (1) The multi-channel lifting commutes with parallel composition - meaning composing components and then lifting yields the same result as lifting each component first and then composing them. (2) The MBT apparatus survives the transformation - conformance relations, test generation procedures, and test verdicts are all preserved by the lifting, specifically for the testable traces that a timeout-based tester can observe.
AI.conclusion: The multi-channel lifting approach successfully extends prior work to handle per-component, per-channel timeouts while preserving key MBT properties. The commutation with parallel composition is a significant theoretical result enabling compositional reasoning. This work bridges the gap between formal timed testing theory and practical MBT by allowing practitioners to work with simple LTS specifications while implicitly obtaining correct timed automata behavior.

title: A Heisenberg Lift Descriptor for Order Sensitive Online Handwriting Recognition
summary: Online handwriting recognition systems typically represent pen trajectories through fixed-length Euclidean shape descriptors that capture the spatial outline of each stroke, but are insensitive to the order in which that outline is produced. Two strokes that trace the same region of the plane in opposite directions are indistinguishable to any such order-blind representation, yet their traversal directions may carry decisive class information in characters where loop orientation and stroke sequencing matter. This paper introduces a Heisenberg-lift framework that addresses this gap through a compact, interpretable, order-sensitive augmentation for online pen-trajectory features. The simplest instance is the terminal signed area, a single parameter-free scalar appended to an existing Euclidean descriptor at negligible computational cost. Evaluated on two standard online handwriting benchmarks, this one-scalar addition, consistently raises classifier accuracy over the Euclidean baseline. On the hardest character pair in our study, the letters o and y, the signed area alone achieves perfect separation while the Euclidean baseline falls short. The advantage grows further under additive coordinate noise, a practically relevant degradation in pen-trajectory data. A richer fifteen-dimensional extension, derived from a noncommutative Heisenberg-group subdivision scheme, provides additional gains in noisy and loop-structured conditions. Dimension-matched statistical controls confirm that all improvements reflect geometric information rather than feature-count inflation. The resulting descriptor is lightweight, closed-form, and directly interpretable, making it a practical augmentation for online handwriting and related document-trajectory classification pipelines in which the direction of stroke execution carries discriminative information.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Heisenberg-lift framework for online handwriting recognition that captures stroke direction information (order-sensitivity) that standard Euclidean shape descriptors miss. The simplest implementation is the "terminal signed area," a single scalar that appends to existing descriptors with minimal computational cost. This addition consistently improves classification accuracy, achieves perfect separation on challenging character pairs (o and y), and performs even better under noisy conditions.
AI.motivation: Current online handwriting recognition systems use fixed-length Euclidean shape descriptors that capture spatial outline but ignore stroke traversal order. Two strokes tracing the same region in opposite directions appear identical, yet directional information may be critical for distinguishing characters where loop orientation and stroke sequencing matter (e.g., 'o' vs 'y').
AI.method: The authors propose a Heisenberg-lift framework that adds order-sensitive geometric information to existing Euclidean descriptors. The simplest instance is the "terminal signed area" - a single scalar parameter computed from the pen trajectory. A richer 15-dimensional extension is also derived using noncommutative Heisenberg-group subdivision. These augmentations are evaluated against dimension-matched statistical controls on two standard online handwriting benchmarks.
AI.result: The terminal signed area scalar consistently raises classifier accuracy over the Euclidean baseline. On the hardest character pair (letters 'o' and 'y'), the signed area alone achieves perfect separation while the Euclidean baseline fails. Performance advantage increases under additive coordinate noise. The 15-dimensional extension provides additional gains in noisy and loop-structured conditions. All improvements are confirmed to reflect genuine geometric information rather than feature-count inflation.
AI.conclusion: The Heisenberg-lift framework provides a lightweight, closed-form, and interpretable augmentation for online handwriting recognition. The terminal signed area is parameter-free, computationally cheap, and effectively captures directional information that Euclidean descriptors miss. This makes it practical for document-trajectory classification pipelines where stroke execution direction carries discriminative information.

title: EvolveTrade: Experience-Driven Policy Refinement for Self-Evolving LLM Trading Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents can combine market data, news, and executable analysis, but their behavior is often controlled by static hand-written tool-use policies that are fixed before deployment. This limits their ability to adapt how they gather evidence, invoke tools, verify signals, and manage risk under changing market regimes. We introduce EvolveTrade, a self-evolving framework that treats the system prompt of a tool-using trading agent as a text-parameterized policy. After each update interval, a Policy Agent revises this policy using accumulated decision traces and realized portfolio feedback, while keeping the backbone LLM fixed. The updated policy is then used for the next batch of trading decisions, enabling the agent to refine its information-acquisition and portfolio-construction procedure over time. Experiments across multiple market regimes and two LLM backbones show that EvolveTrade often improves Sharpe Ratio and Cumulative Return over fixed-policy LLM baselines, achieving the improved SR and CR in most evaluated settings. Behavioral analyses further show that self-evolved policies increase code-mediated analysis and activate regime-relevant computations; case-level policy-to-return attributions trace how policy-induced allocation changes contribute to realized return differences. These results suggest that adapting the reusable procedure governing tool use is a key direction for building more robust LLM trading agents.

AI.tldr: EvolveTrade is a self-evolving framework for LLM trading agents that dynamically adapts the system prompt (tool-use policy) based on accumulated decision traces and portfolio feedback, without changing the backbone LLM. This enables agents to refine their information-acquisition and portfolio-construction procedures over time under changing market regimes.
AI.motivation: LLM trading agents are limited by static hand-written tool-use policies fixed before deployment, preventing them from adapting how they gather evidence, invoke tools, verify signals, and manage risk under changing market regimes.
AI.method: EvolveTrade treats the system prompt of a tool-using trading agent as a text-parameterized policy. A Policy Agent revises this policy after each update interval using accumulated decision traces and realized portfolio feedback, while keeping the backbone LLM fixed. The updated policy is then used for subsequent trading decisions.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple market regimes and two LLM backbones show that EvolveTrade often improves Sharpe Ratio and Cumulative Return over fixed-policy LLM baselines. Behavioral analyses reveal that self-evolved policies increase code-mediated analysis and activate regime-relevant computations. Case-level policy-to-return attributions demonstrate how policy-induced allocation changes contribute to realized return differences.
AI.conclusion: Adapting the reusable procedure governing tool use is a key direction for building more robust LLM trading agents. The framework enables agents to evolve their behavior based on realized performance, improving adaptability across different market conditions.

title: PointGrade: Geometric Priors for Grading MoonBoard Problems
summary: A MoonBoard is a standardized bouldering wall used in gyms around the world. Climbs up the wall limited to only a subset of holds are known as problems. We introduce PointGrade, a novel machine learning approach to predicting the difficulty of a MoonBoard problem. By sampling a point cloud from pre-scanned meshes of every hold, our model combines 3D object classification architecture with existing sequence-based approaches to difficulty grade prediction. Our method captures latent geometric information contained the climb, outperforming other work on the problem that neglect this data.

AI.tldr: PointGrade is a novel machine learning approach that predicts the difficulty of MoonBoard climbing problems by sampling point clouds from 3D-scanned hold meshes and combining 3D object classification architectures with sequence-based methods, capturing geometric information that previous approaches missed.
AI.motivation: MoonBoard is a standardized bouldering wall used globally, but predicting problem difficulty remains challenging. Existing approaches neglect the geometric information available from pre-scanned hold meshes, limiting their predictive accuracy.
AI.method: The method samples point clouds from pre-scanned 3D meshes of climbing holds and combines 3D object classification architecture with existing sequence-based approaches to difficulty grade prediction.
AI.result: The method captures latent geometric information contained in the climb and outperforms other work on the problem that neglect this data.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating 3D geometric data through point cloud sampling significantly improves difficulty prediction for MoonBoard problems compared to approaches that rely solely on sequence-based methods.

title: The Unbearable Weight: Scaling Models and Methods for UAV Audio Classification
summary: As unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) become increasingly prevalent in consumer and defense settings, classifying them reliably from limited, modality-specific data is an urgent challenge. The dominant approach, large pretrained networks fully fine-tuned on task data, carries a substantial computational and memory weight that is hard to bear in resource-constrained UAV deployments, where edge inference and rapid retraining for emerging platforms are both required. This paper systematically scales across both model architectures and fine-tuning methods for UAV audio classification, asking when that weight is justified and when lighter alternatives prevail. Using a custom dataset of 3,100 audio clips spanning 31 drone classes, we evaluate transformer (ViT, AST) and convolutional (custom CNN, ResNet-18/152, MobileNet-V3-S/L, EfficientNet-B0/B7) backbones under full fine-tuning, classifier-only fine-tuning, and four parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods: SSF, IA3, OFT, and selective batch-norm tuning. All configurations are evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation across accuracy, training time, trainable-parameter share, and inference-time memory footprint. Selective batch-norm fine-tuning of EfficientNet-B7 with three-fold augmentations achieves the highest validation accuracy (97.65% +- 0.30) while updating under 0.5% of model parameters. Across the sweep, lightweight CNNs consistently outperform transformers on both accuracy and efficiency. For UAV audio classification under data scarcity, scaling the method outperforms scaling the model.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates efficient approaches for UAV (drone) audio classification under resource constraints, comparing transformer and CNN architectures across various fine-tuning methods. The study finds that selective batch-norm fine-tuning of EfficientNet-B7 achieves 97.65% accuracy while updating less than 0.5% of model parameters, and that lightweight CNNs consistently outperform transformers for this task.
AI.motivation: The dominant approach of large pretrained networks fully fine-tuned on task data is computationally expensive and memory-intensive, which is problematic for resource-constrained UAV deployments requiring edge inference and rapid retraining capabilities.
AI.method: The researchers evaluated multiple model architectures (ViT, AST, custom CNN, ResNet-18/152, MobileNet-V3-S/L, EfficientNet-B0/B7) combined with different fine-tuning strategies (full fine-tuning, classifier-only, and 4 PEFT methods: SSF, IA3, OFT, selective batch-norm tuning) using a custom dataset of 3,100 audio clips across 31 drone classes. All configurations were evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation across accuracy, training time, trainable-parameter share, and inference-time memory footprint.
AI.result: Selective batch-norm fine-tuning of EfficientNet-B7 with three-fold augmentations achieved the highest validation accuracy of 97.65% (±0.30) while updating under 0.5% of model parameters. Lightweight CNNs consistently outperformed transformers on both accuracy and efficiency. The key finding is that scaling the method (fine-tuning strategy) outperforms scaling the model for UAV audio classification under data scarcity.
AI.conclusion: For UAV audio classification under data scarcity, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (particularly selective batch-norm tuning) combined with appropriately-sized CNN architectures (like EfficientNet-B7) provide the best balance of accuracy and efficiency. Lightweight CNNs are preferable to transformers for this task, and optimizing the fine-tuning method is more effective than using larger models.

title: When the Gradient Sees Rank: Provable Necessity, Causal Recruitment, and Composition in Trained Matrix Memories
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Code and archived results: https://github.com/saml212/matrix-memories
summary: Can gradient-based training learn the rank needed to store and compose associations in a matrix memory? In our earlier study, we used a matrix-augmented reasoner on a task that admits a rank-1 solution, leaving this question open. We train matrix memories on $K$ fresh key-value bindings whose exact linear recovery requires $\mathrm{rank}(Z) \geq K$. A fixed linear readout queries a single matrix state without access to the original bindings. Experiments measure recovery by cosine similarity greater than 0.9, a threshold distinct from mathematical equality. Learned effective rank increases with $K$ across the tested grid (Spearman $ρ= 1.0$ at $d = 16$). Training-time rank caps produce a recovery transition near $k = K$: at $d = 8$, $K = 4$, rank 3 gives at most 0.0004 recovery and rank 4 gives 0.97. Four of five seeds retain at least 0.9996 recovery through 21-fold self-application of the trained operator. On the entity subspace, the learned operator has effective rank close to $K$ and approximates the ideal cycle. For the single converged seed capped below $K$, a calculation using the entity-subspace operator and ideal cycle predicts the measured cosine within 0.008 through seven applications. Extending training resolves several initial failures, but recovery still declines at larger matrix dimensions with encoder width fixed.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether gradient-based training can learn the rank necessary to store and compose associations in matrix memories. Using matrix-augmented reasoners trained on K fresh key-value bindings requiring rank(Z) ≥ K for linear recovery, the study finds that learned effective rank increases with K (Spearman ρ=1.0 at d=16). Training-time rank caps produce sharp recovery transitions near k=K, and the trained operator can sustain high recovery (≥0.9996) through 21-fold self-application. However, recovery declines at larger matrix dimensions with fixed encoder width.
AI.motivation: The authors seek to answer whether gradient-based training can learn the rank required to store and compose associations in matrix memories. Their prior work used a matrix-augmented reasoner on a task with a rank-1 solution, leaving this question open. The study aims to determine if neural networks can learn the necessary rank for storing K fresh key-value bindings.
AI.method: Experiments train matrix memories on K fresh key-value bindings requiring rank(Z) ≥ K for exact linear recovery. A fixed linear readout queries a single matrix state without access to original bindings. Recovery is measured by cosine similarity > 0.9. The study tests various configurations: d=8,16 with varying K, and examines training-time rank caps, self-application of the trained operator (up to 21-fold), and entity subspace analysis.
AI.result: Learned effective rank increases with K across the tested grid (Spearman ρ=1.0 at d=16). Training-time rank caps produce recovery transitions near k=K: at d=8, K=4, rank 3 gives at most 0.0004 recovery while rank 4 gives 0.97. Four of five seeds retain at least 0.9996 recovery through 21-fold self-application. On the entity subspace, the learned operator has effective rank close to K and approximates the ideal cycle. For the single converged seed capped below K, a calculation using the entity-subspace operator and ideal cycle predicts measured cosine within 0.008 through seven applications. Extending training resolves initial failures but recovery still declines at larger matrix dimensions with fixed encoder width.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-based training can learn the rank needed to store and compose associations in matrix memories. The learned effective rank scales with K, and trained operators can sustain high recovery through repeated self-application. However, limitations appear at larger matrix dimensions with fixed encoder width, suggesting trade-offs in scalability. The study demonstrates that neural networks can learn rank-appropriate representations for binding and composition in matrix memories.

title: MoQSplat: Adaptive Progressive Streaming of 3D Gaussian Splatting via MoQ
comment: 7 pages. Accepted at IEEE MMSP 2026 (Istanbul, 22-24 September 2026). First three authors contributed equally. Code: https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/MoQSplat
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic novel view synthesis, but transmitting gigabyte-scale scene data remains challenging for immersive applications. Traditional HTTP Adaptive Streaming over TCP introduces Head-of-Line (HOL) blocking and coarse segmenting ill-suited to fine-grained 3DGS delivery. We propose MoQSplat, which maps 3DGS content onto the Media over QUIC (MoQ) transport hierarchy. MoQSplat partitions scenes into spatial Tracks, clusters splats into semantically coherent Groups, and constructs progressive-quality Subgroups mapped to independent QUIC streams to eliminate connection-level HOL blocking. Using a stateless, subscriber-driven adaptation loop, clients dynamically request spatial regions and quality tiers based on six degrees of freedom (6-DoF) frustum visibility, distance, and foveal alignment. We evaluate the core components on a prototype implementation, showing that opacity-based pruning outperforms scale-based pruning for progressive delivery. The source code is available at https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/MoQSplat.

AI.tldr: MoQSplat is a novel streaming system for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) content that addresses the challenge of transmitting gigabyte-scale scene data over networks. It maps 3DGS content onto the Media over QUIC (MoQ) transport hierarchy, partitioning scenes into spatial tracks, semantic groups, and progressive-quality subgroups mapped to independent QUIC streams to eliminate Head-of-Line (HOL) blocking. The system uses a stateless, subscriber-driven adaptation loop that dynamically requests spatial regions and quality tiers based on 6-DoF frustum visibility, distance, and foveal alignment.
AI.motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables photorealistic novel view synthesis, but transmitting gigabyte-scale scene data remains challenging for immersive applications. Traditional HTTP Adaptive Streaming over TCP introduces HOL blocking and coarse segmenting that is ill-suited to fine-grained 3DGS delivery.
AI.method: MoQSplat maps 3DGS content onto the MoQ transport hierarchy by: (1) partitioning scenes into spatial Tracks, (2) clustering splats into semantically coherent Groups, and (3) constructing progressive-quality Subgroups mapped to independent QUIC streams. A stateless, subscriber-driven adaptation loop allows clients to dynamically request spatial regions and quality tiers based on six degrees of freedom (6-DoF) frustum visibility, distance, and foveal alignment.
AI.result: The evaluation shows that opacity-based pruning outperforms scale-based pruning for progressive delivery in 3DGS streaming.
AI.conclusion: MoQSplat successfully eliminates connection-level HOL blocking through independent QUIC streams and enables fine-grained, viewer-adaptive delivery of 3DGS content. The prototype implementation demonstrates the viability of using MoQ transport for immersive 3D content streaming.

title: CARE: A Responsibility-Oriented Architecture for Domain-Scoped Resolution in Modular and Upgradeable Smart Contracts
summary: Modular and upgradeable smart-contract systems enable replaceable execution logic, but modular dispatch alone does not define which components own architectural responsibilities such as coordination, resolution, shared state, reusable services, and observation. This paper presents CARE, a responsibility-oriented architecture that makes these ownership boundaries explicit and introduces domain-scoped capability resolution, separating execution coordination from the authority that selects an execution target. CARE is defined through a formal architectural model from which five structural properties are derived. Its behavioral semantics are further encoded in TLA+ and evaluated with TLC against seven architectural invariants. Intermediate TLC results were used to refine the architectural model before the final validation run. A controlled empirical evaluation against EIP-2535 and a routing only baseline shows that CARE introduces an approximately fixed 7.7k-gas runtime routing premium in the evaluated workloads, while localized capability replacement remains close to the routing-only control and substantially less expensive than the evaluated EIP-2535 reconfiguration path. Adversarial tests further characterize authorization controls and residual risks associated with delegated execution and reentrancy. These results position CARE as an architectural model for explicit responsibility ownership and localized evolution rather than as a universal replacement for existing smart-contract upgradeability mechanisms

AI.tldr: This paper presents CARE, a responsibility-oriented architecture for modular smart-contract systems that makes ownership boundaries explicit between execution coordination and execution target selection. It introduces domain-scoped capability resolution and is validated through formal TLA+ modeling and empirical evaluation against EIP-2535.
AI.motivation: Current modular smart-contract systems enable replaceable execution logic through modular dispatch, but they fail to define which components own critical architectural responsibilities such as coordination, resolution, shared state, reusable services, and observation. This lack of explicit responsibility ownership creates ambiguity in system design and evolution.
AI.method: The research defines CARE through: (1) A formal architectural model from which five structural properties are derived; (2) Behavioral semantics encoded in TLA+ and evaluated with TLC model checker against seven architectural invariants; (3) A controlled empirical evaluation comparing CARE against EIP-2535 (Diamond Standard) and a routing-only baseline; (4) Adversarial testing for authorization controls and residual risks (delegated execution, reentrancy).
AI.result: The evaluation shows CARE introduces an approximately fixed 7.7k-gas runtime routing premium. Localized capability replacement remains close to routing-only controls and substantially less expensive than EIP-2535's reconfiguration path. Adversarial tests characterized authorization controls and residual risks.
AI.conclusion: CARE positions itself as an architectural model for explicit responsibility ownership and localized evolution, rather than a universal replacement for existing smart-contract upgradeability mechanisms. It provides a systematic approach to defining ownership boundaries in modular contract systems.

title: Adaptive Interpolatory Curve Subdivision with Learned Local Angles
summary: Curve subdivision is pivotal in computer graphics for generating smooth geometric objects from control polygons. Interpolatory subdivision is especially attractive because the refined curve is guaranteed to pass through the designer's control points. Classical four-point and six-point schemes preserve this property, but their behaviour is governed by a single global tension parameter, limiting their ability to adapt across flat regions, sharp turns and varying local geometries. We introduce an adaptive local-angle formulation that keeps the interpolatory structure intact while learning how each new vertex should be inserted. A compact edge-wise predictor assigns one insertion angle per edge, while the original vertices are copied exactly at every refinement level. Interpolation is therefore a structural property of the operator and does not depend on the trained weights. The same predictor is used with geometry-specific geodesic primitives on the Euclidean plane, the two-sphere and the Poincaré disk. Under a matched-density evaluation protocol, the method reduces nearest-neighbour error by factors of five to seventeen over the best validation-tuned fixed-tension baseline, and by about 1.8 over centripetal Catmull-Rom in the Euclidean case. It also substantially reduces bending energy and tangent roughness, while remaining competitive with separately trained per-geometry models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an adaptive local-angle formulation for interpolatory curve subdivision that maintains the interpolatory property while learning optimal insertion angles per edge. The method uses a compact edge-wise predictor that assigns insertion angles to new vertices, applied across different geometries (Euclidean plane, two-sphere, Poincaré disk). The approach significantly outperforms traditional fixed-tension schemes and centripetal Catmull-Rom splines in error metrics.
AI.motivation: Classical interpolatory subdivision schemes (four-point, six-point) rely on a single global tension parameter, which limits their ability to adapt to varying local geometries such as flat regions, sharp turns, and different curvature profiles. This one-size-fits-all approach restricts the flexibility needed for high-quality curve generation.
AI.method: The proposed method introduces an adaptive local-angle formulation that maintains the interpolatory structure while learning insertion angles for new vertices. A compact edge-wise predictor assigns one insertion angle per edge, while original vertices are copied exactly at every refinement level. The predictor is applied with geometry-specific geodesic primitives across the Euclidean plane, two-sphere, and Poincaré disk, using a matched-density evaluation protocol.
AI.result: The method achieves significant error reductions: 5-17x improvement in nearest-neighbor error over the best validation-tuned fixed-tension baseline, and approximately 1.8x improvement over centripetal Catmull-Rom in the Euclidean case. Substantial reductions in bending energy and tangent roughness are also observed, while remaining competitive with separately trained per-geometry models.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive local-angle formulation successfully maintains the interpolatory property as a structural feature rather than depending on trained weights. This approach provides a unified framework that adapts to local geometry across different spaces, offering substantial improvements over traditional fixed-tension schemes while maintaining computational efficiency and competitive performance with specialized per-geometry models.

title: One Color Preprocessing Improves DSATUR
