summary: The Graph Coloring Problem (GCP) is NP-hard and DSATUR stands as one of the fastest heuristics for it despite producing colorings that typically use more colors than state-of-the-art coloring algorithms. We propose SSLD (Semidefinite Spectral Learning with DSATUR), which improves DSATUR by preprocessing a first good color class before letting DSATUR complete coloring the rest of the given graph. We obtain this color class from a Semidefinite Programming (SDP), similar to an SDP used to compute the Lovász theta number. To the best of our knowledge, SSLD is the first approach to improve DSATUR by preprocessing through fixed color classes. We evaluate SSLD against DSATUR and against a naive 1-color-class preprocessing algorithm on DIMACS instances, random graphs (Erdős--Rényi, Watts-Strogatz, Barabási--Albert), Frequency Assignment and Job Shop Scheduling instances. SSLD matches or beats DSATUR in almost every case across over 1600 benchmark instances, and out performs the naive GISD baseline, allows us to confirm the value brought by the SDP-guided choice of the first color class. This quality comes at a runtime cost of roughly 195 times slower that DSATUR, but demonstrating that SDP-guided preprocessing of a first color class is a direction for future improvements.

AI.tldr: SSLD improves the DSATUR heuristic for graph coloring by using Semidefinite Programming to preprocess a high-quality first color class before DSATUR completes the coloring. This SDP-guided approach matches or beats DSATUR in over 1600 benchmark instances at the cost of 195x slower runtime.
AI.motivation: DSATUR is a fast heuristic for the NP-hard Graph Coloring Problem but produces colorings using more colors than state-of-the-art algorithms. The authors aim to improve DSATUR's solution quality while maintaining its heuristic nature.
AI.method: The method uses Semidefinite Programming (similar to the SDP for computing the Lovász theta number) to find a high-quality first color class before letting DSATUR color the remainder of the graph. This is the first approach to improve DSATUR by preprocessing through fixed color classes.
AI.result: SSLD matches or beats DSATUR in almost every case across over 1600 benchmark instances (DIMACS, random graphs, Frequency Assignment, Job Shop Scheduling). It also outperforms a naive 1-color-class preprocessing baseline, confirming the value of SDP-guided first color class selection.
AI.conclusion: SDP-guided preprocessing of a first color class is a promising direction for future improvements to DSATUR, though it comes with a runtime cost of roughly 195 times slower than DSATUR.

title: DSD: Learning Diverse and Reusable Motor Skills via Diffusion Skill Discovery
summary: Humans efficiently learn new tasks by reusing a rich repertoire of motor skills across different goals and contexts. A similar strategy can also be used to enable simulated characters to efficiently perform new tasks by leveraging reusable motor skills. To support a wide range of downstream tasks, the learned repertoire should be diverse, consisting of distinct behaviors as well as spatial and temporal variation within each behavior. A commonly used method for learning diverse skills is by maximizing the mutual information between skill latents and the states produced by a policy. The marginal state entropy promotes broad behavioral coverage, while the conditional entropy encourages consistent behaviors from each latent. However, directly estimating the marginal state entropy is intractable in high-dimensional control problems. Prior methods therefore rely on indirect latent-space approximations or coarse estimators of the state distribution. These approximations may not effectively promote broad coverage of the state space, resulting in skills with limited behavioral diversity and reduced utility for downstream tasks. In this work, we propose Diffusion Skill Discovery (DSD), a skill discovery method that uses a diffusion model to approximate the entropy gradient of the policy-induced state distribution through score matching. The resulting objective encourages the discovery of skills that produce a broader range of behaviors for high-dimensional humanoid control. The learned skills are reused in two downstream control settings: hierarchical control with a task-specific high-level policy and zero-shot control through latent selection from offline trajectories. Our experiments show that DSD discovers a broader repertoire of reusable motor skills than prior skill discovery methods, leading to the emergence of complex and agile behaviors that can be reused across downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: A method called Diffusion Skill Discovery (DSD) that uses diffusion models to learn diverse motor skills for simulated characters, enabling better reuse of behaviors for downstream control tasks.
AI.motivation: Humans efficiently reuse motor skills across different tasks, but existing skill discovery methods struggle to produce diverse enough behaviors due to intractable entropy estimation in high-dimensional control problems. Current methods use indirect approximations that don't effectively promote broad state space coverage.
AI.method: Proposes using a diffusion model to approximate the entropy gradient of the policy-induced state distribution through score matching. This enables direct estimation of marginal state entropy for skill discovery. Skills are then applied in two downstream settings: hierarchical control and zero-shot control via latent selection.
AI.result: DSD discovers a broader repertoire of reusable motor skills than prior methods, leading to emergence of complex and agile behaviors that can be reused across downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: The diffusion-based approach to entropy estimation enables more effective skill discovery in high-dimensional humanoid control, producing diverse behaviors useful for downstream tasks.

title: CPR: Combining global composing, local performing and full-sequence refining in piano rendering with continuous autoregressive modelling
summary: Prompt-conditioned piano MIDI-to-Music rendering aims to faithfully render target notes while reproducing the timbre of a reference recording. Existing approaches primarily follow two paradigms: autoregressive (AR) modeling and flow matching (or diffusion). Discrete-codec AR models provide causal temporal modeling, but quantization can discard acoustic detail. Flow matching better preserves acoustic structure in the cost of full-sequence attention costs and worse semantic structure. Continuous autoregressive models operate directly on continuous representations. It not only combines the condition-following ability of AR models and distribution-modeling capacity of flow matching but also bypasses the quantization bottleneck with lower computational costs. Building on this principle, we present Composer--Performer--Refiner (CPR) framework. Composer autoregressively predicts continuous hidden states, Performer generates 24kHz acoustic latents through local flow matching and Refiner then upsamples the waveform to 48 kHz. We further introduce Bottlenecked Representation Alignment (BREPA) and Modality--Time RoPE (MT-RoPE) to strengthen musical semantic structure in Composer hidden states and temporal alignments across modalities. Codes are available at https://github.com/FEAfeatherTHER/CPR_official

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CPR (Composer-Performer-Refiner), a continuous autoregressive framework for piano MIDI-to-Music rendering that combines autoregressive modeling with flow matching to achieve high-quality 48kHz audio synthesis while maintaining musical semantics.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for MIDI-to-Music rendering have trade-offs: autoregressive models provide causal temporal modeling but suffer from quantization loss that discards acoustic detail; flow matching preserves acoustic structure but has high computational costs and weaker semantic structure. A continuous autoregressive approach could combine the strengths of both paradigms while avoiding quantization bottlenecks.
AI.method: The CPR framework consists of three components: (1) Composer autoregressively predicts continuous hidden states, (2) Performer generates 24kHz acoustic latents through local flow matching, and (3) Refiner upsamples the waveform to 48kHz. Two novel techniques are introduced: Bottlenecked Representation Alignment (BREPA) to strengthen musical semantic structure in Composer hidden states, and Modality-Time RoPE (MT-RoPE) for temporal alignments across modalities.
AI.result: The framework achieves high-quality audio synthesis at 48kHz while maintaining faithful note rendering and reference timbre reproduction. The continuous representation approach bypasses quantization bottlenecks with lower computational costs compared to discrete-codec methods.
AI.conclusion: The CPR framework successfully combines the condition-following ability of AR models with the distribution-modeling capacity of flow matching through continuous autoregressive modeling, offering an efficient solution for high-fidelity piano music rendering.

title: Prior-Free Competitive Ratios for Improving Bandits: Scale, Curvature and Horizon Are Free, but Not Jointly Under Noise
summary: In the improving multi-armed bandits problem, each of $k$ arms has an unknown nondecreasing, discretely concave reward curve $f_i$, and pulling arm $i$ for the $t$-th time yields $f_i(t)$. For sufficiently long horizons, Blum and Ravichandran (ALT 2025) proved that randomized algorithms achieve an $O(\sqrt k)$ approximation to the best single arm when the scale $m=f^*(T)$ of the optimal arm is known ($T\ge2k$), and $O(\sqrt k\log k)$ when it is not ($T>4k$), against an $Ω(\sqrt k)$ lower bound. The logarithmic factor is unnecessary: a one-page \emph{probe-and-commit} algorithm achieves competitive ratio $4\sqrt3\,\sqrt k$ for $T\ge2\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor$, without any knowledge of the scale, and we determine the optimal ratio for every horizon, $Θ(\sqrt k+k/T)$, also for unknown horizons. Without noise, \emph{no prior is needed at all}: a random-marginal probing algorithm reading neither the scale $m$, nor the concavity-envelope exponent $β$ of Blum, Garicano, Ravichandran and Sharma (UAI 2026), nor the horizon $T$, achieves the optimal $Θ(k^{β/(1+β)}+k/T)$ simultaneously for every $β$ and every horizon. Under the multiplicative noise model of Blum and Ravichandran, probe-and-commit keeps the same all-horizon order $Θ(\sqrt k+k/T)$ without knowing the noise level (and $Θ(\sqrt k)$ on the same range), but the price of priors jumps: for any fixed noise level $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2]$, the uniform price of adaptation $φ_\varepsilon(k)$ --- the worst case over horizons $T\ge16k$ of the loss relative to $k^{β/(1+β)}$ for algorithms knowing neither $m$ nor $β$ --- is $Θ_\varepsilon(\sqrt{\log k/\log\log k})$, the lower bound asymptotic in $k$ at fixed positive $\varepsilon$ and matched by a nested random-permutation probing algorithm, whereas knowing either $m$ or $β$ alone restores a constant price.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses improving multi-armed bandits where each arm has an unknown nondecreasing, discretely concave reward curve. The authors show that a simple probe-and-commit algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 4√3√k without knowing the scale, and determine the optimal ratio as Θ(√k + k/T) for all horizons. They also provide a random-marginal probing algorithm that achieves optimal Θ(k^{β/(1+β)} + k/T) without any prior knowledge, and analyze the price of adaptation under multiplicative noise.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to improve upon previous work by Blum and Ravichandran (ALT 2025) which achieved O(√k) approximation with known scale and O(√k log k) without. The logarithmic factor was suspected to be unnecessary, and the authors aim to remove it and determine optimal ratios for all horizons.
AI.method: The main methods include: (1) a probe-and-commit algorithm that achieves 4√3√k competitive ratio; (2) a random-marginal probing algorithm for the no-noise case; (3) a nested random-permutation probing algorithm for the noise case. The analysis involves characterizing the optimal competitive ratio as Θ(√k + k/T) and determining the price of adaptation under multiplicative noise.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Probe-and-commit achieves competitive ratio 4√3√k for T ≥ 2⌊√k⌋ without scale knowledge; (2) Optimal ratio is Θ(√k + k/T) for all horizons; (3) Random-marginal probing achieves optimal Θ(k^{β/(1+β)} + k/T) without knowing m, β, or T; (4) Under multiplicative noise, the price of adaptation φ_ε(k) = Θ_ε(√(log k/log log k)) for fixed ε ∈ (0, 1/2], with a matching lower bound and nested random-permutation algorithm.
AI.conclusion: The logarithmic factor in previous work is unnecessary. The optimal competitive ratio is Θ(√k + k/T). Without noise, no prior knowledge is needed. Under multiplicative noise, there is a significant price of adaptation (√(log k/log log k)) for algorithms knowing neither the scale m nor the concavity exponent β, but knowing either alone restores a constant price.

title: Transcribe, Then Reason: Two-Pass Decomposition for Multimodal Review
summary: The natural way to review a long recording or document with a multimodal model is to hand it the raw source and ask for a review in one call. We show that this quietly fails: the model satisfices, dropping roughly a third of the content and embellishing the rest. The failure is not perception--almost all of the dropped content reappears when the same model is simply asked to transcribe the source. The bottleneck is generation under load: a single pass cannot perceive, reason over, and write a long faithful review at the same time, because doing all three competes for one output. We rule out the obvious alternatives. It is not the modality: models read text and an image of the same text equally well. And it is not merely a matter of thinking harder: giving the single pass a far larger reasoning budget does not recover the lost content, because the model spends that budget planning a review rather than writing the source down. What works is to split the labor across two same-weights passes--first transcribe, then review the transcript--so each step gets a full output budget of its own. This transcribe-then-review decomposition improves both faithfulness and coverage across a 21-source suite. The benefit is not uniform: we observe that it helps most where the one-pass baseline is weakest and little where that baseline is already strong, a pattern that also tracks the source's length and modality. Decomposition comes with two failure modes--the review pass running out of room on very long sources, and confabulating from memory once the grounding source is removed.

AI.tldr: When multimodal models are asked to directly review long recordings or documents in a single pass, they drop roughly a third of the content and embellish the rest. This failure is due to generation under load rather than perception issues. The solution is a two-pass approach: first transcribe the source, then review the transcript, giving each step its own output budget.
AI.motivation: The authors observed that models quietly fail when asked to review long recordings or documents in one call, dropping significant content. They wanted to understand why this happens and find a solution, since the same model can transcribe almost all content when simply asked to do so.
AI.method: The authors ruled out alternatives (modality and thinking harder) through experiments. They tested reading text vs. images of text, and gave larger reasoning budgets to single-pass models. They then proposed a transcribe-then-review decomposition using two same-weights passes, tested across a 21-source suite, and analyzed when it helps vs. fails.
AI.result: The transcribe-then-review decomposition improves faithfulness and coverage. The benefit is not uniform - it helps most where the one-pass baseline is weakest (longer sources, certain modalities) and little where baseline is already strong. Two failure modes were identified: review running out of room on very long sources, and confabulating from memory when grounding source is removed.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck is generation under load, not perception. Splitting labor across two passes allows each step to have a full output budget, solving the problem. This decomposition has practical limitations for very long sources and risks confabulation when the source is removed.

title: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Quality Assurance Practices and Gaps in AI Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly used across software engineering, web automation, research, and productivity applications. Their integration of planning, memory, tool use, code execution, and external interactions enables greater autonomy but also introduces new reliability, safety, and security risks. We present a large-scale empirical study of quality assurance (QA) practices in 157 open-source LLM-based agent projects with at least 100 GitHub stars. We analyze documentation, source code, configurations, and tests to characterize QA practices across execution surfaces, safeguards, testing artifacts, risk scenarios, and recurring gaps. We find that current QA primarily focuses on basic functionality and high-risk actions, while coverage remains fragmented. Safeguards are inconsistently applied across equivalent execution routes, tests rarely examine boundary, adversarial, or multi-step tool-use failures, and identified risks are seldom translated into end-to-end QA checks. These findings highlight the need to move beyond feature-level testing toward systematic end-to-end validation that ensures agent workflows remain within intended boundaries when interacting with untrusted inputs, tools, persistent state, and external APIs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a large-scale empirical study analyzing QA practices in 157 open-source LLM-based agent projects. It finds that current QA practices are fragmented, focusing primarily on basic functionality while neglecting boundary conditions, adversarial inputs, and systematic end-to-end validation of agent workflows.
AI.motivation: The increasing deployment of LLM-based agents across software engineering, web automation, research, and productivity applications introduces new reliability, safety, and security risks. However, the current state of QA practices in this domain remains poorly understood, necessitating empirical investigation to identify gaps and improvement opportunities.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale empirical study of 157 open-source LLM-based agent projects with at least 100 GitHub stars. They analyzed documentation, source code, configurations, and tests to characterize QA practices across five dimensions: execution surfaces, safeguards, testing artifacts, risk scenarios, and recurring gaps.
AI.result: The study reveals that current QA practices primarily focus on basic functionality and high-risk actions, with fragmented coverage. Safeguards are inconsistently applied across equivalent execution routes. Tests rarely examine boundary conditions, adversarial scenarios, or multi-step tool-use failures. Identified risks are seldom translated into end-to-end QA checks.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the critical need to move beyond feature-level testing toward systematic end-to-end validation. This will ensure agent workflows remain within intended boundaries when interacting with untrusted inputs, tools, persistent state, and external APIs.

title: DualCount: Structurally Consistent Density and Point Modeling for Zero-Shot Object Counting
summary: Zero-shot object counting aims to estimate the number of objects specified by a text query without category-specific training. Recent approaches primarily rely on density regression or detection-style instance prediction. While effective, density-based models often suffer from spatial ambiguity and background leakage due to weakly regulated mass allocation, leading to fragmented or part-biased representations that increase counting error in complex scenes. In this work, we propose an instance-aware dual-decoder framework that structurally couples density and point representations for zero-shot object counting. Instead of treating density estimation as independent pixel-wise regression, we interpret it as a structured mass allocation problem over a latent set of object instances. Predicted instance centers induce a soft instance-wise decomposition of the density map, upon which we enforce two geometric constraints: (1) per-instance mass conservation, ensuring each object contributes approximately one unit of density mass, and (2) center-of-mass alignment, encouraging each density component to concentrate around its corresponding predicted center. These constraints introduce instance-level geometric consistency and lead to more accurate mass allocation, thereby reducing counting error. Extensive experiments on FSC-147, PUCPR+, and CARPK show that our approach consistently reduces counting error and establishes new state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot object counting.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an instance-aware dual-decoder framework for zero-shot object counting that couples density and point representations through two geometric constraints: per-instance mass conservation and center-of-mass alignment, achieving state-of-the-art performance on FSC-147, PUCPR+, and CARPK datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing density-based zero-shot counting methods suffer from spatial ambiguity and background leakage due to weakly regulated mass allocation, leading to fragmented or part-biased representations that increase counting error in complex scenes.
AI.method: The proposed framework interprets density estimation as a structured mass allocation problem over a latent set of object instances. Instance centers induce soft instance-wise decomposition of the density map, upon which two geometric constraints are enforced: (1) per-instance mass conservation ensuring each object contributes approximately one unit of density mass, and (2) center-of-mass alignment encouraging each density component to concentrate around its corresponding predicted center.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on FSC-147, PUCPR+, and CARPK datasets demonstrate that the approach consistently reduces counting error and establishes new state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: The instance-level geometric consistency introduced by coupling density and point representations with geometric constraints effectively improves mass allocation accuracy, thereby reducing counting error in zero-shot object counting.

title: Physics-Constrained Digital Twins for Sensor Integrity in Urban Pedestrian Flow: Detecting Stealthy False Data Injection with Conformal Guarantees
summary: City pedestrian counting systems now feed economic indicators, planning decisions and safety operations, yet the twins built on top of them treat the incoming stream as ground truth. We study what happens when it is not. We formalise stealthy false data injection for city-scale pedestrian sensing, where the map from latent flow to observation is far more rank deficient than in the power and water networks for which stealth has been characterised. Our twin estimates directed flows on the pedestrian street graph, assimilates counts through a learned graph-localised gain, and is trained against a flow conservation residual that couples metered and unmetered segments. Detection combines the innovation with that residual, and the alarm threshold is set by adaptive conformal calibration rather than by hand. To measure what the physics buys, we define the attack margin, the relative reduction in worst-case corruption of the estimated flow field, achieved against a white-box adversary that optimises directly through the twin. On six years of Melbourne data the margin reaches 0.54 against a single compromised device and falls to 0.19 when a third of the fleet is compromised, on a network where only 1.18 per cent of walkable segments are metered. Replacing the street graph by a distance graph collapses it to 0.09, which shows that the gain comes from the conservation law rather than from locality.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses cybersecurity vulnerabilities in city-scale pedestrian sensing systems. The authors formalize stealthy false data injection attacks for pedestrian networks, which are far more rank deficient than power/water networks. They propose a twin system that estimates directed flows using graph-localized gain and flow conservation residuals, with detection via adaptive conformal calibration. The approach achieves an attack margin of 0.54 against single compromised devices and 0.19 when a third of devices are compromised, demonstrating that conservation laws provide significant protection against data injection attacks.
AI.motivation: City pedestrian counting systems are increasingly used for economic indicators, planning decisions, and safety operations. However, existing "digital twin" systems built on these sensors treat incoming data as ground truth, making them vulnerable to false data injection attacks. The authors note that pedestrian sensing networks are far more rank deficient than power and water networks where such attacks have been previously characterized, creating unique challenges for detection.
AI.method: The authors develop a twin system that: (1) estimates directed flows on a pedestrian street graph; (2) assimilates counts through a learned graph-localized gain; (3) is trained against a flow conservation residual that couples metered and unmetered segments; (4) combines innovation with the residual for detection; and (5) uses adaptive conformal calibration to set alarm thresholds. They define the "attack margin" as the relative reduction in worst-case corruption of the estimated flow field against a white-box adversary.
AI.result: On six years of Melbourne data: the attack margin reaches 0.54 against a single compromised device; falls to 0.19 when one-third of the fleet is compromised; the network has only 1.18% of walkable segments metered; replacing the street graph with a distance graph collapses the margin to 0.09, demonstrating that the protection comes from conservation laws rather than locality alone.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that flow conservation laws provide significant protection against false data injection attacks in pedestrian sensing networks, even when only 1.18% of segments are metered. The conservation law-based approach outperforms pure locality-based methods, achieving meaningful attack margins (0.54-0.19) against adversaries that can compromise multiple devices. This work highlights the importance of incorporating physical constraints into sensing infrastructure for security.

title: CADSplat: Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting Aided by CAD Models for Robust, Photorealistic Digital-Twin Reconstruction
summary: We present CADSplat, a framework that reconstructs photorealistic, geometrically accurate digital twins from sparse ($<15$ views), wide-baseline posed images of an object by regularizing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an explicit CAD shape prior. Using such a prior requires finding a CAD model whose shape resembles the object depicted in the images and determining the pose of each camera relative to the object. We obtain both by matching segmented object silhouettes against silhouettes rendered from a CAD library and keeping the camera-to-object poses of the best-matching model. We then anchor 3D Gaussian primitives to the surface of the retrieved model and jointly optimize the 3DGS parameters, the camera-to-object registration, and a non-rigid deformation field to account for shape differences between the physical object and the CAD model. Across two real-world datasets, CADSplat outperforms unconstrained, few-shot, and mesh-texturing baselines and degrades gracefully to as few as 3 views. Our experiments show that most of the gain in rendering quality comes from how the splats are constrained---a fixed set of splats tied to a surface and moved by a single smooth deformation field---rather than from the CAD shape itself. The CAD model adds shape knowledge where views are scarcest, in the sparsest captures and on strongly self-occluded objects, and it places every camera in the object's own frame. This enables applications beyond novel-view synthesis, such as markerless augmented reality registration, per-image object pose estimation, physical simulations, and the transfer of part labels from the design to the reconstruction.

AI.tldr: CADSplat reconstructs photorealistic 3D digital twins from sparse (<15 views) wide-baseline images by combining 3D Gaussian Splatting with explicit CAD shape priors. The method retrieves a matching CAD model from a library, anchors Gaussian primitives to its surface, and jointly optimizes parameters with a non-rigid deformation field to handle shape differences.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing geometrically accurate and photorealistic 3D models from minimal image captures is challenging. Existing methods struggle with sparse views, leading to artifacts and inaccurate geometry. This work aims to leverage CAD shape priors to constrain the reconstruction while handling shape variations between the physical object and the CAD model.
AI.method: CADSplat works by: (1) Matching segmented object silhouettes against a CAD library to retrieve the best-matching model and camera-to-object poses; (2) Anchoring 3D Gaussian primitives to the retrieved CAD surface; (3) Jointly optimizing 3DGS parameters, camera registration, and a non-rigid deformation field to account for shape differences.
AI.result: CADSplat outperforms unconstrained, few-shot, and mesh-texturing baselines on two real-world datasets. It degrades gracefully to as few as 3 views. The key insight is that the constraint method (fixed splats tied to surface moved by single smooth deformation field) contributes more to rendering quality than the CAD shape itself. The CAD model provides shape knowledge in sparsest captures and enables applications like AR registration, pose estimation, physical simulations, and part label transfer.
AI.conclusion: The combination of 3D Gaussian Splatting with CAD shape priors enables high-quality reconstruction from very sparse views. The deformation-based constraint mechanism is crucial, while the CAD shape primarily provides knowledge where views are scarcest. This approach enables downstream applications beyond novel-view synthesis.

title: Look Less, Hear Better: Jointly Rewarded GRPO for Streaming ASR
summary: Streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR) must be judged jointly on what it transcribes and on how quickly it commits each word. Delayed streams modeling (DSM) has become the dominant paradigm for streaming large audio-language models, exposing a structural delay $τ$ that bounds the decoder's lookahead. We show that $τ$ is a poor proxy for user-perceived latency, and that the alignment-based supervision of DSM leaves latency on the table: the same forced-aligned transcript is used at every $τ$, forcing the model to withhold words it could already commit. We introduce AWED, a word-level emission-delay metric defined relative to the acoustic end of each word, and post-train a DSM recognizer with GRPO under a reward that scores transcription accuracy and measured delay jointly. Trained at a single operating point ($τ=6$ frames), our model dominates both its supervised fine-tuning initialization and the Voxtral Realtime backbone across all evaluated lookahead budgets: it cuts WER by 30.8\% relative at an 80\,ms structural delay, and by 5.7\% relative at 480\,ms while lowering median AWED from 1.17\,s to 1.04\,s. Latency-rewarded post-training thus advances the accuracy--latency Pareto frontier of streaming ASR without architectural change.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses latency issues in streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR) by introducing AWED (Acoustic Word End Delay), a word-level emission-delay metric, and proposes post-training a Delayed Streams Modeling (DSM) recognizer with GRPO under a joint accuracy-latency reward. The method achieves significant improvements across the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: The structural delay τ in Delayed Streams Modeling (DSM) is a poor proxy for user-perceived latency. Additionally, the alignment-based supervision of DSM forces models to withhold words they could already commit, leaving latency on the table. There was a need for a better latency metric and a training approach that jointly optimizes for accuracy and latency.
AI.method: 1) Introduced AWED (Acoustic Word End Delay), a word-level emission-delay metric defined relative to the acoustic end of each word; 2) Post-trained a DSM recognizer using GRPO (Gradient-Rewarded Policy Optimization) with a reward that jointly scores transcription accuracy (WER) and measured delay; 3) Trained at a single operating point (τ=6 frames = 80ms structural delay)
AI.result: The proposed model dominates both its supervised fine-tuning initialization and the Voxtral Realtime backbone across all evaluated lookahead budgets: -30.8% relative WER at 80ms structural delay; -5.7% relative WER at 480ms; median AWED reduced from 1.17s to 1.04s
AI.conclusion: Latency-rewarded post-training via GRPO advances the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier of streaming ASR without requiring architectural changes, demonstrating that aligning training objectives with user-perceived latency leads to better real-time performance.

title: Lecture notes on Physics Informed Neural Networks, Neural Operators, and their applications
comment: 264 pages; Lecture notes for the PhD course Physics Informed Neural Network held at the University of Bozen/Bolzano
summary:
This is the set of lecture notes for the PhD course \href{https://www.unibz.it/en/faculties/engineering/phd-computer-science/study-course-offering/2025/36967}{\textit{Physics Informed Neural Network}, held at the University of Bozen/Bolzano} in the academic year 2025/2026.
  The goal of the course was to introduce the concept of Physics Informed Deep Neural Networks (PINN) and Neural Operators (NOs), discuss their implementation from scratch in PyTorch and using advanced ad-hoc developed open-source libraries such as NVIDia PhysicsNeMo to address real-world problems in various fields (engineering, physics, petroleum reservoir). We discuss recent topics such as Mixture-of-Models, Fourier Neural Operators, Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs) and Fourier Neural Operators.

AI.tldr: Lecture notes for a PhD course on Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and Neural Operators, covering implementation in PyTorch and NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, with topics including Mixture-of-Models, Fourier Neural Operators, and Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs).
AI.motivation: Introduce advanced deep learning methods that integrate physics-based constraints for solving real-world problems in engineering, physics, and petroleum reservoir modeling.
AI.method: Course-based instruction covering: (1) PINN fundamentals and implementation from scratch in PyTorch, (2) Advanced libraries like NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, (3) Recent research topics including Mixture-of-Models, Fourier Neural Operators, and PIKANs.
AI.result: Students gain theoretical understanding and practical skills in physics-informed machine learning methods for various applied domains.
AI.conclusion: The course provides comprehensive training on state-of-the-art neural network approaches that embed physical laws, preparing researchers for advanced applications in computational science and engineering.

title: Visual Autoregressive Priors for RAW-to-sRGB Image Signal Processing
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026 Workshop on Low-Level Vision Frontiers (LoViF). 13 pages, 4 figures
summary: RAW-to-sRGB image signal processing (ISP) must recover perceptually faithful colors and fine details from sensor measurements, often under imperfect spatial alignment and missing camera metadata. This paper presents, to the best of our knowledge, the first application of visual autoregressive (VAR) next-scale prediction over a discrete image codebook to the RAW-to-sRGB ISP task. We adapt a frozen 1.10\,B-parameter VAR backbone for RAW-conditioned ISP with only 32.93\,M trainable parameters (2.99\%), and propose a frequency-decomposed color loss that separately supervises low-frequency tone via wavelet LL cosine similarity and chromatic edges via detail-band $\ell_1$. On the Zurich RAW-to-sRGB benchmark, the method improves PSNR-Y from 21.31 to 21.89\,dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.276 to 0.218 on the full 1,204-image test set. Diagnostic experiments show that the VAR prior preserves structure well, but continuous color transfer remains the dominant bottleneck: oracle affine correction recovers 3.8\,dB, while learned color heads yield marginal gains.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first application of visual autoregressive (VAR) next-scale prediction with a discrete image codebook to the RAW-to-sRGB image signal processing task. Using only 2.99% trainable parameters (32.93M) from a frozen 1.10B-parameter backbone, the method achieves state-of-the-art results on the Zurich RAW-to-sRGB benchmark, improving PSNR-Y from 21.31 to 21.89 dB and reducing LPIPS from 0.276 to 0.218. A novel frequency-decomposed color loss is proposed to separately supervise low-frequency tone and chromatic edges.
AI.motivation: RAW-to-sRGB ISP aims to recover perceptually faithful colors and fine details from sensor measurements, but faces challenges from imperfect spatial alignment and missing camera metadata. Existing methods struggle with this ill-posed inverse problem. This work explores whether visual autoregressive (VAR) models, which have shown success in image generation, can be adapted for this low-level vision task.
AI.method: The authors adapt a frozen 1.10B-parameter VAR backbone (pretrained on next-scale prediction over a discrete image codebook) for RAW-conditioned ISP with only 32.93M trainable parameters (2.99%). They propose a frequency-decomposed color loss that separately supervises: (1) low-frequency tone via wavelet LL cosine similarity, and (2) chromatic edges via detail-band ℓ1 loss.
AI.result: On the Zurich RAW-to-sRGB benchmark (1,204 images), the method improves PSNR-Y from 21.31 to 21.89 dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.276 to 0.218. Diagnostic experiments reveal that the VAR prior preserves structure well, but continuous color transfer remains the dominant bottleneck: oracle affine correction recovers 3.8 dB, while learned color heads yield only marginal gains.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that large-scale VAR pretrained models can be effectively adapted for low-level ISP tasks with minimal fine-tuning. The frequency-decomposed color loss helps, but color transfer is identified as the primary bottleneck. Future work should focus on improving color modeling, as structural preservation is already well-handled by the VAR prior.

title: Detecting Argument-Swap Bugs Using Context-Enhanced Code Representations
comment: Accepted in the 26th IEEE International Conference on Source Code Analysis and Manipulation (SCAM 2026)
summary: Names of source code elements convey rich semantic information and have been widely used in software engineering tasks such as bug detection, code completion, type prediction, and code classification. Prior studies exploit lexical similarity between method arguments and formal parameter names to detect bugs caused by incorrectly ordered arguments, typically relying on establishing mappings between method calls and their corresponding definitions. However, such mappings are often difficult to obtain in dynamically typed languages like Python. In this paper, we present BugProbe, a learning-based approach for detecting incorrectly ordered arguments in Python method calls that does not require call-to-definition mappings. Our approach leverages multiple sources of contextual information, including local context and argument usage context, and combines name-based similarity with machine learning to construct expressive representations of method arguments. We collect a new dataset of 132,739 Python source files from the top-1,000 starred GitHub repositories, yielding 3,371,244 synthetic training examples, and contribute a curated benchmark of 55 real-world argument-swap bugs manually verified from commit histories. We evaluate our approach on this dataset and show that it achieves high accuracy and consistently outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline across standard evaluation metrics. These results demonstrate that effective detection of argument-ordering bugs is possible without relying on explicit call-to-definition resolution, making the approach well suited for dynamically typed language settings.

AI.tldr: BugProbe is a learning-based approach for detecting incorrectly ordered arguments in Python method calls without requiring call-to-definition mappings, leveraging contextual information and name-based similarity with machine learning.
AI.motivation: Prior work on detecting argument-ordering bugs relies on establishing mappings between method calls and definitions, which are difficult to obtain in dynamically typed languages like Python. This limitation motivates the need for an approach that works without explicit call-to-definition resolution.
AI.method: BugProbe combines multiple sources of contextual information (local context and argument usage context) with name-based similarity and machine learning to construct expressive representations of method arguments. It trains on a dataset of 3,371,244 synthetic examples from 132,739 Python source files.
AI.result: BugProbe achieves high accuracy and consistently outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline across standard evaluation metrics on a benchmark of 55 real-world argument-swap bugs manually verified from commit histories.
AI.conclusion: Effective detection of argument-ordering bugs is possible without relying on explicit call-to-definition resolution, making this approach well suited for dynamically typed language settings like Python.

title: Geometry-Driven Shadow Harmonisation for Composited Faces: A Multiplicative, Albedo-Preserving Relighting Pipeline
summary: Face swapping and face compositing pipelines routinely produce a face that is geometrically well aligned but photometrically implausible: the donor face carries flat, near-frontal studio illumination while the host body and background carry directional scene light. Most existing remedies re-synthesise the face through colour transfer, neural relighting, or inverse rendering, and therefore risk altering identity, skin tone, and texture. We present a conservative alternative: geometry-driven form-shadow injection. The pipeline never repaints the face. It estimates a per-pixel gain field $g\in[g_{\min},1]$ from a rasterised 3D face proxy and multiplies it channel-uniformly onto linear RGB, so the operator can only darken and cannot shift chromaticity. A dense landmark mesh is rasterised into a depth buffer, from which we derive surface normals, a cavity term, and screen-space cast shadows. Key-light direction is estimated from host-side cues (body, background, hair halo); on-face cues are downweighted because they recover the donor's lighting. Shadow magnitude is not matched to the host: it is set by a three-parameter transfer $(τ,σ,g_{\min})$. The shading field is divided by its 75th percentile over skin, then gated, scaled, clamped, smoothed, and re-clipped inside a feathered, skin-gated face mask. On an analytic face heightfield, the default $(τ,σ,g_{\min})=(0.90,0.45,0.82)$ modifies 56.5% of face pixels with mean gain 0.938 (0.890 on modified pixels) and drives 3.4% of pixels to the floor. Hue invariance is a corollary of the operator. We analyse the transfer in closed form, ablate its parameters, and discuss failure modes of a monotone, darkening-only formulation, including double-shadowing of non-flat donors.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a conservative method for correcting photometric inconsistencies in face swapping. The approach uses geometry-driven form-shadow injection thatdarkens face regions to match host lighting without altering identity, skin tone, or texture. It estimates a per-pixel gain field from a 3D face proxy and multiplies it channel-uniformly onto linear RGB, ensuring hue invariance while only darkening pixels.
AI.motivation: Face swapping and compositing pipelines produce faces that are geometrically well-aligned but photometrically implausible: the donor face carries flat, near-frontal studio illumination while the host body and background carry directional scene light. Existing remedies (colour transfer, neural relighting, inverse rendering) risk altering identity, skin tone, and texture. The authors seek a conservative alternative that preserves the original face appearance while only adding shadows.
AI.method: The pipeline uses geometry-driven form-shadow injection: (1) A dense landmark mesh is rasterized into a depth buffer to derive surface normals, cavity term, and screen-space cast shadows. (2) A per-pixel gain field g ∈ [g_min, 1] is estimated from a rasterized 3D face proxy and multiplied channel-uniformly onto linear RGB, allowing only darkening without chromaticity shifts. (3) Key-light direction is estimated from host-side cues (body, background, hair halo), downweighting on-face cues that would recover donor lighting. (4) Shadow magnitude is set by a three-parameter transfer (τ, σ, g_min). (5) The shading field is divided by its 75th percentile over skin, then gated, scaled, clamped, smoothed, and re-clipped inside a feathered, skin-gated face mask.
AI.result: On an analytic face heightfield with default parameters (τ, σ, g_min) = (0.90, 0.45, 0.82), the method modifies 56.5% of face pixels with mean gain 0.938 (0.890 on modified pixels) and drives 3.4% of pixels to the floor. Hue invariance is achieved as a corollary of the multiplicative operator.
AI.conclusion: The proposed conservative approach successfully corrects photometric inconsistencies without repainting the face, preserving identity and skin tone. The method provides hue invariance through its monotone, darkening-only formulation. The authors analyze the transfer in closed form, ablate its parameters, and discuss failure modes including double-shadowing of non-flat donors.

title: What You Can't See Is Still What You Learn: A Preregistered Sixty-Society Confirmation That Evidence Masking Drives Compositional Generalization
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Preregistered fresh-world confirmation of arXiv:2608.20054; related companion study: arXiv:2609.11365
summary: Restricting what a module can read may improve what a system learns to compute. We test this in a preregistered confirmation with sixty four-cell systems sharing a frozen language-model backbone and communicating through learned continuous packets. Five conditions vary evidence masking, ownership markers, and replacement of foreign evidence with neutral filler, across six initialization clusters, each with two data orders, on one fresh task world. With markers available in both regimes, masking improved accuracy on held-out two- and three-operation compositions by median paired differences of 0.846 and 0.859; all twelve pairs cleared the required margins, and the full preregistered behavioral criterion passed. The unmarked replication also passed. No globally visible system passed the marker-following check, so the effect of usable role information remains unresolved. The filler condition yielded seven full generalizers, but its decomposition criteria were inconclusive. Packet interventions in all eighteen audited masked systems followed the predicted intermediate-value changes on eligible cases; these finite, success-conditioned audits do not establish mediation. The results confirm a large advantage of the tested masking regime, while leaving its finer attribution and generality open. Protocols, results, and checkpoints are public.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether restricting information access (masking) between modules in a 64-cell system improves learning outcomes. Using a frozen language-model backbone with learned continuous packet communication, the study found that evidence masking significantly improved accuracy on held-out two- and three-operation compositions, with median paired differences of 0.846 and 0.859, passing all preregistered behavioral criteria.
AI.motivation: The researchers investigated whether limiting what a module can read (information masking) could improve what a system learns to compute. This addresses the question of whether controlled information restriction in modular neural systems leads to better generalization and learning outcomes.
AI.method: The study used 64-cell systems with a frozen language-model backbone communicating through learned continuous packets. Five conditions were tested: evidence masking, ownership markers, and replacement of foreign evidence with neutral filler. These were run across six initialization clusters, each with two data orders, on one fresh task world. The study included marker-following checks, filler condition assessments, and packet intervention audits on 18 masked systems.
AI.result: Masking improved accuracy on held-out two- and three-operation compositions with median paired differences of 0.846 and 0.859. All twelve pairs cleared required margins, and the full preregistered behavioral criterion passed. The unmarked replication also passed. The filler condition yielded seven full generalizers, but its decomposition criteria were inconclusive. No globally visible system passed the marker-following check. Packet interventions in all eighteen audited masked systems followed predicted intermediate-value changes, but these finite audits do not establish mediation.
AI.conclusion: The results confirm a large advantage of the tested masking regime. However, the finer attribution of this effect and its generality remain open questions. The effect of usable role information (from ownership markers) remains unresolved. Protocols, results, and checkpoints are made public for reproducibility.

title: CARA: Collision-Aware Resolution Adaptation for Multiresolution Hash Encoding Based Image Fitting
summary: Multiresolution hash encodings have recently enabled fast and high-fidelity implicit neural representations by storing multi-scale features in fixed-size hash tables along a geometric resolution schedule. However, the standard design is data-agnostic: different resolution levels receive identical hash-table capacity despite large differences in image frequency content. As a result, some levels experience severe hash collisions while others underutilize parameters, leading to inefficient capacity allocation. To address this issue, we propose Collision-Aware Resolution Adaptation (CARA), a method that assigns per-level resolutions by balancing the effective information load across hash levels. This adaptive allocation reduces capacity bottlenecks and improves parameter efficiency. In addition, we introduce an invertible pixel-shuffle transform that reduces hash load factors by redistributing spatial information, thereby mitigating collision-induced information loss without enlarging the hash tables. To support evaluation on extremely high-resolution data, we also curate, to the best of our knowledge, the first uncompressed whole-slide image dataset for academic research. Experiments on Kodak images, gigapixel natural images, and raw whole-slide images demonstrate that CARA consistently improves the fidelity-parameter trade-off. Our method matches state-of-the-art performance while using only $27.76%$ of the parameters, and achieves up to $6.11$ dB PSNR improvement at comparable parameter counts. Code is provided in the supplementary.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Collision-Aware Resolution Adaptation (CARA) to optimize hash table capacity allocation in multiresolution hash encodings for implicit neural representations, along with an invertible pixel-shuffle transform to reduce hash collisions. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance with only 27.76% of parameters or up to 6.11 dB PSNR improvement.
AI.motivation: Standard multiresolution hash encodings use data-agnostic design where different resolution levels receive identical hash-table capacity despite varying image frequency content. This causes some levels to experience severe hash collisions while others underutilize parameters, leading to inefficient capacity allocation.
AI.method: Two key contributions: (1) CARA assigns per-level resolutions by balancing effective information load across hash levels to reduce capacity bottlenecks; (2) An invertible pixel-shuffle transform redistributes spatial information to reduce hash load factors without enlarging hash tables. Additionally, a new whole-slide image dataset was curated for evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments on Kodak images, gigapixel natural images, and raw whole-slide images show CARA consistently improves fidelity-parameter trade-off. The method matches state-of-the-art performance using only 27.76% of parameters, and achieves up to 6.11 dB PSNR improvement at comparable parameter counts.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CARA method effectively addresses the inefficiency of data-agnostic hash encoding designs by adaptively allocating capacity across resolution levels, significantly improving parameter efficiency while maintaining or exceeding prior art quality.

title: VoiceTrace: A Benchmark and Retrieval Framework for Who-Said-What Speech Retrieval
summary: Speech retrieval has become increasingly important as spoken content continues to grow across meetings, lectures, podcasts, and videos. Existing benchmarks and models have advanced semantic search over spoken content, but largely focus on \emph{what} is said while overlooking \emph{who} says it. In many real-world scenarios, however, users need to retrieve speech based jointly on semantic content and a target speaker, where the speaker may be specified naturally through a reference speech utterance rather than a predefined identity. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{VoiceTrace-Bench}, a benchmark for hybrid speech retrieval in which each query combines text specifying \emph{what} to retrieve with reference speech specifying \emph{who} to retrieve. This setting requires models to integrate complementary semantic and speaker information directly from heterogeneous query inputs. Motivated by the joint audio-text modeling capabilities of audio-language models (ALMs), we develop \textbf{VoiceTrace}, a two-stage retrieval framework consisting of \textbf{VoiceTrace-Emb}, an embedding model that learns unified representations for efficient large-scale retrieval, and \textbf{VoiceTrace-Reranker}, a reranking model that jointly examines each query--candidate pair for fine-grained relevance estimation. Experiments show that VoiceTrace achieves state-of-the-art performance on established semantic speech retrieval benchmarks, while substantially outperforming cascade-based approaches on VoiceTrace-Bench, demonstrating its effectiveness for both conventional semantic retrieval and the new hybrid retrieval setting.

AI.tldr: VoiceTrace-Bench is a new benchmark for hybrid speech retrieval that combines text queries (semantic content) with reference speech (speaker identity). VoiceTrace is a two-stage framework using an embedding model (VoiceTrace-Emb) for large-scale retrieval and a reranking model (VoiceTrace-Reranker) for fine-grained relevance estimation, achieving state-of-the-art results on both conventional semantic retrieval and the new hybrid retrieval setting.
AI.motivation: Existing speech retrieval benchmarks and models focus on what is said (semantic content) but overlook who says it (speaker identity). In real-world scenarios, users often need to retrieve speech based on both semantic content AND a target speaker, specified naturally through reference speech rather than predefined identities.
AI.method: The paper proposes VoiceTrace, a two-stage retrieval framework leveraging audio-language models (ALMs). Stage 1: VoiceTrace-Emb learns unified representations for efficient large-scale retrieval. Stage 2: VoiceTrace-Reranker jointly examines each query-candidate pair for fine-grained relevance estimation.
AI.result: VoiceTrace achieves state-of-the-art performance on established semantic speech retrieval benchmarks while substantially outperforming cascade-based approaches on the new VoiceTrace-Bench benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that VoiceTrace is effective for both conventional semantic retrieval and the new hybrid retrieval setting that combines semantic content with speaker identity through reference speech.

title: Fathom: Per-Query Read Depth for Sparse Decoding over Offloaded KV Caches
summary: When agentic sessions run to a million tokens with many sessions resident at once, the KV cache and the index that ranks it live in host memory, and the scan that ranks all n keys for a top-k step becomes the traffic that bounds decoding. We present Fathom, a key scan in which each query decides how many bits of each key channel to read. The 4-bit K cache is stored channel-major as bit planes, so a prefix of t planes is exactly the channel's t-bit quantizer, and the query spends its bit budget by reverse water-filling over the variance-weighted importance of its channels. At one million tokens on Qwen3-8B a decode step is 1.67x faster in GPU time than with the 136-bit scans of Double Sparsity, Loki and SparQ r=32, and in the same GPU time as SparQ's 68-bit read (r=16) Fathom reads 18% fewer bytes with lower attention error on six of seven model and context settings. On RULER-style tasks every per-token scan matches exact top-k decoding, and on real coding-agent sessions Fathom reaches the step agreement of the most accurate 136-bit scan at 92 bits. The store is the 4-bit K copy a quantized serving stack already holds, and the method is not faster when the index is resident in GPU memory.

AI.tldr: Fathom is a KV cache key scan method for efficient LLM decoding at scale (1M tokens). It uses adaptive bit allocation where each query decides how many bits to read per key channel, stored as 4-bit bit planes. This achieves 1.67x speedup over 136-bit scans while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: When agentic sessions reach millions of tokens with many concurrent sessions, the KV cache ranking scan becomes the bottleneck. Existing methods use fixed-bit scans (e.g., 136-bit) that are inefficient in both memory bandwidth and computational cost.
AI.method: Fathom stores 4-bit K cache channel-major as bit planes. Each query adaptively decides how many bits of each key channel to read by reverse water-filling over variance-weighted importance of channels. A prefix of t planes serves as the channel's t-bit quantizer.
AI.result: 1.67x faster decode step than 136-bit scans (Double Sparsity, Loki, SparQ r=32) on Qwen3-8B at 1M tokens. At same GPU time as SparQ r=16 (68-bit), Fathom reads 18% fewer bytes with lower attention error on 6/7 model/context settings. Matches exact top-k decoding on RULER tasks. Reaches 136-bit accuracy at only 92 bits on coding-agent sessions.
AI.conclusion: Fathom achieves near-exact attention quality at significantly reduced bit widths by adaptively allocating bits based on channel importance. It leverages existing 4-bit K cache in quantized serving stacks and is particularly effective when index resides in host memory.

title: TTM-Bench: A Framework for Text-to-Music System Performance Benchmarking
summary: Text-to-music (TTM) systems are increasingly used to generate musical audio from natural-language descriptions. Robust evaluation is therefore essential, yet reliable performance comparison remains challenging. This difficulty stems from differences in system architecture, supported conditioning information, and access mode, as well as heterogeneous and fragmented metrics that cannot be applied uniformly across systems. To address these challenges, we introduce TTM-Bench, a framework that defines a common protocol for systematic, reproducible performance benchmarking of contemporary TTM systems. It evaluates performance along two dimensions: musical-content alignment, quantified by interpretable semantic, genre, and musical-descriptor agreement scores against a common musical specification and summarized by an aggregate score; and computational efficiency, characterized by generation latency and real-time factor, alongside resource use for local models and cost for hosted services. We demonstrate the framework through a preliminary comparative case study, illustrating the complementary evidence captured by these dimensions. The results show that higher musical-content alignment does not systematically coincide with lower computational demands, highlighting the importance of assessing TTM performance through distinct, interpretable measures rather than a reductive overall indicator.

AI.tldr: TTM-Bench is a framework for systematic, reproducible benchmarking of text-to-music (TTM) systems, evaluating musical-content alignment and computational efficiency to address challenges in performance comparison due to heterogeneous systems and metrics.
AI.motivation: Text-to-music systems are increasingly used but reliable performance comparison remains challenging due to differences in architecture, conditioning information, access modes, and heterogeneous metrics that cannot be applied uniformly across systems.
AI.method: The framework defines a common protocol for benchmarking TTM systems along two dimensions: 1) Musical-content alignment (semantic, genre, and musical-descriptor agreement scores against a common musical specification, summarized by an aggregate score); 2) Computational efficiency (generation latency, real-time factor, resource use for local models, and cost for hosted services). A preliminary comparative case study demonstrates the framework.
AI.result: Higher musical-content alignment does not systematically coincide with lower computational demands, highlighting the importance of assessing TTM performance through distinct, interpretable measures rather than a reductive overall indicator.
AI.conclusion: The framework captures complementary evidence from both evaluation dimensions, demonstrating that performance assessment requires distinct, interpretable measures rather than a single overall indicator.

title: Experimental Settings in LLM-Based Program Repair: A Study of Inputs, Tool Access, Feedback, and Validation
summary: Evaluations of automated program repair (APR) systems commonly report the benchmark, the number of repaired defects, and the tests used for final patch validation, but these items no longer fully specify the repair task presented to a system. Recent LLM-based systems differ in the information supplied before repair, the repository and testing operations permitted during repair, and the feedback returned after unsuccessful attempts, allowing the same benchmark to instantiate substantially different repair tasks ranging from localized patch generation to repository-level diagnosis and iterative repair. We present a framework for explicitly specifying the experimental settings associated with reported APR results. We analyze reported experimental settings from systems evaluated on Defects4J and SWE-bench and characterize each result by its task unit, fault-localization assumptions, initial input, tool access, repair-time feedback, final validation, and resource budget. Our analysis shows that benchmark identity alone is insufficient to reconstruct the evaluated task or determine the appropriate scope of comparison across reported repair rates. We therefore introduce a machine-readable schema for specifying each experimental setting to improve reproducibility and make the scope of cross-system comparisons explicit.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the lack of standardized experimental settings in automated program repair (APR) evaluations. The authors argue that reported benchmark results are insufficient because different LLM-based systems use varying information, operations, and feedback during repair, leading to substantially different repair tasks. They propose a framework to explicitly specify experimental settings and introduce a machine-readable schema for reproducibility.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to solve the problem of incomparability across APR systems. Current evaluations report benchmark, number of repaired defects, and tests used, but these don't fully specify the repair task. Different systems use different information, repository operations, testing operations, and feedback mechanisms, making cross-system comparisons invalid. The field lacks a standardized way to describe experimental settings.
AI.method: The authors present a framework for explicitly specifying experimental settings in APR evaluations. They analyze reported experimental settings from systems evaluated on Defects4J and SWE-bench benchmarks. They characterize each result by seven dimensions: task unit, fault-localization assumptions, initial input, tool access, repair-time feedback, final validation, and resource budget.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that benchmark identity alone is insufficient to reconstruct the evaluated task or determine the appropriate scope of comparison across reported repair rates. Different systems instantiate substantially different repair tasks from the same benchmark, ranging from localized patch generation to repository-level diagnosis and iterative repair.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that a machine-readable schema is needed to specify each experimental setting to improve reproducibility and make cross-system comparisons explicit. This framework addresses the validity problem in APR system evaluation by making the experimental setup transparent and comparable.

title: How to make effective use of domain experts for image classification?
summary: A lot of expectations have been put for years on integrating domain expert knowledge in image classification models. Several approaches have been explored, Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) opened up a new avenue of research leading to many variants, and more recently to Concept-based Embedding Models (CEMs). CBM consider binary encoding of each concept, while CEM expands this idea by embedding each concept through two vectors. However in real-life scenarii, domain experts' knowledge is usually organized in concepts determined by various attributes, each attribute encoded either with numerical values, or range of values, or binary values, or categorical values. In this work, we first finetune an image feature extractor for classifying attributes representing the downstream object classes, where the class attributes have been specified by experts under various encoding formats. A classification head is then learnt from these various attributes to categorize target objects. We experimentally show that it improves the classification for three datasets: Kaggle fish dataset, AWA2 and a more challenging new wood charcoal dataset. We then propose an automatic selection of potential missclassified data. In this second step, experts are asked for those data to eventually modify the predicted attributes in order to improve the classification.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for integrating domain expert knowledge into image classification models by handling various attribute encoding formats (numerical, range, binary, categorical) specified by experts. The approach finetunes an image feature extractor for attribute classification and includes an automatic selection mechanism for potential misclassified samples that experts can review and correct.
AI.motivation: Current approaches like CBMs use binary concept encoding, while CEMs use two-vector embedding. However, real-world expert knowledge is typically represented through diverse attribute formats (numerical values, value ranges, binary values, categorical values). This work addresses the gap of handling heterogeneous attribute representations in concept-based image classification.
AI.method: The approach involves two stages: (1) Finetune an image feature extractor to classify attributes representing downstream object classes, where class attributes are specified by experts using various encoding formats; (2) Learn a classification head from these diverse attributes to categorize target objects. Additionally, an automatic selection mechanism identifies potentially misclassified samples for expert review and attribute modification.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate improved classification performance across three datasets: Kaggle fish dataset, AWA2, and a newly introduced wood charcoal dataset.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully integrates heterogeneous expert knowledge representations into image classification, achieving performance improvements on multiple datasets. The human-in-the-loop mechanism for expert correction of potentially misclassified samples provides a practical approach for iterative model refinement.

title: CapMem: A Benchmark for Caption-Based Episodic Memory in Egocentric Video
summary: Wearable assistants require episodic memory over egocentric video, yet current vision-language models face bounded frame budgets, growing visual-token costs, and long-context retrieval failures. Under these practical constraints, we study whether textual captions can serve as reusable episodic memory. We define the Episodic Memory Video Caption QA task and introduce CapMem, a human-annotated benchmark with 75 videos totaling 33.7 hours, and 1,000 multiple-choice questions across 16 scenarios. On long videos (>20 min), full-coverage CaptionQA with 30s and 60s caption windows outperforms direct VideoQA for 10/12 and 8/12 models, respectively. On the same video subset, a matched-frame control across six Qwen models retains mean accuracy gains of 3.22 and 2.55 points, respectively. Our caption-guided retrieve-and-verify harness further improves accuracy by up to 5.3 points. These results support the effectiveness of caption memory for episodic reasoning over long egocentric video.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether textual captions can serve as reusable episodic memory for wearable assistants processing egocentric video. The authors introduce CapMem, a benchmark with 75 videos (33.7 hours) and 1,000 multiple-choice questions across 16 scenarios. Results show that caption-based approaches outperform direct VideoQA on long videos (>20 min), with caption-guided retrieval improving accuracy by up to 5.3 points.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models face practical constraints: bounded frame budgets, growing visual-token costs, and long-context retrieval failures when processing egocentric video for wearable assistants. This motivates exploring whether textual captions can serve as efficient and effective episodic memory.
AI.method: The authors define the Episodic Memory Video Caption QA task and introduce CapMem benchmark. They evaluate caption-based approaches (30s and 60s caption windows) against direct VideoQA on long videos (>20 min), using matched-frame controls across six Qwen models. They also test a caption-guided retrieve-and-verify harness.
AI.result: On long videos (>20 min): (1) CaptionQA with 30s windows outperforms direct VideoQA for 10/12 models; (2) CaptionQA with 60s windows outperforms for 8/12 models; (3) Matched-frame controls show mean accuracy gains of 3.22 and 2.55 points respectively; (4) Caption-guided retrieve-and-verify harness improves accuracy by up to 5.3 points.
AI.conclusion: Textual captions can serve as effective reusable episodic memory for episodic reasoning over long egocentric video, offering a practical solution to the token cost and retrieval limitations of current vision-language models.

title: Reflect, Revise, Reuse: Training-Free Skill Evolution for GUI Agents
summary: GUI agents execute long-horizon tasks on dynamic graphical user interfaces, where pop-ups, delayed loads, and relocated widgets routinely invalidate plans fixed before execution. Recent agent-skill frameworks encapsulate reusable procedural knowledge to mitigate this, yet existing skill designs are largely developed without targeting GUI execution dynamics and treat skills as static artifacts produced before deployment rather than living procedural knowledge that improves through it. We argue that what GUI agents need is not better static skills, but skills that can be revised from execution feedback at deployment time, without additional training. We propose \textbf{EvoSkill-GUI}, a training-free framework in which each skill is a structured multi-file package containing retrieval metadata, executable plans, backup localization, failure-recovery rules, accessibility utilities, and failure cases. EvoSkill-GUI operates through a \textbf{\emph{reflect-revise-reuse}} loop: the executor performs instant in-rollout revisions, an isolated critic diagnoses failed trajectories under strict information isolation, and the executor edits specific skill files through a restricted tool interface. Across MobileWorld, AndroidWorld, and OSWorld, three mainstream GUI benchmarks spanning mobile and desktop platforms, EvoSkill-GUI consistently improves multiple base models without any training, with maximum gains of $+16.2\%$, $+6.0\%$, and $+10.5\%$ respectively, and evolved skill libraries continue to benefit related tasks rather than being rebuilt from scratch. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/EvoSkill-GUI.

AI.tldr: EvoSkill-GUI is a training-free framework that enables GUI agents to revise skills from execution feedback at deployment time, rather than relying on static skills. It uses a reflect-revise-reuse loop where an executor performs in-rollout revisions, an isolated critic diagnoses failures, and the executor edits skill files through a restricted interface.
AI.motivation: Current GUI agent-skill frameworks treat skills as static artifacts that cannot adapt to dynamic GUI environments (pop-ups, delayed loads, relocated widgets). The authors argue that GUI agents need skills that can be revised from execution feedback at deployment time without additional training, rather than better static skills.
AI.method: EvoSkill-GUI represents each skill as a structured multi-file package containing retrieval metadata, executable plans, backup localization, failure-recovery rules, accessibility utilities, and failure cases. The framework operates through a reflect-revise-reuse loop: (1) Executor performs instant in-rollout revisions, (2) Isolated critic diagnoses failed trajectories under strict information isolation, (3) Executor edits specific skill files through a restricted tool interface.
AI.result: Across three mainstream GUI benchmarks (MobileWorld, AndroidWorld, OSWorld) spanning mobile and desktop platforms, EvoSkill-GUI consistently improves multiple base models without any training, with maximum gains of +16.2% (MobileWorld), +6.0% (AndroidWorld), and +10.5% (OSWorld). Evolved skill libraries continue to benefit related tasks rather than being rebuilt from scratch.
AI.conclusion: EvoSkill-GUI demonstrates that training-free skill evolution is viable for GUI agents, enabling skills to adapt dynamically to execution feedback. The approach achieves significant performance improvements across diverse platforms and maintains reusable evolved skill libraries that benefit related tasks.

title: GenStream: Semantic Streaming Framework for Generative Reconstruction of Human-centric Media
comment: 9 pages. Published at ACM MM 2025. Code: https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/genstream
summary: Video streaming dominates global internet traffic, yet conventional pipelines remain inefficient for structured, human-centric content such as sports, performance, or interactive media. Standard codecs re-encode entire frames, foreground and background alike, treating all pixels uniformly and ignoring the semantic structure of the scene. This leads to significant bandwidth waste, particularly in scenarios where backgrounds are static and motion is constrained to a few salient actors. We introduce GenStream, a semantic streaming framework that replaces dense video frames with compact, structured metadata. Instead of transmitting pixels, GenStream encodes each scene as a combination of skeletal keypoints, camera viewpoint parameters, and a static 3D background model. These elements are transmitted to the client, where a generative model reconstructs photorealistic human figures and composites them into the 3D scene from the original viewpoint. This paradigm enables extreme compression, achieving over 99.9% bandwidth reduction compared to HEVC for the continuous data stream. We partially validate GenStream on Olympic figure skating footage and demonstrate potential for high perceptual fidelity under minimal data. While acknowledging the significant computational costs shifted to the client and challenges in generalization, GenStream opens new directions in volumetric avatar synthesis, canonical 3D actor fusion across views, and personalized viewing experiences, laying the groundwork for scalable, intelligent streaming in the post-codec era.

AI.tldr: GenStream is a semantic video streaming framework that replaces traditional pixel-based video encoding with compact structured metadata (skeletal keypoints, camera parameters, and 3D background models), enabling a generative model to reconstruct photorealistic human figures client-side, achieving over 99.9% bandwidth reduction compared to HEVC.
AI.motivation: Conventional video codecs inefficiently treat all pixels uniformly, ignoring semantic structure of scenes. This leads to significant bandwidth waste, especially in scenarios with static backgrounds and few salient actors (e.g., sports, performance art).
AI.method: Instead of transmitting pixels, GenStream encodes each scene as: (1) skeletal keypoints, (2) camera viewpoint parameters, and (3) a static 3D background model. These compact metadata elements are transmitted to clients, where a generative model reconstructs photorealistic human figures and composites them into the 3D scene from the original viewpoint.
AI.result: Achieves over 99.9% bandwidth reduction compared to HEVC for continuous data streams. Partially validated on Olympic figure skating footage with high perceptual fidelity under minimal data transmission.
AI.conclusion: GenStream demonstrates a promising paradigm for extreme video compression in the post-codec era. Key challenges remain: significant computational costs shifted to clients and generalization difficulties. Future directions include volumetric avatar synthesis, canonical 3D actor fusion across views, and personalized viewing experiences.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Cost-Efficient Large Language Models on Algorithmic Programming Tasks
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in the IEEE Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Advanced Computing Technologies (ICACT)
summary: This study empirically evaluates whether cost-efficient Large Language Models (LLMs) can be trusted to generate enterprise code to a written specification.
