Three models (Gemini Flash 3, GPT-5.4 mini and Claude Haiku 4.5) were asked to solve 992 algorithmic problems as Java Spring Boot service methods conforming to a mandated signature and data-transfer-object specification, crossing four model and agentic coding tool combinations with two prompt variants to yield eight configurations, with iteration forbidden and hardcoded answers explicitly prohibited. Eight problem statements were withheld to probe how models respond to missing input. The 7,593 resulting methods were classified by an eight-class outcome taxonomy describing what each does about producing an answer, then deployed and executed, giving 7,936 measured requests joined to that classification. Structural conformance approached ceiling, yet 38.4% of methods do not compute the value they returned and only 12.9% of returned answers were correct. Conditioning on outcome class shows that response reliability and correctness are inversely related, whereas genuinely computing methods answered least often and were correct 19.3%. Limitations include single generation runs per configuration, partial harness coverage, single-pass timing, syntactic classification, and probable corpus contamination.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether cost-efficient LLMs can be trusted to generate enterprise code by testing three models (Gemini Flash 3, GPT-5.4 mini, Claude Haiku 4.5) on 992 algorithmic problems as Java Spring Boot services. Across 8 configurations, only 12.9% of returned answers were correct, while 38.4% of methods did not compute the values they returned, raising serious concerns about LLM reliability for enterprise code generation.
AI.motivation: The study aims to empirically evaluate whether cost-efficient Large Language Models can be trusted to generate enterprise code that conforms to written specifications. This is motivated by the increasing adoption of LLMs for code generation in enterprise environments.
AI.method: The researchers tested three LLM models across four model and agentic coding tool combinations with two prompt variants (8 configurations total). They generated 7,593 Java Spring Boot service methods from 992 algorithmic problems, with iteration forbidden and hardcoded answers prohibited. An eight-class outcome taxonomy was used to classify methods, which were then deployed and executed yielding 7,936 measured requests.
AI.result: Structural conformance approached ceiling, but only 12.9% of returned answers were correct. Notably, 38.4% of methods do not compute the value they returned. The study found that response reliability and correctness are inversely related, while genuinely computing methods answered least often (correct 19.3% of the time).
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal significant concerns about trusting LLMs for enterprise code generation. Despite high structural conformance, the actual correctness of outputs is very low, with many methods returning non-computed values. This suggests LLMs cannot yet be reliably trusted for enterprise code generation tasks.

title: Beyond Performance Metrics: Uncertainty Mapping of Label Ambiguity in Fazekas Score Prediction
summary:
Reference labels used to train medical image classification models are not always as certain as they may appear, and this uncertainty has implications on performance metrics. In this study, we propose a framework to analyze model performance for periventricular Fazekas score prediction that goes beyond conventional metrics. The Fazekas score is an ordinal visual rating scale used to assess the severity of white matter hyperintensities and is known to be affected by inter-rater variability. While the best Fazekas score prediction model achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.70, performance varied across data splits and loss functions, making interpretation of model capabilities difficult.
  Rather than interpreting epistemic uncertainty of a model's prediction as an isolated scalar value, our approach of uncertainty mapping relates uncertainty to its position within the learned feature representation. This highlights regions of class-boundary transitions where cases appear more ambiguous and misclassifications are more likely. It also identifies potential label disagreement, including low-uncertainty misclassified cases that expert review found to be inconsistent with the original reference Fazekas score. Therefore, uncertainty mapping allows model behaviour to be examined in relation to class separation and potential model-label disagreement.
  Loss function choice also influenced the uncertainty profile, with some models showing clearer class separation and more localized uncertainty in ambiguous regions than others. These findings suggest that uncertainty mapping for Fazekas score predictions can support model interpretation and targeted dataset review when reference labels are affected by ambiguity/ inter-rater variability.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an "uncertainty mapping" framework to analyze medical image classification models when reference labels are uncertain (due to inter-rater variability in Fazekas scoring). The method relates epistemic uncertainty to feature representation position, identifying class boundaries and potential label disagreements rather than treating uncertainty as a scalar value.
AI.motivation: Reference labels in medical image classification often have hidden uncertainty (inter-rater variability), which affects performance metrics. Conventional metrics like MCC don't capture this ambiguity, making model interpretation difficult.
AI.method: The authors propose uncertainty mapping, which relates a model's epistemic uncertainty to its position within the learned feature representation space. This approach identifies: (1) class-boundary transitions where cases are ambiguous, (2) low-uncertainty misclassified cases suggesting label disagreement, and (3) how loss function choice affects class separation and uncertainty localization.
AI.result: Best Fazekas score prediction model achieved MCC of 0.70. Performance varied across data splits and loss functions. Uncertainty mapping revealed that some models show clearer class separation and more localized uncertainty in ambiguous regions. Expert review confirmed that some low-uncertainty misclassifications were actually inconsistent with the original reference labels.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty mapping can support model interpretation and targeted dataset review when reference labels are affected by ambiguity or inter-rater variability. Loss function choice significantly influences uncertainty profiles and class separation quality.

title: GraphEcho: Structural Redundancy and Evidence Provenance in LLM Graph Agents
summary: A large language model (LLM) agent can follow more graph paths without acquiring more independent evidence. GraphEcho tests whether agents mistake these repeated encounters for additional corroboration. The benchmark varies path counts and evidential origins while holding evidence content fixed, and evaluates both judgments and active exploration. Controlled synthetic experiments reveal model-dependent judgment shifts, but redundant supporting paths increase the share of repeated walks across all evaluated frozen agents. Provenance-aware post-training (PAPT) reduces revisits and improves synthetic accuracy, yet covers fewer distinct sources. On scientific claims, it continues to reduce repetition while accuracy declines. These findings expose a gap between efficient exploration and effective evidence use: an agent can learn to stop repeating itself while overlooking information it needs. GraphEcho provides a controlled way to evaluate both what graph agents conclude and whether their exploration reaches distinct evidential sources.

AI.tldr: GraphEcho is a benchmark testing whether LLM agents incorrectly treat repeated graph path traversals as additional independent evidence. The study reveals that agents confuse redundancy with corroboration, and while provenance-aware training reduces repetition, it may sacrifice coverage of distinct sources - highlighting a fundamental trade-off between efficient exploration and effective evidence utilization.
AI.motivation: To address a critical issue in LLM agents: they may mistake repeated encounters with the same information (via multiple graph paths) for additional independent evidence, leading to overconfidence in their judgments without genuine corroboration.
AI.method: GraphEcho benchmark varies path counts and evidential origins while holding evidence content fixed. Evaluates both judgment accuracy and active exploration behavior across multiple frozen LLMs. Proposes provenance-aware post-training (PAPT) as an intervention.
AI.result: Controlled synthetic experiments reveal model-dependent judgment shifts, with redundant supporting paths increasing repeated walks across all evaluated agents. PAPT reduces revisits and improves synthetic accuracy but covers fewer distinct sources. On scientific claims, PAPT continues to reduce repetition while accuracy declines.
AI.conclusion: There exists a gap between efficient exploration and effective evidence use: agents can learn to stop repeating themselves while overlooking information they need. GraphEcho provides a controlled benchmark to evaluate both agent conclusions and whether exploration reaches distinct evidential sources.

title: Beyond EER: Multi-Dimensional Evaluation of Information Leakage in Speaker De-Identification
summary: Speaker de-identification (SDID) aims to preserve privacy by concealing speaker identity while maintaining speech utility. However, current evaluations often reduce privacy to a single dimension - biometric verification performance - typically measured by Equal Error Rate (EER). This narrow focus ignores critical leakage channels, such as soft biometric inference, embedding-level re-identification, and structural template similarity, which threaten the unlinkability and irreversibility of biometric references. We propose a holistic evaluation framework across five complementary metrics: (i) EER, (ii) soft biometric leakage score , (iii) cumulative match characteristic re-identification analysis, (iv) canonical correlation analysis and Procrustes embedding alignment, and (v) intelligibility via word error rate and semantic similarity. Evaluating five SDID systems from the IARPA ARTS program, we demonstrate that these metrics capture independent dimensions of information leakage. Our results indicate that reliance on a single metric can misrepresent the privacy properties of an SDID system.

AI.tldr: Current speaker de-identification (SDID) evaluations rely solely on Equal Error Rate (EER), which fails to capture full privacy leakage. This paper proposes a holistic evaluation framework with five complementary metrics to assess privacy across multiple dimensions, demonstrating that single-metric evaluation can misrepresent SDID privacy properties.
AI.motivation: Current SDID evaluations reduce privacy to a single dimension (EER), ignoring critical leakage channels like soft biometric inference, embedding-level re-identification, and structural template similarity. This narrow approach threatens unlinkability and irreversibility of biometric references.
AI.method: The authors propose a holistic evaluation framework across five complementary metrics: (i) EER, (ii) soft biometric leakage score, (iii) cumulative match characteristic re-identification analysis, (iv) canonical correlation analysis and Procrustes embedding alignment, and (v) intelligibility via word error rate and semantic similarity. They evaluated five SDID systems from the IARPA ARTS program.
AI.result: These five metrics capture independent dimensions of information leakage. Reliance on a single metric (EER) can misrepresent the privacy properties of an SDID system.
AI.conclusion: A multi-metric evaluation framework is essential for accurately assessing SDID privacy. Single-metric evaluation is insufficient as it fails to capture the full scope of information leakage in speaker de-identification systems.

title: Regularized Least Squares Training of Quadratic Neural Networks with Applications to System Identification
summary: This paper proposes a least squares approach for the training of quadratic neural networks with regularization. The proposed methodology yields a lower bound on the solution of the training optimization problem for the case where the regularization coefficient is positive. Moreover, it yields closed-form expressions for the approximate solution and its sensitivity The lower bound is tight and the approximate solution is the optimal solution when the regularization coefficient is zero. Having a closed-form expression for the weights reduces considerably the computational time when compared with iterative numerical methods such as backpropagation that can get stuck in local minima. The proposed approach has three main contributions, namely, (i) it yields an analytical expression for the weights, (ii) an analytical expression for the sensitivity of the weights to errors in the data is also provided, (iii) it establishes a connection between the optimization to compute a lower bound and nuclear norm minimization. The proposed least squares training is successfully applied to a nonlinear system identification example where the proposed lower bound is compared with the optimal value.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a least squares approach with regularization for training quadratic neural networks, providing closed-form solutions for weights and their sensitivity, with connections to nuclear norm minimization.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address limitations of iterative numerical methods like backpropagation - specifically their computational inefficiency and vulnerability to local minima. The authors seek an analytical solution that reduces computation time and avoids these pitfalls.
AI.method: The method involves a least squares approach with regularization for training quadratic neural networks. It yields a lower bound on the solution when the regularization coefficient is positive, and provides closed-form expressions for both the approximate solution and its sensitivity to data errors.
AI.result: The lower bound is tight and becomes the optimal solution when the regularization coefficient is zero. The approach provides analytical expressions for weights and their sensitivity, and establishes a connection between the optimization for computing the lower bound and nuclear norm minimization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed least squares training method is successfully applied to a nonlinear system identification example, where the lower bound is compared with the optimal value, demonstrating practical applicability.

title: Relationally Guided Use Case Modeling with LLMs
summary: Use case flows are important elements of use case modeling because they support downstream software engineering activities, including requirements analysis, architectural and detailed design, and test case generation. However, constructing them manually is costly and expertise-intensive, while existing automated approaches still struggle to preserve semantic consistency, control-flow logic, data-flow logic, and the intended system boundary, especially when identifying branch points and generating alternative flows. To address this problem, we propose FlowGen for complete use case flow construction. FlowGen uses LLM-based Semantic Information Processing (SIP) to extract semantic elements, constructs a Semantic Relational Graph (SRG) encoded by an enhanced R-GAT for basic flow generation (BFGen), and further supports branch point prediction through BPP and branch-conditioned alternative flow generation through AFGen. Evaluations on 13 public and 7 industrial datasets show that FlowGen consistently outperforms competitive baselines in all three core components. In particular, BFGen improves over the best baseline by 14% in Precision, 7-25% in Recall, 11-30% in F1, and 10-19% in AUC; BPP improves Precision by 30-110%, Recall by 33-91%, and F1 by 32-117%; AFGen improves Precision by 8-23%, F1 by 5-18%, and AUC by 0.6-2.5%. Moreover, we validate the effectiveness of the LLM-based SIP module and the attention preservation factor in BFGen, analyze the impact of requirement completeness on BFGen, and examine how different scopes of branch-related context affect AFGen.

AI.tldr: FlowGen is a novel system for automated use case flow construction that addresses the limitations of manual and existing automated approaches. It leverages LLM-based semantic information processing, graph neural networks (enhanced R-GAT), and specialized modules for branch point prediction and alternative flow generation. The system was evaluated on 20 datasets (13 public, 7 industrial) and demonstrated significant improvements across all three core components.
AI.motivation: Manual construction of use case flows is costly and expertise-intensive. Existing automated approaches struggle to preserve semantic consistency, control-flow logic, data-flow logic, and system boundary, particularly when identifying branch points and generating alternative flows. This gap in automated use case flow generation motivated the development of FlowGen.
AI.method: FlowGen employs a multi-stage approach: (1) LLM-based Semantic Information Processing (SIP) extracts semantic elements from requirements; (2) constructs a Semantic Relational Graph (SRG) encoded by an enhanced R-GAT for basic flow generation (BFGen); (3) Branch Point Prediction (BPP) identifies decision points; (4) Branch-conditioned Alternative Flow Generation (AFGen) creates alternative paths based on branch conditions.
AI.result: FlowGen consistently outperforms competitive baselines across all three core components on 13 public and 7 industrial datasets. BFGen achieves 14% higher Precision, 7-25% higher Recall, 11-30% higher F1, and 10-19% higher AUC. BPP shows 30-110% Precision improvement, 33-91% Recall improvement, and 32-117% F1 improvement. AFGen demonstrates 8-23% Precision improvement, 5-18% F1 improvement, and 0.6-2.5% AUC improvement.
AI.conclusion: The study validates the effectiveness of the LLM-based SIP module and the attention preservation factor in BFGen. Analysis confirms that requirement completeness impacts BFGen performance and that branch-related context scope affects AFGen outcomes. FlowGen presents a comprehensive solution for automated use case flow construction, though future work could explore scalability to larger systems and integration with other requirements engineering tools.

title: Not All Patches Are Equally Forgettable: Spatially Localized Domain Unlearning in Vision-Language Models
summary: Pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong cross-domain recognition performance even without additional training. However, this robustness can also preserve undesirable domain-specific behavior, as domain-related and semantic information often remain entangled within the learned representation space, making selective domain unlearning challenging. Existing approaches typically address this problem through latent-space disentanglement and prompt- or feature-level interventions, without directly attributing and attenuating individual patch-token contributions. However, here we suggest that rather than uniformly suppressing the full representation, it may be more effective to exploit the spatial structure of vision transformers to localize and suppress patch regions that contribute disproportionately to forget-domain prediction. Patches that strongly influence forget-domain prediction may not be equally important for semantic recognition, suggesting that forgetting should be guided according to the domain contribution of different visual regions. Specifically, we propose a two-stage patch-selective framework that first estimates patch-level domain sensitivity and then selectively attenuates patches whose contribution to forget-domain prediction is stronger than their semantic utility. We evaluate our framework on Office-Home, Mini DomainNet, and DomainNet. Experimental results demonstrate improved forgetting-retention tradeoffs compared to prior methods while improving retained-domain recognition by up to 3.8\%. Additional evaluations under visually overlapping and unseen-domain settings further demonstrate improved robustness under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: A two-stage patch-selective framework for selective domain unlearning in pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) that localizes and suppresses patch regions contributing disproportionately to forget-domain prediction while preserving semantic recognition.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained VLMs preserve undesirable domain-specific behavior due to entangled domain-related and semantic information in representation space. Existing methods uniformly suppress representations without considering patch-level contributions, which may unnecessarily degrade semantic recognition.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) Estimate patch-level domain sensitivity, then (2) Selectively attenuate patches whose contribution to forget-domain prediction exceeds their semantic utility. The method exploits the spatial structure of vision transformers.
AI.result: Improved forgetting-retention tradeoffs compared to prior methods, with up to 3.8% improvement in retained-domain recognition. Demonstrated robustness under visually overlapping and unseen-domain settings on Office-Home, Mini DomainNet, and DomainNet datasets.
AI.conclusion: Patch-level selective unlearning outperforms uniform representation suppression, effectively removing domain-specific behavior while preserving semantic capabilities. The spatial structure of ViTs provides meaningful signals for identifying forget-domain-relevant patches.

title: GVD: Governed Versioning and Deduplication for Document Repositories
summary: Document repositories evolve continuously. Guidelines and policies are revised, superseded, and re-uploaded, so the same content recurs in different wording and newer versions refine or contradict earlier ones. These inconsistencies belong to the growing collection rather than to any single document, yet existing work treats versioning, duplicate detection, and contradiction detection as isolated pairwise tasks and stops once a pair is labeled. We present GVD (Governed Versioning and Deduplication), a framework that unifies cross-document version linking with rule-level conflict resolution under an auditable update policy. Incoming documents are assigned to version families through bidirectional rule alignment, and their rules are compared against the family memory to identify duplicates, contradictions, asymmetric refinements, and new knowledge, with Counterfactual Span Probing (CSP) resolving related pairs that inference misclassifies as neutral. Relation-specific policies suppress duplicates and escalate only consequential changes for review, retaining version lineage as an audit trail. The pipeline runs fully locally, with no large language model. On 120 enterprise documents processed as 140 ingestions across 59 version families, GVD reaches an F1 of 0.97 for version-family construction and 0.94 for rule-level consistency, with CSP raising rule consistency from 0.90 to 0.94.

AI.tldr: GVD is a framework that unifies document version linking, duplicate detection, and contradiction detection under an auditable policy. It uses bidirectional rule alignment to assign documents to version families and compares rules against family memory to identify inconsistencies. CSP resolves misclassified neutral relations. The system runs fully locally without LLMs.
AI.motivation: Document repositories evolve continuously with guidelines being revised, superseded, and re-uploaded, causing content to recur in different wording with newer versions potentially contradicting earlier ones. Existing work treats versioning, duplicate detection, and contradiction detection as isolated pairwise tasks, failing to address inconsistencies across the entire collection.
AI.method: GVD framework unifies cross-document version linking with rule-level conflict resolution under an auditable update policy. Incoming documents are assigned to version families through bidirectional rule alignment. Rules are compared against family memory to identify duplicates, contradictions, asymmetric refinements, and new knowledge. Counterfactual Span Probing (CSP) resolves related pairs misclassified as neutral by inference. Relation-specific policies suppress duplicates and escalate only consequential changes for review, retaining version lineage as an audit trail. The pipeline runs fully locally with no large language model.
AI.result: On 120 enterprise documents processed as 140 ingestions across 59 version families, GVD achieves F1 of 0.97 for version-family construction and 0.94 for rule-level consistency, with CSP raising rule consistency from 0.90 to 0.94.
AI.conclusion: GVD successfully unifies version linking, duplicate detection, and contradiction detection into a single framework. It achieves high accuracy (F1 0.97 for version families, 0.94 for rule consistency) while running fully locally without requiring large language models, making it suitable for enterprise document management.

title: Multi-Teacher Distillation for Cross-Domain Streaming Electrolaryngeal Speech Encoding
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at IEEE Spoken Language Technology Workshop (SLT) 2026
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has improved speech representations, yet performance degrades in pathological domains such as electrolaryngeal (EL) speech, and the computational footprint of SSL models limits their applicability in real-time, on-device deployment. We propose a multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework to train a lightweight, streaming content encoder that generalizes across healthy (HE) and EL speech. Two teachers are distilled progressively: a frozen SSL model providing discrete phonetic cluster targets from HE speech, and an EL-fine-tuned speech recognition model supplying continuous bottleneck feature targets. Evaluated via downstream speech recognition, our approach reduces the EL word error rate to 21.2%, compared to 39.3% for the strongest zero-shot SSL baseline. Among causal convolutional, Transformer, Conformer, and Mamba-based student architectures, a Mel-Conformer achieves the best combination of EL accuracy and computational efficiency. The final encoder contains 21.9,M parameters and runs at a real-time factor of 0.30 under ONNX Runtime on a single CPU core.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses two challenges in speech processing: 1) performance degradation of self-supervised learning (SSL) models on pathological electrolaryngeal (EL) speech, and 2) the computational overhead of SSL models preventing real-time on-device deployment. The authors propose a multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework that trains a lightweight student encoder by leveraging knowledge from two teachers - a frozen SSL model and an EL-fine-tuned ASR model.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised learning has improved speech representations, but SSL models perform poorly on pathological speech domains like electrolaryngeal (EL) speech, which is used by patients after laryngectomy. Additionally, the large computational footprint of SSL models makes them unsuitable for real-time, on-device deployment scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework with progressive distillation. Two teachers are used: 1) a frozen SSL model providing discrete phonetic cluster targets from healthy speech, and 2) an EL-fine-tuned speech recognition model supplying continuous bottleneck feature targets. The student is a lightweight streaming content encoder. Among tested architectures (causal convolutional, Transformer, Conformer, and Mamba-based), a Mel-Conformer achieved the best balance of accuracy and efficiency.
AI.result: The approach reduces EL word error rate to 21.2%, compared to 39.3% for the strongest zero-shot SSL baseline - a significant improvement of 18.1 percentage points. The final Mel-Conformer encoder has 21.9M parameters and runs at a real-time factor of 0.30 under ONNX Runtime on a single CPU core, enabling real-time on-device deployment.
AI.conclusion: Multi-teacher knowledge distillation effectively bridges the domain gap between healthy and pathological speech while creating a compact model suitable for real-time on-device applications. The Mel-Conformer architecture provides the best trade-off between EL speech recognition accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: A Study of the Reliability of Agentic AI-Generated Programs
summary: Agentic-AI based software development offers the promise of faster completion of the software, greater programmer efficiency, and more reliable code. The question is how can we verify these claims in an objective way? In this project, we attempted to answer this question based on three practices. First, we applied a typical best-practices agentic AI workflow for software development. Second, our target programs were ten well-known, release-quality human-written Linux utility programs so that we could compare the AI-generated code against a concrete ground truth. Third, we based our measure of reliability on a widely used testing technique, fuzz random testing. For this testing, we used both classic black box, generational testing and more modern coverage guided (gray box, mutational) testing using AFL++. We found that the AI-generated versions of the utility programs were typically as reliable - often more reliable - than the latest human-generated versions of these programs. While the AI-generated versions did have some failures, they were less common than the code from the standard repositories. Interestingly, the AI-generated code was less likely to have failures such as memory errors (such as buffer overflows) but more likely to have hangs such as infinite loops. In addition, we verified that generating robust and reliable software using agentic AI requires careful practice and human supervision. The quality of the code is highly dependent on the prompts and skills used, and how the human directing the process responds. We also demonstrated that using agentic AI workflow for software development (with its prompts and skills) can become a specification of the code that leads to cost-effective sustainability of the software.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether agentic AI can generate reliable software by comparing AI-generated versions of ten Linux utility programs against human-written equivalents using fuzz testing (both black-box generational and gray-box coverage-guided with AFL++). The study finds AI-generated code is typically as reliable or more reliable than human-written code, with fewer memory errors but more infinite loops, while emphasizing the critical role of human supervision and quality prompts.
AI.motivation: To objectively verify claims that agentic-AI based software development offers faster completion, greater programmer efficiency, and more reliable code. The researchers sought a systematic way to measure reliability using established testing techniques.
AI.method: Applied a typical best-practices agentic AI workflow to develop ten well-known, release-quality Linux utility programs. Compared AI-generated code against human-written ground truth using fuzz testing: both classic black-box generational testing and modern coverage-guided (gray-box, mutational) testing using AFL++.
AI.result: AI-generated utility programs were typically as reliable, often more reliable, than the latest human-generated versions. AI-generated code had fewer memory errors (e.g., buffer overflows) but more hangs (e.g., infinite loops). The quality heavily depended on prompts, skills, and human supervision. Agentic AI workflows with prompts and skills can serve as code specifications enabling cost-effective sustainability.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI can generate robust and reliable software, but requires careful practice and human supervision. The quality of output is highly dependent on the prompts and skills used, and how humans direct the process. This workflow can become a specification mechanism for cost-effective software sustainability.

title: AgenTeeth: A Model-Agnostic Framework for Suppressing Hallucination in Frozen Vision-Language Models on Dental X-Rays via Tool Evidence Injection
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) remain largely unreliable on panoramic dental radiographs and can rely on learned anatomical priors rather than evidence in the image. This is particularly problematic for tooth localization and spatial reasoning, and fine-tuned dental VLMs can retain the same spatial biases. We present AgenTeeth, a model-agnostic, tool-augmented framework that grounds frozen VLMs using seven specialized dental vision experts. A question-aware orchestrator selects the relevant tools, whose detections are mapped to FDI tooth numbers or anatomical regions and returned as structured findings together with annotated image overlays. A fresh synthesis call then answers the question using this evidence, without fine-tuning the underlying VLM. On MMOral-OPG-Bench, AgenTeeth improves four backbone VLMs by 12.9-23.0 percentage points over their baselines. Our strongest configuration reaches 65.66% on open-ended VQA, compared with 45.35% for OralGPT-Plus. The advantage also holds at matched scale: a frozen Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with AgenTeeth reaches 48.11%, exceeding OralGPT-Plus built on the same backbone after supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning for tool use. We release the framework, all seven expert models, and a dentist-annotated dataset for alveolar bone-loss detection in panoramic radiographs.

AI.tldr: AgenTeeth is a model-agnostic framework that augments frozen Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with seven specialized dental vision experts for reliable panoramic dental radiograph analysis. A question-aware orchestrator selects relevant tools, maps detections to FDI tooth numbers, and returns structured findings with annotated overlays for synthesis.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models remain unreliable on panoramic dental radiographs and tend to rely on learned anatomical priors rather than actual image evidence. This is particularly problematic for tooth localization and spatial reasoning tasks, and even fine-tuned dental VLMs can retain the same spatial biases.
AI.method: AgenTeeth uses a tool-augmented approach with seven specialized dental vision experts. A question-aware orchestrator selects relevant tools based on the query. Tool detections are mapped to FDI tooth numbers or anatomical regions and returned as structured findings together with annotated image overlays. A fresh synthesis call then answers the question using this evidence, without fine-tuning the underlying VLM.
AI.result: On MMOral-OPG-Bench, AgenTeeth improves four backbone VLMs by 12.9-23.0 percentage points over their baselines. The strongest configuration reaches 65.66% on open-ended VQA, compared with 45.35% for OralGPT-Plus. A frozen Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with AgenTeeth reaches 48.11%, exceeding OralGPT-Plus built on the same backbone after supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: AgenTeeth demonstrates that tool-augmented grounding can significantly improve VLM performance on dental radiographs without requiring fine-tuning. The framework, all seven expert models, and a dentist-annotated dataset for alveolar bone-loss detection are released.

title: NeMo Data Designer: An Extensible Framework for Multimodal Synthetic Data Generation
summary: We present NeMo Data Designer (NDD), an open-source, general-purpose framework for multi-modal synthetic data generation (SDG). Designed to be intuitive to use, NDD provides a declarative configuration format in which human and/or agent users define each dataset column, with column types spanning text, code, structured outputs, images, embeddings, and statistical samplers that are explicitly configured to steer dataset diversity. Additional column types and functionality can be introduced using the framework's flexible plugin system. NDD's configuration is an inspectable artifact, supporting workflow sharing and reproducibility. SDG is an inherently iterative process. NDD therefore builds a preview-and-revision loop into its core workflow, allowing users to generate and inspect a small number of records, refine the specification, and rerun generation at full scale. At runtime, NDD resolves dependencies, schedules calls to user-provided model endpoints, and retries failed requests. We describe NDD's architecture and programming model and present case studies spanning structured, agentic, multimodal, and domain-specialized tasks, including datasets used in Nemotron model development and in production enterprise deployments.

AI.tldr: NeMo Data Designer (NDD) is an open-source, general-purpose framework for multi-modal synthetic data generation (SDG) that uses a declarative configuration format, supports various data types (text, code, images, embeddings), includes a plugin system for extensibility, and features a preview-and-revision iterative workflow for dataset creation.
AI.motivation: Synthetic data generation is inherently iterative and requires handling diverse data types (text, code, images, embeddings) while maintaining reproducibility and ease of use. Existing tools lack flexibility for multi-modal data and a unified workflow for specification, preview, and revision.
AI.method: NDD uses a declarative configuration format where users define dataset columns with specific types (text, code, structured outputs, images, embeddings, statistical samplers). The framework includes: 1) A plugin system for custom column types, 2) A preview-and-revision loop for iterative development, 3) Runtime dependency resolution, 4) Model endpoint scheduling with retry logic for failed requests.
AI.result: NDD has been deployed for structured, agentic, multimodal, and domain-specialized tasks, including datasets used in Nemotron model development and production enterprise deployments.
AI.conclusion: NDD provides a comprehensive, intuitive, and extensible framework for multi-modal synthetic data generation that addresses the iterative nature of SDG through its preview-and-revision workflow, while supporting diverse data types and production-scale deployments.

title: TeleAntiFraud 2.0: A Refreshable, Profile-Grounded, and Audio-Based Benchmark for Telecom Fraud Detection
summary: Telecom fraud scripts evolve rapidly and are often designed to resemble routine service conversations, creating two key requirements for audio-based telecom-fraud evaluation. First, benchmarks must incorporate newly observed scam patterns without overwriting previously established test sets. Second, they must distinguish fraud from lawful, near-domain calls rather than relying on topic-separated negative examples. We present TeleAntiFraud 2.0, constructed with our Mixed-Tree Anti-Fraud Generation Pipeline and evaluated under a monthly frozen evaluation protocol. The pipeline transforms online fraud-case abstracts into profile-grounded scenarios, expands them through mixed-tree generation, realizes fraud and non-fraud dialogue paths under shared contexts, renders validated dialogues as role-matched speech, and freezes the resulting audio, labels, prompts, manifests, and provenance records for each monthly evaluation set. Each frozen set contains 900 Chinese calls, comprising 600 fraud and 300 near-domain non-fraud cases. Controlled text experiments show that three classifiers achieve perfect macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) when evaluated against unrelated or ordinary negatives, but drop to 0.65-0.68 with near-domain sibling negatives. Full-set audio and automatic-speech-recognition plus large-language-model (ASR+LLM) evaluations further reveal class-prior shortcuts, prediction collapse, and snapshot sensitivity. Together, these findings establish near-domain construction and collapse-aware reporting as core requirements for evaluating audio-based telecom-fraud models under realistic confusable conditions. The accompanying research artifact includes the construction code, evaluation scripts, manifests, and documentation. Our dataset and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TeleAntiFraud-2_0-EEB2/.

AI.tldr: TeleAntiFraud 2.0 is a benchmark for evaluating audio-based telecom-fraud detection models. It addresses two key challenges: incorporating evolving scam patterns without overwriting existing test sets, and distinguishing fraud from near-domain legitimate calls rather than topic-separated negatives. The benchmark uses a Mixed-Tree Anti-Fraud Generation Pipeline to create realistic dialogue scenarios with 900 Chinese calls per monthly frozen set (600 fraud, 300 non-fraud). Experiments reveal that classifiers achieve perfect Macro-F1 on standard negatives but drop significantly (0.65-0.68) when evaluated against near-domain sibling negatives, highlighting critical evaluation gaps in current fraud detection systems.
AI.motivation: Current telecom fraud detection benchmarks fail to address two critical requirements: (1) dynamically incorporating new scam patterns without losing historical test sets, and (2) distinguishing fraud from lawful near-domain calls rather than relying on topic-separated negative examples. Existing benchmarks use unrelated or ordinary negatives that don't reflect realistic confusable conditions in actual fraud detection scenarios.
AI.method: The Mixed-Tree Anti-Fraud Generation Pipeline transforms online fraud-case abstracts into profile-grounded scenarios, expands them through mixed-tree generation, realizes fraud and non-fraud dialogue paths under shared contexts, renders validated dialogues as role-matched speech, and freezes the resulting audio, labels, prompts, manifests, and provenance records for each monthly evaluation set. Each frozen set contains 900 Chinese calls (600 fraud, 300 near-domain non-fraud). Evaluation uses a monthly frozen evaluation protocol with both text-based and audio-based (ASR+LLM) assessments.
AI.result: Controlled text experiments show three classifiers achieve perfect macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) when evaluated against unrelated or ordinary negatives, but performance drops to 0.65-0.68 when evaluated against near-domain sibling negatives. Full-set audio and ASR+LLM evaluations further reveal class-prior shortcuts, prediction collapse, and snapshot sensitivity issues.
AI.conclusion: Near-domain construction and collapse-aware reporting are core requirements for evaluating audio-based telecom-fraud models under realistic confusable conditions. The benchmark successfully identifies critical weaknesses in current fraud detection systems that are obscured by traditional evaluation methods. The research artifact includes construction code, evaluation scripts, manifests, documentation, and is publicly available.

title: The Missing "I Don't Know": Why Three Reasoning-Reliability Findings Converge on Calibrated Abstention
comment: 12 pages, 4 tables. Accepted to AACL-IJCNLP 2026 (main conference)
summary: Three recent results describe what look like unrelated LLM reliability problems. Yin et al. (2026) show reasoning RL collapses tool-reliability representations. Suleymanov et al. (2026) show that under safety-constrained generation, large models rewrite flagged spans while small models truncate. Bastounis et al. (2024) prove any consistent-reasoning system without an implicit "I don't know" function must hallucinate infinitely often on broad problem classes. We argue these findings converge on a single intervention: calibrated abstention is what each independently identifies as the missing capability, even though the unavailability they document, a capability gap, a policy gap, and a recursion-theoretic gap, has a different source in each case. Honesty post-training has narrowed the gap in deployed models, but principled closure of the class Bastounis identifies requires a calibrated abstention function whose training signal at the leaderboard level is absent: dominant benchmarks assign zero reward to decline, so the leaderboard gradient that would select for the function does not exist. We propose four changes to evaluation: triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified evaluation, and mandatory calibration metrics. Benchmark reform is necessary, not sufficient, for closing the gap the theorem identifies.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that three seemingly unrelated LLM reliability problems (reasoning RL degrading tool reliability, safety-constrained generation causing model misbehavior, and a theorem proving hallucination is inevitable without an "I don't know" function) all converge on a single missing capability: calibrated abstention. The paper proposes benchmark reform with four evaluation changes to address this fundamental gap.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that three distinct LLM reliability issues (a capability gap, a policy gap, and a recursion-theoretic gap) are actually symptoms of the same underlying problem—the absence of calibrated abstention—and to propose unified solutions through benchmark reform.
AI.method: The paper synthesizes three prior results (Yin et al. 2026, Suleymanov et al. 2026, Bastounis et al. 2024) and identifies their common root cause. It analyzes the training signal gap in current benchmarks and proposes four specific evaluation reforms: triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified evaluation, and mandatory calibration metrics.
AI.result: The paper argues that these three problems, despite having different sources (capability gap, policy gap, recursion-theoretic gap), all point to the same intervention: calibrated abstention. While honesty post-training has partially narrowed the gap, the fundamental theorem identified by Bastounis et al. requires benchmark reform to create the necessary training signals.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark reform is necessary but not sufficient for closing the gap identified by the theorem. Four specific evaluation changes are needed: triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified evaluation, and mandatory calibration metrics to enable proper training signals for calibrated abstention functions.

title: A Study on the Impact of Natural Language Differences in Prompts on Automatic Code Generation Using LLMs
comment: Accepted for publication in Empirical Software Engineering
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in automatic code generation tasks, thereby encouraging new research in this area. Although numerous studies have explored LLM-based code generation, the impact of the natural language in input prompts remains unexplored (language bias). This study aims to (1) quantify how the natural language of input prompts influences LLM-based code generation performance and (2) evaluate a mitigation strategy to reduce language bias in code generation. We assess code generation Accuracy on AtCoder, LeetCode, and BigCodeBench. To quantify the language bias on code generation, each problem is presented in English, Japanese, and Chinese. We use seven LLMs (GPT-4o, o3-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2, Llama-3, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, and GitHub Copilot) and assess their performance in terms of Accuracy (the number of problems for which generated code passes all test cases). We compare Accuracy before and after translation to evaluate the effectiveness of translation as a mitigation strategy. We observed that the natural language of problem statements affects LLM-based code generation performance. Specifically, the languages officially supported by each dataset achieved the highest median Accuracy. Also, translation improved Accuracy, but its effectiveness was not consistent across datasets and model types. We found that AtCoder contained a particularly high proportion of narrative-style problem statements and longer problem statements. Natural language significantly affects LLM code generation accuracy. Translation can mitigate language bias in some settings, but its effectiveness depends on the dataset and model type. Furthermore, the narrative aspects and context length of input prompts are important factors related to language bias and the effectiveness of translation as a mitigation strategy.

AI.tldr: This study investigates language bias in LLM-based code generation by testing how the natural language of input prompts (English, Japanese, Chinese) affects code generation accuracy across 7 LLMs and 3 datasets (AtCoder, LeetCode, BigCodeBench). Translation is evaluated as a mitigation strategy.
AI.motivation: While LLMs have shown strong performance in automatic code generation, the impact of the natural language used in input prompts remains unexplored. This study addresses this gap by quantifying language bias and evaluating mitigation strategies.
AI.method: The researchers tested 7 LLMs (GPT-4o, o3-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2, Llama-3, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, and GitHub Copilot) on 3 datasets (AtCoder, LeetCode, BigCodeBench). Each problem was presented in English, Japanese, and Chinese. Accuracy was measured as the number of problems where generated code passed all test cases. Translation was evaluated as a mitigation strategy by comparing accuracy before and after translation.
AI.result: Natural language significantly affects LLM code generation performance. Officially supported languages achieved the highest median accuracy. Translation improved accuracy but effectiveness varied across datasets and models. AtCoder contained a high proportion of narrative-style and longer problem statements, which correlated with language bias.
AI.conclusion: Language bias exists in LLM code generation and is influenced by narrative aspects and context length of prompts. Translation can mitigate language bias in some settings, but its effectiveness depends on the specific dataset and model type.

title: Wind on Trees: Testing Physical Grounding in Dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Monocular reconstruction of wind-driven vegetation is severely underconstrained: motion along the viewing direction is largely unobservable, a moving canopy offers few reliable correspondences, and nearly the entire scene is dynamic, providing little static reference. Directly-learned deformation fields in 4D Gaussian Splatting therefore optimize photometric consistency rather than recover the motion that produced it. We replace that field with a physically parameterized deformation prior: one damped harmonic oscillator per rigid part, driven by the observed wind and integrated by differentiable RK4, supervised photometrically alone. To test whether such a prior is physically grounded rather than merely well fit, we build a controlled synthetic testbed of three procedurally generated trees spanning an order of magnitude in skeleton complexity, whose per-part natural frequency follows from its own geometry and whose damping ratio is a fixed constant, both held out of training. On it, we measure held-out views, temporal extrapolation, zero-shot transfer to unseen wind speeds, and recovery of the physical parameters themselves. The prior costs appearance fidelity on in-distribution views and extrapolates markedly better outside the training window and the training wind, while parameter recovery is far weaker than it first appears: frequency recovery survives an untrained null control on only the sparsest of the three trees, and damping is not recovered at all.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses monocular reconstruction of wind-driven vegetation by replacing directly-learned deformation fields in 4D Gaussian Splatting with a physically parameterized prior based on damped harmonic oscillators. The method is tested on synthetic trees with varying complexity, evaluating view extrapolation, temporal extrapolation, zero-shot wind transfer, and physical parameter recovery.
AI.motivation: Monocular reconstruction of wind-driven vegetation is severely underconstrained: motion along the viewing direction is unobservable, moving canopies offer few reliable correspondences, and the dynamic nature of the scene provides little static reference. Existing methods using directly-learned deformation fields optimize photometric consistency rather than recovering the actual underlying motion.
AI.method: The authors replace learned deformation fields with a physically parameterized deformation prior: one damped harmonic oscillator per rigid part, driven by observed wind and integrated by differentiable Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4). The method is supervised photometrically alone. They built a controlled synthetic testbed with three procedurally generated trees spanning an order of magnitude in skeleton complexity, where per-part natural frequency derives from its geometry and damping ratio is a fixed constant—both held out of training.
AI.result: The physically parameterized prior costs appearance fidelity on in-distribution views but extrapolates markedly better outside the training window and training wind. However, parameter recovery is far weaker than expected: frequency recovery survives an untrained null control only on the sparsest of the three trees, and damping is not recovered at all.
AI.conclusion: While the physically grounded prior improves extrapolation capabilities, the physical parameters themselves (particularly frequency and damping) are not reliably recoverable from monocular observations alone. This suggests that the prior is useful for better generalization but cannot be used as a true physical inference mechanism for recovering vegetation mechanics from visual data.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of the COTQ Provincial Land Cover Product: Structural Consistency, Spectral Separability, and Relative Positioning Against ESA, ESRI, and Google Products
summary: High-resolution land use and land cover (LULC) products derived from Sentinel-2 imagery are widely used for environmental monitoring and land management, yet their performance can vary across regions with complex ecological gradients and heterogeneous surface conditions. In Quebec, these limitations motivated the development of a provincial 10-m land-cover product, the COTQ, designed to support annual monitoring of land occupation and soil artificialisation. This study presents a systematic evaluation of the COTQ product relative to three global 10-m LULC datasets: ESA WorldCover, ESRI LandCover, and Google DynamicWorld. This paper does not introduce a new mapping methodology but focuses on analysing the behaviour and consistency of the COTQ using complementary evaluation approaches. All products are harmonized under a common legend and compared using structural indicators (object-size distributions, shape complexity, Adjusted Rand Index, and Intersection over Union), spectral separability metrics derived from Sentinel-2 reflectance data, and a targeted photo-interpretation of disagreement areas. The analysis is conducted over eight Sentinel-2 tiles selected to represent the main bioclimatic domains of Québec, from temperate and boreal forests to northern tundra environments. The results show that the COTQ exhibits structural and spectral characteristics most similar to ESA WorldCover among the reference global products, while revealing systematic differences linked to class definitions and thematic priorities, particularly for urban areas, wetlands, and rocky or cryptogamic surfaces. This multi-criteria evaluation provides an objective characterization of the COTQ product and clarifies its relative positioning with respect to existing global land-cover datasets for operational land monitoring in Québec.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates a provincial 10-m land-cover product (COTQ) from Quebec against three global 10-m LULC datasets (ESA WorldCover, ESRI LandCover, Google DynamicWorld) using multi-criteria evaluation approaches including structural indicators, spectral separability, and photo-interpretation.
AI.motivation: Global LULC products derived from Sentinel-2 have performance limitations in regions with complex ecological gradients and heterogeneous surface conditions, necessitating the development of province-specific products like COTQ for annual monitoring of land occupation and soil artificialisation in Quebec.
AI.method: Harmonized all products under a common legend; compared using structural indicators (object-size distributions, shape complexity, Adjusted Rand Index, IoU), spectral separability metrics from Sentinel-2 reflectance, and targeted photo-interpretation of disagreement areas across eight Sentinel-2 tiles representing Québec's main bioclimatic domains.
AI.result: COTQ exhibits structural and spectral characteristics most similar to ESA WorldCover among reference global products, with systematic differences linked to class definitions and thematic priorities, particularly for urban areas, wetlands, and rocky or cryptogamic surfaces.
AI.conclusion: This multi-criteria evaluation provides an objective characterization of the COTQ product and clarifies its relative positioning with respect to existing global land-cover datasets for operational land monitoring in Québec.

title: FRAUDSkill: Structured Frozen-Weight Skill Optimization for Audio Anti-Fraud Detection
summary: Large audio-language models have shown promise for anti-fraud detection by directly processing speech and reasoning over fraud-related evidence. Their deployment, however, requires predictions to follow a predefined label space and a structured decision protocol consisting of service-scenario identification, fraud detection, and conditional fraud-type classification. Existing fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches typically encode task knowledge, constraints, and decision rules into model parameters or manually maintained prompts, making them difficult to adapt as fraud patterns and labeling policies evolve. To this end, we propose FRAUDSkill, a structured frozen-weight adaptation framework that leaves the underlying audio-language model unchanged while optimizing an external layer of skill programs, route-specific policies, and decision rules. We further combine structured output control with validation-guided multi-path inference to ensure protocol-compliant predictions. On the TeleAntiFraud benchmark, FRAUDSkill achieves 73.50% Macro-F1, outperforming the shared frozen-model baseline by 31.96% while reducing invalid outputs to 1.94%. Extensive experiments demonstrate that external skill optimization provides an effective and adaptable solution for structured audio anti-fraud detection without modifying the underlying model. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FRAUDSKILL-114514.

AI.tldr: FRAUDSkill is a structured frozen-weight adaptation framework for audio-language models in anti-fraud detection. It optimizes external skill programs, route-specific policies, and decision rules without modifying the underlying model, combined with structured output control and validation-guided multi-path inference to ensure protocol-compliant predictions.
AI.motivation: Current fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches for anti-fraud detection encode task knowledge into model parameters or manually maintained prompts, making them difficult to adapt as fraud patterns and labeling policies evolve. Deployment also requires predictions to follow predefined label spaces and structured decision protocols.
AI.method: FRAUDSkill uses frozen-weight adaptation that leaves the underlying audio-language model unchanged while optimizing an external layer consisting of skill programs, route-specific policies, and decision rules. It combines structured output control with validation-guided multi-path inference to ensure protocol-compliant predictions.
AI.result: On the TeleAntiFraud benchmark, FRAUDSkill achieves 73.50% Macro-F1, outperforming the shared frozen-model baseline by 31.96% while reducing invalid outputs to 1.94%.
AI.conclusion: External skill optimization provides an effective and adaptable solution for structured audio anti-fraud detection without modifying the underlying model, offering better adaptability to evolving fraud patterns and labeling policies.

title: Accelerating Diffusion Sampling via Speculative Draft Trees
summary: Speculative sampling accelerates diffusion model generation by drafting inexpensive candidate states and correcting them under a coupling that preserves the target distribution exactly, reducing the number of expensive target evaluations. Existing diffusion samplers, notably those based on reflection maximal coupling, are topologically constrained: their lookahead drafts form a chain graph, a single linear sequence, which inherently limits the acceptance rate per target evaluation. We connect speculative sampling in diffusion models to relative entropy coding (REC). This perspective shows the lookahead need not be linear and motivates our central contribution, draft trees, which enrich the candidates considered per round and lower the target function evaluations. We further adopt greedy rejection sampling, an REC algorithm, as the draft-target coupling, improving acceptance while guaranteeing exact target samples. Experiments across diverse target and draft models demonstrate up to 8.3% acceleration over the reflection coupling baseline in practical settings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "draft trees" to accelerate diffusion model generation by replacing the linear lookahead chain used in reflection maximal coupling with a tree-structured candidate generation approach, connected to relative entropy coding (REC). Using greedy rejection sampling as the draft-target coupling, the method achieves up to 8.3% acceleration over baseline while preserving exact target distribution.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion samplers based on reflection maximal coupling are topologically constrained: their lookahead drafts form a chain graph (single linear sequence), which inherently limits the acceptance rate per target evaluation. This constraint reduces the efficiency of speculative sampling in diffusion models.
AI.method: The paper connects speculative sampling to relative entropy coding (REC) theory, which reveals that the lookahead need not be linear. The central contribution is "draft trees" - enriching candidates per round using tree structures rather than linear sequences. The method adopts greedy rejection sampling (an REC algorithm) as the draft-target coupling to improve acceptance while guaranteeing exact target samples.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse target and draft models demonstrate up to 8.3% acceleration over the reflection coupling baseline in practical settings.
AI.conclusion: The tree-structured lookahead approach, combined with greedy rejection sampling coupling, provides a more efficient alternative to linear reflection coupling for speculative sampling in diffusion models, offering meaningful speedups while preserving exact sampling correctness.

title: From Component Snapshots to Lifecycle Traces: Agent-Based Software Composition Analysis
summary: Software supply-chain security requires accurate identification of third-party components and an understanding of how they evolve from development to execution. Existing software composition analysis (SCA) approaches examine manifests, build environments, release artifacts, containers, or runtime states, but typically produce only stage-specific views of software composition. As dependencies are resolved, removed, repackaged, and transformed across lifecycle stages, a single snapshot cannot capture both where a component originates and where it ultimately ends up. Combining snapshots from multiple stages still leaves their cross-stage relationships unresolved. We present SCA-Agent, an agent-based approach to lifecycle-aware SCA that reconstructs evidence-backed component lifecycle traces across Code, Build, Release, Deploy, and Runtime. SCA-Agent adaptively explores project-specific analysis paths, gathers stage-specific evidence, and correlates observations across stages to recover component identities, versions, introduction paths, propagation relationships, and final lifecycle states. We evaluate SCA-Agent on 105 real-world projects from the Java, JavaScript, and Python ecosystems. SCA-Agent achieves the highest component detection F1 across all lifecycle stages and ecosystems. For vulnerability exposure assessment, it reaches an F1 score of 96.69%, exceeding the best traditional SCA tool by 18.76 percentage points. These results show that lifecycle-aware SCA supports traceable component provenance and more accurate software supply-chain risk assessment.

AI.tldr: SCA-Agent is an agent-based approach to lifecycle-aware software composition analysis that reconstructs component lifecycle traces across Code, Build, Release, Deploy, and Runtime stages. It addresses the limitation of existing SCA tools that only provide stage-specific views by correlating observations across stages to recover component identities, versions, introduction paths, and final lifecycle states.
AI.motivation: Existing SCA approaches examine software components at specific lifecycle stages but produce only stage-specific views. Dependencies are resolved, removed, repackaged, and transformed across stages, so single snapshots cannot capture both where a component originates and where it ends up. Combining snapshots from multiple stages still leaves cross-stage relationships unresolved.
AI.method: SCA-Agent uses an agent-based approach that adaptively explores project-specific analysis paths, gathers stage-specific evidence, and correlates observations across stages to recover component identities, versions, introduction paths, propagation relationships, and final lifecycle states.
AI.result: Evaluated on 105 real-world projects from Java, JavaScript, and Python ecosystems, SCA-Agent achieves the highest component detection F1 across all lifecycle stages and ecosystems. For vulnerability exposure assessment, it reaches an F1 score of 96.69%, exceeding the best traditional SCA tool by 18.76 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Lifecycle-aware SCA supports traceable component provenance and more accurate software supply-chain risk assessment. The approach demonstrates significant improvements in both component detection and vulnerability exposure assessment compared to traditional SCA tools.

title: GazeDiT: Gaze-Accurate Diffusion Image Generation for Eye Tracking via Spatial Conditioning
summary: Diffusion models are increasingly used to generate synthetic training data, but precise label control remains difficult when the conditioning signal is low-dimensional and coarse. Text-conditioned images are judged by broad prompt consistency, whereas supervised training requires precise correspondence between each image and its numerical label. This is challenging in eye tracking, where a 4D binocular gaze is expressed through subtle, spatially localized pupil and iris geometry. We introduce GazeDiT, a diffusion model that generates images for a requested 4D gaze through an internally constructed spatial condition that grounds the global gaze label in this local geometry. During training, a frozen SegFormer extracts pupil/iris geometry from diverse real images, allowing the model to learn realistic appearance conditioned on that geometry. At inference, a physical eye renderer samples gaze-consistent geometries by varying anatomy and camera state, enabling diverse synthesis without a source image. GazeDiT achieves substantially lower tail gaze-label error than other diffusion baselines, approaching the error of the same frozen gaze estimator on real images. Its generated data also improves the downstream eye tracker, reducing gaze error on difficult cases from 3.05° to 2.80° in the smallest cohort.

AI.tldr: GazeDiT is a diffusion model for generating synthetic eye tracking training data with precise 4D gaze label control. It uses a frozen SegFormer to extract pupil/iris geometry as conditioning, and a physical eye renderer at inference for diverse synthesis without source images.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models struggle with precise label control when conditioning signals are low-dimensional and coarse. In eye tracking, 4D binocular gaze requires precise correspondence between images and numerical labels, which is challenging because gaze is expressed through subtle, spatially localized pupil and iris geometry.
AI.method: 1) Training: Use a frozen SegFormer to extract pupil/iris geometry from diverse real images, enabling the model to learn realistic appearance conditioned on this geometry. 2) Inference: Use a physical eye renderer to sample gaze-consistent geometries by varying anatomy and camera state, enabling diverse synthesis without source images.
AI.result: GazeDiT achieves substantially lower tail gaze-label error than other diffusion baselines, approaching the error of the same frozen gaze estimator on real images. Generated data improves the downstream eye tracker, reducing gaze error on difficult cases from 3.05° to 2.80° in the smallest cohort.
AI.conclusion: GazeDiT successfully enables precise 4D gaze control in synthetic eye image generation, with generated data that can improve downstream eye tracking performance, particularly for difficult cases in small cohorts.

title: Imitation Learning for Autonomous Driving in CARLA
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures. Code, data samples and trained policy: https://github.com/JordyKieto/carla-imitation-learning
summary: Behavioral cloning trains a policy offline on expert demonstrations, but deployment is closed loop: each action affects the observations the policy receives next. We study how much closed-loop driving competence a compact multimodal policy can acquire from offline demonstrations in the CARLA simulator. The policy uses five-frame histories of RGB images, LiDAR, vehicle telemetry, and lane waypoints to predict throttle, brake, and steering at 20 Hz. Demonstrations were collected in three stages, ending with a systematic route-generation procedure that enumerates spawn points and feasible maneuvers and verifies completed autopilot routes. The released 1.36 million parameter policy was trained on 236,882 windows, representing about 3.3 hours of driving from 448 captures. The resulting policy drives autonomously for hours on training and held-out routes. In our runs, it did so without collisions and also transferred qualitatively to an unseen CARLA town with different road geometry. We also observed recovery from large trajectory deviations, although we do not claim systematic recovery without controlled evaluation. We report offline metrics and distinguish measured results from qualitative closed-loop observations. We release the code, trained checkpoint, ONNX model, data sample, and an evidence audit for the reported claims.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a compact multimodal behavioral cloning policy for autonomous driving in CARLA simulator. The 1.36M parameter policy uses 5-frame histories of RGB images, LiDAR, vehicle telemetry, and lane waypoints to predict throttle, brake, and steering at 20 Hz. Trained on ~3.3 hours of driving data (236,882 windows from 448 captures), the policy can drive autonomously for hours on training and held-out routes without collisions, transfers to unseen towns, and recovers from large trajectory deviations.
AI.motivation: Behavioral cloning is trained offline on expert demonstrations but deployed in closed-loop settings where each action affects future observations. The authors aim to study how much closed-loop driving competence a compact multimodal policy can acquire from offline demonstrations in the CARLA simulator.
AI.method: 1) Collect expert demonstrations in three stages using a systematic route-generation procedure that enumerates spawn points and feasible maneuvers and verifies completed autopilot routes. 2) Train a compact multimodal policy using five-frame histories of RGB images, LiDAR, vehicle telemetry, and lane waypoints to predict throttle, brake, and steering at 20 Hz. 3) Evaluate offline metrics and perform qualitative closed-loop observations.
AI.result: The resulting policy drives autonomously for hours on training and held-out routes without collisions in the authors' runs. It transfers qualitatively to an unseen CARLA town with different road geometry. Recovery from large trajectory deviations was also observed, although without controlled evaluation.
AI.conclusion: A compact multimodal policy trained via behavioral cloning can achieve significant closed-loop driving competence in CARLA, including generalization to unseen towns and recovery from deviations. The authors release code, trained checkpoint, ONNX model, data sample, and evidence audit for reproducibility.

title: Variable-Rate Harmonic-Percussive Time-Scale Modification with Real-Time Playback in Python
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Open-source implementation: https://github.com/HMC-MIR/TSMRealTime
summary: Time-scale modification (TSM) has a number of open-source implementations, but these are designed almost exclusively for offline use, in which a recording is processed at a fixed rate and written out ahead of time. Applications such as automatic musical accompaniment require a different setting, which we call variable-rate playback: the recording to be stretched is known in advance, but the playback rate is not, and must change continuously in response to a live performer. The few implementations that generate output in real time are written in C++ and optimized for speed rather than for ease of modification, experimentation, and integration with the primarily Python-based research ecosystem. This paper describes a Python implementation of the widely used harmonic-percussive TSM method for the variable-rate playback setting. Harmonic-percussive separation is performed offline as a preprocessing step on the known input recording, while synthesis and playback are carried out in real time with a time-scale factor that may change at every frame. We further propose a family of variants that reduce runtime by replacing the phase vocoder's analysis-stage FFT and instantaneous frequency calculations with lookups into precomputed tables. Subjective listening tests with 24 participants (1114 pairwise ratings) show that these approximations become perceptually indistinguishable from the exact implementation once the precomputed hop size is sufficiently small, while reducing total runtime by roughly half. We characterize the resulting tradeoffs among precomputation, runtime, memory, and perceptual quality to guide algorithm selection, and we release our implementation as an open-source package.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Python implementation of harmonic-percussive time-scale modification (TSM) designed for variable-rate playback applications like automatic musical accompaniment. Unlike existing offline or C++ implementations, this work enables real-time playback with continuously changing rates in response to live performers. The authors also propose computational approximations using precomputed lookup tables that reduce runtime by ~50% while maintaining perceptual quality.
AI.motivation: Existing TSM implementations are either offline-only (processing fixed-rate recordings) or written in C++ optimized for speed but not for easy integration with Python-based research. Applications like automatic musical accompaniment require variable-rate playback where the recording is known but playback rate must change dynamically in response to a live performer.
AI.method: The implementation uses harmonic-percussive separation as preprocessing on the known input, then performs real-time synthesis with a time-scale factor that can change at each frame. The paper proposes variants that replace the phase vocoder's analysis-stage FFT and instantaneous frequency calculations with precomputed lookup tables to reduce computational load.
AI.result: Subjective listening tests with 24 participants (1114 pairwise ratings) demonstrated that the approximations become perceptually indistinguishable from the exact implementation when the precomputed hop size is sufficiently small, while reducing total runtime by approximately 50%.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a practical open-source Python implementation for variable-rate TSM, with characterized tradeoffs among precomputation, runtime, memory, and perceptual quality to guide algorithm selection. The implementation is released as an open-source package.

title: Composite-Gradient Learning for Shared Control Authority Between Deep Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control
summary: Integrated deep reinforcement learning (DRL) and model predictive control (MPC) methods are increasingly used to control autonomous systems by combining their complementary capabilities. DRL learns control policies through interaction with the environment. MPC uses a system model to optimize control inputs while accounting for constraints. In DRL-MPC frameworks with shared control authority, both the DRL agent and the MPC controller each determine part of the control inputs. However, common learning formulations treat MPC as part of the environment and therefore do not explicitly account for MPC's contribution to control or its interaction with the DRL agent. This paper proposes a novel composite-gradient learning (CGL) method that integrates the MPC controller into the learning process by representing the DRL and MPC control inputs as a joint action and accounting for their interaction when updating the DRL agent during training. CGL is evaluated on two multi-class freeway traffic networks with different strengths of interaction between the DRL and MPC control inputs and it is compared with alternative methods that treat MPC as part of the environment or that only partially incorporate MPC into learning. The results show that CGL offers limited benefit under weak interaction, but learns higher-performing control policies than the alternative methods in a subset of training runs under strong interaction, although the average control-performance gains remain modest.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a composite-gradient learning (CGL) method that integrates model predictive control (MPC) into the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) training process, rather than treating MPC as part of the environment. The method is evaluated on freeway traffic networks, showing modest performance gains under strong interaction conditions.
AI.motivation: Current DRL-MPC frameworks treat MPC as part of the environment, failing to explicitly account for MPC's contribution to control or its interaction with the DRL agent. This limits the learning effectiveness when both DRL and MPC share control authority.
AI.method: The proposed CGL method represents DRL and MPC control inputs as a joint action and explicitly accounts for their interaction when updating the DRL agent during training. Evaluation was conducted on two multi-class freeway traffic networks with different interaction strengths.
AI.result: CGL offers limited benefit under weak interaction between DRL and MPC inputs. Under strong interaction, CGL learns higher-performing control policies than alternative methods in a subset of training runs, though average control-performance gains remain modest.
AI.conclusion: The CGL method shows promise for DRL-MPC integration, particularly under strong interaction conditions, but the average performance improvements are modest. Further research may be needed to enhance the method's consistency and magnitude of performance gains.
