title: Evaluating the Health of Open-Source Smart City Platforms
comment: Accepted at the 12th IEEE International Smart Cities Conference (ISC2 2026)
summary:
To manage the complexity of smart cities, a variety of smart city platforms (SCPs), both proprietary and open-source, have been proposed. Typically acting as middleware between IoT devices at a lower layer and smart services at a higher layer, these platforms simplify the management of smart cities by reifying a variety of requirements common to different municipalities. Open-source software (OSS) is typically free of charge, making open-source SCPs an attractive option for municipalities with smaller budgets that still wish to improve efficiency and quality of life for residents and visitors. Furthermore, using an OSS SCP promotes digital sovereignty, since municipalities can control where the data will reside and will be less prone to vendor lock-in.
  A lack of support for OSS hinders its adoption by municipalities' IT teams, often with scarce technical resources. An active (aka "healthy") ecosystem, including well-orchestrated developers and users, the availability of installation and user manuals, non-vulnerable and documented code, test batteries, and other artifacts, is an important decision factor before adopting an OSS SCP. In this paper, we evaluate different open-source SCPs using the concept of "OSS health", covering several of the aforementioned characteristics.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates open-source smart city platforms (SCPs) using the concept of "OSS health" to help municipalities with limited technical resources make informed adoption decisions.
AI.motivation: Open-source SCPs offer cost benefits and digital sovereignty for municipalities, but a lack of support and unclear ecosystem health hinder adoption by IT teams with limited technical resources.
AI.method: The paper evaluates different open-source SCPs using "OSS health" criteria, covering: developer/user community activity, installation/user documentation quality, code vulnerability and documentation, test battery availability, and other ecosystem artifacts.
AI.result: Not provided in the abstract - this appears to be the main contribution of the paper.
AI.conclusion: A healthy OSS ecosystem is a critical decision factor for municipalities considering open-source SCPs, as it addresses the support and technical resource challenges they face.

title: CALIPER: Metric-Grounded Model-Free Recognition of Visually Similar Industrial Parts
summary: Fine-grained recognition of visually similar industrial parts is challenging when classes differ primarily in physical dimensions. Normalizing detected object crops to a fixed input size suppresses absolute scale, while CAD models and large class-specific datasets may be unavailable in evolving industrial inventories. We present CALIPER, a model-free RGB-D framework that couples support-based appearance matching with metric size evidence. Each training class is onboarded from a single turntable RGB-D video and one to two labeled real images; 3D reconstruction provides novel-view appearance support, while aligned depth yields a class-specific metric size profile. At inference, a coarse YOLOv8n-seg model localizes parts, and a frozen DINOv2 backbone with an episodically trained embedding head performs fine-grained support matching. Margin-conditioned metric fusion activates probabilistic size evidence only for appearance-ambiguous decisions. New classes are enrolled from a small RGB-D support set without updating network parameters. We evaluate CALIPER on 18 visually similar industrial parts: 16 classes are used for training, while two screws are reserved for training-free enrollment. CALIPER achieves 88.2% closed-set accuracy with 99.8% localization recall and 85.7% overall accuracy after 10-shot enrollment of the two unseen screws. Metric fusion improves unseen-class accuracy by up to 37.4 percentage points without statistically significant degradation of the original inventory. Robot-arm deployment identifies 17/18 parts without deployment-specific retraining.

AI.tldr: CALIPER is a model-free RGB-D framework for fine-grained recognition of visually similar industrial parts, using support-based appearance matching combined with metric size evidence. It handles cases where classes differ primarily in physical dimensions, using 3D reconstruction for novel-view appearance support and aligned depth for metric size profiles. The system achieves 88.2% closed-set accuracy and 85.7% overall accuracy including 2 unseen classes enrolled without network retraining.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained recognition of industrial parts is challenging when classes differ primarily in physical dimensions. Current methods normalize detected object crops to fixed input sizes, which suppresses absolute scale information. Additionally, CAD models and large class-specific datasets are often unavailable in evolving industrial inventories. The authors aim to address these limitations by developing a model-free framework that leverages both appearance and metric size evidence.
AI.method: CALIPER couples support-based appearance matching with metric size evidence. Training classes are onboarded from a single turntable RGB-D video and 1-2 labeled real images, where 3D reconstruction provides novel-view appearance support and aligned depth yields a class-specific metric size profile. At inference, YOLOv8n-seg localizes parts, a frozen DINOv2 backbone with an episodically trained embedding head performs fine-grained support matching, and margin-conditioned metric fusion activates probabilistic size evidence only for appearance-ambiguous decisions. New classes are enrolled from small RGB-D support sets without updating network parameters.
AI.result: CALIPER achieves 88.2% closed-set accuracy with 99.8% localization recall on 18 industrial parts (16 training classes). After 10-shot enrollment of 2 unseen screws, overall accuracy reaches 85.7%. Metric fusion improves unseen-class accuracy by up to 37.4 percentage points without significant degradation of the original inventory. Robot-arm deployment successfully identifies 17/18 parts without deployment-specific retraining.
AI.conclusion: CALIPER effectively addresses fine-grained recognition of visually similar industrial parts by combining appearance matching with metric size evidence. The model-free approach enables training-free enrollment of new classes, and the margin-conditioned metric fusion particularly benefits unseen-class recognition. The system's ability to deploy on a robot arm without retraining demonstrates practical applicability in industrial settings.

title: SAGE: Governed Artifact Generation from Enterprise Guidelines
summary: Enterprise guideline documents mix narrative text, complex tables, and embedded images, and converting them into structured work artifacts still takes two to three days of manual effort each. Current language and vision-language models extract from such documents but offer no governed workflow beyond extraction: no validation, no consistency checking, no traceable artifact generation. We introduce SAGE, a governed multi-stage LLM pipeline organized around a shared versioned rule store with stable identifiers, schema-validated inter-stage contracts, and end-to-end provenance tracking. Extracted rules undergo deterministic structural validation and LLM-based semantic scoring, then a consistency module that removes duplicates, flags contradictions, and surfaces specification gaps; only uncertain or flagged items reach reviewers, while high-confidence outputs are auto-approved. On 120 documents, SAGE cuts turnaround from days to 20-100 minutes, achieving a 96% document-level success rate with 3.2% hallucination, extracting 3,896 rules and producing 812 artifacts ready for human review; without governance, hallucination rises to 15.7%.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a governed multi-stage LLM pipeline that automates the extraction of structured work artifacts from enterprise guideline documents, reducing turnaround time from 2-3 days to 20-100 minutes while maintaining high accuracy (96% success rate, 3.2% hallucination rate).
AI.motivation: Enterprise guideline documents are complex (narrative text, tables, images) and converting them into structured artifacts requires 2-3 days of manual effort. Existing language and vision-language models can extract content but lack governed workflows with validation, consistency checking, and traceable artifact generation.
AI.method: SAGE uses a governed multi-stage LLM pipeline with: (1) shared versioned rule store with stable identifiers, (2) schema-validated inter-stage contracts, (3) end-to-end provenance tracking. Extracted rules undergo deterministic structural validation and LLM-based semantic scoring. A consistency module removes duplicates, flags contradictions, and surfaces specification gaps. High-confidence outputs are auto-approved; only uncertain or flagged items reach human reviewers.
AI.result: On 120 documents, SAGE achieved: 96% document-level success rate, 3.2% hallucination rate, extracted 3,896 rules, produced 812 artifacts ready for human review. Turnaround reduced from days to 20-100 minutes. Without governance, hallucination rises to 15.7%.
AI.conclusion: SAGE demonstrates that governed LLM pipelines with validation, consistency checking, and provenance tracking can significantly reduce manual effort while maintaining high accuracy. The governance layer is critical - without it, hallucination increases 5x. The system successfully balances automation (for high-confidence outputs) with human review (for uncertain items).

title: What Affects the Performance of Fake Audio Detection? Analyzing Factors in a Continual Learning Setting
summary: The increasing sophistication of deepfake audio generation technologies makes it important to develop robust fake audio detection systems that can adapt over time. This study examines how various factors impact the performance of detection systems in a continual learning setting. We focus on factors such as attacker architectures, attackers' training datasets, speaker diversity, and task order. We evaluate the performance of three detection models trained with four different strategies, including direct fine-tuning, one-class classification, random replay, and Learning without Forgetting. Results show that artifacts from the fake audios might arise from the attackers' training datasets, and simply changing attacker architectures does not sufficiently challenge detection systems. Moreover, task order and speaker diversity can significantly influence performance, with varying degrees of sensitivity across different detection models and training strategies. These insights underline the need for careful consideration of these factors when developing robust detection systems.

AI.tldr: This study investigates factors affecting deepfake audio detection systems in a continual learning setting, including attacker architectures, training datasets, speaker diversity, and task order. Three detection models were evaluated using four training strategies.
AI.motivation: The increasing sophistication of deepfake audio generation technologies necessitates robust detection systems that can adapt over time to counter evolving threats.
AI.method: The study evaluates three detection models trained with four different strategies: direct fine-tuning, one-class classification, random replay, and Learning without Forgetting. It examines how attacker architectures, attackers' training datasets, speaker diversity, and task order impact detection performance.
AI.result: Key findings indicate that artifacts in fake audios may originate from attackers' training datasets, and simply changing attacker architectures does not sufficiently challenge detection systems. Task order and speaker diversity significantly influence performance, with varying sensitivity across different detection models and training strategies.
AI.conclusion: Careful consideration of attacker training data, task ordering, and speaker diversity is essential when developing robust deepfake audio detection systems in continual learning environments.

title: REVERSAL-BENCH: A Reversibility Axis and Reset Oracle for Measuring the Reset-Free RL Cliff
summary: A central goal of autonomous reinforcement learning is continuous policy training without external resets. However, existing paradigms largely depend on underlying environmental reversibility, a property absent in real world manipulation, where events such as pushing objects off tables or spilling granular substances cannot be undone. We introduce REVERSAL-BENCH, a benchmark that controls reversibility via a continuous parameter $ρ\in [0, 1]$ and provides a reset oracle, a ground-truth verification mechanism to test state recoverability across eight manipulation settings in five physics engines. Evaluating a broad spectrum of policy architectures, including standard actor-critic algorithms, safe RL, and specialized reset-free frameworks, reveals a sharp reversibility cliff: reset-free agents are consistently absorbed into irrecoverable states as $ρ$ increases, whereas episodic agents maintain steady learning. We see this failure mode across autonomous reset-free baselines and constrained RL. Because reset-free agents lack external resets, any transition into an irrecoverable state results in permanent absorption, leaving the agent trapped where further learning halts. We show that this absorption phenomenon persists in full physics simulations under learned manipulation policies. By evaluating against geometrically identical reversible counterparts, we confirm that this breakdown is causally driven by irreversibility rather than obstacle complexity. We release the benchmark suite, a large multi-simulator dataset labeled with recoverability and a reset oracle. We also evaluate a safety shield that intervenes before irreversible failures occur, showing that while recoverability can be predicted accurately, active recovery primarily succeeds only when the agent can physically steer clear of the trap

AI.tldr: REVERSAL-BENCH is a benchmark that controls environmental reversibility via a continuous parameter ρ∈[0,1] to evaluate reset-free autonomous reinforcement learning. The study reveals a "reversibility cliff" where reset-free agents become trapped in irrecoverable states as irreversibility increases, while episodic agents maintain stable learning. This failure persists across all tested frameworks (actor-critic, safe RL, reset-free baselines) and in full physics simulations.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous RL assumes environmental reversibility, which is absent in real-world manipulation tasks (e.g., pushing objects off tables, spilling substances). The research aims to understand how irreversible events affect reset-free policy training and whether existing frameworks can handle such scenarios.
AI.method: The authors created REVERSAL-BENCH, a benchmark with 8 manipulation settings across 5 physics engines, controlling reversibility via parameter ρ∈[0,1]. They evaluated various policy architectures including standard actor-critic algorithms, safe RL, and specialized reset-free frameworks. They also tested a safety shield that predicts recoverability and intervenes before irreversible failures.
AI.result: A sharp "reversibility cliff" was discovered: as ρ increases, reset-free agents are consistently absorbed into irrecoverable states, while episodic agents maintain steady learning. This failure occurs across all autonomous reset-free baselines and constrained RL methods. The safety shield can predict recoverability accurately, but active recovery only succeeds when the agent can physically avoid the trap.
AI.conclusion: Reset-free RL fundamentally fails in irreversible environments because any transition into an irrecoverable state results in permanent absorption, halting further learning. The breakdown is causally driven by irreversibility rather than obstacle complexity. Future work should focus on safety shields and recovery mechanisms that help agents avoid irreversible states.

title: ProgramDistill: From Interactive Web Apps to Verifiable Reference-Guided SWE Tasks
summary: Coding agents are typically evaluated with desired behavior specified through issues or instructions. In practical web development, however, agents may need to infer behavior from working software and implement it in an incomplete application. We introduce ProgramDistill, a benchmark evaluating coding agents on features discovered through interaction with fully functional reference applications. We build ProgramDistill by factorizing applications into features of different granularities, each associated with replayable behaviors executable via its gold patch. Our pipeline, mine-craft-patch, discovers 1,975 replay-verified behaviors across 26 applications and constructs 4,063 tasks without human intervention. Across nine frontier coding agents, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 achieve 49.2% and 28.8% success on cumulative workflows in full-application reconstruction. In partial-application reconstruction, success falls from 100% to 64.0% and from 96% to 32% as restoration depth increases from 1 to 8. ProgramDistill thus provides a scalable benchmark with controlled difficulty for evaluating and diagnosing coding agents, and a natural basis for future curriculum-based training.

AI.tldr: ProgramDistill is a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on inferring and implementing features from working reference applications, without explicit instructions. It uses an automated pipeline to create 4,063 tasks from 1,975 behaviors across 26 applications. Top agents like GPT-6 Astra achieve ~49% success on full reconstruction tasks.
AI.motivation: Current coding agent benchmarks use explicit instructions/issues, but real-world web development requires agents to infer behavior from existing software and implement it in incomplete applications. There was a need for a benchmark that evaluates this practical inference capability.
AI.method: The authors developed "mine-craft-patch" pipeline that: 1) Factorizes applications into features of different granularities, 2) Associates each feature with replayable behaviors executable via gold patches, 3) Automatically discovers 1,975 replay-verified behaviors across 26 applications, 4) Constructs 4,063 tasks without human intervention. Two evaluation settings: full-application reconstruction (cumulative workflows) and partial-application reconstruction (varying restoration depth).
AI.result: Across nine frontier coding agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.2% and Claude Opus 5 achieves 28.8% success on cumulative workflows in full-application reconstruction. In partial-application reconstruction, success decreases from 100% to 64.0% (GPT-6) and from 96% to 32% (Claude) as restoration depth increases from 1 to 8.
AI.conclusion: ProgramDistill provides a scalable benchmark with controlled difficulty for evaluating and diagnosing coding agents. It enables natural curriculum-based training and reveals significant gaps in current agents' ability to infer behavior from working software.

title: RoboVAD: A Large Cross-Domain Evaluation Benchmark for Anomaly Detection in Robotic Arm Manipulation Videos
summary: Video anomaly detection (VAD) is an actively studied task, having wide applications in typical scenarios such as public surveillance and road traffic safety. The task is also relevant for robotic arm interactions, where it has several downstream applications, including learning better interaction and manipulation abilities, triggering recovery procedures when anomalies occur, etc. Despite its relevance, the exploration of anomaly detection in robotic arm manipulation videos is limited by the low number of available resources. To this end, we introduce RoboVAD, a large-scale benchmark for video anomaly detection that comprises challenging cross-domain evaluation scenarios, where certain actions (tasks executed by a robotic arm) and anomaly types (mistakes that occur while performing certain tasks) remain unseen during training. RoboVAD is designed to benchmark VAD methods in realistic scenarios, where robotic arms can perform unforeseen tasks, and thereby encounter new anomaly types. We train and evaluate several state-of-the-art VAD methods, including a novel method specifically adapted for robotic arm manipulation. While the proposed method outperforms many state-of-the-art competitors, all methods remain below a micro-averaged frame-level AUC threshold of 70% in the most challenging evaluation setup, confirming the difficulty of the proposed benchmark. We publicly release our dataset and code at https://zenodo.org/records/22754659.

AI.tldr: RoboVAD is a large-scale benchmark for video anomaly detection in robotic arm manipulation, featuring challenging cross-domain evaluation scenarios where certain actions and anomaly types remain unseen during training. Despite a novel method outperforming competitors, all methods fail to exceed 70% micro-averaged frame-level AUC in the most challenging setup.
AI.motivation: Video anomaly detection is important for applications like public surveillance and road traffic safety, and has additional relevance for robotic arms in learning better interaction abilities and triggering recovery procedures. However, anomaly detection in robotic arm manipulation videos is under-explored due to limited available resources.
AI.method: The paper introduces RoboVAD, a large-scale benchmark with cross-domain evaluation scenarios where certain tasks and anomaly types remain unseen during training. They also propose a novel VAD method specifically adapted for robotic arm manipulation and evaluate several state-of-the-art VAD methods on this benchmark.
AI.result: The proposed method outperforms many state-of-the-art competitors, but all methods remain below a micro-averaged frame-level AUC threshold of 70% in the most challenging evaluation setup.
AI.conclusion: RoboVAD confirms the difficulty of detecting anomalies in robotic arm manipulation videos, especially when encountering unseen tasks and anomaly types. The benchmark is designed to evaluate VAD methods in realistic scenarios where robotic arms perform unforeseen tasks. The dataset and code are publicly released at https://zenodo.org/records/22754659.

title: FairCompressAgent: An Agentic Framework for Fairness-Aware Model Compression for FPGA Deployment
summary: Fairness-aware model compression requires selecting methods and configurations that balance accuracy, fairness, and deployment cost. These decisions become more difficult when compression methods are composed or the user's requirements change. In this paper, we propose FairCompressAgent (FCA), an agentic framework that integrates fairness-aware pruning, incremental quantization, and sparse low-rank factorization through a common operator interface. A language-model planner uses model profiles and measured outcomes to select compression configurations, while an execution layer performs compression, fine-tuning, evaluation, and constraint-based selection. FCA also supports requirement updates and reports the remaining violation when a request cannot be satisfied. Experiments on Fitzpatrick-17k with VGG-11 compare four search methods over 40 measured configurations. Under the accuracy-constrained request, FCA selects a compressed model with 59.54% less inference tensor storage, while validation average precision increases from 0.5141 to 0.5233 and equalized opportunity (EOpp) decreases from 0.2251 to 0.2168. It reaches the same final selection as one-shot planning with 7.33 versus 12 candidate evaluations on average, under their respective stopping policies. Repeated fine-tuning, held-out testing, and online requirement updates characterize the stability and interactive use of this compression workflow. The results demonstrate how measured feedback and explicit constraints support the selection and interactive refinement of fairness-aware compression configurations.

AI.tldr: FairCompressAgent (FCA) is an agentic framework for fairness-aware model compression that integrates multiple compression methods (pruning, quantization, sparse low-rank factorization) through a common interface. It uses a language-model planner to select compression configurations based on model profiles and measured outcomes, supporting requirement updates and constraint reporting.
AI.motivation: Fairness-aware model compression requires balancing accuracy, fairness, and deployment cost. This becomes challenging when compression methods are composed or user requirements change. Existing approaches lack an integrated framework that can handle multiple compression techniques while explicitly considering fairness constraints.
AI.method: FCA integrates three compression methods (fairness-aware pruning, incremental quantization, sparse low-rank factorization) through a common operator interface. A language-model planner selects compression configurations using model profiles and measured outcomes. An execution layer performs compression, fine-tuning, evaluation, and constraint-based selection. Experiments on Fitzpatrick-17k with VGG-11 compared four search methods over 40 configurations.
AI.result: Under accuracy-constrained request, FCA achieved 59.54% less inference tensor storage. Validation average precision increased from 0.5141 to 0.5233, and equalized opportunity (EOpp) decreased from 0.2251 to 0.2168 (improved fairness). FCA reached the same final selection as one-shot planning with 7.33 versus 12 candidate evaluations on average, demonstrating efficiency. The framework supports repeated fine-tuning, held-out testing, and online requirement updates.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that measured feedback and explicit constraints effectively support selection and interactive refinement of fairness-aware compression configurations. FCA successfully balances accuracy, fairness, and deployment cost while being more efficient than one-shot planning approaches.

title: Instrument Classification of Solo Sheet Music Images
summary: This paper studies instrument classification of solo sheet music. Whereas previous work has focused on instrument recognition in audio data, we instead approach the instrument classification problem using raw sheet music images. Our approach first converts the sheet music image into a sequence of musical "words" based on the bootleg score representation, and then treats the problem as a text classification task. We show that it is possible to significantly improve classifier performance by training a language model on unlabeled data, initializing a classifier with the pretrained language model weights, and then finetuning the classifier on labeled data. In this work, we train AWD-LSTM, GPT-2, and RoBERTa models on solo sheet music images from IMSLP for eight different instruments. We find that GPT-2 and RoBERTa slightly outperform AWD-LSTM, and that pretraining increases classification accuracy for RoBERTa from 34.5% to 42.9%. Furthermore, we propose two data augmentation methods that increase classification accuracy for RoBERTa by an additional 15%.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses instrument classification in solo sheet music images by converting sheet music to musical "words" using bootleg score representation and treating it as a text classification problem. The approach uses pretrained language models (AWD-LSTM, GPT-2, RoBERTa) with fine-tuning on labeled data.
AI.motivation: Previous work focused on instrument recognition in audio data, but this paper tackles the novel problem of classifying instruments directly from raw sheet music images, which has not been previously explored.
AI.method: The approach converts sheet music images into sequences of musical "words" using the bootleg score representation, then treats the problem as text classification. Models are trained in three stages: (1) pretrain language model on unlabeled data, (2) initialize classifier with pretrained weights, (3) finetune on labeled data. Two data augmentation methods are also proposed.
AI.result: GPT-2 and RoBERTa slightly outperform AWD-LSTM. Pretraining increases RoBERTa accuracy from 34.5% to 42.9% (8.4% improvement). The proposed data augmentation methods boost RoBERTa accuracy by an additional 15%.
AI.conclusion: It is possible to effectively classify instruments from sheet music images using language model-based approaches. Pretraining on unlabeled data significantly improves performance, and data augmentation provides substantial additional gains. The dataset used contains solo sheet music from IMSLP for eight instruments.

title: SAM-on-the-Curve: Sharpness-Aware Mode Connectivity for Robust Weight-Space Interpolation
summary: Deep neural networks that are independently trained to similar performance can be connected by low-loss parametric curves in weight space, a phenomenon known as Mode Connectivity (MC). This geometric property underpins practical techniques such as weight averaging, model ensembling, and model merging. We argue that low-loss connectivity is an incomplete geometric criterion: it controls loss only along a one-dimensional trajectory while leaving the surrounding weight-space neighborhood unconstrained, so the optimized curve may traverse sharp ridges that become fragile under distribution shift. We therefore reformulate mode connectivity as a neighborhood-robust path optimization problem, seeking a curve whose entire local neighborhood maintains low loss. We propose Sharp Mode Connectivity (SMC), which applies a first-order sharpness-aware approximation to the resulting minimax functional, enforcing flatness along the entire curve rather than only on it. We derive a practical optimization algorithm for connectivity paths under this sharpness-aware objective. Under severe blur corruptions from CIFAR-10-C, SMC achieves up to 6.09\% absolute accuracy improvement over standard MC. Remarkably, SMC produces negative loss barriers, meaning that models obtained at interior points of the optimized path can outperform the average endpoint loss. These results, validated across ResNet-18, VGG16-BN, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100, establish path-wise flatness as a practical principle for robust weight-space interpolation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Sharp Mode Connectivity (SMC), a reformulation of Mode Connectivity that seeks weight-space curves whose entire local neighborhood maintains low loss, rather than just the curve itself. This addresses the limitation that standard MC only controls loss along a 1D trajectory while leaving surrounding weight-space neighborhoods unconstrained and fragile under distribution shift. SMC uses a first-order sharpness-aware approximation to enforce flatness along the entire curve. Under severe blur corruptions on CIFAR-10-C, SMC achieves up to 6.09% absolute accuracy improvement over standard MC.
AI.motivation: The authors argue that low-loss connectivity is an incomplete geometric criterion because it only controls loss along a one-dimensional trajectory while leaving the surrounding weight-space neighborhood unconstrained. The optimized curve may traverse sharp ridges that become fragile under distribution shift. This motivates the need for a robustness criterion that considers the entire neighborhood rather than just the path itself.
AI.method: The authors reformulate mode connectivity as a neighborhood-robust path optimization problem. They propose Sharp Mode Connectivity (SMC), which applies a first-order sharpness-aware approximation to the resulting minimax functional. This enforces flatness (low sharpness) along the entire curve rather than only on the curve itself. They derive a practical optimization algorithm for connectivity paths under this sharpness-aware objective.
AI.result: Under severe blur corruptions from CIFAR-10-C, SMC achieves up to 6.09% absolute accuracy improvement over standard MC. Remarkably, SMC produces negative loss barriers, meaning that models obtained at interior points of the optimized path can outperform the average endpoint loss. These results are validated across ResNet-18, VGG16-BN, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that path-wise flatness is a practical principle for robust weight-space interpolation. SMC provides a way to find connectivity paths that are robust to distribution shift by enforcing flatness in the surrounding neighborhood of the entire path, not just the path itself.

title: Removing Noise or Introducing Bias? The Hidden Cost of MSR Filtering
summary: OSS platforms like GitHub serve as a primary data source for MSR research. As the platform is widely used by different users, spanning from student to developer, not all repositories are actual engineered projects. Therefore, to avoid such noise, researchers often apply several criteria, which may fundamentally change the sample demographics. To understand such biases, this study aims to uncover the hidden cost originating from these arbitrary thresholds or criteria. We analyzed 1.57 million repositories from the SEART platform and constructed several datasets from the thresholds often applied in MSR research. We identify the maintenance bias in these filtering processes, which masks the true abandonment (73.42%) realities of OSS projects. Also, these strategies favor some ecosystems and governance styles. Moreover, the sampling strategy also distorts the relationship between variables, suffering from relational biases. Therefore, to avoid such biases, the researchers should shift towards stratified sampling and refining the criteria for noise detection.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hidden biases introduced by common filtering criteria used in Mining Software Repositories (MSR) research when sampling GitHub repositories. Through analysis of 1.57 million repositories, the study reveals that standard filtering thresholds mask the true abandonment rate of OSS projects (73.42%) and introduce maintenance, ecosystem, governance, and relational biases.
AI.motivation: Researchers often apply arbitrary thresholds or criteria to filter GitHub repositories for MSR studies, aiming to remove "noise" (non-engineered projects). However, this practice may introduce systematic biases that fundamentally alter sample demographics and distort research findings. The motivation is to uncover these hidden costs and understand how filtering strategies affect research validity.
AI.method: The researchers analyzed 1.57 million repositories from the SEART platform. They constructed several datasets using common thresholds and filtering criteria typically applied in MSR research. They then compared these datasets to identify how different filtering strategies affect the sample composition, including maintenance patterns, ecosystem distribution, governance styles, and variable relationships.
AI.result: The study identified four key biases introduced by common filtering practices: (1) Maintenance bias - standard filters mask the true abandonment rate of 73.42% of OSS projects; (2) Ecosystem bias - filtering strategies favor certain software ecosystems; (3) Governance bias - certain governance styles are preferred by current filtering approaches; (4) Relational bias - sampling strategies distort relationships between variables, affecting research conclusions.
AI.conclusion: To avoid such biases in MSR research, researchers should shift towards stratified sampling methods and refine the criteria for noise detection rather than relying on arbitrary thresholds. This will help produce more representative samples and valid research findings about open-source software ecosystems.

title: Investigating Adversarial Robustness of Heterogeneous Cooperative Perception
summary: Heterogeneous cooperative perception (CP) enables connected vehicles with diverse sensor setups to share spatial awareness via compact feature maps, where receivers reconcile these maps using learned translation modules for fusion and inference. Prior attacks against CP in a homogeneous setting reveal that the data exchange introduces a critical attack surface: a single malicious agent can transmit crafted features that erase real objects from a neighbor's fused scene. Yet, it is widely hypothesized that heterogeneity naturally defends against these attacks, as the attacker lacks knowledge of the victim's detector and the translation module scrambles adversarial gradients. We demonstrate that this protection is largely an illusion. Using a matched-objective harness to standardize the perturbation budget, objective, and forward path, we show that properly tuned iterative attacks close or reverse the apparent robustness gap. However, these optimization-based attacks require ground-truth labels and iterative backpropagation, meaning they do not represent a practical field threat running in real-time. To bridge this gap, we introduce HetPoison, a learned generator that crafts a removal perturbation in a single, label-free forward pass. HetPoison transfers across major heterogeneous designs without requiring access to the victim's detector, matching or exceeding the effectiveness of expensive optimizer-based attacks. Since heterogeneity itself is not a defense, we propose HetShield, a lightweight trust layer that validates the spatiotemporal consistency across features, recovering 83--95% of the accuracy degraded by attacks, outperforming prior art.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that heterogeneous cooperative perception (CP) systems in connected vehicles are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, despite a common hypothesis that sensor heterogeneity provides natural defense. The authors show that optimization-based attacks can overcome this apparent robustness gap, and introduce HetPoison, a learned generator that achieves effective removal attacks in a single forward pass without labels. They also propose HetShield, a defense mechanism that recovers 83-95% of attack-degraded accuracy.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a critical security vulnerability in cooperative perception systems for connected autonomous vehicles. Prior work showed that homogeneous CP systems are vulnerable to attacks where malicious agents can erase real objects from neighbors' fused scenes. The widely held hypothesis was that heterogeneity (diverse sensor setups) naturally defends against these attacks because attackers lack knowledge of victims' detectors and translation modules scramble adversarial gradients. This paper challenges that hypothesis by proving the protection is largely illusory.
AI.method: The authors introduce a matched-objective harness to standardize perturbation budget, objective, and forward path across heterogeneous designs. They evaluate iterative optimization-based attacks that require ground-truth labels and backpropagation, then develop HetPoison - a learned generator that crafts removal perturbations in a single label-free forward pass. For defense, they propose HetShield - a lightweight trust layer validating spatiotemporal consistency across features.
AI.result: Iterative attacks close or reverse the apparent robustness gap from heterogeneity. HetPoison successfully transfers across major heterogeneous designs without requiring access to the victim's detector, matching or exceeding the effectiveness of expensive optimizer-based attacks. HetShield recovers 83-95% of the accuracy degraded by attacks, outperforming prior art.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneity alone is not a sufficient defense against adversarial attacks in cooperative perception. The field needs active defense mechanisms like HetShield that validate spatiotemporal consistency. The research demonstrates both the severity of the threat (with practical single-pass attacks via HetPoison) and a viable defense pathway.

title: A Four-Stage Decomposition of Word-Problem Solving and Mechanistic Fragility in LLM Math Reasoning
summary: Large language models solve grade-school math word problems with high accuracy, yet a single irrelevant clause inserted into the problem can collapse it. We reconcile these observations with a mechanistic account. We show that the model's internal computation decomposes into a four-stage sequential pipeline, Schema Abstraction, Operation Planning, Operand Binding, and Computation, each stage producing a distinct intermediate representation in an identifiable band of layers. Using the same scaffold to diagnose distractor-induced failure, we localize the corruption to a single stage, Operation Planning, implemented by a set of attention heads whose causal role we validate bidirectionally. In short, we provide a mechanistic interpretation of math word problem reasoning in LLMs, and their failure when distracted.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a mechanistic interpretation of how LLMs solve math word problems, identifying a four-stage pipeline (Schema Abstraction → Operation Planning → Operand Binding → Computation) in specific layer bands. Failure from irrelevant distractors is traced to the Operation Planning stage, implemented by specific attention heads whose causal role is validated bidirectionally.
AI.motivation: To understand why large language models (LLMs) that excel at grade-school math problems fail dramatically when a single irrelevant clause is added, reconciling the apparent contradiction between high accuracy and extreme fragility to distractors.
AI.method: Mechanistic analysis using a scaffold to diagnose model behavior, identifying distinct processing stages through layer-wise analysis, and validating causal roles bidirectionally through intervention on specific attention heads.
AI.result: The model's internal computation decomposes into four sequential pipeline stages: Schema Abstraction, Operation Planning, Operand Binding, and Computation, each producing distinct intermediate representations in identifiable layer bands. Distractor-induced failure localizes to a single stage—Operation Planning—implemented by specific attention heads.
AI.conclusion: The researchers provided a complete mechanistic account of math word problem reasoning in LLMs, showing that distractor-induced failure stems from corruption in the Operation Planning stage, enabling precise diagnosis of where and why reasoning fails in these models.

title: Modular Deep Learning Mechanisms for Auditable Next-Day Wildfire Spread Prediction
summary: Next-day wildfire prediction requires models whose forecasts can be evaluated alongside the assumptions and historical evidence used in their computation. Although deep learning can learn spatial patterns from remote-sensing data, predictive performance alone does not establish physical fidelity or operational trustworthiness. This study investigates three modular augmentations for next-day active-fire prediction: wind- and slope-conditioned attention biases, physics-feature retrieval-augmented output correction, and fire conditioned dual-stream gating. The attention biases expose prescribed directional preferences, while the retrieval module selects historical tiles using a nine-dimensional environmental and fire-state descriptor and applies a learned correction to a frozen model's logits. The modules are evaluated across five backbones on the Next Day Wildfire Spread benchmark, using staged ablations, directional audits, retrieval perturbations, calibration measures, and computational comparisons. The three-seed mean F1 score and area under the precision--recall curve (AUC-PR) of a SwinUNETR model with all three augmentations are 0.4216 and 0.3673. Then, a mixed ensemble (two augmented architectures and one non-augmented architecture) model achieves 0.4292 and 0.3790. Benefits vary across architectures, and retrieval-related improvements in AUC-PR do not consistently translate into higher F1. The constructed wind bias aligns closely with input wind, but its alignment with observed next-day fire displacement is much weaker, distinguishing prior inspectability from predictive physical fidelity. The study contributes a framework for exposing and evaluating selected domain-informed components within wildfire prediction models. Together, the results presented show that predictive performance, operational trustworthiness, and computational practicality need not be competing objectives.

AI.tldr: This study develops and evaluates three modular augmentations for next-day active-fire prediction: wind- and slope-conditioned attention biases, physics-feature retrieval-augmented output correction, and fire-conditioned dual-stream gating. These modules aim to improve both predictive performance and operational trustworthiness by incorporating domain-informed components into deep learning models.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the gap between predictive performance and physical fidelity in deep learning wildfire prediction models. While deep learning can learn spatial patterns from remote-sensing data, performance metrics alone do not establish operational trustworthiness or physical fidelity. The study seeks to create interpretable, domain-informed components that can be evaluated alongside their predictions.
AI.method: The study implements three modular augmentations: (1) wind- and slope-conditioned attention biases that expose prescribed directional preferences, (2) a physics-feature retrieval module that selects historical tiles using a nine-dimensional environmental and fire-state descriptor and applies learned correction to frozen model logits, and (3) fire-conditioned dual-stream gating. These modules were evaluated across five backbones on the Next Day Wildfire Spread benchmark using staged ablations, directional audits, retrieval perturbations, calibration measures, and computational comparisons.
AI.result: The SwinUNETR model with all three augmentations achieved a three-seed mean F1 score of 0.4216 and AUC-PR of 0.3673. A mixed ensemble (two augmented and one non-augmented architecture) achieved 0.4292 F1 and 0.3790 AUC-PR. Benefits varied across architectures, and retrieval improvements in AUC-PR did not consistently translate to higher F1. The wind bias aligned closely with input wind but showed weak alignment with observed next-day fire displacement, distinguishing inspectability from predictive physical fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a framework for exposing and evaluating domain-informed components within wildfire prediction models. The key conclusion is that predictive performance, operational trustworthiness, and computational practicality can be achieved simultaneously without competing objectives. The study provides tools for evaluating physical fidelity beyond standard metrics.

title: Code Consistency Preference Optimization Verification for Language Model Alignment
summary: Execution-based verification enhances large language models' mathematical reasoning through computational soundness and dependency-aware filtering. However, prior preference optimization methods relying on Bradley-Terry reward models fail to capture the logical dependencies and execution consistency needed for scientific tasks. We propose a method that generates computationally sound solutions with dependency graphs for execution-consistent preference optimization. We first build a scientific reasoning dataset using UltraFeedback prompts, model generations, verification, and consistency results. Then we extract reasoning step expressions, prerequisites, and derivability relationships to construct dependency graphs and compute execution consistency scores. These scores are appended to each step, creating paired training data. Fine-tuning Llama-3-8B and DeepSeekMath-7B yields significant gains: +17.0% on MATH and +15.1% on GSM8K. Extending our Scientific Feasibility Control framework achieves 50.1% accuracy on PhyX multimodal physics reasoning, surpassing DeepSeek-R1 (49.8%) and OpenAI o3-mini (48.2%), with 91.7% scientific validity coverage at alpha=0.10 and 73% fewer scientific law violations, resulting in the CCPO model family.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel execution-consistent preference optimization (CCPO) method that uses dependency graphs to enhance large language models' mathematical and scientific reasoning capabilities. It addresses limitations in prior Bradley-Terry reward models by incorporating computational soundness and execution consistency scoring.
AI.motivation: Prior preference optimization methods using Bradley-Terry reward models fail to capture logical dependencies and execution consistency needed for scientific tasks. Execution-based verification exists but lacks proper dependency-aware filtering for training LLM reasoning.
AI.method: The researchers built a scientific reasoning dataset using UltraFeedback prompts, model generations, verification, and consistency results. They extracted reasoning step expressions, prerequisites, and derivability relationships to construct dependency graphs and compute execution consistency scores. These scores were appended to each step to create paired training data, which was used to fine-tune Llama-3-8B and DeepSeekMath-7B, resulting in the CCPO model family.
AI.result: Fine-tuning achieved significant gains: +17.0% on MATH and +15.1% on GSM8K. The Scientific Feasibility Control framework achieved 50.1% accuracy on PhyX multimodal physics reasoning, surpassing DeepSeek-R1 (49.8%) and OpenAI o3-mini (48.2%). It also achieved 91.7% scientific validity coverage at alpha=0.10 and reduced scientific law violations by 73%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CCPO method successfully integrates dependency graphs with execution consistency scoring into preference optimization, significantly improving LLM performance on mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks while maintaining higher scientific validity and reducing law violations.

title: Lumen: Parameter-Efficient Alignment of Pretrained Vision and Language Encoders for Zero-Shot Computational Pathology
summary: Pathology vision-language models are commonly built by pretraining or fine-tuning large encoders on paired image-caption data. We asked whether a pathology vision-language model can instead be assembled by parameter-efficient alignment of frozen unimodal foundation models, leaving their pretrained representations untouched. Here we present Lumen, which aligns frozen Virchow2 and BioMedBERT backbones using rank-4 adapters and projection heads, training only 0.40% of the total parameters on the public QUILT-1M corpus. Across nine public zero-shot patch benchmarks, Lumen achieved the highest mean chance-corrected balanced accuracy, 0.546 versus 0.461 for the strongest baseline (paired difference 0.086, 95% CI 0.042-0.136). On lymph-node metastasis detection, Lumen reached an AUROC of 0.964 (95% CI 0.956-0.971) on 4,214 held-out internal slides and 0.955 (95% CI 0.942-0.966) on 2,368 slides across nine external cohorts and six organs. At the internally calibrated threshold, it outperformed all vision-language baselines, with a balanced accuracy of 0.909 (95% CI 0.896-0.923) internally and 0.915 (95% CI 0.902-0.929) externally. Lumen performed competitively across the evaluations, with the exception of cross-modal retrieval, where it ranked third behind CONCH and PathGen-L/14. Fully fine-tuning both encoders gave Lumen no consistent benefit over low-rank adaptation, although it improved retrieval. Aligning frozen unimodal foundation models therefore yields strong and transferable performance at patch and slide level while training only a small fraction of the parameters.

AI.tldr: Lumen is a pathology vision-language model that achieves state-of-the-art performance by aligning frozen unimodal foundation models (Virchow2 and BioMedBERT) using rank-4 adapters, training only 0.40% of total parameters on QUILT-1M corpus.
AI.motivation: The authors investigate whether a pathology VLM can be assembled by parameter-efficient alignment of frozen unimodal foundation models rather than pretraining or fine-tuning large encoders, aiming to preserve pretrained representations while reducing computational cost.
AI.method: Lumen aligns frozen Virchow2 (vision) and BioMedBERT (text) backbones using rank-4 adapters and projection heads, training only 0.40% of total parameters on the public QUILT-1M corpus. The approach uses low-rank adaptation (LoRA) for parameter efficiency.
AI.result: Lumen achieved the highest mean chance-corrected balanced accuracy of 0.546 on nine zero-shot patch benchmarks (vs 0.461 baseline). For lymph-node metastasis detection, it achieved AUROC of 0.964 on 4,214 internal slides and 0.955 on 2,368 external slides across 9 cohorts and 6 organs. Balanced accuracy was 0.909 internally and 0.915 externally. The exception was cross-modal retrieval where it ranked third behind CONCH and PathGen-L/14.
AI.conclusion: Aligning frozen unimodal foundation models yields strong and transferable performance at patch and slide level while training only a small fraction of parameters. Full fine-tuning provided no consistent benefit over low-rank adaptation, although it improved retrieval. This demonstrates a parameter-efficient approach to building competitive pathology VLMs.

title: Learning Heterogeneous Preferences
summary: Learning from human feedback has become a central paradigm for training modern AI systems, where models of human utility are used as reward models in policy learning. Existing methods typically assume a \emph{universal utility} function shared across a population and treat disagreement between annotators as stochastic variation. While suitable for objective tasks, this assumption breaks down in subjective domains where preferences vary systematically across individuals. We study the problem of subjective preference learning, in which observed choices arise from heterogeneous but internally consistent utility functions. Drawing upon rational choice theory, RCT \parencite{tversky1981framing}, we introduce \emph{individuated utility} functions conditioned on both the individual and their decision context, and propose a novel multi-stage architecture for estimating them from multi-modal data. We evaluate our framework on a newly collected dataset of more than $575{,}000$ pairwise aesthetic judgments from $2{,}398$ participants comparing automotive wheel designs. Our experiments show that individuated utility models substantially outperform universal utility models including foundation model baselines. Our results demonstrate that disagreement reflects meaningful preference heterogeneity rather than annotation noise. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of collecting annotator attributes and learning individuated utility functions, enabling reward models that explicitly account for whose preferences they represent and faithfully capture human decision diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses a fundamental limitation in learning from human feedback: the assumption of a universal utility function across all individuals. The authors propose a novel framework for learning "individuated utility" functions that capture heterogeneous but internally consistent preferences across different people, evaluated on a large dataset of 575,000+ pairwise aesthetic judgments about automotive wheel designs from 2,398 participants.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for learning from human feedback assume a universal utility function shared across a population, treating annotator disagreement as stochastic noise. This assumption works for objective tasks but fails in subjective domains where preferences vary systematically across individuals. The authors aim to capture meaningful preference heterogeneity rather than treating disagreement as noise.
AI.method: The authors introduce individuated utility functions conditioned on both the individual and their decision context, drawing upon rational choice theory. They propose a novel multi-stage architecture for estimating these utility functions from multi-modal data. The framework is evaluated on a newly collected dataset of more than 575,000 pairwise aesthetic judgments from 2,398 participants comparing automotive wheel designs.
AI.result: Individuated utility models substantially outperform universal utility models, including foundation model baselines. The results demonstrate that disagreement reflects meaningful preference heterogeneity rather than annotation noise.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of collecting annotator attributes and learning individuated utility functions. This enables reward models that explicitly account for whose preferences they represent and faithfully capture human decision diversity, moving beyond the universal utility assumption in subjective domains.

title: Principled Koopman Representations with Kalman Inference for Efficient Time-Series Prediction
summary: The Koopman operator has been widely used for time-series prediction in dynamical systems. However, prior work that learns latent ``Koopman spaces'' using neural networks often did not construct a valid Koopman space for forecasting, as these representations may be mathematically inconsistent with the operator-theoretic formulation and fail to capture the intrinsic low-rank structure of system dynamics. To address this issue, we introduce K$^2$SVD, a method that explicitly learns the leading singular functions of the Koopman operator by optimizing a Hilbert-Schmidt objective. This yields a well-defined low-rank approximation of the Koopman operator with an interpretable linear combination, featuring a compact latent space with less than $10\%$ of the dimensions used in previous work. In the learned Koopman space, K$^2$SVD further captures temporal evolution with a linear Gaussian state-space model and performs inference via Kalman filtering, mitigating noise accumulation during multi-step prediction. Empirical results show that K$^2$SVD outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets, with significantly faster prediction speeds and lower computational cost than previous efficiency-focused models. This highlights the benefits of principled low-rank Koopman representations and opens up broader potential for applications.

AI.tldr: K²SVD is a method for learning valid low-rank Koopman operator representations by optimizing a Hilbert-Schmidt objective to capture leading singular functions, combined with a linear Gaussian state-space model for inference via Kalman filtering.
AI.motivation: Prior neural network approaches for learning Koopman spaces in dynamical systems often fail to construct mathematically valid Koopman spaces that are consistent with operator-theoretic formulation and cannot capture the intrinsic low-rank structure of system dynamics.
AI.method: K²SVD learns the leading singular functions of the Koopman operator by optimizing a Hilbert-Schmidt objective, yielding a well-defined low-rank approximation with interpretable linear combination and compact latent space (<10% of previous work dimensions). Temporal evolution is captured using a linear Gaussian state-space model with inference performed via Kalman filtering to mitigate noise accumulation in multi-step prediction.
AI.result: K²SVD outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets, with significantly faster prediction speeds and lower computational cost than previous efficiency-focused models.
AI.conclusion: Principled low-rank Koopman representations provide significant benefits, demonstrating the value of mathematical consistency in operator-theoretic formulations and opening potential for broader applications.

title: Can VLMs Reliably Assess Sidewalk Accessibility Attributes from Pedestrian-Level Imagery?
summary: An important component of urban accessibility, particularly for wheelchair users and people with reduced mobility, is sidewalk compliance with measurable requirements. We test whether effective width, longitudinal slope, cross slope, and pavement condition can be assessed reliably from pedestrian-level imagery using vision-language models (VLMs). We present the first application of sampling-based conformal prediction (CP) for VLM-based accessibility assessment. We evaluate four VLMs on 514 sidewalk images from Seoul, South Korea, with field-measured ground truth. Conformal calibration attains the nominal 90% coverage for all models and attributes, but the calibrated regions differ in informativeness. Effective width yields the most informative estimates, with a mean interval half-width of about 1.0 m for the best model. Since every model overestimates width, asymmetric calibration shortens the intervals by up to 33% at unchanged coverage. Longitudinal slope is marginally informative, cross-slope intervals are too wide to resolve regulatory thresholds, and pavement-condition sets degenerate to all five grades (A-E) for three of the four models. Uncalibrated intervals from raw sampling dispersion cover only 17-47% of field-measured values at a nominal 90% level. Among the images with the most self-consistent responses, these intervals miss the field-measured value in up to 96% of cases. Response self-consistency is therefore not evidence of accuracy, and sampling dispersion cannot be interpreted as uncertainty until it has been calibrated against field-measured ground truth. No quantitative attribute reaches the precision required for general compliance assessment, but CP identifies from calibration data alone which attributes can support screening of segments far from the thresholds. We release the annotated pedestrian-level images and their corresponding field-measured attribute values.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether vision-language models (VLMs) can reliably assess sidewalk accessibility attributes (effective width, longitudinal slope, cross slope, and pavement condition) from pedestrian-level imagery. Using 514 sidewalk images from Seoul with field-measured ground truth, they apply sampling-based conformal prediction (CP) for the first time to VLM-based accessibility assessment. The study finds that while CP achieves nominal 90% coverage, no attribute achieves precision sufficient for general compliance assessment, though CP can identify which attributes are useful for screening segments far from regulatory thresholds.
AI.motivation: Urban sidewalk accessibility is critical for wheelchair users and people with reduced mobility. Current compliance assessment requires expensive field measurements. This research explores whether AI vision-language models can automate this process using readily available pedestrian-level imagery, potentially enabling large-scale accessibility mapping at lower cost.
AI.method: The study evaluated four VLMs on 514 sidewalk images from Seoul, South Korea, with field-measured ground truth for four attributes: effective width, longitudinal slope, cross slope, and pavement condition. They applied sampling-based conformal prediction (CP) to generate calibrated uncertainty intervals and compared these against raw sampling dispersion. They also tested asymmetric calibration to improve interval efficiency.
AI.result: Conformal calibration achieved nominal 90% coverage for all models and attributes. Effective width produced the most informative estimates (mean interval half-width ~1.0m), but all models overestimated width. Asymmetric calibration shortened intervals by up to 33%. Longitudinal slope was marginally informative; cross-slope intervals were too wide to resolve regulatory thresholds; pavement-condition sets degenerated to all five grades for three of four models. Uncalibrated intervals covered only 17-47% of field-measured values, and self-consistent responses showed up to 96% error rate.
AI.conclusion: Vision-language models alone cannot yet provide sufficient precision for general sidewalk accessibility compliance assessment. However, conformal prediction is valuable for identifying which attributes can serve as screening tools for segments clearly far from regulatory thresholds. The key insight is that response self-consistency does not indicate accuracy—calibration against ground truth is essential for reliable uncertainty quantification. The authors release their annotated dataset for future research.

title: SNOMED CT Concept Recommendation from Masked Clinical Context
summary: Standardizing clinical language to SNOMED CT supports interoperability, analytics, and reusable phenotyping, but concept recommendation remains difficult when relevant concepts are rare or absent from training data. We present a masked-concept recommendation benchmark using the SNOMED CT Entity Linking Challenge v1.2.1 data derived from MIMIC-IV-Note. The dataset contains 75,491 annotations across 272 discharge summaries, with 204 notes used for training and 68 for historical testing. For each unique note-concept pair, the target mention is masked from a local clinical context and the system ranks SNOMED CT concepts observed during training. We compare a popularity baseline, sparse TF-IDF concept prototypes, dense latent semantic analysis embeddings, sparse-dense fusion, retrieved-note evidence, and a retrieval-augmented hybrid. Sparse TF-IDF performs best, achieving Recall@1 of 14.81%, Recall@10 of 33.43%, MRR of 0.2114, and nDCG@10 of 0.2297. Retrieval augmentation does not improve this baseline, with Recall@10 of 31.99% and MRR of 0.1937. Performance is strongly affected by concept frequency: Recall@10 is 7.74% for concepts appearing in only one or two training notes versus 43.90% for concepts appearing in more than ten. In addition, 9.66% of test note-concept pairs contain concepts unseen during training. These findings show that local lexical context and terminology coverage are major determinants of recommendation quality in low-resource settings and provide a reproducible baseline for future ontology-grounded and biomedical-encoder retrieval systems.

AI.tldr: A benchmark for SNOMED CT concept recommendation in clinical notes shows sparse TF-IDF achieves best performance (Recall@10=33.43%), with performance heavily dependent on concept frequency (7.74% for rare vs 43.90% for frequent concepts). Retrieval augmentation provides no improvement, and 9.66% of test concepts are unseen during training.
AI.motivation: Standardizing clinical language to SNOMED CT supports interoperability and analytics, but concept recommendation remains difficult when relevant concepts are rare or absent from training data.
AI.method: Created a masked-concept recommendation benchmark using SNOMED CT Entity Linking Challenge v1.2.1 data from MIMIC-IV-Note (75,491 annotations across 272 discharge summaries). Compared six approaches: popularity baseline, sparse TF-IDF, dense LSA embeddings, sparse-dense fusion, retrieved-note evidence, and retrieval-augmented hybrid.
AI.result: Sparse TF-IDF performs best: Recall@1=14.81%, Recall@10=33.43%, MRR=0.2114, nDCG@10=0.2297. Retrieval augmentation does not improve baseline (Recall@10=31.99%, MRR=0.1937). Performance strongly affected by concept frequency: Recall@10 is 7.74% for concepts in 1-2 training notes vs 43.90% for concepts in >10 notes. 9.66% of test pairs contain unseen concepts.
AI.conclusion: Local lexical context and terminology coverage are major determinants of recommendation quality in low-resource settings. This benchmark provides a reproducible baseline for future ontology-grounded and biomedical-encoder retrieval systems.

title: The Free Inference Dimension: Complexity Measure for Zero-Collision Navigation under Hypothesis Mixtures
summary:
Solomonoff induction frames prediction as a mixture over computable hypotheses, typically leading to identification of the true environment. In a finite meta-reinforcement learning setting with nested constraint families, in our previous work, we observe a different regime: a value-mixture (VM) agent achieves near-optimal, zero-collision navigation without identifying the true environment, a phenomenon we call Free Inference. This regime persists up to a sharp density threshold, beyond which performance degrades and posterior-mode selection (PMS) becomes preferable.
  We formalize this behavior via the Free Inference dimension dFI(S,N), a combinatorial measure of the environmental complexity a VM agent can handle while preserving trajectory coherence. We prove dFI is strictly smaller than the VC-dimension and relates to the Natarajan dimension up to a path-length factor, capturing the cost of non-decomposable loss. A PAC-style relaxation yields generalization bounds driven by dFI^(epsilon,delta). We also define a complementary PMS identification dimension and show that a hybrid strategy---averaging until the first collision, then switching to selection---is optimal, with links to Littlestone-type dimensions supported by grid-world experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper explores a phenomenon called "Free Inference" in meta-reinforcement learning, where a value-mixture (VM) agent achieves near-optimal performance without identifying the true environment. It introduces the Free Inference dimension (dFI) as a combinatorial complexity measure, proves its relationships with VC-dimension and Natarajan dimension, and shows a hybrid strategy (averaging then switching to selection) is optimal.
AI.motivation: The authors observed that in finite meta-reinforcement learning with nested constraint families, VM agents can achieve zero-collision navigation without identifying the true environment - a phenomenon that persists up to a sharp density threshold. This contrasts with classical Solomonoff induction where the true environment is typically identified. The motivation is to formalize and understand this anomalous behavior.
AI.method: The paper uses theoretical analysis combining: 1) Combinatorial complexity measures (defining dFI dimension), 2) Comparative analysis with established dimensions (VC-dimension, Natarajan dimension), 3) PAC-style generalization bounds, and 4) Empirical validation through grid-world experiments.
AI.result: The key results include: 1) dFI is strictly smaller than VC-dimension, 2) dFI relates to Natarajan dimension up to a path-length factor, 3) A sharp density threshold exists beyond which VM performance degrades, 4) A hybrid strategy (averaging until first collision, then switching to selection) is optimal, with links to Littlestone-type dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a theoretical framework for understanding Free Inference in meta-RL, introducing dFI as a meaningful complexity measure that captures environmental complexity a VM agent can handle while preserving trajectory coherence. The hybrid strategy provides optimal performance across different regimes.

title: Zing-0.5: Toward Playable Worlds with Real-Time Joint Action and Text Control
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures. Authors listed alphabetically by surname. Project: https://zing.loopit.me/ ; Code: https://github.com/seedleap/zing-world-model ; Models: https://huggingface.co/seedleap/zing-0.5 ; Serving: https://github.com/seedleap/Zing-SGLang
summary: We introduce Zing-0.5, a 5B autoregressive world model designed for playability: users can explore generated worlds, influence unfolding events, and respond to the resulting feedback through joint keyboard and online text control. Our approach brings together three technical contributions: (1) Unified action and text conditioning, combining magnitude-aware keyboard inputs with temporally aligned text instructions and jointly annotated videos to learn navigation and event control within the same sequence; (2) Event-scale supervision for incremental generation, using a segment-level teacher trained on connected multi-prompt videos to supervise a block-level causal student through distribution-matching distillation; and (3) Low-cost real-time interaction, combining four-step generation with context-preserving streaming to support 832 x 480 inference at 24 FPS at an estimated server rental cost of approximately USD 0.009 per stream-minute. Zing-0.5 achieves an overall score of 81.0 and a consistency score of 88.5 across 158 WBench Navigation cases. A joint-control demonstration shows a text-directed event change during continued navigation without restarting generation. We release the model weights, inference code, and Zing-SGLang serving implementation to support further work on playable generated worlds.

AI.tldr: Zing-0.5 is a 5B autoregressive world model enabling playable generated worlds where users can explore, influence events, and interact through joint keyboard and text controls. It achieves 81.0 overall score and 88.5 consistency score on 158 WBench Navigation cases, with real-time inference at 24 FPS.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to create playable generated worlds where users can actively explore, influence unfolding events, and receive feedback through combined keyboard and online text control - moving beyond passive video generation toward interactive experiences.
AI.method: Three technical contributions: (1) Unified action and text conditioning combining magnitude-aware keyboard inputs with temporally aligned text instructions and jointly annotated videos; (2) Event-scale supervision using segment-level teacher to supervise block-level causal student through distribution-matching distillation; (3) Low-cost real-time interaction combining four-step generation with context-preserving streaming for 832x480 at 24 FPS.
AI.result: Zing-0.5 achieves an overall score of 81.0 and consistency score of 88.5 across 158 WBench Navigation cases. Joint-control demonstration shows text-directed event change during continued navigation without restarting generation. Estimated server cost of ~$0.009 per stream-minute.
AI.conclusion: The model enables interactive world generation with real-time performance at low cost. Release of model weights, inference code, and Zing-SGLang serving implementation supports further work on playable generated worlds.

title: The Inference Engineering Pareto Atlas: Which Optimizations Dominate the Cost, Quality, and Latency Frontier?
summary: LLM inference optimizations report speedups on different models, GPUs, prompts, and quality metrics, making them hard to compare or combine. We build a cost, quality, and latency Pareto atlas to identify the best configurations for different deployment constraints. Since exhaustive testing is impractical, we measure 54 configurations of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct running on vLLM 0.12 across L4, A100, and H100 GPUs and use these anchors to calibrate a simulator. It reproduces measurements at anchored batch sizes, with cross campaign drift below 1.5 percent. A separate quality evaluation tests FP16, AWQ 4bit, FP8 weights, and FP8 KV cache on 200 GSM8K questions with five examples per prompt. Sparse attention is evaluated only in simulation. On the calibrated grid, 18 of 36 configurations reach the Pareto frontier. Combined methods reach it more often than individual methods, with 9 of 15 combinations versus 9 of 21 single methods. Quality testing changes the winners. AWQ 4bit reduces per token latency to 0.34 times baseline on L4 but loses 5.9 percent of strict GSM8K accuracy, narrowly missing the 95 percent quality floor within sampling uncertainty. Flexible answer extraction matches FP16 accuracy, suggesting the loss comes from formatting rather than arithmetic. FP8 weights retain 99.4 percent of baseline accuracy at 0.61 to 0.65 times baseline latency across all three GPUs and appear in three of four regime winners. A naive FP8 KV cache maintains normal throughput but answers none of the 200 questions correctly, showing why speed alone is insufficient. Under two prompt designs, n gram speculative decoding measures at 0.90 to 0.98 times baseline and adds no benefit on this stack. The best choice depends on the constraint and GPU: H100 wins for tight latency, while A100 wins for throughput and low cost at 0.106 dollars per million tokens.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic framework for comparing LLM inference optimizations by building a cost, quality, and latency Pareto atlas. The authors test 54 configurations of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on vLLM across L4, A100, and H100 GPUs, evaluating various quantization methods (FP16, AWQ 4bit, FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache) and speculative decoding on GSM8K benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLM inference optimizations report inconsistent speedups across different models, GPUs, prompts, and quality metrics, making them difficult to compare or combine. There was a need for a systematic approach to identify optimal configurations for different deployment constraints.
AI.method: The authors measured 54 configurations on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct running vLLM 0.12 across L4, A100, and H100 GPUs. They used these measurements to calibrate a simulator that reproduces measurements with cross-campaign drift below 1.5%. Quality evaluation tested FP16, AWQ 4bit, FP8 weights, and FP8 KV cache on 200 GSM8K questions with five examples per prompt. Sparse attention was evaluated only in simulation.
AI.result: 18 of 36 configurations reached the Pareto frontier. Combined methods (9/15) reached Pareto more often than single methods (9/21). AWQ 4bit reduced per-token latency to 0.34x baseline on L4 but lost 5.9% GSM8K accuracy, missing the 95% quality floor. FP8 weights retained 99.4% baseline accuracy at 0.61-0.65x latency across all GPUs and appeared in three of four regime winners. FP8 KV cache failed completely (0% accuracy). N-gram speculative decoding showed no benefit (0.90-0.98x baseline). H100 wins for tight latency; A100 wins for throughput and low cost ($0.106 per million tokens).
AI.conclusion: The optimal LLM inference configuration depends heavily on deployment constraints and GPU type. Combined optimization methods outperform individual methods. FP8 weights offer the best balance of speed and accuracy, while AWQ 4bit provides fastest inference but at acceptable quality loss. Quality metrics must be considered alongside speed metrics—FP8 KV cache demonstrates that speed alone is insufficient. H100 is best for latency-critical applications, while A100 offers the best cost-efficiency for throughput-focused workloads.

title: NObSP: Functional Decomposition of Neural Networks via Oblique Subspace Projections
comment: 24 pages, including 6 pages of supplementary material. Code available at https://github.com/santialferez/nobsp_lib
summary: Understanding how deep neural networks make decisions remains a fundamental challenge. We present NObSP (Nonlinear Oblique Subspace Projections), a framework that decomposes predictions into explicit per feature contribution functions and an interaction residual. NObSP exploits the linear final layer of a trained network and uses oblique projections in sample space to reduce double counting when learned feature subspaces overlap, thereby supporting both local explanations and global functional analysis. We establish connections to functional ANOVA and the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem and derive an efficient partial regression algorithm for out of sample evaluation. For convolutional networks, NObSP-CAM produces class activation maps without backward passes after a one time calibration. Experiments on tabular and vision benchmarks show faithfulness comparable to established attribution methods. On a synthetic benchmark with known component functions, NObSP obtains a Function Reproduction Score of 0.989, compared with 0.966 for KernelSHAP and 0.922 for Integrated Gradients. On TinyImageNet, contribution vector embeddings improve mean nearest neighbor class purity from 0.654 for raw activations to 0.713 and reduce mean neighbor distance by more than half.
