These results indicate that NObSP complements scalar attribution methods by recovering functional contribution profiles with separable positive and negative evidence.

AI.tldr: NObSP (Nonlinear Oblique Subspace Projections) is a framework that decomposes deep neural network predictions into explicit per-feature contribution functions and an interaction residual, using oblique projections to address overlapping feature subspaces.
AI.motivation: Understanding how deep neural networks make decisions remains a fundamental challenge, requiring methods that can decompose predictions into interpretable components.
AI.method: NObSP exploits the linear final layer of trained networks and uses oblique projections in sample space to reduce double counting when learned feature subspaces overlap. It supports both local explanations and global functional analysis, with connections to functional ANOVA and Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. An efficient partial regression algorithm is derived for out-of-sample evaluation. For convolutional networks, NObSP-CAM produces class activation maps without backward passes after one-time calibration.
AI.result: Experiments on tabular and vision benchmarks show faithfulness comparable to established attribution methods. On a synthetic benchmark with known component functions, NObSP achieves a Function Reproduction Score of 0.989, compared with 0.966 for KernelSHAP and 0.922 for Integrated Gradients. On TinyImageNet, contribution vector embeddings improve mean nearest neighbor class purity from 0.654 to 0.713 and reduce mean neighbor distance by more than half.
AI.conclusion: NObSP complements scalar attribution methods by recovering functional contribution profiles with separable positive and negative evidence, providing both local explanations and global functional analysis capabilities.

title: Face-voice Association across LAnguages and Gender (FLAG) 2027 Challenge Evaluation Plan
summary: Face--voice association models may rely on language or gender cues in the voice rather than on speaker-specific voice characteristics, which can lead to a performance deterioration when the model has to identify a multilingual speaker or distinguis same-gender speakers. To investigate these issues, we introduce the Face-voice Association across LAnguages and Gender (FLAG) 2027 Challenge. The challenge formulates face--voice association as a cross-modal verification task: given a voice, identify the speaker's face from a ``gallery'' of faces consisting of the speaker's face and a set of negative samples. Models are evaluated on identities not present in the training data (``unseen'') and both for languages present or absent from the training data (``heard'' and ``unheard''). Two evaluation settings are used to test models' reliance on gender: a standard, unconstrained and a gender-constrained one, where the latter uses a same-gender gallery. The performance of existing, baseline models in these settings reveals that models performance degrades under language shifts and in gender-constrained settings, highlighting the need to foster the development of models that capture identity-specific aspects beyond language and gender. The challenge provides a benchmark dataset, pretrained baseline models, and an evaluation framework to advance face--voice association.

AI.tldr: The FLAG 2027 Challenge addresses face-voice association by testing models across different languages and gender settings. It reveals that current models rely too heavily on language and gender cues rather than speaker-specific identity characteristics, leading to performance degradation when handling multilingual speakers or same-gender comparisons.
AI.motivation: Face-voice association models may incorrectly rely on language or gender cues in voices rather than speaker-specific voice characteristics, causing performance issues when identifying multilingual speakers or distinguishing same-gender speakers.
AI.method: The challenge formulates face-voice association as a cross-modal verification task: given a voice, identify the speaker's face from a gallery containing the speaker's face and negative samples. Evaluation uses unseen identities with both "heard" (languages in training) and "unheard" (languages not in training) languages. Two settings are tested: standard/unconstrained and gender-constrained (same-gender gallery).
AI.result: Existing baseline models show performance degradation under language shifts and in gender-constrained settings, highlighting that current models fail to capture identity-specific aspects beyond language and gender cues.
AI.conclusion: The challenge provides a benchmark dataset, pretrained baseline models, and an evaluation framework to advance face-voice association research, specifically requiring models that capture identity-specific characteristics beyond language and gender.

title: Do Frontier Models Seek Safety Evidence Before Acting?
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, with supplementary appendices. Code and data available at the repository linked in the paper
summary: Frontier models are often evaluated on how they respond to safety information once it is already in context. We study an earlier decision point: whether models choose to acquire safety-relevant evidence before acting. We introduce SAFE, a controlled benchmark in which models make deployment decisions with optional evidence that varies in retrieval cost, probability, severity, and presentation. Across GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, we find distinct evidence-acquisition policies: Opus inspects nearly by default, o3 is the most skip-heavy and threshold-sensitive, and GPT-5.5 and Sonnet occupy intermediate regimes. Inspection increases strongly with severity and decreases with retrieval cost, whereas probability has much weaker behavioral influence: increasing the stated likelihood of a problem from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points. Despite these differences, Stage 1 rationales are dominated by expected-value reasoning across models. A cost-obligation decomposition further shows that avoidance is driven primarily by retrieval friction and explicit threats to the deployment payoff rather than by the remediation duties created by knowing. Counterfactual interventions reveal a further mismatch between behavior and explanation: evidence framing can strongly change decisions near the inspection boundary while going largely unmentioned, whereas probability is frequently cited despite having little causal influence. These results suggest that deployment-time safety depends not only on how models respond to known risks, but also on whether they acquire the evidence needed to know that acting is safe.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SAFE benchmark to study whether AI models choose to acquire safety evidence before acting. Testing GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, researchers found distinct evidence-acquisition policies, with inspection driven more by severity and retrieval cost than by probability. A key mismatch exists between stated reasoning (often citing probability) and actual causal factors (retrieval friction and deployment payoff threats). The study reveals that deployment safety depends on whether models proactively seek safety evidence, not just how they respond to known risks.
AI.motivation: Current AI safety evaluations focus on how models respond to safety information already in context. However, this ignores an earlier critical decision point: whether models choose to acquire safety-relevant evidence before acting. The research addresses this gap by studying the "pre-action" evidence acquisition phase.
AI.method: The authors introduce SAFE, a controlled benchmark where models make deployment decisions with optional evidence. The evidence varies across four dimensions: retrieval cost, probability, severity, and presentation. They evaluated four models: GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. They used cost-obligation decomposition and counterfactual interventions to analyze behavior.
AI.result: The study found distinct evidence-acquisition policies across models: Opus inspects nearly by default, o3 is most skip-heavy and threshold-sensitive, while GPT-5.5 and Sonnet occupy intermediate regimes. Inspection increases strongly with severity and decreases with retrieval cost. Interestingly, probability has weak behavioral influence—increasing stated likelihood from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points. Stage 1 rationales are dominated by expected-value reasoning across models. Cost-obligation decomposition shows avoidance is driven primarily by retrieval friction and explicit threats to deployment payoff, not by remediation duties. Counterfactual interventions reveal mismatches: evidence framing strongly changes decisions near inspection boundary but goes unmentioned, while probability is frequently cited despite having little causal influence.
AI.conclusion: Deployment-time safety depends not only on how models respond to known risks, but also on whether they acquire evidence needed to know acting is safe. The findings highlight a previously overlooked dimension of AI safety—models' willingness to proactively seek safety-relevant information before making deployment decisions.

title: Procedural Pretraining for Molecular Property Prediction
summary: Molecular property prediction is often limited by the small size of labeled downstream datasets, motivating pretraining on large corpora of unlabeled molecules. In this work, we ask whether useful inductive biases can instead be learned from abstract, procedurally generated data before a model sees any molecular data. We introduce a three-stage training pipeline consisting of procedural pretraining, molecular pretraining on SMILES, and downstream fine-tuning, and evaluate several procedural tasks spanning sequence structure, cellular automata, and graph reasoning. We find that procedural pretraining can improve molecular property prediction even after subsequent molecular pretraining: on Lipophilicity, \textsc{Reverse} reduces test error by 4.8\%. For context, the magnitude of this improvement is roughly 90\% of the performance difference between our 250K-molecule baseline and the publicly released MoLFormer checkpoint pretrained on approximately 100M molecules. Our analysis shows that the benefit is strongest under downstream data scarcity, depends on the structure of the procedural data rather than only surface-level statistics, and does not increase monotonically with additional procedural training. Instead, transfer typically peaks at an intermediate procedural budget and deteriorates as the model approaches convergence on the procedural task. We further find that, for several tasks, much of the transferable information is localized in the attention layers, while feed-forward layers can contribute to over-specialization. These results show that procedural data can provide transferable structure for molecular learning and offer a complementary route to improving performance when labeled molecular data are limited.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether abstract, procedurally generated data can provide useful inductive biases for molecular property prediction before a model sees any molecular data. They propose a three-stage pipeline (procedural pretraining → molecular pretraining → fine-tuning) and find that procedural pretraining can reduce test error by 4.8% on Lipophilicity, with benefits strongest under data scarcity and peaking at intermediate procedural training budgets.
AI.motivation: Molecular property prediction is limited by small labeled datasets. While pretraining on large unlabeled molecular corpora helps, this work explores whether abstract procedural data can provide transferable inductive biases before any molecular data is introduced, potentially offering a complementary approach to improve performance when labeled molecular data are limited.
AI.method: Three-stage training pipeline: (1) Procedural pretraining on abstract tasks (sequence structure, cellular automata, graph reasoning), (2) Molecular pretraining on SMILES strings, (3) Downstream fine-tuning on molecular property prediction tasks. They evaluated several procedural tasks and analyzed where transferable information localizes (attention vs. feed-forward layers).
AI.result: Procedural pretraining improves molecular property prediction even after subsequent molecular pretraining. On Lipophilicity, Reverse reduces test error by 4.8% (roughly 90% of the improvement gap between a 250K-molecule baseline and MoLFormer pretrained on 100M molecules). Benefits are strongest under data scarcity, depend on structural complexity of procedural data, and peak at intermediate procedural training budgets rather than converging.
AI.conclusion: Procedural data can provide transferable structure for molecular learning, offering a complementary route to improving performance when labeled molecular data are limited. The transferable information is largely localized in attention layers, while feed-forward layers may contribute to over-specialization. This work demonstrates that abstract procedural pretraining is a viable alternative or complement to large-scale molecular pretraining.

title: Audio for Sports Highlight Detection: A Comparative Empirical Study
comment: Accepted at ACM Multimedia Workshop on Multimedia Content Analysis in Sports (MMSports) 2026
summary: Sports highlight detection aims to identify the most exciting and meaningful moments from long sports videos. While existing methods often emphasize visual or visual-language representations, sports videos contain rich audio cues, including commentator speech, crowd reactions, whistles, ball impacts, and referee calls. In this work, we revisit the role of audio in sports highlight detection and ask a simple question: how far can audio alone go? We construct lightweight audio-only baselines using pretrained audio representations and compare them with visual-only and audio-visual methods on the SV-Highlights benchmark. Surprisingly, our audio-only GRU baseline achieves strong performance and outperforms several existing audio-visual methods under our supervised evaluation setting. Furthermore, a simple audio-visual fusion baseline achieves the best performance across all metrics, indicating that audio and visual cues provide complementary information. To better understand the contribution of audio, we conduct source-separated analysis and show that vocal/commentary audio is more informative than background-only audio, while their combination performs best. We also analyze interpretable audio cues and find that highlight clips exhibit higher RMS loudness, peak loudness, and mid-frequency energy than non-highlight clips, although substantial distribution overlap indicates that loudness alone is insufficient. Our findings suggest that audio is an underexplored but highly informative modality for sports highlight detection and should be treated as a primary signal rather than merely an auxiliary cue.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the effectiveness of audio-only methods for sports highlight detection, comparing audio-only, visual-only, and audio-visual approaches on the SV-Highlights benchmark. Surprisingly, a simple audio-only GRU baseline achieves competitive performance and outperforms several existing audio-visual methods, while audio-visual fusion achieves the best results overall.
AI.motivation: Existing sports highlight detection methods emphasize visual or visual-language representations, but sports videos contain rich audio cues (commentator speech, crowd reactions, whistles, ball impacts). The authors revisit the role of audio and ask how far audio alone can go in highlight detection.
AI.method: The authors construct lightweight audio-only baselines using pretrained audio representations (GRU architecture) and compare them with visual-only and audio-visual methods on the SV-Highlights benchmark under supervised evaluation. They also conduct source-separated analysis to understand contribution of different audio types (vocal/commentary vs background-only) and analyze interpretable audio cues (RMS loudness, peak loudness, mid-frequency energy).
AI.result: Audio-only GRU baseline achieves strong performance and outperforms several existing audio-visual methods. Simple audio-visual fusion achieves best performance across all metrics. Source-separated analysis shows vocal/commentary audio is more informative than background-only audio, while their combination performs best. Highlight clips exhibit higher RMS loudness, peak loudness, and mid-frequency energy than non-highlight clips, though substantial distribution overlap indicates loudness alone is insufficient.
AI.conclusion: Audio is an underexplored but highly informative modality for sports highlight detection and should be treated as a primary signal rather than merely an auxiliary cue. Audio and visual cues provide complementary information.

title: ERPBench: A State-Grounded Evaluation Paradigm for Computer-Use Agents in Enterprise Software
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables, submitted for review to 2027 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
summary: Computer-use agents that operate through screenshots and simulated actions are advancing rapidly, yet their evaluation remains anchored to general desktop and web tasks. Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems run the finance, procurement, inventory, and customer operations of organizations worldwide, and pose distinct challenges for computer-use agents: dense interfaces, coordinated multi-step interactions, and errors that alter persistent business records rather than surfacing on screen. Existing enterprise benchmarks rely on proprietary platforms or on simulated approximations of such software. We introduce ERPBench, a benchmark that evaluates screenshot-only agents on a live and reproducible ERP system and scores each task against ground-truth values in its database. Beyond the benchmark, we present a production-grade harness that gates agent actions behind human approval for safe deployment, which ERPBench runs autonomously. Evaluating six closed and open-source agents, we demonstrate that strong general GUI performance does not transfer to enterprise reliability. Even when an agent reaches the right form and saves it, the stored record is often wrong: some agents save in up to 85% of runs but write the correct value in as few as 3%. We further characterize failure modes specific to enterprise workflows.

AI.tldr: ERPBench is a benchmark for evaluating screenshot-based computer-use agents on live ERP systems, addressing the gap that general desktop benchmarks don't capture enterprise-specific challenges like dense interfaces, multi-step workflows, and persistent data errors.
AI.motivation: Existing computer-use agent benchmarks focus on general desktop/web tasks, but enterprise ERP systems pose unique challenges: dense interfaces, coordinated multi-step interactions, and errors that corrupt persistent business records rather than appearing on screen. Current enterprise benchmarks rely on proprietary platforms or simulations, lacking a realistic evaluation framework.
AI.method: The authors developed ERPBench, a benchmark using a live and reproducible ERP system that evaluates screenshot-only agents by scoring tasks against ground-truth values in the database. They also created a production-grade harness that gates agent actions behind human approval for safe deployment. Six closed and open-source agents were evaluated.
AI.result: Strong general GUI performance does not transfer to enterprise reliability. Agents achieve high save rates (up to 85%) but write correct values in as few as 3% of runs. Failure modes specific to enterprise workflows were identified, showing that reaching the right form and saving it doesn't guarantee correct data entry.
AI.conclusion: ERPBench reveals a critical gap between general GUI agent capabilities and enterprise software requirements. The benchmark provides a practical tool for evaluating agents on real ERP systems, and the safety harness enables safe autonomous testing. The findings highlight the need for enterprise-specific evaluation frameworks rather than relying on general-purpose benchmarks.

title: Adaptive hybrid coupling with operator inference, the overlapping Schwarz alternating method and reinforcement learning
summary: Hybrid domain decomposition methods provide a flexible framework for coupling full order models (FOMs) and reduced order models (ROMs), but typically assume the model assigned to each subdomain is fixed throughout a simulation. This is limiting for transient problems in which localized features propagate through the domain and the regions requiring high-fidelity resolution change over time. We introduce a reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach for online adaptation of FOM-ROM models coupled via the overlapping Schwarz alternating method (O-SAM), an iterative domain decomposition method that solves subdomain-local problems while exchanging solution information through transmission boundary conditions on overlapping interfaces. Deep Q-networks (DQNs) are trained offline to select among subdomain-local FOMs and pre-trained Operator Inference (OpInf) ROMs using a reward balancing accuracy, cost, and model-switching frequency. Once trained, the policies are deployed predictively on problem instances not seen during training, without requiring a reference FOM solution. We demonstrate the approach on two examples: a 1D advection-diffusion problem with a moving front, and a 3D linear elastic wave propagation problem implemented in the Norma.jl solid mechanics code. For the advection-diffusion benchmark, the learned policy dynamically allocates high-fidelity resolution as the front propagates and outperforms static FOM/ROM assignments; letting the agent also adapt the domain decomposition provides no further benefit. For the elastic wave benchmark, learned policies for two and three subdomain decompositions track the propagating wave by assigning FOMs to subdomains containing the wave and ROMs elsewhere, as expected. Our results demonstrate the potential of RL to enable predictive online adaptation of model fidelity within Schwarz-based hybrid simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-based approach for online adaptation of hybrid full order model (FOM) and reduced order model (ROM) couplings in domain decomposition methods. Deep Q-networks are trained to dynamically select between FOMs and ROMs for different subdomains based on accuracy, computational cost, and model-switching frequency, enabling predictive adaptation without requiring reference solutions.
AI.motivation: Traditional hybrid domain decomposition methods assume fixed model assignments throughout simulations, which is limiting for transient problems where localized features (like moving fronts or waves) propagate through the domain and regions requiring high-fidelity resolution change over time.
AI.method: The authors use Deep Q-networks (DQNs) trained offline to select among subdomain-local FOMs and pre-trained Operator Inference (OpInf) ROMs. The reward function balances accuracy, computational cost, and model-switching frequency. The method is applied to the overlapping Schwarz alternating method (O-SAM), an iterative domain decomposition method that exchanges solution information through transmission boundary conditions on overlapping interfaces.
AI.result: For the 1D advection-diffusion benchmark with a moving front, the learned policy dynamically allocates high-fidelity resolution as the front propagates and outperforms static FOM/ROM assignments. Interestingly, letting the agent also adapt the domain decomposition provides no further benefit. For the 3D linear elastic wave propagation problem, learned policies for two and three subdomain decompositions successfully track the propagating wave by assigning FOMs to subdomains containing the wave and ROMs elsewhere.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning can enable predictive online adaptation of model fidelity within Schwarz-based hybrid simulations. The approach successfully balances accuracy and computational cost by dynamically allocating high-fidelity resolution to regions where it is most needed (e.g., where waves or fronts are present).

title: Rapid Loss of the Sierra Nevada's Largest Trees Driven by Fire
summary: Large trees disproportionately contribute to biomass storage, habitat structure, and ecosystem functioning. However, their distribution and health dynamics remain poorly quantified at a regional scale. Here, a deep learning model (U-Net-ID) and canopy height models derived from sub-meter aerial imagery from 2020 were used to delineate all individual trees with crown area $\geq$ 100 m$^2$ across the Sierra Nevada Floristic Province. The model was trained using more than 3.3 million synthetic tree crowns and achieved a median Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.602 when validated against an independent dataset of 20,273 crowns. A total of 6,515,705 large trees were mapped, occurring across approximately 78.7% of the Sierra Nevada Floristic Province. The spatial distribution of large trees showed associations with elevation, temperature, and precipitation. Using Sentinel-2 time series from 2020 to 2025, tree health dynamics were characterized by extracting spectral trajectories for each crown and applying BFAST breakpoint detection algorithm combined with a disturbance classification framework to identify mortality, disturbance, and recovery trajectories of individual trees. Wildfires, estimated from CAL FIRE fire perimeters, were identified as the dominant driver of large-tree mortality, killing 10% of all large trees in the Sierra Nevada, with mortality strongly concentrated during the extreme 2020-2021 fire seasons.

AI.tldr: A deep learning model mapped 6.5 million large trees across the Sierra Nevada using aerial imagery, then analyzed their health dynamics from 2020-2025 using satellite time series, finding wildfires caused 10% mortality.
AI.motivation: Large trees are critical for biomass storage, habitat structure, and ecosystem functioning, but their regional distribution and health dynamics remain poorly quantified despite their ecological importance.
AI.method: Used U-Net-ID deep learning model with canopy height models from sub-meter aerial imagery (2020) to delineate individual trees with crown area ≥100 m². Trained on 3.3 million synthetic tree crowns, validated on 20,273 crowns. Tree health dynamics were analyzed using Sentinel-2 time series (2020-2025) with BFAST breakpoint detection and a disturbance classification framework. Wildfire impacts were assessed using CAL FIRE fire perimeters.
AI.result: Model achieved median IoU of 0.602. Mapped 6,515,705 large trees covering 78.7% of the province. Spatial distribution associated with elevation, temperature, and precipitation. Wildfires identified as dominant mortality driver, killing 10% of all large trees, with mortality concentrated during extreme 2020-2021 fire seasons.
AI.conclusion: This study provides the first regional-scale quantification of large tree distribution and mortality dynamics in the Sierra Nevada, demonstrating that extreme wildfire events are the primary driver of large-tree mortality, with significant implications for ecosystem management and conservation.

title: OBC-Prune: Outcome-Based Calibration for Large Reasoning Model Pruning
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate long chain-of-thought traces before answering, creating significant inference overhead. Pruning can reduce this cost, but its effectiveness depends on the calibration data used to estimate parameter importance. Recent work calibrates on the model's own rollouts instead of generic dataset, but treats all reasoning tokens uniformly, regardless of whether they contribute to successful reasoning. As a result, pruning protects weights by statistical salience rather than by their contribution to correct reasoning, so weights behind erroneous computation survive as readily as those behind correct computation. These erroneous patterns then get carried into the pruned model, degrading reasoning quality, producing both lower accuracy and longer reasoning traces. We propose Outcome-Based Calibration for Large Reasoning Model Pruning (OBC-Prune) to close this gap. OBC first constructs difficulty-matched pairs of correct and incorrect rollouts from problems the model answers inconsistently. It then estimates the causal importance of each reasoning sentence through intervention-based analysis, quantifying how removing its influence affects subsequent predictions. These causal importance scores are converted into per-token weights that rescale the calibration activations used by one-shot pruning methods (SparseGPT, Wanda, ALPS), without modifying the underlying pruning algorithms. Experiments on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, and 14B models at 40\% and 50\% sparsity demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art calibration baselines across most model sizes and sparsity levels on MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and AIME 2025. These results indicate that preserving causally important reasoning circuits is a substantially more effective pruning objective than uniformly preserving observed activations.

AI.tldr: OBC-Prune introduces outcome-based calibration for pruning large reasoning models by using causal importance scores to identify reasoning tokens that actually contribute to correct answers, rather than just preserving statistically salient tokens. This method rescal calibration activations for one-shot pruning methods without modifying the algorithms themselves.
AI.motivation: Current LRM pruning calibrates on model rollouts but treats all reasoning tokens uniformly, regardless of whether they contribute to correct reasoning. This causes weights behind erroneous computation to survive pruning, degrading reasoning quality with lower accuracy and longer reasoning traces.
AI.method: OBC-Prune constructs difficulty-matched pairs of correct and incorrect rollouts from problems the model answers inconsistently. It estimates causal importance of each reasoning sentence through intervention-based analysis, quantifying how removing its influence affects subsequent predictions. These causal importance scores are converted into per-token weights that rescale calibration activations used by one-shot pruning methods (SparseGPT, Wanda, ALPS).
AI.result: Experiments on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, and 14B models at 40% and 50% sparsity demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art calibration baselines across most model sizes and sparsity levels on MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and AIME 2025.
AI.conclusion: Preserving causally important reasoning circuits is a substantially more effective pruning objective than uniformly preserving observed activations. The method successfully improves reasoning quality in pruned models by targeting weights that actually contribute to correct reasoning.

title: Hybrid coupling with numerics-informed neural networks and the overlapping Schwarz alternating method
summary: We develop a hybrid modeling framework for coupling pre-trained numerics-informed neural networks (NINNs) with classical full order models (FOMs) using the overlapping Schwarz alternating method. We consider the two-dimensional advection-diffusion equation in the advection-dominated, Peclet-number 10^6 regime. We first demonstrate that, unlike the corresponding physics-informed neural network (PINN), a monolithic NINN can be accurately trained on our model problem without domain decomposition. We then employ overlapping multiplicative Schwarz as a deployment mechanism for coupling a pre-trained, subdomain-local NINN with a neighboring FOM, with the NINN weights held fixed throughout the Schwarz iteration. We consider two training approaches for the subdomain-local NINNs: a top-down approach, in which boundary data are obtained from a coupled Schwarz solve on the full domain with a FOM on each subdomain (FOM-FOM Schwarz), and a bottom-up approach, in which boundary traces are generated synthetically on the NINN subdomain without requiring any full-domain solves. The resulting hybrid NINN-FOM solutions agree closely with the corresponding FOM-FOM Schwarz solutions, with the top-down and bottom-up training approaches yielding comparable accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid modeling framework that couples pre-trained numerics-informed neural networks (NINNs) with classical full order models (FOMs) using the overlapping Schwarz alternating method, applied to the advection-dominated 2D advection-diffusion equation (Peclet number 10^6).
AI.motivation: The work addresses the challenge of training physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in advection-dominated regimes, which typically suffer from accuracy issues. The motivation is to develop a scalable and efficient hybrid approach that combines the strengths of neural networks with traditional numerical methods.
AI.method: The authors develop a hybrid framework using overlapping multiplicative Schwarz method to couple a pre-trained subdomain-local NINN with a neighboring FOM. They compare two training approaches: (1) a top-down approach where boundary data is obtained from coupled Schwarz solve with FOM on each subdomain, and (2) a bottom-up approach where boundary traces are generated synthetically without full-domain solves. The NINN weights remain fixed during Schwarz iteration.
AI.result: The monolithic NINN can be accurately trained without domain decomposition, unlike PINNs. Both top-down and bottom-up training approaches yield hybrid NINN-FOM solutions that agree closely with corresponding FOM-FOM Schwarz solutions, with comparable accuracy between the two approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid NINN-FOM framework successfully combines neural networks with classical numerical methods, offering a promising approach for solving high Peclet number problems. The comparable performance of top-down and bottom-up training approaches provides flexibility in practical implementation.

title: EDCT-Bench: Uncovering Faithfulness Gaps in VLMs via Explanation-Driven Counterfactual Testing
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can produce Natural Language Explanations (NLEs) that sound plausible yet remain inconsistent with the visual evidence they cite. We present Explanation-Driven Counterfactual Testing (EDCT), an intervention-based protocol that extracts visual concepts cited in a model's explanation, applies verified minimal edits to them, and tests whether the resulting answer and explanation remain consistent with the edited image. Using this protocol, we create EDCT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark spanning three complementary domains: knowledge-intensive visual question answering (OK-VQA), safety-critical driving (DriveLM), and 3D spatial reasoning (3DSRBench). Across the evaluated VLMs, EDCT reveals substantial faithfulness gaps, with models frequently producing responses inconsistent with verified visual changes. Finally, our fine-tuning study suggests that EDCT-generated counterfactuals provide high-impact training signals.

AI.tldr: EDCT is an intervention-based protocol that tests whether Vision-Language Models produce explanations consistent with visual evidence by creating counterfactual images through minimal edits to cited visual concepts and evaluating if model responses remain faithful to the edited images.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language Models can produce plausible-sounding Natural Language Explanations (NLEs) that are actually inconsistent with the visual evidence they cite, raising concerns about the faithfulness of model explanations.
AI.method: EDCT protocol extracts visual concepts cited in model explanations, applies verified minimal edits to those concepts in the image, and tests whether the resulting answer and explanation remain consistent with the edited image. Using this method, they create EDCT-Bench spanning three domains: OK-VQA (knowledge-intensive VQA), DriveLM (safety-critical driving), and 3DSRBench (3D spatial reasoning).
AI.result: EDCT reveals substantial faithfulness gaps across evaluated VLMs - models frequently produce responses inconsistent with verified visual changes. Fine-tuning study shows EDCT-generated counterfactuals provide high-impact training signals.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that intervention-based testing is essential for evaluating VLM explanation faithfulness, and EDCT-generated counterfactuals can serve as effective training data to improve model consistency between explanations and visual evidence.

title: Collaborative Memory for Multi-Agent VLM Systems
summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents combine specialized perception, tools, and reasoning to address complex visual tasks. In multi-agent settings, different agents inspect different image regions, video frames, or visual representations, so collaboration extends beyond distributed reasoning to distributed perception. This makes shared visual context a central problem in VLM agent collaboration. In this paper, we frame memory hierarchy, cross-agent sharing, and consistency mechanisms around the need to reconcile interpretations and update dependent reasoning. Effective collaboration requires agents to build on contributions from other agents, recover missing visual context, and reconcile differing interpretations as new evidence emerges. Shared visual memory preserves not only images or textual summaries but also the dependencies among observations, agent interpretations, and subsequent reasoning. Together, these design considerations shape how information flows and evolves across VLM agents. The proposed framework provides a foundation for building reliable and resource-efficient agent teams.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses collaboration challenges in multi-agent Vision-language model (VLM) systems where different agents inspect different visual regions. The authors propose a framework centered on shared visual memory that preserves not just images or summaries but also dependencies among observations, agent interpretations, and reasoning chains.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent VLM settings, collaboration extends beyond distributed reasoning to distributed perception, making shared visual context a central problem. Effective collaboration requires agents to build on contributions from others, recover missing visual context, and reconcile differing interpretations as new evidence emerges.
AI.method: The paper frames memory hierarchy, cross-agent sharing, and consistency mechanisms around the need to reconcile interpretations and update dependent reasoning. The proposed framework addresses how information flows and evolves across VLM agents.
AI.result: The framework provides a foundation for building reliable and resource-efficient agent teams in multi-agent VLM settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework addresses the core challenges of distributed perception in VLM agent collaboration by maintaining dependencies among observations, interpretations, and reasoning, enabling effective reconciliation of different agent perspectives.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for Open-World Intent Discovery Under an evolving Label Space
summary: Real-world intelligent systems increasingly operate under open-world conditions, where user intents are not fixed or exhaustively known a priori and may evolve as new interaction patterns emerge. This paper proposes a unified uncertainty-aware probabilistic framework for continual new intent discovery under an evolving label space. Each utterance is encoded through an adaptive $β$-VAE into a latent mean, used for classification and density modelling and a posterior uncertainty estimate acting as a global reliability signal. Classifier confidence, posterior uncertainty and DP-GMM likelihood are combined through a multi-signal decision mechanism to distinguish known intents from potentially novel samples. Candidate novel instances are clustered through a density-based discovery module and only reliable clusters are promoted to new labels, enabling controlled label-space expansion. Replay and Elastic Weight Consolidation mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve previously acquired knowledge. The paper formalises continual intent discovery as a structured multi-phase open-world problem, introduces adaptive label-space expansion under stability--plasticity constraints and uses posterior uncertainty to regulate trusted-sample selection, pseudo-labelling, novelty admission and replay. Experiments show high novelty precision, stable adaptation across sequential phases and limited forgetting. Near-zero NMI and ARI indicate limited reconstruction of the complete fine-grained intent taxonomy, consistent with the framework's conservative promotion strategy. Qualitative analyses nevertheless reveal dense and locally coherent semantic clusters, showing that reliable novel structures can be discovered without exhaustive recovery of the underlying taxonomy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified uncertainty-aware probabilistic framework for continual new intent discovery under evolving label spaces in open-world conversational AI systems. The framework uses adaptive β-VAE for encoding, combines classifier confidence, posterior uncertainty, and DP-GMM likelihood through a multi-signal decision mechanism, and employs replay and EWC to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Real-world intelligent systems operate under open-world conditions where user intents are not fixed and may evolve over time. The key challenge is to continuously discover new intents while preserving knowledge of previously learned ones, without exhaustive a priori knowledge of all possible intents.
AI.method: The paper proposes: (1) Adaptive β-VAE encoding producing latent mean for classification/density modeling and posterior uncertainty as reliability signal; (2) Multi-signal decision mechanism combining classifier confidence, posterior uncertainty, and DP-GMM likelihood to distinguish known from novel intents; (3) Density-based clustering module for candidate novel instances with controlled cluster promotion; (4) Replay and Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) for catastrophic forgetting mitigation; (5) Formalization of continual intent discovery as structured multi-phase open-world problem.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate high novelty precision, stable adaptation across sequential phases, and limited forgetting. Near-zero NMI and ARI indicate incomplete recovery of fine-grained intent taxonomy, consistent with the conservative promotion strategy. Qualitative analysis shows dense, locally coherent semantic clusters, indicating reliable novel structure discovery without exhaustive taxonomy recovery.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully enables controlled label-space expansion under stability-plasticity constraints using posterior uncertainty to regulate trusted-sample selection, pseudo-labeling, novelty admission, and replay. The conservative promotion strategy prioritizes reliability over completeness, discovering meaningful novel clusters while limiting false novel detections.

title: Newer Is Not Fairer: Gender Stereotyping in Text-to-Image AI Across Model Generations
summary: Text-to-image generative models are widely used in professional and creative settings, yet how they represent gender across occupations -- and whether newer models are fairer -- remains poorly understood across multiple generations. We evaluate gender representation across 20 occupations, 5 prompt templates, and 4 Stable Diffusion model generations (SD 1.5, SD 2.1, SDXL, SD 3 Medium), generating 8,000 images with n = 100 per occupation-model cell (5 prompts x 20 images), and classifying all with DeepFace. Across the 8,000 open-source images, 76.4% show male subjects (95% CI [75.1%, 78.7%], p < 2.2 x 10^-16, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted). More strikingly, 57.6% of images for historically female-coded occupations show male subjects (raw p = 3.43 x 10^-22, BH-adjusted p = 1.71 x 10^-21). All nine significant tests reported in this paper survive BH correction across 10 tests. When compared against U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics workforce data, models underrepresent women by 20-46pp on average, with particularly large deviations for near gender-balanced occupations: scientist (48% female in BLS, 82-99% male in model outputs) and cleaner (46% female in BLS, 80-92% male in outputs). Model generations do not improve steadily: bias worsens from SD 1.5 to SDXL before partially recovering in SD 3 Medium. A preliminary comparison with GPT-image-1 on five occupations suggests lower bias than open-source models, though the practical effect is small (Cramer's V = 0.080) and the comparison is exploratory. No model achieves gender parity.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates gender bias in text-to-image generative models (Stable Diffusion generations) across 20 occupations, finding significant male overrepresentation (76.4% of images show male subjects) and substantial underrepresentation of women (20-46pp below BLS workforce data). Bias does not improve steadily across model generations.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image generative models are widely used but their representation of gender across occupations is poorly understood, especially across multiple model generations. The researchers wanted to quantify this bias and determine if newer models are fairer.
AI.method: The researchers generated 8,000 images using 4 Stable Diffusion model generations (SD 1.5, SD 2.1, SDXL, SD 3 Medium), 20 occupations, and 5 prompt templates (n=100 per occupation-model cell). They classified all images using DeepFace and compared results against U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics workforce data. All 9 significant tests survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
AI.result: 76.4% of images show male subjects (95% CI [75.1%, 78.7%], p < 2.2 x 10^-16). 57.6% of images for historically female-coded occupations show male subjects. Models underrepresent women by 20-46pp on average. Large deviations found for scientist (48% female in BLS vs 82-99% male in models) and cleaner (46% female in BLS vs 80-92% male). Bias worsens from SD 1.5 to SDXL before partially recovering in SD 3 Medium. GPT-image-1 showed lower bias but small effect (Cramer's V = 0.080). No model achieves gender parity.
AI.conclusion: All tested text-to-image models exhibit significant gender bias, with systematic underrepresentation of women across occupations. Newer model generations do not consistently improve fairness; bias actually worsens from SD 1.5 to SDXL before partial recovery in SD 3 Medium. No model achieves gender parity, indicating a persistent problem in generative AI.

title: Measuring AI Leadership: Development and Validation of a Multidimensional Measure for AI-Native Organizations
summary: AI is changing what leaders must judge, explain, learn, and coordinate, yet existing measures do not capture these behaviors at the level needed to study leadership in AI-enabled work. We develop the AI Leadership Battery, which organizes 36 behaviorally specific subdimensions into 11 theory-specified content families. Following established scale-development procedures, the research used deductive item generation; content validation of definitional correspondence and definitional distinctiveness; exploratory factor analysis and item reduction; confirmatory factor analysis in independent samples; and tests of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and criterion-related and incremental validity. Across the development and validation studies, the analyses provided evidence for the Battery's content, multidimensional structure, reliability, and distinction from selected orbiting constructs. The Battery also contributed additional information beyond orbiting constructs across organizational growth, decision speed, customer/stakeholder response capability, AI-enabled team performance, AI-enabled work experience, AI security and risk management, and AI adoption and integration. The resulting measure provides researchers with a behavioral framework for examining how leaders in AI-enabled work regulate judgment, learning, adaptation, transparency, and accountability.

AI.tldr: The paper develops the AI Leadership Battery, a comprehensive measurement tool with 36 subdimensions organized into 11 content families, designed to assess leadership behaviors specific to AI-enabled work environments.
AI.motivation: AI is transforming leadership requirements (judgment, explanation, learning, coordination), but existing measures fail to capture these emerging behaviors at the necessary level of specificity to study leadership in AI-enabled contexts.
AI.method: The research followed established scale-development procedures: deductive item generation; content validation (definitional correspondence and distinctiveness); exploratory factor analysis with item reduction; confirmatory factor analysis in independent samples; and tests of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and criterion-related/incremental validity.
AI.result: The Battery demonstrated evidence for content validity, multidimensional structure, reliability, and distinction from orbiting constructs. It provided additional predictive information beyond existing constructs across organizational growth, decision speed, customer/stakeholder response capability, AI-enabled team performance, AI-enabled work experience, AI security/risk management, and AI adoption/integration.
AI.conclusion: The AI Leadership Battery provides researchers with a behavioral framework for examining how leaders in AI-enabled work regulate judgment, learning, adaptation, transparency, and accountability—offering a validated tool for future leadership research in AI contexts.

title: Dataset-Dependent Effects of Cross-Depth Aggregation and Soft-Routed Experts in EEG Foundation Model Fine-Tuning
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
summary: EEG decoding tasks can rely on different temporal dynamics and cross-channel relationships. We test whether specialized modules improve a fully fine-tuned EEG foundation model by augmenting CBraMod with cross-depth Attention Residuals (AttnRes) and two soft-routed expert banks. Across matched three-seed experiments on FACED, ISRUC, SEED-V, and PhysioNet-MI, the complete model changes mean balanced accuracy relative to full fine-tuning by -0.12, +1.27, +0.77, and -1.27 points, respectively. AttnRes alone improves mean balanced accuracy on three datasets, whereas adding experts on top of AttnRes helps only FACED and SEED-V. These gains come with substantial overhead: AttnRes requires 2.11 to 2.88x runtime and 1.78 to 2.67x memory, while the complete model requires 2.41 to 3.04x runtime and 1.86 to 2.85x memory. Overall, the added modules produce dataset-dependent, sometimes opposing effects rather than consistent gains over full fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether specialized modules (cross-depth Attention Residuals and soft-routed expert banks) can improve a fully fine-tuned EEG foundation model (CBraMod) for EEG decoding tasks. The study conducts experiments across four datasets (FACED, ISRUC, SEED-V, PhysioNet-MI) and finds dataset-dependent, sometimes opposing effects rather than consistent improvements over full fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether specialized modules can improve EEG decoding performance by leveraging temporal dynamics and cross-channel relationships beyond what full fine-tuning of a foundation model provides.
AI.method: The study augments CBraMod with cross-depth Attention Residuals (AttnRes) and two soft-routed expert banks. Experiments were conducted across four datasets (FACED, ISRUC, SEED-V, PhysioNet-MI) using matched three-seed experiments. Performance was measured using mean balanced accuracy, and computational overhead was assessed in terms of runtime and memory usage.
AI.result: The complete model showed mixed results: -0.12 (FACED), +1.27 (ISRUC), +0.77 (SEED-V), -1.27 (PhysioNet-MI) points change in mean balanced accuracy. AttnRes alone improved performance on three datasets, while adding experts on top of AttnRes helped only FACED and SEED-V. However, these gains came with substantial computational overhead: AttnRes required 2.11-2.88x runtime and 1.78-2.67x memory, while the complete model required 2.41-3.04x runtime and 1.86-2.85x memory.
AI.conclusion: The added modules (AttnRes and expert banks) produce dataset-dependent, sometimes opposing effects rather than consistent gains over full fine-tuning. The computational overhead is substantial, and the benefits are not universal across datasets.

title: IRIS: Implicit Rendering Matters for Pose-Free Novel View Synthesis
summary: Novel view synthesis from unposed multi-view images remains challenging, as the model must jointly learn scene representations and camera parameters without pose supervision. Existing approaches largely fall into two extremes: implicit latent-space rendering is flexible and easy to optimize, but often yields weakly grounded camera estimation; explicit 3D representations provide stronger geometric grounding, but introduce heavier parameterization and more fragile optimization. In this paper, we present IRIS, a fully self-supervised framework that provides a practical middle ground between these two paradigms. Instead of decoding free latent tokens or reconstructing fully explicit 3D primitives, IRIS represents the scene as a latent neural field and renders novel views by querying this field under self-predicted cameras. Specifically, projected features from reference views are aggregated at sampled 3D points to form point-wise latent features, which are then composed along target rays for rendering. This design preserves the flexibility and optimization stability of implicit modeling, while introducing stronger geometric structure than unconstrained latent rendering. Extensive experiments show that IRIS achieves strong novel view synthesis quality with competitive pose accuracy under fully self-supervised learning. Our project page: https://leo-frank.github.io/IRIS

AI.tldr: IRIS is a fully self-supervised framework for novel view synthesis from unposed multi-view images. It represents scenes as a latent neural field and renders novel views by querying this field under self-predicted cameras, combining the flexibility of implicit modeling with stronger geometric structure.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for novel view synthesis from unposed images fall into two extremes: implicit latent-space rendering (flexible but weak camera estimation) or explicit 3D representations (stronger geometry but fragile optimization). There is a need for a practical middle ground that combines the benefits of both paradigms.
AI.method: IRIS represents scenes as a latent neural field. It renders novel views by: (1) aggregating projected features from reference views at sampled 3D points to form point-wise latent features, then (2) composing these features along target rays for rendering. The framework uses self-predicted cameras without pose supervision.
AI.result: IRIS achieves strong novel view synthesis quality with competitive pose accuracy under fully self-supervised learning.
AI.conclusion: IRIS provides a practical middle ground between implicit latent-space rendering and explicit 3D representations, preserving the flexibility and optimization stability of implicit modeling while introducing stronger geometric structure than unconstrained latent rendering.

title: Memory Has Geometry: Non-Uniform Geometric Memory for Long-Horizon Personalized AI
comment: Accepted to the IEEE ICDM 2026 (BlueSky). 6 pages, 2 figures, and 2 tables
summary: Long-term memory is becoming a core substrate for personalized AI, yet most systems still represent personalization as discrete records in a largely static latent space, accessed under one global similarity notion. For data mining, this creates a mismatch: the evidence is a temporal event stream, while the dominant abstraction is a searchable record set. We argue that long-horizon personalization should instead model memory as a user-specific dynamical state space with locally heterogeneous geometry. Geometry here is a computational language, not a literal claim about cognition: it captures stable versus volatile regions, variable-rate drift, heterogeneous neighborhoods, and uncertainty about current user state. Profiles and isolated events remain useful as points, but interaction, feedback, and elapsed time induce trajectories. Memory access then becomes trajectory-conditioned reconstruction of the relevant user state, not only nearest-neighbor lookup.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that long-term memory in personalized AI should be modeled as a user-specific dynamical state space with heterogeneous geometry rather than static discrete records. This would better capture temporal dynamics, user state uncertainty, and variable-rate drift in personalization.
AI.motivation: The current paradigm represents personalization as discrete records in a static latent space with global similarity, creating a mismatch with temporal event stream data. This limits the ability to model user dynamics over long horizons.
AI.method: Proposes modeling memory as a user-specific dynamical state space where geometry serves as a computational language capturing: stable vs volatile regions, variable-rate drift, heterogeneous neighborhoods, and state uncertainty. Memory access becomes trajectory-conditioned reconstruction rather than nearest-neighbor lookup.
AI.result: The paper establishes a new conceptual framework where profiles/events are points, but interactions/feedback/time induce trajectories, enabling more nuanced modeling of user evolution.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon personalization should shift from searchable record sets to trajectory-conditioned state reconstruction, better matching the temporal nature of user interaction data.

title: Long-Context Demonstration Selection Using State Space Models
summary: We study the problem of demonstration selection, which involves selecting a subset of examples for prepending to a query to a language model. This problem is closely related to in-context learning and language model inference. Since the inference cost of a transformer model scales quadratically with sequence length, the selection problem becomes especially challenging in a long-context scenario. In this paper, we tackle this problem by building on state space models (SSMs), which require only linear inference time given the input. Our approach involves two algorithms. The first learns a small set of SSMs through distillation of a (trained) transformer model. We partition all the layers into consecutive groups. Then for each group, we estimate a separate state space model to replicate the input-output behavior within the adjacent layers. Second, we map the distilled model outputs to a small set of tokens, and apply these embeddings for demonstration selection in downstream applications. We perform extensive experiments in both synthetic and real-world datasets to validate our approach. We demonstrate that the distilled SSMs only incur an approximation error of less than $0.7\%$ relative to the true output. In downstream evaluation, we show that on several text classification and reasoning tasks, our approach reduces FLOPs by $14.2\times$ and improves accuracy by $6.48\%$ relative to baseline demonstration selection methods.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles demonstration selection for in-context learning in long-context scenarios by distilling a transformer model into state space models (SSMs). The approach involves learning SSMs to replicate transformer layer behavior and using the distilled outputs as token embeddings for demonstration selection, achieving less than 0.7% approximation error, 14.2× FLOPs reduction, and 6.48% accuracy improvement.
AI.motivation: Demonstration selection for in-context learning is important but challenging in long-context scenarios due to the quadratic scaling of transformer inference cost with sequence length. There needs to be a more efficient approach for selecting demonstrations.
AI.method: Two-algorithm approach: (1) Distill a trained transformer into SSMs by partitioning layers into consecutive groups and estimating separate SSMs for each group to replicate input-output behavior; (2) Map distilled model outputs to a small set of tokens and use these embeddings for demonstration selection in downstream tasks.
AI.result: The distilled SSMs incur less than 0.7% approximation error relative to the true transformer outputs. In downstream evaluation on text classification and reasoning tasks, the approach achieves 14.2× FLOPs reduction and 6.48% accuracy improvement compared to baseline demonstration selection methods.
AI.conclusion: SSM-based distillation provides an effective solution for demonstration selection in long-context scenarios, offering both computational efficiency and improved accuracy over baseline methods.

title: SetPlanner: A Lightweight Plug-in Point-Set Planner for Frozen SAM
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
summary: Segment Anything Models provide reusable priors, yet they require user prompts and cannot support fully automatic instrument segmentation. Automatic prompting is difficult for thin, articulated, reflective, and partly occluded tools, where several configurations can be valid. We formulate automatic prompting as lightweight point-set planning and isolate the point source under a frozen pathway. To this end, we present SetPlanner, a 1.52M-parameter plug-in point-set planner for frozen SAM. The plug-in preserves SAM's point-prompt interface and enables reuse across backbones. SetPlanner plans complete unordered K-point sets from geometry-aware targets with a permutation-aware conditional flow. SAM decodes eight candidates; their consensus readout yields a ground-truth-free prediction. Across three endoscopic datasets, SetPlanner wins all six transfer routes over a LoRA-adapted system. Under our frozen-pathway protocol, SetPlanner reaches 0.934 Dice on Kvasir-Instrument and recovers 96% of a 44.4-point localization gap, while candidate disagreement ranks low-Dice cases at AUROC 0.969.

AI.tldr: SetPlanner is a lightweight 1.52M-parameter plug-in that enables fully automatic instrument segmentation with frozen SAM by planning complete K-point sets from geometry-aware targets using permutation-aware conditional flow, achieving 0.934 Dice on Kvasir-Instrument and winning all six transfer routes across three endoscopic datasets.
AI.motivation: Segment Anything Models (SAM) provide reusable priors but require user prompts and cannot support fully automatic instrument segmentation. Automatic prompting is particularly challenging for thin, articulated, reflective, and partly occluded tools where multiple valid configurations exist.
AI.method: The authors formulate automatic prompting as lightweight point-set planning and isolate the point source under a frozen pathway. SetPlanner preserves SAM's point-prompt interface and enables reuse across backbones by planning complete unordered K-point sets from geometry-aware targets using a permutation-aware conditional flow. SAM decodes eight candidates, and their consensus readout yields ground-truth-free prediction.
AI.result: SetPlanner wins all six transfer routes over a LoRA-adapted system across three endoscopic datasets. Under the frozen-pathway protocol, SetPlanner reaches 0.934 Dice on Kvasir-Instrument and recovers 96% of a 44.4-point localization gap, while candidate disagreement ranks low-Dice cases at AUROC 0.969.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SetPlanner successfully enables fully automatic instrument segmentation with frozen SAM, achieving state-of-the-art performance while preserving SAM's modularity and reusability across different backbones. The method demonstrates that lightweight point-set planning can effectively address the automatic prompting challenge for complex medical instruments.

title: When to Call an LLM: A Confidence-Gated Hybrid for Cost-Effective Emotion Recognition in Conversational AI
summary: Emotion recognition in conversation (ERC) is a production capability behind agent-assist prompts, escalation routing, and post-call analytics in contact-center-as-a-service (CCaaS) platforms, where cost and latency constraints matter as much as accuracy. We report a systems-level comparison of three deployment options for dialogue-contextual ERC: a low-cost stacked ensemble (sentence embeddings, windowed context, RandomForest/XGBoost/logistic-regression stacking), off-the-shelf LLM prompting (GPT-4o-mini; zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought), and a confidence-gated hybrid that escalates only the ensemble's least-confident predictions to the LLM - modeled on IVA-to-human-agent escalation policies used in production contact centers. On IEMOCAP, the ensemble significantly outperforms every LLM configuration (0.595 vs. 0.460-0.536 weighted F1, p < 0.0001) at a fraction of the cost and sub-10ms latency; on MELD and CMU-MOSI the ranking reverses, showing neither pure system is a safe default. The confidence-gated hybrid resolves this by Pareto-dominating both pure systems on all three datasets (0.620, 0.643, 0.824 weighted F1) while routing the majority of traffic through the near-zero-cost ensemble, translating to roughly $10-85 per million utterances versus $99-170 for an LLM-only pipeline. The escalation policy is not an opaque cost/accuracy dial: escalated turns disproportionately follow an emotion or sentiment shift, giving operators an interpretable, auditable routing signal, and the ensemble's confidence is well-calibrated and safely under- rather than over-confident. The pattern holds across three datasets and two LLM providers. Confidence-gated cascading is established in general ML systems; our contribution is showing it transfers cleanly to dialogue-contextual ERC, yielding a concrete deployment recipe for CCaaS and conversational-AI platforms deciding how to allocate LLM spend.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three deployment options for emotion recognition in conversation (ERC) in contact center settings: a low-cost stacked ensemble, off-the-shelf LLM prompting (GPT-4o-mini), and a confidence-gated hybrid that routes uncertain predictions to the LLM. The hybrid Pareto-dominates both pure systems across three datasets while significantly reducing costs ($10-85 vs $99-170 per million utterances).
AI.motivation: Address the practical challenge of deploying ERC in CCaaS platforms where cost and latency matter as much as accuracy. Existing methods either sacrifice accuracy for cost/latency or are too expensive/slow for production use.
AI.method: Systems-level comparison of three approaches: (1) Stacked ensemble using sentence embeddings, windowed context, and RandomForest/XGBoost/logistic-regression; (2) LLM prompting (GPT-4o-mini) with zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought configurations; (3) Confidence-gated hybrid that escalates only ensemble's least-confident predictions to LLM. Evaluated on IEMOCAP, MELD, and CMU-MOSI datasets.
AI.result: On IEMOCAP, ensemble significantly outperforms all LLM configurations (0.595 vs 0.460-0.536 weighted F1, p<0.0001). On MELD and CMU-MOSI, LLM outperforms ensemble. The confidence-gated hybrid Pareto-dominates both pure systems on all three datasets (0.620, 0.643, 0.824 weighted F1) with sub-10ms latency and $10-85 per million utterances vs $99-170 for LLM-only.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-gated cascading transfers cleanly to dialogue-contextual ERC, providing a concrete deployment recipe for CCaaS and conversational-AI platforms. The escalation policy is interpretable and auditable, with ensemble confidence being well-calibrated and safely under-confident. Emotion/sentiment shifts disproportionately trigger escalation.

title: TabPFN-3.5: Technical Report
summary: We introduce TabPFN-3.5, our new flagship Tabular Foundation Model. It significantly outperforms its predecessor, TabPFN-3, and all existing baselines across a broad range of tabular problems. TabPFN-3.5 sets a new state of the art on standard tabular prediction in TabArena, and extends it to the data practitioners encounter in practice: non-i.i.d. data with temporal or grouped splits, tables with strings, text and images, high-cardinality categorical features, and wide tables with many features. These gains carry over to our task-specific harnesses: state of the art on relational data and stronger time-series forecasting. For faster inference, our variant TabPFN-3.5-Fast runs up to 3x faster than TabPFN-3 while keeping most of the accuracy gains. In addition, we upgrade TabPFN-3.5-Plus, expanding our multimodal capabilities with advanced text and date handling alongside proprietary inference optimizations. Finally, we release a new version of our Thinking mode, TabPFN-3.5-Thinking, which scales inference-time computation to push the state of the art further. It benefits from our stronger base model and from inference-time improvements that make it up to 12x faster than TabPFN-3-Thinking.

AI.tldr: TabPFN-3.5 is a new tabular foundation model that significantly outperforms its predecessor TabPFN-3 and all existing baselines across various tabular prediction tasks. It sets new state-of-the-art performance on standard tabular prediction in TabArena and extends capabilities to practical data scenarios including non-i.i.d. data with temporal/grouped splits, tables with strings/text/images, high-cardinality categorical features, and wide tables. The paper also introduces faster variants (TabPFN-3.5-Fast, up to 3x faster) and an upgraded version (TabPFN-3.5-Plus with advanced text/date handling). Additionally, TabPFN-3.5-Thinking is released, scaling inference-time computation for better performance while being up to 12x faster than TabPFN-3-Thinking.
AI.motivation: To address limitations of previous tabular models and meet the needs of data practitioners dealing with real-world complex data scenarios including non-i.i.d. data, multimodal tables, high-cardinality features, and wide tables.
AI.method: Development of a new flagship Tabular Foundation Model (TabPFN-3.5) with variants optimized for speed (TabPFN-3.5-Fast) and enhanced capabilities (TabPFN-3.5-Plus with advanced text/date handling). Also introduced TabPFN-3.5-Thinking which scales inference-time computation.
AI.result: TabPFN-3.5 achieves state-of-the-art performance on TabArena for standard tabular prediction, extends capabilities to practical data scenarios (non-i.i.d. data, multimodal tables, high-cardinality features, wide tables), achieves state-of-the-art on relational data and stronger time-series forecasting. TabPFN-3.5-Fast runs up to 3x faster while retaining most accuracy gains. TabPFN-3.5-Thinking is up to 12x faster than TabPFN-3-Thinking while pushing state-of-the-art further.
AI.conclusion: TabPFN-3.5 represents a significant advancement in tabular foundation models, setting new benchmarks across standard and practical tabular prediction tasks while offering variants optimized for speed and enhanced capabilities.

title: CoAtNet-DeepMoE: A Convolution-Attention Hybrid with DeepSeek Mixture-of-Experts for Parameter-Efficient Tomato Disease Classification
summary: The world population is growing rapidly, and technology is improving in parallel. Meeting the huge demand for food for these 7 billion people not only depends on increasing food production but also on reducing food loss. Crop losses due to disease affect both the food supply and the financial and economic stability of a country. Tomatoes are among the top food-producing crops globally, and a significant portion of this production is lost due to disease. People have used Machine Learning techniques for feature extraction and early diagnosis of tomato diseases, and nowadays, Deep Learning-based models are widely used for disease recognition. However, most existing models are highly parameter-intensive, which increases the time required for training and inference. As a result, while lightweight models are more suitable for user-friendly applications, they often show a reduction in performance. To balance performance and model size, we propose CoAtNet-DeepMoE, a Convolution-Attention hybrid architecture for rich feature extraction, further enhanced with a DeepSeek Mixture of Experts to substantially reduce the number of parameters without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate our model on both balanced and imbalanced datasets from Kaggle and PlantVillage, demonstrating robustness and achieving 99.80% accuracy, 99.80% precision, 99.80% recall, and 99.80% F1-score on Kaggle, and 99.83% accuracy, 99.85% precision, 99.76% recall, and 99.80% F1-score on PlantVillage, representing state-of-the-art performance with only 2.47M parameters. The source code will be available at https://github.com/nadimbrur/CoAt-MoE.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CoAtNet-DeepMoE, a lightweight deep learning model combining Convolution-Attention hybrid architecture with DeepSeek Mixture of Experts for tomato disease detection. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance (99.80%+ accuracy) while using only 2.47M parameters, addressing the trade-off between model size and accuracy.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the challenge of balancing model performance and size in tomato disease detection. Existing deep learning models are parameter-intensive, increasing training/inference time, while lightweight models often suffer from reduced accuracy. The authors aim to reduce parameters without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: The proposed method combines: 1) CoAtNet architecture (Convolution-Attention hybrid) for rich feature extraction, 2) DeepSeek Mixture of Experts (MoE) to substantially reduce parameters. The model was evaluated on both balanced and imbalanced datasets from Kaggle and PlantVillage.
AI.result: The model achieved: On Kaggle - 99.80% accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score; On PlantVillage - 99.83% accuracy, 99.85% precision, 99.76% recall, and 99.80% F1-score. These represent state-of-the-art results with only 2.47M parameters.
AI.conclusion: CoAtNet-DeepMoE successfully balances performance and model size, achieving SOTA accuracy while being lightweight enough for user-friendly applications. The model demonstrates robustness on both balanced and imbalanced datasets.

title: Contiguity, Not Importance: Budgeted Repair of Stale KV Caches After Document Edits
summary: KV-cache reuse can reduce inference cost in retrieval-augmented generation and agentic systems, but cached contexts may become stale when retrieved knowledge, working memory, or user state is edited. Under causal self-attention, even a local edit can affect downstream KV states. A full re-prefill reliably restores consistency but is costly, whereas refreshing only the edited span can leave downstream dependencies stale. We formulate in-place repair as budgeted recomputation and compare training-free position-selection policies on a factual RAG benchmark with matched direct and derived edits. Across three model families, all policies repair direct cases, but derived cases clearly separate them. At the primary budget, a contiguous edit-local window recovers at least 0.94 of the post-edit answer margin and substantially outperforms attention-based, KV-deviation, and structural selectors. Mechanistic analysis shows that position sets effective under clean-state transplantation can fail under actual recomputation because scattered positions inherit surrounding staleness. The edit-local advantage also depends on adjacency and largely disappears when the answer-bearing text moves downstream. Because answer-relevant edits almost always corrupt model behavior, failure severity is difficult to predict, and repair is 13-21 times faster than full re-prefill, our results support unconditional edit-local repair when the dependent text remains adjacent to the edit.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses KV-cache staleness in retrieval-augmented generation and agentic systems when cached contexts are edited. The authors formulate in-place repair as budgeted recomputation and compare training-free position-selection policies. A contiguous edit-local window policy outperforms attention-based, KV-deviation, and structural selectors, achieving ≥0.94 of the post-edit answer margin while being 13-21× faster than full re-prefill.
AI.motivation: KV-cache reuse can reduce inference cost in RAG and agentic systems, but cached contexts become stale when retrieved knowledge, working memory, or user state is edited. Under causal self-attention, even local edits affect downstream KV states. Full re-prefill is costly, while refreshing only edited span leaves downstream dependencies stale.
AI.method: The authors formulate in-place repair as budgeted recomputation and compare training-free position-selection policies on a factual RAG benchmark with matched direct and derived edits. They test across three model families and analyze mechanistic behavior.
AI.result: All policies repair direct cases, but derived cases clearly separate them. At the primary budget, a contiguous edit-local window recovers at least 0.94 of the post-edit answer margin and substantially outperforms attention-based, KV-deviation, and structural selectors. Position sets effective under clean-state transplantation can fail under actual recomputation because scattered positions inherit surrounding staleness. The edit-local advantage depends on adjacency and largely disappears when answer-bearing text moves downstream. Repair is 13-21 times faster than full re-prefill.
AI.conclusion: The results support unconditional edit-local repair when dependent text remains adjacent to the edit, as answer-relevant edits almost always corrupt model behavior and failure severity is difficult to predict.

title: Walking the Score Manifold: Continuous-time Generative Dynamics on Learned Data Manifolds
summary: Generative modeling of time-dependent data is typically formulated on a discrete temporal grid, restricting supervision to the observed timestamps in the training data. We instead frame generation as continuous-time evolution on a learned data manifold. To this end, we leverage pretrained score-based models as geometric priors and learn a vector field that evolves data along score-induced interpolation paths. Because these dynamics follow transitions that respect the geometry learned by the score model, they support generation at arbitrary timestamps and temporal super-resolution beyond the discretization of the training data. Moreover, this geometric formulation allows us to train the vector field simulation-free through a regression objective. To improve long-horizon rollout robustness, we introduce an objective that promotes path-relative transverse exponential stability. While motivated by stability theory, it admits a practical interpretation as denoising score matching transverse to the interpolation path. Further, we extend the framework to a probabilistic setting that models a distribution over plausible future trajectories. We demonstrate the method on natural video and scientific dynamical data, including temporal super-resolution, PDE-based spatiotemporal fields, and molecular dynamics. Our results show that score-based priors provide a strong foundation for learning stochastic continuous-time generative dynamics.
