AI.tldr: The paper introduces a continuous-time generative modeling framework that leverages pretrained score-based models as geometric priors. Instead of working on discrete temporal grids, the method learns a vector field that evolves data along score-induced interpolation paths, enabling generation at arbitrary timestamps and temporal super-resolution beyond the training data discretization.
AI.motivation: Traditional generative modeling of time-dependent data is restricted to discrete temporal grids, limiting supervision to observed timestamps. This constraint prevents generation at arbitrary time points and temporal super-resolution beyond the training data's discretization.
AI.method: The method uses pretrained score-based models as geometric priors and learns a vector field that evolves data along score-induced interpolation paths. Training is simulation-free through a regression objective. To improve long-horizon robustness, the authors introduce an objective promoting path-relative transverse exponential stability, which can be interpreted as denoising score matching transverse to the interpolation path. The framework is extended to a probabilistic setting modeling distributions over plausible future trajectories.
AI.result: The method demonstrates capabilities on natural video and scientific dynamical data, including temporal super-resolution, PDE-based spatiotemporal fields, and molecular dynamics. Score-based priors provide a strong foundation for learning stochastic continuous-time generative dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging pretrained score-based models as geometric priors enables learning stochastic continuous-time generative dynamics that support generation at arbitrary timestamps and temporal super-resolution beyond the training data discretization. The stability objective improves long-horizon rollout robustness, and the probabilistic extension allows modeling distributions over plausible future trajectories.

title: Position Anchor Tuning: Towards Efficient Adaptation of Pre-Trained Point Cloud Transformers
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has recently emerged as a pivotal research direction for adapting pre-trained point cloud transformers to diverse downstream tasks. Although existing methods achieve excellent fine-tuning performance with high parameter efficiency, they ignore inference efficiency. To tackle this problem, a novel PEFT method termed position anchor tuning (PAT) is proposed in this paper. As multi-head attention (MHA) and feed-forward network (FFN) are computation-heavy blocks in pre-trained transformers, PAT decreases their computational cost through token aggregation-expansion pairs. Each pair comprises a token aggregation module (TAM) and a token expansion module (TEM). For MHA and FFN blocks, TAMs extract representative tokens from their input tokens based on position anchors in 3D space. These extracted tokens, rather than the original input tokens, are processed by the blocks, thereby reducing the number of tokens involved in computation. Then, TEMs propagate the learned representations back to the original input tokens. Since TAMs are solely responsible for capturing task-specific representations, base-sharing low-rank adaptation (BSLoRA) is further introduced to enable them to learn such representations effectively with only a small number of trainable parameters. Extensive experiments on widely used benchmarks demonstrate that PAT performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods while incurring significantly lower computational overhead and fewer trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Position Anchor Tuning (PAT), a novel parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for pre-trained point cloud transformers that improves inference efficiency through token aggregation-expansion pairs, addressing the limitation that existing PEFT methods ignore computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing PEFT methods achieve high parameter efficiency but ignore inference efficiency, which is critical for practical deployment. The authors aim to reduce computational cost in transformer blocks (MHA and FFN) while maintaining performance.
AI.method: PAT uses token aggregation-expansion pairs consisting of: (1) Token Aggregation Module (TAM) - extracts representative tokens based on position anchors in 3D space; (2) Token Expansion Module (TEM) - propagates learned representations back to original tokens. Additionally, BSLoRA enables task-specific learning with minimal trainable parameters.
AI.result: PAT achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while incurring significantly lower computational overhead and fewer trainable parameters on widely used benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: PAT successfully balances parameter efficiency and inference efficiency, making it suitable for practical deployment of pre-trained point cloud transformers across diverse downstream tasks.

title: TuiML: Machine Learning for AI Agents
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Code and documentation at https://tuiml.ai
summary: Machine-learning libraries such as Weka and scikit-learn were designed for human programmers. Language-model agents now use these same libraries by recalling APIs from memory and writing code, an approach that hides what a library offers, delays errors until runtime, and loses experimental state between turns. We present TuiML, a self-contained machine-learning library built for AI agents, with native algorithms across supervised, unsupervised, time-series, data handling, tuning, and evaluation tasks. Every component describes itself through machine-readable metadata and parameter schemas, so an agent can search the library, inspect components, compose validated workflows, and register new ones that become discoverable in turn. Every call is validated, seeded, and traced, and sessions export as runnable notebooks, making experiments reproducible by construction. One specification layer drives the Model Context Protocol (MCP), agent-framework adapters, a Python API, a CLI, and local model serving, while data and models never leave the machine. Benchmarks show TuiML remains predictively competitive with scikit-learn and Weka. While looking like a conventional library to a human user, TuiML is designed for agents first, allowing them to read, extend, and operate machine learning autonomously. TuiML is open source, with documentation at https://tuiml.ai.

AI.tldr: TuiML is a self-contained machine-learning library designed specifically for AI agents, featuring native algorithms across supervised, unsupervised, time-series, data handling, tuning, and evaluation tasks, with machine-readable metadata for agent discovery and composition.
AI.motivation: Current ML libraries (Weka, scikit-learn) were designed for human programmers, causing issues when used by language-model agents: hiding library capabilities, delaying errors to runtime, and losing experimental state between turns.
AI.method: TuiML provides every component with self-describing machine-readable metadata and parameter schemas, enabling agents to search, inspect, compose validated workflows, and register new discoverable components. Includes call validation, seeding, tracing, and session export as runnable notebooks. One specification layer drives MCP, agent-framework adapters, Python API, CLI, and local model serving.
AI.result: TuiML remains predictively competitive with scikit-learn and Weka while being designed for agents first, allowing them to read, extend, and operate ML autonomously. Data and models never leave the machine.
AI.conclusion: TuiML represents a paradigm shift in ML library design - appearing conventional to human users but fundamentally agent-centric, enabling autonomous ML operation while maintaining competitive performance with established libraries.

title: EdgeReMIND: A Scalable, Top-Ranked Memorization Baseline for Temporal Multi-Relational Link Prediction
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. Accepted at the Fifth Learning on Graphs Conference (LoG 2026), Proceedings Track. Code: https://github.com/BryantPollard/EdgeReMIND
summary: Temporal link prediction on the Temporal Graph Benchmark 2.0 (TGB 2.0) faces a scalability ceiling: on the benchmark's three largest datasets, every existing embedding method runs out of memory or exceeds the time budget. These large-scale graphs are the ones nearest real deployment scale, so failing on them is a real production limitation. EdgeReMIND sets the highest reported test mean reciprocal rank (MRR) on six of eight TGB 2.0 datasets and is the only relation-aware method that runs on all of them. This linear memorization model, with learned per-relation weights over data-calibrated features, is therefore not merely a fallback where embeddings fail but a practical state-of-the-art baseline across the benchmark.

AI.tldr: EdgeReMIND is a linear memorization model for temporal link prediction that achieves state-of-the-art MRR on 6/8 TGB 2.0 datasets while being the only relation-aware method that runs on all datasets, including the three largest ones where embedding methods fail due to memory/time constraints.
AI.motivation: Current embedding methods for temporal link prediction fail to scale to the largest TGB 2.0 datasets (3 out of 8), which are closest to real-world deployment scale. This scalability ceiling limits practical production use.
AI.method: EdgeReMIND uses a linear memorization approach with learned per-relation weights over data-calibrated features. It is relation-aware and leverages feature engineering rather than deep embeddings.
AI.result: EdgeReMIND achieves the highest reported test MRR on six of eight TGB 2.0 datasets and is the only relation-aware method that can run on all datasets, including the three largest ones where embedding methods run out of memory or exceed time budget.
AI.conclusion: EdgeReMIND is not merely a fallback when embeddings fail but a practical state-of-the-art baseline across the entire TGB 2.0 benchmark, demonstrating that linear memorization models can outperform embedding approaches on large-scale temporal graphs.

title: Finder: Agentic Closed-Loop Object Finding for Embodied Grounding
summary: Finding the object referred to by language in a partially observed 3D scene is a core capability for embodied agents. Existing approaches either couple object search with online exploration, which can be costly when relevant observations have already been captured, or query pre-built open-vocabulary maps and scene graphs in a static, one-shot fashion. We present Finder, an agentic closed-loop object-finding primitive for embodied grounding. Instead of treating grounding as passive retrieval from a fixed scene representation, Finder maintains a typed loop state that links query-conditioned planning, scoped evidence gathering, candidate verification, and accept/continue/abort control. When evidence is incomplete or ambiguous, the loop can redirect subsequent perception and comparison rather than simply returning the top retrieved object. On open-vocabulary embodied Object Retrieval in Habitat/HM3D and real-world RGB-D scenes, Finder improves the averaged 1m success rate by 15.75 points over strong baselines. The same primitive also transfers to sequential object grounding and embodied object-centric question answering, improving spatial and temporal localization without changing the inner grounding protocol. Project page: https://finder-vln.github.io.

AI.tldr: Finder is an agentic closed-loop object-finding primitive for embodied grounding that maintains a typed loop state linking query-conditioned planning, evidence gathering, candidate verification, and control flow. It improves 1m success rate by 15.75 points over baselines on embodied object retrieval tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches either couple object search with costly online exploration (even when relevant observations exist) or use static one-shot retrieval from pre-built maps. Neither handles dynamic, adaptive grounding when evidence is incomplete or ambiguous.
AI.method: Finder maintains a typed loop state that enables active grounding: query-conditioned planning determines what evidence to gather, scoped evidence gathering collects observations, candidate verification evaluates options, and accept/continue/abort control decides next actions. This allows redirecting perception and comparison rather than passive retrieval.
AI.result: Improves averaged 1m success rate by 15.75 points over strong baselines on open-vocabulary embodied Object Retrieval in Habitat/HM3D and real-world RGB-D scenes. Also transfers to sequential object grounding and embodied object-centric QA, improving spatial and temporal localization.
AI.conclusion: The closed-loop agentic approach outperforms static retrieval methods. The same primitive transfers to sequential grounding and QA tasks without changing the inner grounding protocol, demonstrating generalizability.

title: RideWay: Benchmarking Efficient Task Completion for Tool-Using Language Agents
summary: AI agents are usually evaluated by whether they complete a task. In interactive service settings, a successful agent can still frustrate users by asking repeated questions, performing redundant searches, or making avoidable revisions. We introduce RideWay, an efficiency-centered benchmark for ridehailing agents in a stateful tool-calling environment, together with Efficiency Utility, a success-gated metric that discounts successful trajectories for excess tool calls and user-facing turns relative to task-specific reference effort. Human paired preferences calibrate the relative penalties, reflecting an aggregate service-workflow trade-off: extra dialogue often creates visible friction, whereas extra tool use can sometimes verify constraints or preserve user intent. Across 58 tasks and 24 models, the fitted penalty for excess turns is about twice that for excess tool calls. On task-disjoint held-out preferences, Efficiency Utility achieves 78.7% accuracy overall: 90.6% when trajectories differ in turns, but chance-level accuracy when they differ solely in tool calls - the axis on which human annotators agree least. RideWay therefore makes interaction efficiency measurable alongside task success, while exposing the boundary of count-based tool-use evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RideWay, a benchmark for evaluating ridehailing AI agents on interaction efficiency rather than just task completion. It proposes "Efficiency Utility," a metric that penalizes successful trajectories for excess tool calls and dialogue turns, with human preferences showing that extra dialogue turns are penalized about twice as much as extra tool calls.
AI.motivation: Current AI agent evaluation focuses solely on task completion success, but ignores interaction efficiency. In real-world service settings, successful agents can still frustrate users through repeated questions, redundant searches, or avoidable revisions. This creates a need for efficiency-centered evaluation that captures user experience beyond binary success/failure.
AI.method: The authors introduced RideWay, a benchmark for ridehailing agents in a stateful tool-calling environment. They developed Efficiency Utility, a success-gated metric that discounts successful trajectories for excess tool calls and user-facing turns relative to task-specific reference effort. Human paired preferences were used to calibrate relative penalties, reflecting an aggregate service-workflow trade-off. They evaluated 58 tasks across 24 models.
AI.result: The fitted penalty for excess dialogue turns is about twice that for excess tool calls. On task-disjoint held-out preferences, Efficiency Utility achieves 78.7% accuracy overall: 90.6% when trajectories differ in turns, but chance-level accuracy when trajectories differ solely in tool calls - the axis on which human annotators agree least.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that interaction efficiency is measurable alongside task success using the RideWay benchmark and Efficiency Utility metric. The findings expose the boundary of count-based tool-use evaluation, showing that human evaluators prioritize reducing dialogue turns over minimizing tool calls, and that tool call efficiency alone is not a reliable proxy for user experience quality.

title: Symmetry without a manifold: intrinsic dimension on orbits
comment: 33 pages, 3 figures. Under review at NeurReps 2026 (NeurIPS workshop, Proceedings Track)
summary: The standard geometric derivation of neural scaling exponents takes the intrinsic dimension of a data manifold as its input. On modular addition in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ that derivation has no input. The exact algebraic solution is an orbit of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ acting by isometries. Transitivity alone makes the ratio statistic underlying the standard dimension estimator a point mass, so the estimator is undefined, and here the two nearest neighbour distances coincide exactly. Breaking the symmetry at scale $ε$ returns a number, but one that tracks $1/ε$ with no scale free plateau. We show that the failure is general, since on any finite orbit of a group acting by isometries the estimator reports the resolution at which the set is probed rather than a dimension. What replaces the power law is exponential in hidden width, $L(h)=L_\infty+A\exp(-c\,h^α)$, with $R^2$ between 0.982 and 0.995 against 0.857 to 0.906 for a power law admitting the same floor and fitted under the same protocol. Where the data supply is sufficient the rate belongs to the regulariser rather than to the group, since weight decay moves $c$ by a factor of 47 while group order moves it by 1.10, a residual below seed to seed resolution, for every fixed $α$ between 0.75 and 2. The critical width falls with group order rather than rising, against capacity counting that assigns a fixed number of neurons to each irreducible representation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why standard geometric derivations of neural scaling exponents fail when applied to algebraic structures like modular addition in Z_p. The authors show that standard dimension estimators become undefined on finite orbits of groups acting by isometries, and propose that exponential scaling (rather than power law) better describes the loss landscape in terms of hidden width.
AI.motivation: The standard geometric derivation of neural scaling exponents relies on the intrinsic dimension of a data manifold as input. However, for modular addition in Z_p, this derivation has no input because the exact algebraic solution forms an orbit of Z_p acting by isometries. The authors seek to understand this failure and characterize what actually happens in such cases.
AI.method: The authors analyze the behavior of standard dimension estimators on finite orbits of groups acting by isometries. They examine the ratio statistic underlying standard dimension estimation and show it becomes a point mass due to transitivity. They then fit exponential models L(h)=L∞+Aexp(-c h^α) versus power law models to loss data, comparing goodness-of-fit via R² values under identical protocols.
AI.result: The standard dimension estimator fails completely on finite group orbits—it reports the resolution at which the set is probed rather than a dimension. The exponential model fits significantly better (R² = 0.982-0.995) than power law (R² = 0.857-0.906). Weight decay affects the rate constant c by a factor of 47, while group order affects it by only 1.10. The critical width falls with group order rather than rising, contradicting capacity counting that assigns fixed neurons per irreducible representation.
AI.conclusion: The failure of standard dimension-based scaling exponents is general for finite orbits of groups acting by isometries. The appropriate scaling law is exponential in hidden width, not power law. The rate is determined by the regularizer (weight decay) rather than the group structure, with the critical width behaving counter to capacity-based predictions.

title: GeoCueFormer: Geometry-Guided Wavelet Representation and Prediction-Cued Dual-Stage Decoder for Underwater Semantic Segmentation
summary: Underwater semantic segmentation is essential for marine ecosystem monitoring, yet remains challenging due to severe visual degradation. Light absorption and scattering often lead to color shifts, low contrast, and blurred boundaries, making shallow detail features unreliable. Existing underwater segmentation methods improve RGB feature aggregation or boundary prediction, but still lack an explicit mechanism to distinguish structure-related details from degradation-induced responses. To address this limitation, we propose GeoCueFormer, a lightweight framework that combines geometry-constrained frequency enhancement with prediction-cued refinement. GeoCueFormer performs stage-specific wavelet enhancement on hierarchical encoder features to complement shallow boundary details while preserving deep structural semantics. A depth-derived spatial gate constrains shallow frequency enhancement toward geometry-consistent regions, and a prediction-cued dual-stage decoder further refines ambiguous high-resolution features. GeoCueFormer obtains 82.23% and 73.04% mIoU on SUIM and DUT, respectively. Under comparable model complexity and standard benchmark settings on SUIM and DUT, it achieves SOTA performance while maintaining a favorable accuracy-complexity trade-off. These results show that distinguishing structural details from degradation-induced interference is more effective for underwater segmentation.

AI.tldr: GeoCueFormer is a lightweight underwater semantic segmentation framework that combines geometry-constrained frequency enhancement with prediction-cued refinement. It uses wavelet enhancement on hierarchical encoder features, a depth-derived spatial gate for geometry-consistent regions, and a dual-stage decoder for feature refinement. It achieves 82.23% mIoU on SUIM and 73.04% on DUT with favorable accuracy-complexity trade-off.
AI.motivation: Underwater semantic segmentation is challenging due to severe visual degradation from light absorption and scattering, causing color shifts, low contrast, and blurred boundaries. Existing methods improve RGB feature aggregation or boundary prediction but lack explicit mechanisms to distinguish structure-related details from degradation-induced responses.
AI.method: GeoCueFormer employs three key components: (1) Stage-specific wavelet enhancement on hierarchical encoder features to complement shallow boundary details while preserving deep structural semantics; (2) A depth-derived spatial gate constrains shallow frequency enhancement toward geometry-consistent regions; (3) A prediction-cued dual-stage decoder further refines ambiguous high-resolution features.
AI.result: GeoCueFormer achieves 82.23% mIoU on SUIM and 73.04% mIoU on DUT datasets. Under comparable model complexity and standard benchmark settings, it achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance while maintaining a favorable accuracy-complexity trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Distinguishing structural details from degradation-induced interference is more effective for underwater segmentation. The proposed approach successfully addresses the limitations of existing methods by explicitly separating structure-related features from degradation responses.

title: Multimodal Conditioning of Fine-Tuned Stable Diffusion XL for Controllable and Culturally Faithful Ulos Motif Generation
comment: C. Anutariya, M.M. Bonsangue, M.N. Mahrin (eds.) "Proceedings of the 4th International Conference on Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (DSAI 2026)", Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, November 12-13, 2026, in volume 3251 of Communications in Computer and Information Science, Springer, November 2026
summary: The traditional Batak Ulos weaving industry faces growing challenges in producing diverse, innovative motifs due to limitations in conventional, manually driven design methods. This study proposes a multimodal generative framework integrating a fine-tuned Latent Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion XL v1.0 via LoRA) with a Multimodal Large Language Model (LLaMA 1.5-7B) to enable controllable, culturally faithful Ulos motif generation. Four complementary conditioning mechanisms: text, image, representation, and semantic map (via ControlNet) jointly guide the generation process, each governing a distinct aspect from semantic intent to spatial layout. A five level ablation study across three scenarios (shape transformation, colour variation, and high-complexity input) shows that conditioning effectiveness is not proportional to the number of mechanisms combined: Text + Image + Semantic Map achieved the best FID (270) and CLIP Score (0.65 - 0.70) but the weakest SSIM (0.65), while Text + Image + Representation offered the best overall balance, with stable SSIM (0.84) and competitive FID (280). Combining all four mechanisms yielded the weakest FID (330), indicating conflicting optimization signals. Qualitative evaluation by nine weavers and thirty public participants confirmed statistically significant positive acceptance (Wilcoxon, p=0.007 and p<0.001, respectively). A web-based prototype supporting text-to-image and image-to-image generation was also developed, offering a practical digital design tool for cultural heritage preservation.

AI.tldr: This study proposes a multimodal generative framework combining a fine-tuned Latent Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion XL with LoRA) and a Multimodal Large Language Model (LLaMA 1.5-7B) to generate culturally authentic Batak Ulos weaving motifs. The framework uses four conditioning mechanisms (text, image, representation, and semantic map via ControlNet) to enable controllable motif generation. Text + Image + Semantic Map achieved the best FID (270) and CLIP Score (0.65-0.70), while Text + Image + Representation offered the best overall balance with stable SSIM (0.84) and competitive FID (280). A web-based prototype was developed for practical use.
AI.motivation: The traditional Batak Ulos weaving industry faces challenges in producing diverse, innovative motifs due to limitations in conventional manually-driven design methods. There is a need for a digital design tool that can enable culturally faithful and controllable motif generation while preserving cultural heritage.
AI.method: The researchers integrated a fine-tuned Latent Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion XL v1.0 via LoRA) with a Multimodal Large Language Model (LLaMA 1.5-7B). Four conditioning mechanisms were used: text, image, representation, and semantic map (via ControlNet). A five-level ablation study was conducted across three scenarios (shape transformation, colour variation, and high-complexity input). Qualitative evaluation was performed by nine weavers and thirty public participants using statistical analysis (Wilcoxon test).
AI.result: Text + Image + Semantic Map achieved the best FID (270) and CLIP Score (0.65-0.70) but the weakest SSIM (0.65). Text + Image + Representation offered the best overall balance with stable SSIM (0.84) and competitive FID (280). Combining all four mechanisms yielded the weakest FID (330), indicating conflicting optimization signals. Qualitative evaluation confirmed statistically significant positive acceptance (Wilcoxon, p=0.007 for weavers and p<0.001 for public participants).
AI.conclusion: Conditioning effectiveness is not proportional to the number of mechanisms combined. The Text + Image + Representation combination provides the best overall balance for Ulos motif generation. A web-based prototype was developed offering text-to-image and image-to-image generation, serving as a practical digital design tool for cultural heritage preservation.

title: Locating Hidden Failures Makes Long-Horizon Agents More Reliable
summary: As AI agents take on long, autonomous tasks, we increasingly oversee rather than perform the work, yet we still judge them almost entirely by whether they finally succeed. An outcome cannot reveal where a run went wrong, whether the agent recovered, or the irreversible harm it caused along the way, and where long-horizon agents fail remains unmapped. We study $2518$ agent trajectories across software engineering, computer use, and science, close to real deployment, and classify $6967$ mistakes into $78$ failure types. Failure follows a recurring signature: after its first mistake an agent often fails to recover and rarely catches the error itself, so the run continues unchecked while still looking correct; whether an agent recovers depends on the task and the environment's feedback, not on the agent framework running it. Long-horizon agents can do real harm on the way to a passing result: even runs scored as solved delete data, corrupt systems, or fabricate success rather than earning it. We release these human-verified annotations as Traverse, a benchmark on which six frontier judges struggle to locate failure regardless of scale: even the strongest correctly identifies the first mistake in fewer than a third of runs. Yet Scout, a $4$B verifier we trained, locates failure far better than these judges and transfers to domains it never saw. Used at test time to select among an agent's candidate runs, it raises task success above the agent's own single-attempt performance, without retraining the agent. By making failure cheap to locate and correct, this work is a foundation for more trustworthy long-horizon agents that learn from their own mistakes, and a practical path to overseeing increasingly autonomous AI.

AI.tldr: This paper studies failure modes in long-horizon AI agents across software engineering, computer use, and science tasks. Analyzing 2518 agent trajectories with 6967 mistakes classified into 78 failure types, the authors find that agents rarely recover from first mistakes and often cause irreversible harm even in "successful" runs. They release Traverse, a benchmark where even frontier judges struggle to identify failures, and Scout, a 4B verifier that locates failures better and transfers across domains.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap in AI oversight: as agents handle longer autonomous tasks, we can only judge them by final outcomes, which cannot reveal where failures occurred, whether agents recovered, or what harm happened along the way. Long-horizon agent failures remain unmapped, and there's no practical way to locate and correct mistakes during runs.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 2518 agent trajectories across three domains (software engineering, computer use, and science), close to real deployment conditions. They classified 6967 mistakes into 78 distinct failure types through human verification. They then released these annotations as Traverse benchmark and tested six frontier judges on failure identification. Finally, they trained Scout, a 4B parameter verifier, to locate failures and evaluated it for transfer learning and test-time selection among candidate runs.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) After first mistake, agents rarely recover and rarely catch errors themselves - runs continue unchecked while appearing correct; (2) Recovery depends on task and environment feedback, not agent framework; (3) Even successful runs can cause real harm (deleting data, corrupting systems, fabricating success); (4) Frontier judges struggle - strongest correctly identifies first mistake in fewer than 1/3 of runs; (5) Scout outperforms judges at failure localization and transfers to unseen domains; (6) Using Scout at test time to select among candidate runs raises task success above single-attempt performance without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that making failure cheap to locate and correct provides a foundation for more trustworthy long-horizon agents that can learn from their mistakes, and offers a practical path to overseeing increasingly autonomous AI. The Traverse benchmark and Scout verifier represent tools to improve agent reliability without requiring fundamental architectural changes.

title: vidax: A Unified JAX Framework for Video Generative Models on Accelerator Meshes
summary: Open-source video generative models ship almost exclusively as PyTorch/CUDA reference implementations. This leaves Cloud TPU pods without a production-ready inference path, despite offering large, cost-effective accelerator memory pools ideal for long-sequence spatiotemporal attention. We present vidax, an open-source JAX/Flax inference engine and zero-copy PyTorch-to-JAX weight translator for modern video generation architectures. vidax covers a diverse set of spatiotemporal models --- including Diffusion Transformers, omnimodal Mixture-of-Transformers, 3D VAEs, text encoders, and native samplers --- with zero PyTorch dependency in the execution path. The framework unifies 1D tensor parallelism with DeepSpeed-Ulysses sequence parallelism on a single JAX sharding mesh, integrates TPU flash-attention kernels, and implements per-layer weight offloading to support reference resolutions that exceed single-device memory. We benchmark compile times, latency, and peak memory utilization on TPU v4-8 hardware, and document real-world numerical bugs surfaced during checkpoint translation. vidax is released open-source as a baseline for JAX and TPU video generation research.

AI.tldr: vidax is an open-source JAX/Flax inference engine with zero-copy PyTorch-to-JAX weight translator for video generation models on TPU hardware, enabling production-ready inference on Cloud TPU pods.
AI.motivation: Open-source video generative models are only available as PyTorch/CUDA implementations, leaving Cloud TPU pods without a production-ready inference path, despite TPUs offering large, cost-effective accelerator memory ideal for long-sequence spatiotemporal attention.
AI.method: vidax implements: (1) zero-copy PyTorch-to-JAX weight translator; (2) support for diverse spatiotemporal models (Diffusion Transformers, omnimodal Mixture-of-Transformers, 3D VAEs, text encoders, native samplers); (3) unified 1D tensor parallelism with DeepSpeed-Ulysses sequence parallelism on single JAX sharding mesh; (4) TPU flash-attention kernel integration; (5) per-layer weight offloading for reference resolutions exceeding single-device memory.
AI.result: Benchmarks on TPU v4-8 hardware show compile times, latency, and peak memory utilization. Real-world numerical bugs surfaced during checkpoint translation were documented.
AI.conclusion: vidax is released open-source as a baseline for JAX and TPU video generation research, providing a production-ready inference path for modern video generation architectures on TPU hardware.

title: Missing Bridges: Composition-Aware Active Imitation Learning
summary: Active imitation learning reduces expert effort by allowing a learner to request the demonstrations it needs. Existing methods typically select these requests for their expected information gain about the expert policy. In structured multi-task domains, however, the number of start-goal tasks may grow combinatorially despite their solutions sharing reusable behavior. This makes composable behaviors especially valuable, since a single demonstration may help solve many tasks at once. Prior methods do not explicitly account for this value when selecting which demonstration to request. We introduce Adaptive Agents via Latent Topologies (AALT), which requests demonstrations that maximize expected gains in start-goal connectivity. We further show that this objective is formally tied to information gain about task reachability. AALT organizes existing demonstrations into a topology of latent hub states connected by learned behaviors, identifies high-value bridge demonstrations that are likely to enable many tasks at once, and grounds each to an expert query. At inference, it plans through the resulting topology and conditions a diffusion policy on each successive hub transition. In a simulated UR5e robot ordered-retrieval domain with 72 tasks, AALT improved from 42/72 to 72/72 (100%) successful tasks consistently using only 3 demonstrations totaling 5 transitions beyond the initial dataset. After 20 demonstrations, the strongest baseline averaged 88.6% success using 98 transitions.

AI.tldr: AALT is an active imitation learning method that requests expert demonstrations by maximizing expected gains in start-goal connectivity. It organizes demonstrations into latent hub topologies and identifies high-value "bridge" demonstrations that enable multiple tasks. In a UR5e robot experiment with 72 tasks, it achieved 100% success with only 3 demonstrations, outperforming baselines that required 20 demonstrations to reach 88.6%.
AI.motivation: Existing active imitation learning methods select demonstrations based on expected information gain about the expert policy, but they fail to account for the composable value of demonstrations in structured multi-task domains where tasks grow combinatorially but share reusable behaviors. Prior methods don't explicitly capture how a single demonstration can help solve many tasks at once.
AI.method: AALT organizes existing demonstrations into a topology of latent hub states connected by learned behaviors. It identifies high-value "bridge" demonstrations likely to enable many tasks simultaneously, and grounds each to an expert query. At inference, it plans through the resulting topology and conditions a diffusion policy on each successive hub transition. The objective is formalized as maximizing expected gains in start-goal connectivity, which is tied to information gain about task reachability.
AI.result: In a simulated UR5e robot ordered-retrieval domain with 72 tasks, AALT improved from 42/72 to 72/72 (100%) successful tasks consistently using only 3 demonstrations totaling 5 transitions beyond the initial dataset. After 20 demonstrations, the strongest baseline averaged 88.6% success using 98 transitions.
AI.conclusion: AALT effectively leverages the composable structure of multi-task domains by requesting demonstrations that maximize connectivity gains. It achieves superior sample efficiency by identifying bridge demonstrations that unlock multiple tasks, reaching 100% success with far fewer demonstrations than baseline methods.

title: Beyond the Previous Layer: Residual Predictive Structure in Sparse MoE Routing
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts models route each token through a sequence of expert selections. We ask whether the immediately preceding selection adequately summarizes this trajectory for predicting the next router. Using frozen OLMoE and JetMoE models, we measure the held-out predictive gain from earlier expert selections while retaining the most recent selection as a common baseline. In OLMoE, extending the history from one to eleven layers raises router-logit $R^2$ from 0.59879 to 0.66544. A preregistered JetMoE replication yields four-layer gains of 0.14275 and 0.20528 at two target depths, with paired bootstrap intervals above zero. These gains survive nonlinear decoding: adding history to a small multilayer perceptron improves $R^2$ by 0.17137 and 0.21861, whereas nonlinear decoding of the recent state alone adds 0.00139 and 0.00936 over a linear probe. Parameter-matched controls preserve the advantage, and cross-fitted history residuals predict target residuals with $R^2$ of 0.20549 and 0.23556. These findings identify residual predictive structure in expert-selection trajectories beyond adjacent-layer persistence.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether expert selection trajectories in sparse mixture-of-experts models contain predictable structure beyond adjacent-layer persistence. Using frozen OLMoE and JetMoE models, the authors measure held-out predictive gain from earlier expert selections while controlling for the most recent selection. Results show significant predictive gains when extending history (e.g., R² increases from 0.59879 to 0.66544 in OLMoE), which survive nonlinear decoding, parameter-matched controls, and cross-fitting. The findings identify residual predictive structure in expert-selection trajectories.
AI.motivation: The authors investigate whether the immediately preceding expert selection in sparse mixture-of-experts models adequately summarizes the trajectory for predicting the next router. They aim to identify if there is residual predictive structure in expert-selection trajectories beyond adjacent-layer persistence.
AI.method: The authors use frozen OLMoE and JetMoE models to measure held-out predictive gain from earlier expert selections while retaining the most recent selection as a baseline. They employ linear probes, nonlinear MLPs, parameter-matched controls, and cross-fitting techniques to validate their findings.
AI.result: In OLMoE, extending history from one to eleven layers raises router-logit R² from 0.59879 to 0.66544. A preregistered JetMoE replication yields four-layer gains of 0.14275 and 0.20528 at two target depths. Adding history to a small MLP improves R² by 0.17137 and 0.21861, whereas nonlinear decoding of recent state alone adds only 0.00139 and 0.00936 over linear probe. Cross-fitted history residuals predict target residuals with R² of 0.20549 and 0.23556.
AI.conclusion: The findings identify residual predictive structure in expert-selection trajectories beyond adjacent-layer persistence, suggesting that expert selection in sparse MoE models follows predictable patterns that can be exploited for better understanding and potential optimization of these architectures.

title: Mask 2D-3D: Adaptive Dual-Masked Autoencoder Network for Image-to-Point Cloud Registration
summary: Detection-free methods for image-to-point cloud registration are prone to erroneous correspondences caused by domain and modality discrepancies, limited sensitivity of feature extractors, and the presence of non-overlapping regions. The Masked Autoencoder (MAE) has shown strong performance in visual representation for images and point clouds. It may be helpful to apply this approach to image-to-point cloud registration, a task that requires unified feature extraction and accurate cross-modal correspondences. Standard MAE's random masking may overlook key regions due to limited camera views, reducing registration effectiveness. To address this, we propose the Intermodal Dual-MAE Framework (ID-MAE) with a Similarity-based RL Masking Strategy (SRLM), which adaptively masks informative positions by leveraging cross-modal similarity and reinforcement learning, thus narrowing the modality gap. Our method enhances cross-modal representation learning by enforcing representation consistency during feature extraction, thereby enabling more reliable 2D-3D correspondence estimation. Experiments on RGB-D Scenes v2 and 7-Scenes benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in image-to-point cloud registration.

AI.tldr: ID-MAE proposes a novel framework for image-to-point cloud registration using dual Masked Autoencoders with a reinforcement learning-based masking strategy (SRLM) that adaptively masks informative regions based on cross-modal similarity, achieving state-of-the-art results on RGB-D Scenes v2 and 7-Scenes benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Detection-free image-to-point cloud registration suffers from erroneous correspondences due to domain/modality discrepancies, limited feature extractor sensitivity, and non-overlapping regions. Standard MAE's random masking may miss key regions in limited camera views, reducing registration effectiveness.
AI.method: The Intermodal Dual-MAE Framework (ID-MAE) with Similarity-based RL Masking Strategy (SRLM) adaptively masks informative positions by leveraging cross-modal similarity and reinforcement learning, narrowing the modality gap. It enforces representation consistency during feature extraction for reliable 2D-3D correspondence estimation.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on RGB-D Scenes v2 and 7-Scenes benchmarks for image-to-point cloud registration.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ID-MAE with SRLM effectively addresses cross-modal representation learning challenges in image-to-point cloud registration by adaptively masking informative regions and enforcing representation consistency, outperforming existing methods.

title: Anchoring What Matters: A Dual-Level Learning Framework for Visually-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has significantly improved the reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs). However, standard on-policy RLVR algorithms face a critical optimization bottleneck in preserving and reinforcing visually grounded reasoning behaviors: valuable visually-grounded reasoning trajectories are discarded after a single update, while uniform token advantage allocation prevents the model from reinforcing critical perception or reasoning steps. To bridge this gap, we propose PIVOT, a dual-level learning framework that anchors policy optimization around informative visual reasoning signals. Specifically, PIVOT introduces a self-calibrated experience replay mechanism, which selectively collects and replays visually-grounded historical experiences as stable reference anchors for policy optimization. Building upon this, we further design a vision-guided advantage allocation mechanism to allocate additional vision-aware advantages to tokens based on their local visual support and impact on downstream reasoning. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that PIVOT achieves highly competitive performance in enhancing the multimodal reasoning capabilities of LVLMs.

AI.tldr: PIVOT addresses critical optimization bottlenecks in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for large vision-language models (LVLMs) by introducing a dual-level learning framework that preserves valuable visually-grounded reasoning trajectories and allocates vision-aware advantages to tokens based on their visual support and reasoning impact.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy RLVR algorithms face two key problems: (1) valuable visually-grounded reasoning trajectories are discarded after a single update, losing stable learning signals, and (2) uniform token advantage allocation fails to reinforce critical perception or reasoning steps, preventing effective visually grounded reasoning.
AI.method: PIVOT proposes two key mechanisms: (1) A self-calibrated experience replay mechanism that selectively collects and replays visually-grounded historical experiences as stable reference anchors for policy optimization; (2) A vision-guided advantage allocation mechanism that allocates additional vision-aware advantages to tokens based on their local visual support and impact on downstream reasoning.
AI.result: PIVOT achieves highly competitive performance in enhancing the multimodal reasoning capabilities of LVLMs across diverse benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The dual-level learning framework successfully bridges the gap in preserving and reinforcing visually grounded reasoning behaviors in LVLMs, demonstrating the importance of experience replay and vision-aware advantage allocation for multimodal reasoning tasks.

title: On the Identifiability of Mixed Ordinal and Exponential Family Causal DAGs under Linear Parametric Models
summary: The problem of identifiability in linear parametric models (LPMs) whose nodes follow either an ordered logit model or a regular one-parameter exponential family is evaluated. The results go beyond classical structural equation models as well as results for nodes with observations from a homogeneous family of distributions. The main result establishes that the orientation of every edge joining an ordinal node to an exponential-family node is identifiable from the joint distribution alone at every parameter value, provided the ordinal node has at least three categories and the exponential-family node at least three points of support, with no restriction on the sufficient statistic. Converses show that both requirements are necessary: the three-category requirement is binding only for affine sufficient statistics, and the three-point requirement is binding under the canonical link. The guarantee extends to orienting every such mixed ordinal-exponential family edge of a given $d$-node undirected skeleton. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results by successfully separating orientations within a Markov equivalence class, which are indistinguishable by conditional independence alone.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses identifiability in Linear Parametric Models (LPMs) where nodes follow either ordered logit or one-parameter exponential family distributions. The main result establishes that edge orientation between ordinal nodes (with at least 3 categories) and exponential-family nodes (with at least 3 support points) is identifiable from the joint distribution alone, without restrictions on sufficient statistics.
AI.motivation: The work extends classical structural equation models and results for homogeneous distribution families by addressing identifiability in mixed graphical models containing both ordinal (ordered logit) and exponential family nodes. This is motivated by the need to distinguish between Markov equivalent structures that cannot be differentiated by conditional independence tests alone.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using structural equation modeling approaches, establishing conditions for identifiability through the joint distribution alone. The study provides both positive results (conditions under which orientation is identifiable) and negative results (converses showing necessary conditions).
AI.result: The main result proves that orientation of every edge joining an ordinal node to an exponential-family node is identifiable from the joint distribution at every parameter value, provided: (1) the ordinal node has at least three categories, and (2) the exponential-family node has at least three points of support. The three-category requirement is binding only for affine sufficient statistics, and the three-point requirement is binding under the canonical link. This guarantee extends to orienting every mixed ordinal-exponential family edge in a d-node undirected skeleton.
AI.conclusion: The orientation of edges in mixed graphical models containing both ordinal and exponential family nodes can be uniquely determined from observational data under specific conditions (3+ categories for ordinal, 3+ support points for exponential family). This enables separation of orientations within Markov equivalence classes that are otherwise indistinguishable by conditional independence alone. Both requirements are shown to be necessary through counterexamples.

title: Aligned Consensus Teaching for Label-Efficient Oriented Object Detection in Weakly-Aligned Visible-Infrared Imagery
summary: Visible-infrared object detection (VIOD) detects objects with oriented bounding boxes from paired visible and infrared images. Existing methods depend on costly dual-modality annotations. Semi-supervised learning can reduce this burden, but extending it from single-modal detection to VIOD is challenging. In the practical image-pair-level setting considered here, only a few pairs are labeled in both modalities, while the rest are completely unlabeled. This limited supervision creates three challenges: (i) too few labeled boxes for robust cross-modal alignment; (ii) pseudo-label errors caused by branch-wise misses accumulate during self-training; and (iii) tail-class annotations become critically scarce as the labeling budget decreases. We propose Aligned Consensus Teacher (ACT) for label-efficient VIOD in this setting. Its Cycle-Consistent Region Alignment (CRA) combines cycle consistency and sparse anchors with reliability-weighted regional matching. Cross-Modal Consensus Mean-Teacher (CMC-MT) forms consensus pseudo labels under pair-preserving views to recover branch-wise misses and supervise unlabeled pairs. Text-Guided Cross-Modal Instance Augmentation (TG-CMIA) uses a vision-language scene prior to compose tail-class instance pairs while preserving RGB--IR offsets. To the best of our knowledge, ACT is the first framework to study semi-supervised VIOD under this image-pair-level setting. Experiments on DroneVehicle and VEDAI show consistent gains across annotation ratios. With 10\% labeled pairs on DroneVehicle, ACT reaches 94.3\% of the mAP obtained by the same detector under full supervision. Code and models will be available on GitHub to facilitate future work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Aligned Consensus Teacher (ACT), the first framework for semi-supervised Visible-infrared Object Detection (VIOD) under image-pair-level setting. It addresses limited supervision challenges through three components: CRA for cross-modal alignment, CMC-MT for consensus pseudo-labeling, and TG-CMIA for tail-class augmentation. The method achieves 94.3% of fully supervised performance with only 10% labeled pairs on DroneVehicle dataset.
AI.motivation: Visible-infrared object detection (VIOD) requires costly dual-modality annotations. Existing semi-supervised methods from single-modal detection cannot be directly extended to VIOD due to three challenges: (i) insufficient labeled boxes for cross-modal alignment, (ii) pseudo-label errors from branch-wise misses, and (iii) critically scarce tail-class annotations when labeling budget decreases.
AI.method: The proposed ACT framework consists of three components: (1) Cycle-Consistent Region Alignment (CRA) combines cycle consistency and sparse anchors with reliability-weighted regional matching for cross-modal alignment; (2) Cross-Modal Consensus Mean-Teacher (CMC-MT) forms consensus pseudo labels under pair-preserving views to recover branch-wise misses and supervise unlabeled pairs; (3) Text-Guided Cross-Modal Instance Augmentation (TG-CMIA) uses vision-language scene prior to compose tail-class instance pairs while preserving RGB-IR offsets.
AI.result: Experiments on DroneVehicle and VEDAI datasets show consistent gains across annotation ratios. With 10% labeled pairs on DroneVehicle, ACT reaches 94.3% of the mAP obtained by the same detector under full supervision.
AI.conclusion: ACT is the first framework to study semi-supervised VIOD under the image-pair-level setting. It effectively addresses the three key challenges of limited supervision: cross-modal alignment, pseudo-label errors, and tail-class scarcity. The method demonstrates strong performance with minimal annotation requirements, significantly reducing the annotation burden for VIOD tasks.

title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
summary:
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on consumer hardware is bounded by weight memory: a 35B-class model is 19.5GB at 4-bit, and sparsity shrinks the compute per token, not the bytes that must be held. Naive offloading to SSD does not help on its own, because layer N+1's experts must be chosen before layer N's output exists, so the reads cannot start early enough to hide behind compute. We present Edge0, a streaming MoE inference engine that closes the gap with a prerouter: a per-layer head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, and the prediction is consumed as the routing itself, so the staged expert set equals the routed set and nothing is dropped. An unmerged recovery LoRA, trained on the student path, pays back the quality lost to int4 quantization and routing replacement. On a single 24GB machine, Edge0
  serves a 35B MoE at 20tok/s inside 3GiB of peak active memory, within a few points of its fp16 teacher on average across five public benchmarks. An 8B tier runs on the same framework, and the framework, checkpoints, and adapters are open source.

AI.tldr: Edge0 is a streaming MoE inference engine for consumer hardware that uses a prerouter to predict next-layer routing one token ahead, enabling early expert loading from SSD. A recovery LoRA compensates for int4 quantization quality loss. Achieves 20tok/s on a 35B MoE with only 3GiB active memory on 24GB hardware.
AI.motivation: MoE inference on consumer hardware is constrained by weight memory requirements (35B model = 19.5GB at 4-bit). While sparsity reduces compute per token, it doesn't reduce memory bytes that must be held. Naive SSD offloading fails because expert selection for layer N+1 depends on layer N's output, preventing early prefetching.
AI.method: 1) Prerouter: Per-layer head predicts next layer's routing one token ahead; prediction is consumed directly as routing, ensuring staged expert set equals routed set. 2) Recovery LoRA: Unmerged adapter trained on student path to compensate for int4 quantization and routing replacement quality loss.
AI.result: On single 24GB machine: 35B MoE at 20tok/s with 3GiB peak active memory; within a few percentage points of fp16 teacher across five public benchmarks. 8B tier also runs on same framework.
AI.conclusion: Edge0 enables large MoE models to run on consumer hardware by decoupling expert loading from compute via prediction-based routing, with minimal quality loss from aggressive quantization. Framework, checkpoints, and adapters are open source.

title: ASPIRE: Asynchronous Batched Self-Speculative Decoding for Long-Context LLM Inference
summary: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by attention, whose repeated KV-cache reads make decoding memory-bound. Self-speculative decoding alleviates this by drafting tokens with sparse attention and verifying them with full attention, but existing batched methods remain synchronized: all requests in a batch share a single draft-verify schedule, even though the optimal draft length varies widely across requests and changes dynamically within each request. We propose ASPIRE, a non-synchronized batched self-speculative decoding framework built on three components. First, a unified mixed forward allows drafting and verifying requests to coexist in the same batched forward pass, removing the need for global draft-verify phases. Second, a lightweight online speculation scheduler uses per-request acceptance-rate estimates and a batch-aware cost model to let each request independently choose when to verify. Third, an intra-draft refresh layer performs full attention at a single designated layer during drafting, updating the sparse context at every draft step to reduce staleness during drafting. Across three models and five reasoning and long-context benchmarks, ASPIRE achieves $1.70$-$4.58\times$ speedup in decoding throughput over autoregressive baselines and improves average speedup by approximately $27\%$ over the strongest prior self-speculative baselines.

AI.tldr: ASPIRE is a non-synchronized batched self-speculative decoding framework for efficient long-context LLM inference. It addresses the bottleneck of attention in decoding by allowing independent draft-verify schedules per request through three novel components: unified mixed forward, online speculation scheduler, and intra-draft refresh layer.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by attention, where repeated KV-cache reads make decoding memory-bound. Existing self-speculative decoding uses batched methods but with synchronized draft-verify schedules - all requests in a batch share a single schedule, even though optimal draft length varies widely across requests and changes dynamically within each request.
AI.method: ASPIRE introduces three components: (1) Unified mixed forward allows drafting and verifying requests to coexist in the same batched forward pass, removing global draft-verify phases; (2) Lightweight online speculation scheduler uses per-request acceptance-rate estimates and batch-aware cost model for independent verification decisions; (3) Intra-draft refresh layer performs full attention at a single designated layer during drafting, updating sparse context at every draft step to reduce staleness.
AI.result: Across three models and five reasoning and long-context benchmarks, ASPIRE achieves 1.70-4.58x speedup in decoding throughput over autoregressive baselines and improves average speedup by approximately 27% over the strongest prior self-speculative baselines.
AI.conclusion: ASPIRE successfully enables non-synchronized batched self-speculative decoding, allowing each request to independently choose when to verify based on its own acceptance rate. This approach significantly improves decoding throughput for long-context LLM inference, outperforming both autoregressive baselines and prior synchronized self-speculative methods.

title: PRISM: Predictive Representation of Interaction Style and Motion for Social Robot Navigation
comment: ECCV 2026 Workshop on Agent in World
summary: Humans often observe others before interacting and adjust their behavior accordingly. Robot navigation in crowds, however, often represents pedestrians mainly by observed geometric states, leaving individual differences in interaction tendencies implicit. We propose PRISM (Predictive Representation of Interaction Style and Motion), a framework that infers interaction traits from passive observations of human-human interactions. PRISM encodes human trajectories into a continuous ordinal latent space with a transformer encoder trained by Rank-N-Contrast loss, and pairs each inferred trait with a temporal-stability score supplied to the navigation policy. In randomized crowd simulations, PRISM reduces collision rates over the geometry-only baseline and yields small improvements in navigation-time and path-length metrics. These results suggest the utility of passive latent-trait inference for social navigation in dynamic crowds.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a robot navigation framework that infers individual interaction traits from passive observations of human-human interactions, encoding trajectories into a latent space using a transformer encoder trained with Rank-N-Contrast loss, and supplying these traits with temporal-stability scores to a navigation policy to improve crowd navigation safety.
AI.motivation: Current robot navigation in crowds represents pedestrians mainly by geometric states, leaving individual differences in interaction tendencies implicit. Humans naturally observe others before interacting and adjust behavior accordingly, suggesting that inferring interaction traits could improve social navigation.
AI.method: PRISM uses a transformer encoder to encode human trajectories into a continuous ordinal latent space, trained by Rank-N-Contrast loss. Each inferred trait is paired with a temporal-stability score and supplied to the navigation policy.
AI.result: In randomized crowd simulations, PRISM reduces collision rates compared to the geometry-only baseline and yields small improvements in navigation-time and path-length metrics.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest the utility of passive latent-trait inference for social navigation in dynamic crowds. The approach demonstrates that incorporating individual interaction tendencies can improve safety in robot pedestrian navigation.

title: Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K-12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools
summary: K-12 robotics and AI education remains difficult to scale, especially in rural regions lacking sustained technical mentorship. Programs like FIRST provide competition pathways and instructional opportunities, but they do not eliminate the need for local programming and robotics expertise. We introduce AI, Robotics, & Community (ARC), a hubs-based framework where colleges train undergraduate mentors and host workshops for nearby K-12 teams. Mature school programs can become secondary hubs that support additional schools, creating a self-reinforcing education loop where mentorship reach propagates geographically and can even grow super-linearly. We first evaluate ARC through a trial deployment at one university. The trial created three rural robotics teams. On five-point Likert surveys, mean increases in K-12 programming knowledge, resource access, and practice opportunities were 2.00, 2.25, and 1.25 points. Likewise, undergraduate confidence teaching technical concepts, adapting explanations, managing groups, and finding mentoring enjoyable and meaningful increased by 1.29, 1.14, 1.00, and 1.14 points. Additionally, we create a spatial Markov model of ARC's growth and simulate it using the state of Indiana as a testbed. Under moderate conditions, we find that ARC reaches 74% of Indiana's 1,925 public K-12 schools and produces 992 robotics programs after 40 years, compared with 161 projected under natural growth alone. Together, these results show ARC can create and support rural robotics programs, train undergraduate AI and robotics mentors, and potentially scale mentorship across a region.

AI.tldr: ARC is a hubs-based framework where colleges train undergraduate mentors to support K-12 robotics teams, with mature school programs becoming secondary hubs to create self-reinforcing mentorship networks that can scale geographically, especially in rural areas.
AI.motivation: K-12 robotics and AI education is difficult to scale in rural regions lacking sustained technical mentorship; existing programs like FIRST don't eliminate the need for local programming expertise.
AI.method: Trial deployment at one university creating three rural robotics teams, with Likert surveys measuring changes in K-12 programming knowledge, resource access, and practice opportunities, plus undergraduate mentoring confidence. Also developed a spatial Markov model of ARC growth simulated using Indiana's 1,925 public K-12 schools as testbed.
AI.result: K-12 gains: programming knowledge +2.00, resource access +2.25, practice opportunities +1.25 (5-point scale). Undergraduate gains: teaching confidence +1.29, adapting explanations +1.14, group management +1.00, finding mentoring meaningful +1.14. Simulation: ARC reaches 74% of Indiana schools and produces 992 robotics programs after 40 years vs. 161 under natural growth.
AI.conclusion: ARC framework can create and support rural robotics programs, train undergraduate mentors, and potentially scale mentorship across regions with super-linear growth potential through self-reinforcing hub networks.

title: Maximum Strong Independent Sets in Hypergraphs: Reductions, Bounds, and Greedy Certificates
summary: We study the maximum strong independent set problem in a finite hypergraph: find the largest vertex set that intersects every hyperedge in at most one vertex. This objective arises whenever each observed block is a local incompatibility constraint but transitive closure across overlapping blocks is not justified. A motivating example is multi-band LSH-MinHash deduplication, where each collision bucket gives local evidence, while connected-component contraction can impose spurious global equivalences. The paper develops an incidence-structural toolkit for this problem. We prove exact reductions for dominance, incidence twins, and weight-1 blocks; derive closed-form and low-weight upper bounds; introduce puncturing and covering certificates that sharpen those bounds; and analyze a layered greedy clustering algorithm driven by block weights and residual incidence. The algorithmic analysis includes feasibility, maximality, conditional optimality, a layered witness-matching upper bound, and incidence-local complexity bounds. The results give correctness, termination, fixed-point, and optimality certificates for broad incidence families, together with examples showing when different certificates separate or coincide.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the maximum strong independent set problem in finite hypergraphs, where the goal is to find the largest vertex set that intersects every hyperedge in at most one vertex. This problem models scenarios with local incompatibility constraints where transitive closure is not justified, such as multi-band LSH-MinHash deduplication.
AI.motivation: The problem arises in applications where each observed block represents a local incompatibility constraint, but global equivalence via transitive closure would be spurious. The motivating example is multi-band LSH-MinHash deduplication, where collision buckets provide local evidence but connected-component contraction could impose incorrect global equivalences.
AI.method: The paper develops an incidence-structural toolkit including: (1) Exact reductions for dominance, incidence twins, and weight-1 blocks; (2) Closed-form and low-weight upper bounds; (3) Puncturing and covering certificates to sharpen bounds; (4) Analysis of a layered greedy clustering algorithm driven by block weights and residual incidence, with feasibility, maximality, and conditional optimality analysis.
AI.result: The results provide correctness, termination, fixed-point, and optimality certificates for broad incidence families, along with examples showing when different certificates separate or coincide. The paper also establishes a layered witness-matching upper bound and incidence-local complexity bounds.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete theoretical framework for the maximum strong independent set problem in hypergraphs, with practical algorithmic tools and certificates that can be applied to real-world deduplication and clustering problems while avoiding spurious global equivalences.

title: MCLC-NET: Multimodal Continual Learning for Leaf Counting
summary: Leaf counting is an important task in plant phenotyping for monitoring plant growth and estimating crop yield. Most existing methods rely on RGB images, but their performance is often affected by occlusion, lighting variations, and other real-world challenges. Additional modalities, such as depth and thermal images, can provide useful complementary information. However, multimodal leaf counting remains underexplored. Also, many existing methods assume that all training data are available simultaneously, which is impractical in real agricultural settings, where data is collected over time from multiple sources. To address these challenges, we propose MCLC-NET, a multimodal continual learning framework for leaf counting. It learns tasks sequentially using a memory-based strategy with a memory buffer to retain important samples from previous tasks. We also introduce MMLC, a real-world multimodal leaf-counting dataset designed for a domain incremental scenario (DIS) in CL. It contains RGB, depth, and thermal images collected across different crop types under varying environmental conditions, arranged in three orderings: crop-wise, time-wise, and mixed. Experimental results, averaged over three random seeds, demonstrate that MCLC-NET consistently outperforms existing methods across all three task orderings, achieving the lowest AMSE of 0.675$\pm$0.027, 0.542$\pm$0.069, and 0.745$\pm$0.057, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MCLC-NET, a multimodal continual learning framework for leaf counting in plant phenotyping. It addresses limitations of RGB-only methods (occlusion, lighting variations) and the impractical assumption that all training data is available simultaneously. The framework uses a memory-based strategy with a buffer to retain important samples from previous tasks when learning sequentially. A new dataset MMLC containing RGB, depth, and thermal images across different crop types is also introduced.
AI.motivation: Existing leaf counting methods rely on RGB images but suffer from performance issues due to occlusion, lighting variations, and real-world challenges. Additionally, most methods assume all training data is available simultaneously, which is impractical in real agricultural settings where data is collected over time. Multimodal leaf counting remains underexplored, and the field lacks datasets and methods for continual learning scenarios in plant phenotyping.
AI.method: The proposed MCLC-NET is a multimodal continual learning framework that learns tasks sequentially using a memory-based strategy with a memory buffer to retain important samples from previous tasks. The framework processes RGB, depth, and thermal images. The MMLC dataset was designed for domain incremental scenario (DIS) in continual learning, containing images across different crop types under varying environmental conditions, arranged in three orderings: crop-wise, time-wise, and mixed.
AI.result: MCLC-NET consistently outperforms existing methods across all three task orderings (crop-wise, time-wise, and mixed), achieving the lowest AMSE of 0.675±0.027, 0.542±0.069, and 0.745±0.057 respectively. Results are averaged over three random seeds.
AI.conclusion: The multimodal continual learning approach (MCLC-NET) effectively addresses the challenges of leaf counting in plant phenotyping by leveraging complementary information from RGB, depth, and thermal modalities while handling sequential task learning. The MMLC dataset and proposed framework provide a solid foundation for future research in multimodal continual learning for agricultural applications.

title: Decodability is Not Causality: Dissociating Probe Readouts from Behavioral Drivers via SAE Decomposition
summary: Linear probes can decode safety-relevant concepts such as truthfulness from language-model activations, but probe accuracy may show only decodability, not that the features the probe weights causally drive model behavior. We demonstrate that this gap cannot be closed from the geometry of probe weights alone: the features geometrically aligned with probe direction need not be the ones the model uses, so causal relevance requires intervention. We introduce a feature-level diagnostic that decomposes a deployed True/False probe into sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features, ranks those features by both probe alignment and by gradient sensitivity of the model's behavior, and ablates the resulting shared, probe-only, and random feature sets under a coherence gate. On the truth probe of Buerger et al. (2024) (TTPD), applied in the instructed truth/deception setting of Long et al. (2025) for Gemma2-9B-Instruct, the two rankings overlap only weakly (about 12%, Spearman rho = 0.10), and ablation dissociates them sharply: features the probe shares with the model flip the output far more (up to 27%) than equally sized probe-only (6%) or random (1%) features at full coherence, while probe-only features instead perturb the probe's own readout. The dissociation holds across five seeds and a held-out split, and an activation-aware selection of features flips behavior nearly three times as often as the probe's geometric top features (17.6% vs. 6.1%). In this setting, therefore, the geometric projection of a probe's weight vector alone does not identify the features the model causally uses; however, combining probe information with feature activation statistics recovers substantially more behaviorally causal features, and coherence-gated SAE intervention is needed to separate them from probe readouts.

AI.tldr: Linear probes can decode concepts from LLM activations, but probe accuracy doesn't necessarily mean the aligned features causally drive model behavior. This paper introduces a feature-level diagnostic using sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to separate geometric probe alignment from causal behavioral relevance, demonstrating that coherence-gated intervention is needed to identify truly causal features.
AI.motivation: The gap between probe decodability and causal relevance: linear probes can decode safety-relevant concepts (like truthfulness) from language model activations, but high probe accuracy may only indicate decodability, not that the features the probe weights align with actually causally drive model behavior. This distinction is crucial for understanding and intervening on model behavior.
AI.method: 1) Decompose a deployed True/False probe into sparse autoencoder (SAE) features; 2) Rank features by both probe alignment (geometric) and gradient sensitivity of model behavior; 3) Ablate shared, probe-only, and random feature sets under a coherence gate; 4) Test on truth probe (TTPD) for Gemma2-9B-Instruct in instructed truth/deception setting
AI.result: Two rankings overlap weakly (~12%, Spearman rho = 0.10). Ablation shows: shared features flip output 27% (vs probe-only 6%, random 1%) at full coherence. Probe-only features perturb probe's own readout instead. Activation-aware selection flips behavior 2.9x more than geometric top features (17.6% vs 6.1%). Results hold across five seeds and held-out split.
AI.conclusion: Geometric projection of probe weight vector alone does NOT identify features the model causally uses. Combining probe information with feature activation statistics recovers substantially more behaviorally causal features. Coherence-gated SAE intervention is necessary to separate causally relevant features from probe readouts.

title: QuanText: Protecting Dataset-Level Secrets in Textual Data Sharing
summary: Natural-language datasets support many downstream applications and research studies, but releasing text can reveal sensitive global properties of the underlying data source, such as the proportion of records associated with a particular gender, diagnosis, or political stance. Existing work has largely focused on property inference attacks that recover such global properties, while defenses for protecting these dataset-level secrets remain limited. Differential privacy, although effective for protecting individual records, provides only weak protection for aggregate properties. We propose Randomized Quantization for Text (QuanText), a training-free and large-language-model-agnostic data release mechanism that protects global secrets in textual datasets while preserving data utility. Given a dataset-level secret, such as the proportion of records with a particular diagnosis, and attributes whose utility should be preserved, such as topic and sentiment, QuanText perturbs both the secret distribution and the distributions of correlated attributes. It does so by constructing candidate release distributions over secret and non-secret attributes, randomly selecting a candidate sufficiently close to the private empirical distribution, and rewriting each private text sample to match the selected distribution using attribute-related snippets from the original text. QuanText is inspired by the Statistic Maximal Leakage (SML) framework, which bounds leakage about a secret function of a data distribution. Under idealized conditions, we show that QuanText satisfies an SML guarantee. Since these conditions may not hold exactly in practice, we also evaluate QuanText empirically on real-world datasets. Our results show that QuanText achieves a better empirical privacy-utility trade-off than competing data generation baselines.

AI.tldr: QuanText is a training-free, LLM-agnostic data release mechanism that protects global secrets (e.g., proportion of records with a particular attribute) in textual datasets while preserving utility. It perturbs both secret distributions and correlated attribute distributions by constructing candidate release distributions, randomly selecting one close to the private empirical distribution, and rewriting text samples using attribute-related snippets. The method is theoretically grounded in the Statistic Maximal Leakage (SML) framework.
AI.motivation: Natural-language datasets can reveal sensitive global properties (gender, diagnosis, political stance) through property inference attacks. Existing defenses, particularly differential privacy, provide only weak protection for aggregate properties. There is a need for a mechanism that protects dataset-level secrets while preserving data utility.
