AI.method: QuanText works by: (1) Given a dataset-level secret (e.g., proportion of records with a particular diagnosis) and utility-preserved attributes (e.g., topic, sentiment), (2) Constructing candidate release distributions over secret and non-secret attributes, (3) Randomly selecting a candidate sufficiently close to the private empirical distribution, (4) Rewriting each private text sample to match the selected distribution using attribute-related snippets from original text. The method is inspired by the Statistic Maximal Leakage (SML) framework.
AI.result: Under idealized conditions, QuanText satisfies an SML guarantee. Empirically, QuanText achieves a better privacy-utility trade-off than competing data generation baselines on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: QuanText provides an effective training-free solution for protecting global secrets in textual datasets while preserving utility. Its theoretical grounding in SML provides formal guarantees, and empirical evaluation demonstrates superior performance compared to existing baselines.

title: Stealthy in Semantics, Antagonistic in Space: Attacking Visible-Infrared Object Detectors via Object-Level Misalignment
summary: Visible-infrared object detectors are used for robust perception under challenging illumination and weather conditions. Current physical attacks apply conspicuous patches to spatially aligned target regions, which are noticeable to human observers. Meanwhile, most of these methods only perturb the appearance within the aligned region, without explicitly targeting the correspondence between modalities or the fusion process. In this paper, we propose CamoShift, an adversarial framework for visible-infrared object detection. By combining visual camouflage with object-level infrared shifting, CamoShift breaks cross-modal spatial alignment and disrupts fusion. Specifically, the Semantic Camouflage Module (SCM) generates a stealthy camouflaged patch that can be attached to the host object and maintains its effectiveness in the infrared branch through an RGB-IR adapter. The Object-level Spatial Decoupling Module (OSDM) shifts the infrared target evidence in a scale-aware manner, so as to break object-level correspondence and disrupt cross-modal fusion. Then, the Harmonic Adversarial loss (HarAdv loss) further balances attack strength and visual stealth during optimization. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to target both visual stealthiness and attack success in visible-infrared object detection. Extensive experimental results show that CamoShift achieves a superior balance between attack effectiveness and visual stealth. Code and models will be available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: CamoShift is an adversarial attack framework for visible-infrared object detection that achieves a superior balance between attack effectiveness and visual stealth by combining semantic camouflage with object-level infrared shifting.
AI.motivation: Current physical attacks on visible-infrared object detectors are conspicuous (noticeable to humans) and fail to explicitly target cross-modal correspondence or fusion processes. There is a need for attacks that are both visually stealthy and effective at disrupting cross-modal detection.
AI.method: CamoShift consists of three components: (1) Semantic Camouflage Module (SCM) generates stealthy camouflaged patches with an RGB-IR adapter to maintain effectiveness in infrared; (2) Object-level Spatial Decoupling Module (OSDM) shifts infrared target evidence in a scale-aware manner to break object-level correspondence; (3) Harmonic Adversarial loss (HarAdv loss) balances attack strength and visual stealth during optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experimental results demonstrate that CamoShift achieves a superior balance between attack effectiveness and visual stealth in visible-infrared object detection.
AI.conclusion: This is the first work to simultaneously target both visual stealthiness and attack success in visible-infrared object detection, introducing a novel adversarial framework that breaks cross-modal spatial alignment and disrupts fusion through combined visual camouflage and infrared shifting.

title: When Is Graph Structure Worth Its Cost? The Case for Structure Pricing in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary:
Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can help answer questions that require information from many documents. However, building a graph often requires many language-model calls during ingestion. It is therefore important to ask whether its quality gains justify the additional cost.
  We present EffiRAG, a graph-based RAG system designed to reduce this cost. It uses the graph to locate relevant passages and generates answers from the original text. This design preserves source information while keeping graph construction and query processing lightweight.
  We evaluate EffiRAG on UltraDomain, which contains 120 open-ended questions from four domains. Compared with LightRAG-hybrid, EffiRAG produces the preferred answer on 93 questions. LightRAG is preferred on 7, and the remaining 20 are splits. EffiRAG also reduces total system cost by 57 percent, from USD 0.952 to USD 0.408. The cost includes language-model calls during ingestion and querying.
  The advantage remains as the corpus grows. At 10 and 20 documents per domain, EffiRAG uses a lightweight, non-LLM filter to skip low-salience chunks. It remains preferred over LightRAG-hybrid. It costs 4.2 times and 4.5 times less, respectively.
  The comparisons identify different quality-cost trade-offs. Graph-based RAG systems should therefore be evaluated by both answer quality and cost. The results favor graph structure that locates and preserves source evidence.

AI.tldr: EffiRAG is a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that reduces the high language-model call costs associated with traditional graph-based RAG. It uses the graph structure to locate relevant passages while generating answers directly from original text, keeping both graph construction and query processing lightweight.
AI.motivation: Graph-based RAG systems can answer complex multi-document questions but require many language-model calls during ingestion, raising questions about whether the quality gains justify the additional computational cost. The researchers aimed to address this cost-quality tradeoff.
AI.method: EffiRAG uses the graph structure to locate relevant passages and generates answers from the original text, preserving source information. At larger corpus sizes (10 and 20 documents per domain), it employs a lightweight, non-LLM filter to skip low-salience chunks.
AI.result: On UltraDomain (120 questions from four domains): EffiRAG was preferred on 93 questions, LightRAG-hybrid on 7, with 20 ties. Total system cost reduced by 57% (from $0.952 to $0.408). At 10 documents per domain, EffiRAG costs 4.2x less; at 20 documents per domain, it costs 4.5x less, while remaining preferred over LightRAG-hybrid.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based RAG systems should be evaluated by both answer quality and cost. The results favor graph structures that locate and preserve source evidence, as EffiRAG demonstrates superior cost-efficiency while maintaining or exceeding answer quality compared to LightRAG.

title: The Attention Within: Consensus Dynamics in Selective State Space Models
summary:
Selective state space models (SSMs) have recently emerged as a compelling alternative to transformers, combining competitive performance with substantially improved inference efficiency. At each SSM layer, a sequence of hidden states are propagated by a recurrence, mixing information of different tokens. Despite using a different mechanism, this mixing plays a role analogous to attention in transformers. In fact, recent works have shown that the two architectures may be closer than they first appear, as this recurrence admits a formulation akin to linear attention. In transformers, attention is known to drive the tokens to cluster, i.e., to reach consensus, collapsing in the limit to a single direction. Thus, we ask: does the recurrence at the core of SSMs drive the tokens to consensus, as attention does in transformers?
  To answer this question, we take a dynamical systems perspective on SSMs, modeling the evolution of tokens across layers as an ordinary differential equation. By exploiting input-to-state stability arguments, we establish local exponential stability of the consensus equilibria and characterize their domain of attraction for time-varying weight matrices, a setting not addressed by previous results. We thereby show that the resemblance between SSMs and transformers does run deeper: the recurrence at the core of SSMs aggregates tokens just as attention does. Numerical experiments on a pretrained Mamba-2 model point to the output gate as the component that regulates the extent of this consensus, preventing the tokens from reaching it in full.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether Selective State Space Models (SSMs) drive tokens to consensus like attention mechanisms do in transformers. Using dynamical systems theory and input-to-state stability analysis, the authors prove that SSM recurrences do aggregate tokens toward consensus, similar to transformers, but the output gate component regulates this tendency, preventing full collapse.
AI.motivation: The authors seek to understand the similarity between SSMs and transformers. While prior work noted SSM recurrences can be formulated similarly to linear attention, it remains unclear whether SSMs exhibit the same token consensus behavior that attention exhibits in transformers (where tokens cluster and collapse to a single direction).
AI.method: The authors adopt a dynamical systems perspective, modeling token evolution across SSM layers as an ordinary differential equation. They employ input-to-state stability arguments to establish local exponential stability of consensus equilibria and characterize their domain of attraction, particularly for time-varying weight matrices.
AI.result: The analysis proves that SSM recurrences do aggregate tokens toward consensus, similar to attention in transformers. Numerical experiments on a pretrained Mamba-2 model reveal that the output gate component regulates the extent of this consensus, preventing tokens from reaching full consensus.
AI.conclusion: The resemblance between SSMs and transformers runs deeper than previously recognized: the recurrence at the core of SSMs aggregates tokens just as attention does in transformers. The output gate acts as a regulatory mechanism that controls the degree of consensus, providing a structural way to balance information aggregation with token diversity.

title: Multi-View Mixture-of-Experts with Vision-Language Reranking for Cross-View Object Geo-Localization
summary: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) locates a target in satellite imagery using drone or street-view queries. Existing methods train separate detectors for each viewpoint, leading to parameter redundancy and impeding cross-view knowledge sharing. Moreover, top-ranked satellite candidates are often visually similar, so visual appearance and categorical labels alone are insufficient to resolve such ambiguity. To address these, we propose MVLGeo, an efficient framework designed to unify multiple viewpoints and reduce model redundancy. First, we introduce environmental contextual text from the query view as cues to distinguish visually similar candidates via Vision-Language Reranking (VL-Rerank). Second, we design a multi-view Mixture-of-Experts architecture (MV-MoE) with a shared encoder and view-specific experts to reduce redundancy and promote knowledge sharing, while cross-view contrastive learning aligns their representations for consistency. Third, we introduce an adaptive elliptical prior (ESAM-Prior) as auxiliary positional encoding for anisotropic geometric perception. Extensive experiments on the CVOGL benchmarks confirm that MVLGeo, as a unified model for multiple query viewpoints, achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating robustness to input degradation and generalization across viewpoints. Code and models will be available on GitHub to facilitate future work.

AI.tldr: MVLGeo is a unified framework for cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) that locates targets in satellite imagery using drone or street-view queries. It addresses two key challenges: parameter redundancy from training separate detectors per viewpoint, and ambiguity from visually similar top-ranked satellite candidates.
AI.motivation: Existing CVOGL methods train separate detectors for each viewpoint, causing parameter redundancy and hindering cross-view knowledge sharing. Additionally, top-ranked satellite candidates are often visually similar, making visual appearance and categorical labels insufficient for disambiguation.
AI.method: The paper proposes three key innovations: (1) Vision-Language Reranking (VL-Rerank) uses environmental contextual text from query views to distinguish visually similar candidates; (2) Multi-view Mixture-of-Experts architecture (MV-MoE) employs a shared encoder with view-specific experts to reduce redundancy and enable knowledge sharing, with cross-view contrastive learning aligning representations; (3) Adaptive elliptical prior (ESAM-Prior) provides auxiliary positional encoding for anisotropic geometric perception.
AI.result: MVLGeo achieves state-of-the-art performance on CVOGL benchmarks, demonstrating robustness to input degradation and generalization across viewpoints while operating as a unified model for multiple query viewpoints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MVLGeo framework successfully unifies multiple viewpoints, reduces model redundancy, and improves localization accuracy through vision-language reranking, mixture-of-experts architecture, and adaptive elliptical positional encoding.

title: AutoTuneBench: Trustworthy Measurement for Agent Auto-Tuning of LLM Serving Engines
comment: 15 pages, 7 tables, 6 figures. Code and measurement corpus: https://github.com/li-ch/autotunebench (tag v1.0.0)
summary: Large language model agents tune GPU kernels and serving engines through a closed loop of propose, measure, and keep, but the measurements behind this loop are not trustworthy. We characterize four failure modes from a four-day pilot corpus of 619 model calls: strawman baselines manufacture speedups, absolute times do not transfer across machines, saturated tasks nullify comparisons, and infrastructure defects impersonate science. We present AutoTuneBench, a benchmark and measurement protocol that makes trust architectural. The protocol is frozen as code with test-enforced provenance; a database-level validator rejects out-of-protocol results; anti-cheat checks run outside the agent's modification surface; comparisons follow pre-registered readouts; and measurements anchor to externally published results, grounded in paired-seed statistics with a 5\% cross-run coefficient-of-variation cap. Honest measurement rewrites the headlines: our best kernel reads 10.6x against a naive baseline but 2.03x against the honest one; one configuration delivers 1.174x on one machine and 1.0049x on another; a pre-registered on/off comparison nulls at a shared wall (2.4840 vs 2.4957\,ms); and the KernelBench Level-1 suite admits 51\% of tasks with median speedup 1.0001x over PyTorch eager. The protocol, the two-engine corpus (vLLM and SGLang), and its audit trail are released as open artifacts.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses untrustworthy measurements in LLM agent-based GPU kernel and serving engine tuning. The authors identify four failure modes in existing benchmarking practices and propose AutoTuneBench, a rigorous measurement protocol with architectural trust guarantees. The key finding is that honest measurement significantly reduces claimed speedups: from 10.6x to 2.03x for the best kernel, and that 51% of KernelBench Level-1 tasks show negligible speedup (1.0001x) over PyTorch eager mode.
AI.motivation: The measurement loop (propose, measure, keep) used by LLM agents to tune GPU kernels and serving engines produces untrustworthy results. The authors observed a four-day pilot corpus of 619 model calls revealing systematic measurement failures that inflate claimed performance improvements.
AI.method: The authors characterized four failure modes from empirical observation, then designed AutoTuneBench with five trust mechanisms: (1) protocol frozen as code with test-enforced provenance, (2) database-level validator for out-of-protocol results, (3) anti-cheat checks outside agent's modification surface, (4) pre-registered readouts for comparisons, and (5) measurements anchored to external results with 5% cross-run coefficient-of-variation cap. They evaluated using two serving engines (vLLM and SGLang) and the KernelBench Level-1 suite.
AI.result: Four failure modes identified: (1) strawman baselines inflate speedups, (2) absolute times don't transfer across machines (1.174x vs 1.0049x), (3) saturated tasks invalidate comparisons, (4) infrastructure defects masquerade as scientific results. With honest measurement: best kernel drops from 10.6x to 2.03x; pre-registered on/off comparison nulls (2.4840 vs 2.4957 ms); 51% of KernelBench Level-1 tasks show median 1.0001x speedup.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agent tuning results are largely unreliable due to measurement artifacts. The proposed AutoTuneBench protocol, with its architectural trust mechanisms, can serve as a standard for reproducible performance evaluation. The authors release the protocol, two-engine corpus (vLLM and SGLang), and audit trail as open artifacts.

title: Structural Inference under Hidden Agents
summary: Recovering latent interaction structures from multi-agent dynamics is important for understanding and predicting interacting systems. Trajectory-based structural inference has achieved promising performance, but conventional formulations assume that the trajectories of all modeled agents are available. In practice, agents may become unobserved at deployment because of limited sensing, occlusion, or communication failure. Existing studies have considered unseen-node estimation, structural inference under partial observations, and missing-value imputation, yet the joint recovery of hidden-agent trajectories and their interactions remains underexplored. We formulate this problem as structural inference under hidden agents. Its key difficulty is a circular dependency: recovering interactions involving a hidden agent requires an estimate of its trajectory, while trajectory reconstruction can itself benefit from structural information. To address this challenge, we propose Structural Inference under Hidden Agents (SIHA), which combines structure-agnostic initialization with structure-guided iterative refinement. SIHA reconstructs hidden trajectories from visible observations, infers interactions using Neural Relational Inference, and feeds the estimated structure back into hidden-state reconstruction through multi-strength structural attention and iterative state--structure updates. Experiments on three benchmark dynamical systems demonstrate consistent improvements in visible-to-visible structural inference, while also showing benefits in hidden-state reconstruction and future prediction. Motion-capture experiments with simulated whole-limb occlusion further demonstrate its effectiveness in realistic hidden-agent settings.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem of recovering latent interaction structures in multi-agent systems when some agents are hidden/unobserved. It proposes SIHA (Structural Inference under Hidden Agents), which iteratively reconstructs hidden trajectories and infers interactions through a combination of structure-agnostic initialization and structure-guided refinement using Neural Relational Inference and multi-strength structural attention.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent dynamics, trajectory-based structural inference typically assumes all agents are observable. However, in practice, agents may become unobserved due to limited sensing, occlusion, or communication failure. The key challenge is a circular dependency: recovering interactions involving hidden agents requires their trajectories, while trajectory reconstruction can benefit from structural information. This joint recovery problem remains underexplored.
AI.method: The proposed method SIHA combines structure-agnostic initialization with structure-guided iterative refinement. It reconstructs hidden trajectories from visible observations, infers interactions using Neural Relational Inference, and feeds the estimated structure back into hidden-state reconstruction through multi-strength structural attention and iterative state-structure updates.
AI.result: Experiments on three benchmark dynamical systems demonstrate consistent improvements in visible-to-visible structural inference, while also showing benefits in hidden-state reconstruction and future prediction. Motion-capture experiments with simulated whole-limb occlusion further demonstrate its effectiveness in realistic hidden-agent settings.
AI.conclusion: SIHA effectively addresses the problem of structural inference under hidden agents by breaking the circular dependency through iterative refinement between trajectory reconstruction and interaction inference. The method shows improvements across multiple tasks and validates effectiveness in realistic occlusion scenarios.

title: CapMap-MS-TTA: 3rd Place Solution for the MUMU Track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge at ECCV 2026
summary: The MUMU track of the 8th Large-scale Video Object Segmentation (LSVOS) Challenge requires a single unified multimodal model to jointly solve image tagging (Task A), open-vocabulary object detection (Task B), and English captioning (Task C) under strict resource constraints (<=0.5B parameters and <=8 GB peak GPU memory). We present CapMap-MS-TTA, a training-free submission built on Microsoft Florence-2-base (~231M parameters), combining caption keyword mapping with multi-scale flip test-time augmentation. Task C uses the native <DETAILED_CAPTION> pathway with length/token sanitization. Task A maps the same detailed caption into the official quality/scene/event vocabularies via an expanded keyword lexicon with whole-word matching and a lightweight expand-hints stage. Task B runs Florence-2 open detection (<OD>) with multi-scale and horizontal-flip test-time augmentation (TTA), followed by label-aware non-maximum suppression (NMS). Without fine-tuning, the system improves our reproduced Florence-2 baseline from 15.16 to a best public score of 16.4815, and ranks 3rd on the final MUMU leaderboard.

AI.tldr: CapMap-MS-TTA is a training-free multimodal system for the LSVOS Challenge MUMU track, solving image tagging, open-vocabulary detection, and captioning using Florence-2-base with multi-scale flip TTA. Achieved 16.4815 score (3rd place) without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Address the MUMU track challenge requiring a single unified multimodal model to jointly solve image tagging (Task A), open-vocabulary object detection (Task B), and English captioning (Task C) under strict resource constraints (<=0.5B parameters, <=8GB GPU memory).
AI.method: Built on Microsoft Florence-2-base (~231M parameters). Task C uses native <DETAILED_CAPTION> pathway with length/token sanitization. Task A maps detailed captions into quality/scene/event vocabularies via expanded keyword lexicon with whole-word matching and expand-hints stage. Task B runs Florence-2 open detection (<OD>) with multi-scale and horizontal-flip TTA, followed by label-aware NMS.
AI.result: Improved from reproduced baseline of 15.16 to 16.4815 (best public score), ranking 3rd on final MUMU leaderboard. All within constraints of ~231M parameters and <=8GB peak GPU memory.
AI.conclusion: Training-free approach using pre-trained Florence-2-base with caption keyword mapping and multi-scale flip TTA effectively solves the unified multimodal task within strict resource constraints, achieving competitive results without fine-tuning.

title: Designing Agentic AI Workflow Portfolios under Imperfect Selection and Compute Cost
summary: Agentic AI systems often approach the same task through multiple workflows that differ in reasoning strategy, verification structure, and compute cost. A natural deployment policy is to use the workflow with the highest average performance, but this can be suboptimal because different workflows may succeed on different instances. We study a portfolio-and-selector paradigm in which a firm runs multiple workflow executions and selects the final answer after observing their outputs. Additional executions may uncover correct answers that the best standalone workflow misses, but they consume compute and introduce plausible distractors that complicate final selection. We formulate this as a workflow portfolio problem in which the firm jointly chooses run size and allocation across workflow types. We summarize selector quality through an odds-lift index and derive sharp bounds on the value of workflow variety. For finite workflow pools, we develop exact formulations, linear programming relaxations, randomized rounding procedures, and computable performance certificates. For large implicit workflow classes, we derive a finite-dimensional dual and an ellipsoid method using a pricing oracle to identify workflows with high weighted accuracy net of recurring compute cost. Under a weak condition, the method obtains a near-optimal solution to the relaxation with polynomially many oracle calls. We evaluate the framework on three datasets: ABCD, Schema-Guided Dialogue, and HotpotQA. Relative to the best standalone workflow, portfolio optimization improves held-out selector accuracy by 3.1, 7.5, and 0.9 percentage points, respectively. Dual-guided workflow generation adds 3.5 points on ABCD and 24.1 on HotpotQA, with no additional gain on Schema-Guided Dialogue.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the workflow portfolio problem in agentic AI systems, where multiple reasoning strategies can be applied to the same task. The authors propose a portfolio-and-selector paradigm that runs multiple workflows and selects the best answer, rather than relying on a single best workflow. They develop optimization formulations, LP relaxations, randomized rounding procedures, and a dual-based ellipsoid method with pricing oracle for large workflow classes. Experiments on three datasets show meaningful improvements in selector accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current deployment uses the highest average performance workflow, but this is suboptimal because different workflows succeed on different instances. The authors recognize that running multiple workflows can uncover correct answers missed by the best single workflow, but introduces compute costs and plausible distractors that complicate selection.
AI.method: The authors formulate the workflow portfolio problem as a joint optimization of run size and allocation across workflow types. They introduce an "odds-lift index" to summarize selector quality. For finite pools, they develop exact formulations, linear programming relaxations, and randomized rounding procedures. For large implicit workflow classes, they derive a finite-dimensional dual and an ellipsoid method using a pricing oracle to identify high weighted accuracy workflows net of compute cost.
AI.result: Portfolio optimization improved held-out selector accuracy by 3.1 percentage points on ABCD, 7.5 on Schema-Guided Dialogue, and 0.9 on HotpotQA relative to the best standalone workflow. Dual-guided workflow generation added 3.5 points on ABCD and 24.1 on HotpotQA, with no gain on Schema-Guided Dialogue.
AI.conclusion: The portfolio-and-selector paradigm outperforms using single best workflows. The dual-guided approach using pricing oracle can efficiently identify high-quality workflows for large implicit classes under weak conditions, achieving near-optimal solutions with polynomially many oracle calls. The framework provides both theoretical bounds and practical improvements.

title: Regional Explanations via Causal Sufficiency and Necessity
summary: Model explainability is essential for understanding and trusting machine learning models. Existing explainable AI methods often explain predictions through feature importance, counterfactual explanations, or rules. However, a region-level characterization of when and only when a prediction behavior arises remains less explored. This paper proposes Causal Sufficient and Necessary Regional Explanations (SNRE), a framework that learns an input region $A$ and output region $B$ such that membership in $A$ is both sufficient and necessary for the model output to fall in $B$. Motivated by the classical Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency (PNS), we formulate a region-level PNS measure through stochastic interventions and derive a differentiable finite-sample estimator for optimization. SNRE parameterizes the input-output region pair with explicit and interpretable algebraic region families, together with a learnable feature mask, balancing expressiveness and interpretability. Experiments demonstrate that SNRE learns region pairs with strong sufficiency-necessity performance, robust explanation behavior, and practical utility for model analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SNRE (Causal Sufficient and Necessary Regional Explanations), a novel framework that learns input-output region pairs (A→B) where membership in A is both sufficient and necessary for model predictions to fall in B. It addresses the gap in region-level model explanations by formulating a differentiable PNS-based measure through stochastic interventions.
AI.motivation: Existing explainable AI methods focus on feature importance, counterfactual explanations, or rules, but lack a systematic way to characterize when and only when specific prediction behaviors arise at the region level. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing causal sufficient and necessary regional explanations.
AI.method: The paper formulates a region-level Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency (PNS) measure through stochastic interventions and derives a differentiable finite-sample estimator for optimization. SNRE uses explicit and interpretable algebraic region families parameterized with a learnable feature mask to balance expressiveness and interpretability.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that SNRE learns region pairs with strong sufficiency-necessity performance, robust explanation behavior, and practical utility for model analysis.
AI.conclusion: SNRE provides a novel causal framework for region-level model explanations that captures both sufficiency and necessity conditions, offering more comprehensive and interpretable explanations than traditional feature importance or counterfactual methods.

title: Understanding Dynamic Scenes at Gigapixel Scale: Wide-Area Spatio-Temporal Perception from UAVs
summary: UAV-borne imaging has advanced from megapixel to gigapixel sensors, shifting aerial perception from recognizing individual targets to understanding entire dynamic scenes. We characterize this demand as Wide-area Spatio-temporal Scene Understanding (WSTU), which requires wide-area coverage, per-target resolution, and temporal continuity at once, a combination existing datasets lack. To fill this gap, we introduce an ultra-High-resolution (12768x9564) Airborne Remote-sensing Dataset (HARD) annotated at three levels for object detection, multi-object tracking, and scene-level visual question answering. Ultra-high-resolution imagery raises per-frame processing time to seconds. At that scale latency can no longer be ignored in evaluation. Thus, we propose a latency-aware metric for multi-object tracking called streaming-HOTA (s-HOTA). Extensive baseline experiments show how ultra-high-resolution processing reshapes each task. For detection, the end-to-end pipeline affects accuracy and speed as much as the detector itself does. For tracking, high latency charges the association axis far more unevenly than the detection axis, and association is where pipelines diverge. As a result, the pipeline that performs best offline can lose its lead under s-HOTA. For VQA, vision-language models remain weak at cross-frame identity binding and cannot transfer their single-frame gains to it. Together these findings show that the baselines we evaluate fall short of WSTU. HARD provides the data and the systematic baselines to advance it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HARD (High-resolution Airborne Remote-sensing Dataset), an ultra-high-resolution (12768x9564) aerial imagery dataset with three-level annotations for object detection, multi-object tracking, and scene-level visual question answering. It also proposes s-HOTA, a latency-aware tracking metric, and provides baseline experiments revealing that existing methods fall short for wide-area spatio-temporal scene understanding (WSTU).
AI.motivation: UAV-borne imaging has advanced to gigapixel sensors, requiring a shift from recognizing individual targets to understanding entire dynamic scenes. This demand is characterized as Wide-area Spatio-temporal Scene Understanding (WSTU), which requires wide-area coverage, per-target resolution, and temporal continuity simultaneously—a combination existing datasets lack.
AI.method: The authors created HARD dataset with ultra-high-resolution imagery (12768x9564) annotated at three levels: (1) object detection, (2) multi-object tracking, and (3) scene-level visual question answering. They proposed streaming-HOTA (s-HOTA), a latency-aware metric for multi-object tracking that accounts for processing time at ultra-high resolution. Extensive baseline experiments were conducted to evaluate how ultra-high-resolution processing affects each task.
AI.result: For detection, the end-to-end pipeline affects accuracy and speed as much as the detector itself. For tracking, high latency makes the association axis more uneven than the detection axis, and association is where pipelines diverge—the best offline pipeline can lose its lead under s-HOTA. For VQA, vision-language models struggle with cross-frame identity binding and cannot transfer single-frame gains to multi-frame scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The baselines evaluated fall short of WSTU requirements. HARD dataset provides the data and systematic baselines to advance research in wide-area spatio-temporal scene understanding.

title: Symbolic Temporal Supervision of LLM Agents Using Contracts
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents augmented by tools can automate complex, multi-step tasks, such as web navigation, code generation, and workflow orchestration, by acting on external systems through tool calls. However, hallucinations, distributional instability, and adversarial manipulations in LLMs, and the irreversible consequences of certain tool calls can lead to harmful outcomes. Existing safeguards either grade recorded trajectories post hoc with stochastic LLM judges or block unsafe actions one call at a time, and no single deterministic artifact supports both roles. We present ContrAgent, a contract-based framework for symbolic temporal supervision of LLM agents. ContrAgent captures an agent's behavior as a sequence of tool calls and formalizes it as a trace over a fixed set of checkable predicates. It then specifies required behaviors using assume-guarantee contracts in linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTLf). Each contract is compiled to a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that serves two roles: gating agent actions online and evaluating recorded traces offline. A contract library, acting as a reusable knowledge base, is maintained independently of the agent's model and can be applied across different agents within the same task domain. We show the effectiveness of our approach on four benchmarks spanning both roles, where ContrAgent matches state-of-the-art LLM-judge and rule-based guardrail baselines while producing deterministic, reproducible verdicts and, in the online mode, orders-of-magnitude lower per-call latency.

AI.tldr: ContrAgent is a contract-based framework that uses LTLf (Linear Temporal Logic over Finite Traces) and deterministic finite automata (DFA) to provide symbolic temporal supervision of LLM agents. It serves dual roles: gating agent actions online and evaluating recorded traces offline, with a reusable contract library independent of the agent's model.
AI.motivation: LLM agents augmented by tools can automate complex multi-step tasks, but face challenges including hallucinations, distributional instability, and adversarial manipulations. Additionally, irreversible consequences of certain tool calls can lead to harmful outcomes. Existing safeguards have limitations: they either grade trajectories post hoc using stochastic LLM judges or block unsafe actions one call at a time, with no single deterministic artifact supporting both roles.
AI.method: ContrAgent captures an agent's behavior as a sequence of tool calls formalized as a trace over checkable predicates. Required behaviors are specified using assume-guarantee contracts in LTLf. Each contract is compiled to a DFA that serves dual roles: gating agent actions online and evaluating recorded traces offline. A contract library acts as a reusable knowledge base maintained independently of the agent's model and can be applied across different agents within the same task domain.
AI.result: ContrAgent was evaluated on four benchmarks spanning both online and offline roles. It matches state-of-the-art LLM-judge and rule-based guardrail baselines while producing deterministic, reproducible verdicts. In online mode, it achieves orders-of-magnitude lower per-call latency.
AI.conclusion: ContrAgent provides an effective solution for LLM agent supervision by combining formal methods (LTLf, DFA) with practical contract-based reasoning. It achieves comparable performance to existing approaches while offering deterministic results and significant latency improvements in online mode, with the added benefit of a reusable contract library that is model-independent.

title: Beyond Embedding Transfer: Component Roles in Grokking Transfer and Stability
summary: Warm-start transfer can make algorithmic tasks generalize rapidly, yet it is unclear which model components provide the gain and whether that gain remains stable under continued optimization. We study cross-operator transfer on modular arithmetic and separate efficacy (early velocity) from stability (post-reach drawdown). In a scale-matched 108-run battery across 12 seed blocks (96-run 2^3 factorial plus 12-run scale control), transferring internal attention/MLP weights (B) alongside token embeddings and readout (E+U) improves early accuracy by 5.46 pp (Holm p=0.0039) and cuts confirmation latency by 558 steps (Holm p=0.0088). While readout plus internal-block transfer satisfies the pre-specified +/-500-step latency equivalence criterion in 1-layer models (TOST p=0.0011, though Full is faster in 11/12 paired seeds), a prospective 2-layer replication confirms the internal-block advantage (12/12 seeds, +704.67 integral units, p=4.88x10^-4) while revealing an architectural boundary: omitting donor embeddings falls 4475.6 units below Full, outside the +/-250-unit margin. Continued target training frequently triggers severe post-grokking relapse. Freezing transferred representation carriers (E, U) nearly eliminates offline relapse (19.40% -> 0.07%, Holm p=0.005859). Online validation-triggered gating slashes True Max Drawdown from 22.06% to 0.60% on 2a+b (p=0.000488), with prospective confirmations extending protection across affine, nonlinear quadratic, and 2-layer targets (10.94-23.47 pp reductions), distinguishing continual stabilization from static early stopping. In non-abelian S_5, unshielded transfer surges transiently (95.4% peak), but a prospective shielding cohort yields no confirmed benefit (+0.15 +/- 1.14 pp). These results establish a component-level dissociation between transfer acceleration and trajectory stability, and expose the empirical boundaries of parameter shielding.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates warm-start transfer learning in neural networks, specifically examining which model components (attention/MLP weights, token embeddings, readout) provide generalization gains and whether those gains remain stable during continued optimization. The study reveals a dissociation between transfer acceleration (early velocity) and trajectory stability (post-reach drawdown), with freezing transferred representations nearly eliminating relapse and validation-triggered gating providing continual stabilization.
AI.motivation: Warm-start transfer can make algorithmic tasks generalize rapidly, but it is unclear: (1) which specific model components provide the gain, and (2) whether that gain remains stable under continued optimization. The researchers aimed to dissociate efficacy (early velocity) from stability (post-reach drawdown).
AI.method: A scale-matched 108-run battery across 12 seed blocks (96-run 2^3 factorial plus 12-run scale control) was conducted on modular arithmetic tasks. They tested cross-operator transfer with different component combinations: internal attention/MLP weights (B), token embeddings (E), and readout (U). They also tested freezing transferred representations and validation-triggered gating to address post-grokking relapse. Experiments included 1-layer and 2-layer models, as well as non-abelian S_5 groups.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Transferring B+E+U improves early accuracy by 5.46 pp (Holm p=0.0039) and cuts confirmation latency by 558 steps (Holm p=0.0088); (2) 2-layer replication confirms internal-block advantage (12/12 seeds, +704.67 units, p=4.88x10^-4); (3) Omitting donor embeddings falls 4475.6 units below Full, outside the +/-250-unit margin; (4) Freezing E and U reduces offline relapse from 19.40% to 0.07% (Holm p=0.005859); (5) Online validation-triggered gating reduces True Max Drawdown from 22.06% to 0.60% on 2a+b (p=0.000488); (6) In non-abelian S_5, prospective shielding yields no confirmed benefit (+0.15 +/- 1.14 pp).
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a component-level dissociation between transfer acceleration and trajectory stability. Internal attention/MLP weights (B) combined with embeddings and readout (E+U) provide the best transfer acceleration. However, continued target training frequently triggers severe post-grokking relapse. Freezing transferred representations (E, U) nearly eliminates offline relapse, while validation-triggered gating provides continual stabilization across various target types. The results expose the empirical boundaries of parameter shielding, showing it is effective in some contexts (abelian groups) but not others (non-abelian S_5).

title: WISE: A Lightweight, Weakly-Supervised Model for Onboard Fire Smoke Detection and Localization
summary: Wildfire smoke detection from satellite imagery is critical for early warning and rapid response. For onboard satellite deployment, detection systems must operate under strict memory and latency constraints while providing spatially informative outputs for downstream decision-making. Existing tile-level classification methods are computationally efficient but lack spatial localization, whereas pixel-level segmentation approaches provide detailed masks yet are typically too computationally demanding for real-time onboard execution. To address this gap, we propose WISE (Weakly-supervised Inference-efficient Smoke Extraction), a deployment-oriented framework for onboard fire smoke detection and localization. WISE leverages only tile-level annotations through a teacher-student distillation strategy, where an offline teacher provides soft spatial supervision to a lightweight WISE-Student optimized for efficient onboard inference. The student jointly predicts tile-level smoke presence and smoke probability maps within a single forward pass, enabling spatially informative detection under strict computational constraints. WISE was evaluated through in-orbit execution aboard the ISS-mounted IMAGIN-e payload. Three model variants achieve average inference times of 0.10 s, 0.14 s, and 0.26 s per tile, indicating near-real-time per-tile inference within onboard resource limits. Ground-based experiments on Landsat 5 and Landsat 8 imagery further indicate effective detection and spatially informative localization. The best-performing variant achieves a mean tile-level F1 score of 0.964 and a mean pixel-level F1 score of 0.750 across 10 runs, while containing only 0.12M parameters and requiring approximately 3 GFLOPs. Together, these results indicate that WISE is a practical candidate for low-latency wildfire smoke monitoring from space under onboard resource constraints.

AI.tldr: WISE is a deployment-oriented framework for onboard wildfire smoke detection and localization from satellite imagery, using teacher-student distillation to achieve both tile-level classification and pixel-level localization in a single forward pass with minimal computational resources (0.12M parameters, ~3 GFLOPs).
AI.motivation: Existing methods face a trade-off: tile-level classification is computationally efficient but lacks spatial localization, while pixel-level segmentation provides detailed masks but is too computationally demanding for real-time onboard execution. There is a need for a spatially informative detection system that operates under strict memory and latency constraints for onboard satellite deployment.
AI.method: WISE employs a teacher-student distillation strategy using only tile-level annotations. An offline teacher provides soft spatial supervision to a lightweight WISE-Student model optimized for efficient onboard inference. The student jointly predicts tile-level smoke presence and smoke probability maps within a single forward pass, enabling spatially informative detection under computational constraints.
AI.result: WISE was evaluated through in-orbit execution aboard the ISS-mounted IMAGIN-e payload. Three model variants achieve average inference times of 0.10s, 0.14s, and 0.26s per tile. The best-performing variant achieves a mean tile-level F1 score of 0.964 and a mean pixel-level F1 score of 0.750 across 10 runs, with only 0.12M parameters and approximately 3 GFLOPs. Ground-based experiments on Landsat 5 and Landsat 8 imagery show effective detection and localization.
AI.conclusion: WISE is a practical candidate for low-latency wildfire smoke monitoring from space under onboard resource constraints, successfully bridging the gap between computationally efficient tile-level classification and spatially informative pixel-level segmentation.

title: Time-Aligned Evolving Concept Graphs for Scientific Relation Forecasting
summary: Forecasting scientific relations can guide discovery by identifying promising connections before they emerge. Existing approaches often model concept semantics and graph structure separately or summarize semantics over coarse historical snapshots, leaving semantic representations potentially misaligned with rapidly evolving graph evidence. We propose a time-aligned evolving concept graph framework that jointly models semantic and structural evolution. Its core idea is to treat dated papers as shared update events, reconstructing semantic and structural states from the same publication history through each prediction time. Pair-level fusion combines these states to forecast first co-occurrence, relation formation, and conditional relation type. Holding architecture and training fixed, refreshing context alongside graph updates improves mean relation AUPRC by 16.6% over frozen context. On a graph built from 187,848 papers with 270,687 concepts and 7.45 million co-occurrence links, the complete framework improves mean relation AUROC from 0.9290 for the strongest evaluated baseline to 0.9722, with mean population-weighted AUPRC 0.005778.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a time-aligned evolving concept graph framework for forecasting scientific relations (e.g., first co-occurrence, relation formation, relation type) by jointly modeling semantic and structural evolution from publication history. The framework treats dated papers as shared update events to reconstruct aligned semantic and structural states. It achieves significant improvements: 16.6% AUPRC improvement from refreshing context, and AUROC improved from 0.9290 to 0.9722 on a dataset of 187,848 papers with 270,687 concepts and 7.45M co-occurrence links.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches model concept semantics and graph structure separately or summarize semantics over coarse historical snapshots, causing semantic representations to become misaligned with rapidly evolving graph evidence. This misalignment limits the accuracy of forecasting scientific relations.
AI.method: The proposed time-aligned evolving concept graph framework jointly models semantic and structural evolution by treating dated papers as shared update events. Semantic and structural states are reconstructed from the same publication history through each prediction time. Pair-level fusion combines these states to forecast first co-occurrence, relation formation, and conditional relation type.
AI.result: Refreshing context alongside graph updates improves mean relation AUPRC by 16.6% over frozen context. On a graph built from 187,848 papers with 270,687 concepts and 7.45 million co-occurrence links, the complete framework improves mean relation AUROC from 0.9290 (strongest baseline) to 0.9722, with mean population-weighted AUPRC of 0.005778.
AI.conclusion: The time-aligned evolving concept graph framework effectively addresses the misalignment between semantic and structural representations by jointly modeling their evolution from shared publication history. This approach significantly outperforms existing baselines in forecasting scientific relations, demonstrating the value of maintaining temporal alignment between semantic context and graph structure.

title: FedPGT: Progressive Gradient Transmission for Vehicular Federated Learning over Time-Varying Channels
summary: Vehicular federated learning (VFL) enables privacy-preserving collaborative model training for intelligent transportation systems, where communication resource allocation and gradient sparsification techniques have been explored to reduce communication overhead. However, vehicle mobility leads to rapidly varying channel conditions and transmission capacity, rendering predetermined resource allocation and sparsification decisions ineffective. In this paper, we propose FedPGT, a progressive gradient transmission scheme for VFL over time-varying channels, where vehicles progressively transmit high-magnitude gradient entries in response to instantaneous channel conditions. We establish a convergence bound that characterizes the impact of transmitted gradient entries and reveals diminishing-return behavior governed by a power-law decay. Motivated by this result, we formulate a stochastic optimization problem for online decision-making, where the main challenge lies in a cumulatively coupled, non-separable objective. To handle this challenge, we introduce per-slot surrogate transmission variables to decouple the long-term dependence across time slots and convert the original objective into an additive per-slot optimization problem, enabling a Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty approach for online scheduling. We further develop a low-complexity resource allocation algorithm for efficient online implementation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves a 3.65% accuracy improvement on the CIFAR-10 image classification task and a 12.66% reduction in average displacement error on the Argoverse trajectory prediction task compared with state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating its applicability to diverse learning tasks under highly dynamic vehicular environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FedPGT, a progressive gradient transmission scheme for vehicular federated learning (VFL) that adapts to time-varying channel conditions by progressively transmitting high-magnitude gradient entries based on instantaneous channel quality. The approach uses Lyapunov optimization for online scheduling and achieves significant performance improvements on image classification and trajectory prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Vehicle mobility causes rapidly varying channel conditions and transmission capacity, making predetermined resource allocation and gradient sparsification decisions ineffective in VFL systems. Existing methods cannot adapt to these dynamic conditions in real-time.
AI.method: The paper establishes a convergence bound revealing diminishing-return behavior with power-law decay. It introduces per-slot surrogate transmission variables to decouple long-term dependence across time slots, converting the problem into an additive per-slot optimization solvable via Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty approach. A low-complexity resource allocation algorithm enables efficient online implementation.
AI.result: The proposed FedPGT achieves 3.65% accuracy improvement on CIFAR-10 image classification and 12.66% reduction in average displacement error on Argoverse trajectory prediction compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: The scheme demonstrates effective adaptation to highly dynamic vehicular environments and applicability to diverse learning tasks. The Lyapunov-based approach successfully handles the cumulatively coupled, non-separable objective in online decision-making for VFL over time-varying channels.

title: Unified Response Geometry for Structured Pruning
summary: Structured pruning is commonly formulated as ranking individual channels, although channel responses can be complementary or cancel through downstream mixing. Motivated by these response interactions, we formulate pruning as the selection of a subset with large joint response capacity, followed by a separate functional realization step. Our unified response geometry maps each candidate set to \(M(D,R)=D^{1/2}RD^{1/2}\) and uses its determinant together with Schur-greedy residuals to select non-redundant coordinates. The same construction yields two information-conditioned instances: an unlabeled instance based on activation covariance, and a task-conditioned instance that combines activation and gradient variance for response scale with gradient correlation for complementarity. To convert the selected subset into an executable network, we fold predictable removed responses into successor weights through ridge compensation and recalibrate batch-normalization statistics, without fine-tuning the network. On ImageNet ResNet-50, the unlabeled instance reaches \(65.4\%\) and \(53.9\%\) Top-1 accuracy at 30\% and 40\% deletion, versus \(59.8\%\) and \(43.1\%\) for strength-only selection; the task-conditioned instance reaches \(67.7\%\) and \(56.3\%\) under the same protocol. A six-family screen shows architecture-dependent behavior, with positive relative contrasts in several convolutional and expansion-layer settings and clear boundary cases in windowed attention. These results support response geometry as a conditional principle for structured pruning, with its benefit determined jointly by the observed response and the architecture in which that response is realized.

AI.tldr: A new structured pruning method based on response geometry that selects non-redundant channels using determinant-based metrics (M(D,R)=D^{1/2}RD^{1/2}) with Schur-greedy residuals, achieving 65.4%/67.7% Top-1 at 30% deletion on ResNet-50 versus 59.8% for strength-only selection.
AI.motivation: Traditional channel pruning ranks individual channels, but channel responses can be complementary or cancel through downstream mixing. The authors propose selecting subsets with large joint response capacity rather than individual channels.
AI.method: Unified response geometry mapping using M(D,R)=D^{1/2}RD^{1/2} with determinant and Schur-greedy residuals for selecting non-redundant coordinates. Two instances: (1) unlabeled using activation covariance, (2) task-conditioned combining activation/gradient variance with gradient correlation. Uses ridge compensation and batch-normalization recalibration for network conversion without fine-tuning.
AI.result: On ImageNet ResNet-50 at 30%/40% deletion: unlabeled instance achieves 65.4%/53.9% Top-1 (vs 59.8%/43.1% for strength-only); task-conditioned achieves 67.7%/56.3%. Six-family screen shows architecture-dependent behavior with positive contrasts in convolutional/expansion layers and boundary cases in windowed attention.
AI.conclusion: Response geometry serves as a conditional principle for structured pruning, where benefit is determined jointly by observed response and the architecture realizing that response. The method significantly outperforms strength-only selection, with effectiveness varying across architectures.

title: WFM: Wiki Foundation Model for Complex Agentic Reasoning
summary: Real-world agents fundamentally require persistent non-parametric knowledge for dynamic reasoning, i.e., long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation. While graphs have shown reliable advantages in providing structured evidence, the sparse graph representations naturally restrict machine readability and semantic density required for complex agentic workflows. Driven by this limitation, the entire industry is witnessing a paradigm shift from traditional sparse graphs to LLM Wiki, an agent-native knowledge representation that couples dense document contexts with markdown files containing multi-layered topological linkages. However, parameterizing such rich semantics is challenging to encode dense textual contexts using traditional sparse graph embeddings. Moreover, learning LLM Wiki with existing graph encoders could overwhelm distributed system overheads that hinder deployment in large-scale commercial scenarios. To this end, we propose a novel paradigm Wiki Foundation Model, i.e., WFM, tailored for scalable, agent-native representation and retrieval. Specifically, (i) we formalize a Wiki Graph schema that seamlessly bridges fine-grained structures with dense contexts, maintaining explicit topologies alongside continuous semantics; (ii) A query-conditioned attentive aggregation is tailored for rich wiki message passing and explicit attention variance regularization; (iii) We engineer an infrastructural NCCL boundary exchange protocol that hoists static partition indices and leverages fixed-shape GPU-to-GPU collectives, bypassing CPU serialization and memory copy overheads. Extensive evaluations across five long-term agent memory and multi-hop reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the remarkable performance of WFM, while achieving a 10.5 times training acceleration on distributed clusters.

AI.tldr: WFM (Wiki Foundation Model) is a novel paradigm for scalable, agent-native knowledge representation that bridges sparse graphs with dense document contexts using a Wiki Graph schema, query-conditioned attention aggregation, and NCCL-based distributed training.
AI.motivation: Traditional sparse graphs have limited semantic density and machine readability for complex agentic workflows; existing graph encoders struggle to encode dense textual contexts and create distributed system overhead that hinders large-scale deployment.
AI.method: Three key contributions: (i) Wiki Graph schema that bridges fine-grained structures with dense contexts, maintaining explicit topologies alongside continuous semantics; (ii) Query-conditioned attentive aggregation for rich wiki message passing with attention variance regularization; (iii) NCCL boundary exchange protocol that hoists static partition indices and leverages fixed-shape GPU-to-GPU collectives, bypassing CPU serialization overhead.
AI.result: Remarkable performance on five long-term agent memory and multi-hop reasoning benchmarks, with 10.5x training acceleration on distributed clusters.
AI.conclusion: WFM represents a paradigm shift from traditional sparse graphs to LLM Wiki for scalable, agent-native representation and retrieval, effectively addressing both encoding challenges and distributed system overhead.

title: Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch
summary: Autonomous research loops such as AutoResearch show that one coding agent can improve a training setup unattended. Run several of them and each session starts from scratch, so more agents tend to mean more duplicated search rather than more discovery. Agora is a shared memory for such agents: research is recorded as an append-only directed acyclic graph (DAG) stored in Git, so that every claim is a commit anyone can check out and rerun. Each result, insight, hypothesis, verification, and report is an immutable commit whose parent edges say what it builds on; a derived index exposes the frontier, the neglected branches, and the verification status of each claim, and a diversity-aware selection rule keeps the community from collapsing onto one leader. We describe the system and report its first sustained use: a run of nearly 12 days in which 13 language-model workers, with no assigned tasks and no central planner, worked on a weight-transfer problem. Given 141 pretrained donor models and a frozen 119.6M-parameter attention-SSM hybrid whose dimensions match no donor, the workers had to initialize the target without training data or gradient updates. They published 1,703 contributions and drove the evaluator from 3.39 to 1.899 bits per byte, closing 62% of the gap to a trained GPT-2 124M. The winning recipe compresses donor next-token statistics into the target's embedding and output head, then adds a short-range context signal through sparse edits to attention, feed-forward, and state-space blocks. Its 145-commit ancestry spans 15 accounts, and 165 independent reproductions were posted, none of which failed. We describe the single mid-run human intervention that pulled the community out of a monoculture, what the trace does and does not establish, and the controlled comparison that would settle whether shared research state improves discovery per unit of compute.

AI.tldr: Agora is a shared memory system for autonomous research agents that stores research as an append-only DAG in Git, enabling collaboration without central planning. In a 12-day experiment with 13 language-model workers solving a weight-transfer problem, the system produced 1,703 contributions that improved performance from 3.39 to 1.899 bits per byte (62% of GPT-2 gap), with 145 commits spanning 15 accounts and 165 independent reproductions all successful.
AI.motivation: Autonomous research loops (e.g., AutoResearch) allow a single coding agent to improve training setups, but running multiple agents results in duplicated search rather than shared discovery, as each session starts from scratch. The goal was to create a system that enables collaborative research among autonomous agents without centralized coordination.
AI.method: Agora provides a shared memory using an append-only directed acyclic graph (DAG) stored in Git, where each research contribution (claim, hypothesis, verification, report) is an immutable commit with parent edges showing dependencies. A derived index exposes the frontier, neglected branches, and verification status. A diversity-aware selection rule prevents community collapse onto one leader. The experiment used 13 language-model workers with no assigned tasks or central planner, working on initializing a 119.6M-parameter attention-SSM hybrid using 141 pretrained donor models without training data or gradient updates.
AI.result: The 13 workers produced 1,703 contributions over nearly 12 days, driving the evaluator from 3.39 to 1.899 bits per byte, closing 62% of the gap to a trained GPT-2 124M. The winning recipe compresses donor next-token statistics into the target's embedding and output head, with sparse edits to attention, feed-forward, and state-space blocks adding short-range context. The ancestry spans 145 commits across 15 accounts, with 165 independent reproductions posted, none failing.
AI.conclusion: Agora demonstrates that shared research state among autonomous agents can improve discovery per unit of compute. The single mid-run human intervention that pulled the community out of a monoculture is notable. However, a controlled comparison would be needed to definitively establish whether shared research state improves discovery. The system successfully enabled collaborative problem-solving without central planning, with strong reproducibility (165/165 successful reproductions).

title: Evolving Error States: Failure-Aware Progressive Repair for Ultrasound Lesion Segmentation
summary: Reliability under sparse and heterogeneous failures remains a fundamental challenge for medical image segmentation. High average accuracy can conceal a small set of structurally distinct and clinically consequential errors. Existing post-hoc correction methods alleviate this problem, but typically estimate false-positive and false-negative corrections from the same fixed prediction. This ignores the dynamic evolution of error states and limits the correction of complex cases. Inspired by iterative error feedback in structured prediction, we propose Failure-Aware Progressive Repair (FAPR). FAPR represents the current segmentation mask as a dynamic failure state and models each repair operation as a state-transition operator. Each accepted correction forms a new prediction state for subsequent error diagnosis and repair, enabling later operations to adapt to preceding changes. Conditional routing selectively activates necessary state transitions, while failure replay exposes the model to rare error states. By keeping the base segmentor frozen, FAPR preserves its established segmentation capability while improving difficult cases. Across three public ultrasound lesion segmentation benchmarks, FAPR improves mean DSC by 1.52%. On the very-hard subsets of BUSI and TN3K, the average gain reaches 13.77%.

AI.tldr: FAPR (Failure-Aware Progressive Repair) addresses reliability issues in medical image segmentation by modeling segmentation corrections as iterative state transitions rather than single-stage post-hoc fixes. The method maintains a dynamic failure state that evolves with each accepted correction, allowing subsequent repairs to adapt to preceding changes.
AI.motivation: High average accuracy in medical image segmentation can conceal a small set of structurally distinct and clinically consequential errors. Existing post-hoc correction methods estimate false-positive and false-negative corrections from the same fixed prediction, which ignores the dynamic evolution of error states and limits correction of complex cases.
AI.method: FAPR represents the current segmentation mask as a dynamic failure state and models each repair operation as a state-transition operator. Each accepted correction forms a new prediction state for subsequent error diagnosis and repair, enabling later operations to adapt to preceding changes. Conditional routing selectively activates necessary state transitions, while failure replay exposes the model to rare error states. The base segmentor remains frozen to preserve its established segmentation capability.
AI.result: Across three public ultrasound lesion segmentation benchmarks, FAPR improves mean DSC by 1.52%. On the very-hard subsets of BUSI and TN3K, the average gain reaches 13.77%.
AI.conclusion: FAPR effectively improves segmentation performance on difficult cases while preserving the base segmentor's capability. The progressive repair mechanism allows the system to handle complex error patterns that static correction methods cannot address.

title: Re2A: Situated Conversational Recommendation via Rubric-based Preference Reasoning and Alignment
summary: Real-world recommendation scenarios are commonly grounded in shared physical environments during user-recommender interactions. This motivates situated conversational recommendation (SCR), a complex task requiring recommender assistants to jointly reason over dialogue history, co-observed scenes, and in-scene item attributes. However, current approaches struggle with this setting due to two intertwined challenges: accurately understanding situated user preferences throughout the conversation and generating responses that simultaneously satisfy user needs and grounded situations. To this end, we propose Re2A, a framework that formulates SCR as a structured reason-then-align process. We introduce rubric-based preference reasoning, which uses automated rubrics to guide the model toward producing explicit preference states. Based on these states, we propose a preference-conditioned optimization to align response generation with dual objectives: user preference satisfaction and situation consistency. Extensive experiments on two SCR datasets demonstrate that Re2A consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering more precise, context-aware conversational recommendations. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongdingLin/Re2A.

AI.tldr: Re2A is a framework for situated conversational recommendation (SCR) that formulates the task as a structured reason-then-align process. It addresses two key challenges: understanding situated user preferences and generating contextually appropriate responses. The framework uses rubric-based preference reasoning to produce explicit preference states, then applies preference-conditioned optimization to align response generation with dual objectives of user preference satisfaction and situation consistency.
AI.motivation: Real-world recommendation scenarios often occur in shared physical environments where users and recommenders interact. Current approaches struggle with SCR due to two intertwined challenges: accurately understanding situated user preferences throughout conversations and generating responses that simultaneously satisfy user needs and grounded situations.
AI.method: The proposed Re2A framework consists of two main components: (1) Rubric-based preference reasoning - uses automated rubrics to guide the model toward producing explicit preference states; (2) Preference-conditioned optimization - aligns response generation with dual objectives: user preference satisfaction and situation consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two SCR datasets demonstrate that Re2A consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering more precise, context-aware conversational recommendations.
AI.conclusion: Re2A effectively addresses the challenges of SCR by combining structured reasoning about user preferences with alignment optimization. The framework achieves superior performance over existing methods, providing more accurate and contextually grounded conversational recommendations.

title: iMINDBench: iEEG Multi-Institution Neural Decoding Benchmark
summary: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) is widely used to record electrical activity directly from electrodes inside the human brain, making it an attractive modality for neural decoding. However, progress in iEEG decoding, especially toward general-purpose foundation models, remains difficult to measure reliably: datasets are task- or institution-specific, limiting evidence of generalization across tasks and recording environments, and preprocessing choices can strongly influence performance, making model improvements difficult to distinguish from preprocessing gains. Thus, we introduce iMINDBench, an iEEG Multi-Institution Neural Decoding Benchmark that evaluates models on a shared suite of fifteen decoding tasks across three naturalistic movie-watching datasets. The benchmark additionally defines standardized preprocessing tracks and fixed evaluation splits to support consistent model comparisons. Using iMINDBench, we find that the evaluated pretrained systems generally outperform baselines within their respective preprocessing tracks, while strong spectral baselines remain competitive across institutional datasets. In our scaling study, adding up to 25 times more supervised data from other subjects or institutions yields only small or task-dependent gains over within-session training. Together, these findings highlight the need for iEEG models that improve on strong preprocessing baselines and make more effective use of data across subjects and institutions. Project website: https://imindbench.github.io/

AI.tldr: iMINDBench is a multi-institution benchmark for intracranial EEG (iEEG) neural decoding, featuring 15 decoding tasks across 3 naturalistic movie-watching datasets with standardized preprocessing tracks. The benchmark reveals that while pretrained systems generally outperform baselines, strong spectral baselines remain competitive across institutions, and scaling with more data yields only modest gains.
AI.motivation: Progress in iEEG neural decoding is difficult to measure reliably due to: (1) datasets being task- or institution-specific, limiting evidence of generalization, and (2) preprocessing choices strongly influencing performance, making model improvements hard to distinguish from preprocessing gains.
AI.method: The authors introduce iMINDBench, an iEEG Multi-Institution Neural Decoding Benchmark that: (1) evaluates models on 15 decoding tasks across three naturalistic movie-watching datasets, (2) defines standardized preprocessing tracks, and (3) uses fixed evaluation splits for consistent comparisons. They conducted scaling studies adding up to 25x more supervised data from other subjects/institutions.
AI.result: Evaluated pretrained systems generally outperform baselines within their respective preprocessing tracks, while strong spectral baselines remain competitive across institutional datasets. Adding up to 25 times more supervised data yields only small or task-dependent gains over within-session training.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the need for iEEG models that: (1) improve on strong preprocessing baselines, and (2) make more effective use of data across subjects and institutions. The benchmark provides a standardized framework for evaluating iEEG decoding models.

title: MS-RFD: Multi-Signal Release Frame Detection in Hammer Throw from Reconstructed 3D Trajectories
summary: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and computer vision are reshaping sports performance analysis by enabling automated detection, tracking, and performance analysis. In hammer throw, performance is strongly determined by the kinematic conditions at release, particularly release speed, release angle, and release height. However, identifying the release instant from video typically requires manual frame-by-frame inspection, which is subjective and cumbersome in real-world training scenarios. In this paper, we present a fully automatic multi-signal release frame detection (MS-RFD) method for hammer throw using reconstructed 3D hammer trajectories. The proposed method integrates four complementary kinematic signals: speed dynamics, angular velocity transition, radial distance relative to the rotation center, and post-release trajectory linearity. These signals are fused to score and verify candidate release frames. MS-RFD is evaluated through the throwing-distance estimation error obtained from the release parameters estimated at the detected frame. An ablation study analyzes the contribution of each signal and compares alternative candidate selection strategies. The results show that speed dynamics and radial expansion provide the strongest signals for release frame detection, while angular velocity and post-release linearity provide smaller refinements.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MS-RFD, a fully automatic multi-signal method for detecting the release frame in hammer throw using reconstructed 3D hammer trajectories. The method integrates four kinematic signals (speed dynamics, angular velocity transition, radial distance, and post-release trajectory linearity) to score and verify candidate release frames.
AI.motivation: In hammer throw, performance is determined by release conditions (speed, angle, height), but identifying the release instant from video traditionally requires manual frame-by-frame inspection, which is subjective and cumbersome for real-world training scenarios.
AI.method: The proposed MS-RFD method integrates four complementary kinematic signals: (1) speed dynamics, (2) angular velocity transition, (3) radial distance relative to rotation center, and (4) post-release trajectory linearity. These signals are fused to score and verify candidate release frames. Evaluation is performed through throwing-distance estimation error.
AI.result: Speed dynamics and radial expansion provide the strongest signals for release frame detection, while angular velocity and post-release linearity provide smaller refinements. An ablation study analyzes the contribution of each signal.
AI.conclusion: The multi-signal approach successfully enables fully automatic release frame detection in hammer throw, with the combination of speed dynamics and radial distance being the most critical signals for accurate detection.

title: REPAIR: Resolving Long-Tail Confusion in Scientific Retrievers via Fact-Verified Iterative Refinement
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 30 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Code: https://github.com/yerimoh/REPAIR
summary: Precise retrieval of scientific information is fundamentally constrained by long-tailed concepts and high fact-sensitivity of scientific corpora. These challenges often limit the effectiveness of dense retrievers and hallucination-prone LLM augmentation. To address this, we present REPAIR, a self-evolving data augmentation framework for scientific dense retrievers. REPAIR iteratively synthesizes training data to address knowledge gaps by cycling through diagnosis of long-tail concepts, API-guided evidence expansion, and differentiation via hard negative mining. This process effectively grounds retrieval in factual reality to resolve fine-grained distinctions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REPAIR significantly outperforms 19 strong baselines on nine materials science and biomedical benchmarks. Our work highlights that diagnosing and factually augmenting data to long-tail deficits is essential for robust scientific retrieval.

AI.tldr: REPAIR is a self-evolving data augmentation framework designed to improve scientific dense retrievers by addressing long-tail concepts and fact-sensitivity challenges through iterative training data synthesis, evidence expansion, and hard negative mining.
AI.motivation: Scientific information retrieval is constrained by long-tailed concepts and high fact-sensitivity of scientific corpora, limiting the effectiveness of dense retrievers and hallucination-prone LLM augmentation.
AI.method: REPAIR uses an iterative cycle: (1) diagnosing long-tail concepts, (2) API-guided evidence expansion to gather factual information, and (3) differentiation via hard negative mining to create training data that addresses knowledge gaps and grounds retrieval in factual reality.
AI.result: REPAIR significantly outperforms 19 strong baselines on nine materials science and biomedical benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Diagnosing and factually augmenting data to address long-tail deficits is essential for robust scientific retrieval. The framework effectively grounds retrieval in factual reality to resolve fine-grained distinctions.

title: FoundAna: A GNN-assisted Foundation Model for Graph Anomaly Detection
