summary: Graph anomaly detection aims to identify graph structures (e.g., nodes, edges, or subgraphs) that deviate significantly from expected patterns, which supports critical applications in fraud detection, spam identification, network intrusion, etc. Despite the growing methods in the field, existing approaches follow a one-model-per-dataset paradigm, limiting their transferability across diverse real-world scenarios due to task heterogeneity, label scarcity, and domain variability. In this work, we introduce FoundAna, a GNN-assisted Foundation Model for Graph Anomaly Detection - the first foundation model framework designated for generalizable, cross-graph anomaly detection by combining GNNs and transformers. FoundAna integrates an anomaly detection-specific GNN component with a standard transformer encoder augmented by four complementary positional encodings, which enable the model to capture both local and global structural information. Specifically, the positional encoding enriched node representations are passed through attribute and adjacency decoders, and the reconstruction errors serve as the anomaly score. Extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets spanning financial, social, and citation network domains demonstrate that FoundAna consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code implementation and Supplementary materials are here: https://github.com/FoundAna331/FoundAna.

AI.tldr: FoundAna is the first foundation model for generalizable, cross-graph anomaly detection, combining GNNs with transformers and four complementary positional encodings to capture both local and global structural information. It uses attribute and adjacency decoders where reconstruction errors serve as anomaly scores.
AI.motivation: Existing graph anomaly detection approaches follow a one-model-per-dataset paradigm, limiting transferability across diverse real-world scenarios due to task heterogeneity, label scarcity, and domain variability. There was a need for a generalizable foundation model for cross-graph anomaly detection.
AI.method: FoundAna integrates an anomaly detection-specific GNN component with a standard transformer encoder augmented by four complementary positional encodings. The positional encoding enriched node representations are passed through attribute and adjacency decoders, and reconstruction errors serve as the anomaly score.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets spanning financial, social, and citation network domains demonstrate that FoundAna consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: FoundAna represents the first foundation model framework designated for generalizable, cross-graph anomaly detection, successfully combining GNNs and transformers to achieve superior performance across diverse domains.

title: Decoder-Agnostic Token Merging for Vision Transformers: A Systematic Study of G2TM
comment: Extended version of https://cea.hal.science/cea-05578363, to be published in Communications in Computer and Information Science (CCIS), Springer. Codes are available at https://github.com/vbercy/g2tm
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a range of computer vision tasks, mainly thanks to the self-attention mechanism. However, its complexity, increasing quadratically with the number of tokens, remains the major obstacle to ViT efficiency and deployment at scale. Token merging reduces this cost by aggregating redundant tokens. Yet existing methods are typically evaluated within a single architecture, leaving open whether their effectiveness stems from the merging mechanism itself or from the specific decoder they are paired with. We extend Graph-Guided Token Merging (G2TM), a single module inserted early in a ViT-based network, beyond its original Segmenter setting. We evaluate G2TM across three semantic segmentation frameworks (Segmenter, SETR, EoMT) and three decoder families (Linear, Transformer-, convolution-based), as well as standard ViT image classification. Our results show that G2TM's behavior and accuracy-efficiency trade-off are consistent across every tested architecture for a given backbone size, indicating that its effectiveness is a property of the encoder rather than the decoder. G2TM also generalizes well to image classification, achieving an even smaller degradation in accuracy compared to semantic segmentation. We further find that G2TM's optimal hyperparameters, resulting in a consistent drop in GFLOPs of 22-47% and an increase in throughput by up to 74% for segmentation models on ADE20K dataset, depend primarily on the backbone's pre-training recipe and on the target dataset, rather than on the decoder choice.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates Graph-Guided Token Merging (G2TM) across multiple semantic segmentation frameworks (Segmenter, SETR, EoMT) and decoder families (Linear, Transformer-, convolution-based), as well as ViT image classification, to determine whether G2TM's effectiveness stems from the merging mechanism or the specific decoder it's paired with.
AI.motivation: Token merging reduces the quadratic complexity of self-attention in Vision Transformers, but existing methods are only evaluated within single architectures. It was unclear whether effectiveness came from the merging mechanism itself or from specific decoder interactions.
AI.method: Extended G2TM (originally for Segmenter) across three semantic segmentation frameworks and three decoder families, plus standard ViT image classification. Tested across different backbone sizes and analyzed hyperparameter optimization.
AI.result: G2TM's behavior and accuracy-efficiency trade-off are consistent across all tested architectures for a given backbone size, indicating effectiveness is a property of the encoder rather than the decoder. G2TM generalizes well to image classification with smaller accuracy degradation. Optimal hyperparameters depend on backbone's pre-training recipe and target dataset, not decoder choice. Achieved 22-47% GFLOPs reduction and up to 74% throughput increase on ADE20K.
AI.conclusion: G2TM's effectiveness is intrinsic to the encoder rather than decoder-dependent. The method consistently improves efficiency across architectures while maintaining accuracy. Optimal hyperparameters are primarily determined by backbone pre-training and dataset characteristics, not decoder architecture.

title: BENCHCOMPASS: From Scores to Signals for Training and Harness Decisions in Payment-Domain LLMs
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Payment operations are a critical financial infrastructure, but the value of large language models in this domain remains unclear because payment rules change quickly, evidence is fragmented, and decisions depend on transaction state, participant role, region, and payment rail. Existing benchmarks do not isolate whether failures come from missing payment-rule knowledge, poor use of supplied evidence, or brittleness under imperfect harness inputs. We introduce BENCHCOMPASS, a payment-domain benchmark whose construction pipeline builds scenario-grounded tasks from typed evidence packs, applies LLM-based quality checks, creates task-input attack variants, and reserves final item admission for domain experts. The release contains an expert-reviewed Pro benchmark covering payment knowledge, context-grounded scenario reasoning, and Attacked Open robustness, plus a lower-assurance Normal pool for inspection and future curation. Across 16 model variants, BENCHCOMPASS shows qualitatively different failure modes: missing parametric payment knowledge, incomplete reasoning over supplied rules, and failure to reject plausible but invalid workflows. The benchmark remains unsaturated: the best frontier model reaches 89.6% on Open Context-Grounded Reasoning and 81.7% under attacked inputs, while a representative 32B open-weight model reaches 69.8% and 42.6%. Benchmark data and code are available at https://github.com/ant-intl/BenchCompass.

AI.tldr: BENCHCOMPASS is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large language models on payment operations, addressing gaps in existing benchmarks by isolating failure modes (missing knowledge, poor evidence use, brittleness under attack). It contains expert-reviewed tasks covering payment knowledge, context-grounded reasoning, and robustness under adversarial inputs.
AI.motivation: Payment operations are critical financial infrastructure, but LLM value in this domain remains unclear due to rapid rule changes, fragmented evidence, and complex decision factors (transaction state, participant role, region, payment rail). Existing benchmarks fail to isolate whether failures stem from missing knowledge, poor evidence utilization, or brittleness under imperfect inputs.
AI.method: The construction pipeline: (1) Builds scenario-grounded tasks from typed evidence packs, (2) Applies LLM-based quality checks, (3) Creates task-input attack variants, (4) Reserves final item admission for domain experts. Tests across 16 model variants.
AI.result: Best frontier model achieves 89.6% on Open Context-Grounded Reasoning and 81.7% under attacked inputs. A representative 32B open-weight model reaches 69.8% and 42.6% respectively. Identified failure modes: missing parametric payment knowledge, incomplete reasoning over supplied rules, and failure to reject plausible but invalid workflows.
AI.conclusion: BENCHCOMPASS reveals qualitatively different failure modes in LLMs for payment operations. The benchmark remains unsaturated, with significant room for improvement. The release includes an expert-reviewed Pro benchmark and a lower-assurance Normal pool for future curation.

title: Learning Fractional-Order Dynamics from a Single Trajectory
summary: Many real-world processes exhibit long-range dependence, where the current state depends on a slowly decaying trace of past states rather than on the most recent state alone. This paper studies system identification for discrete-time fractional-order linear time-invariant systems from a single observed trajectory of length $t$, a setting that captures such non-Markovian dynamics through the Grünwald--Letnikov difference operator. Unlike Markovian systems, fractional-order systems couple estimation across the entire history, making both statistical analysis and practical identification more challenging. We propose \emph{Fractional-Order Ordinary-Least-Squares Grid-Search (FO-GS)}, a simple two-stage estimator that exploits the diagonal structure of the fractional-difference operator to decouple the identification problem row-wise. Under the stability assumption, we establish high-probability, non-asymptotic error bounds for estimating both the fractional order and the system matrix in the heterogeneous setting, with both estimation errors scaling as \(\mathcal{O}(t^{-1/2})\). Through experiments, we show that \emph{FO-GS} outperforms existing baselines in recovering both the fractional order and the underlying system dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FO-GS (Fractional-Order Ordinary-Least-Squares Grid-Search), a two-stage estimator for identifying discrete-time fractional-order linear time-invariant systems from a single observed trajectory. The method exploits the diagonal structure of the fractional-difference operator to decouple the identification problem row-wise, addressing the challenge of long-range dependence in non-Markovian dynamics.
AI.motivation: Many real-world processes exhibit long-range dependence, where current states depend on slowly decaying traces of past states rather than recent states alone. Fractional-order systems capture this through the Grünwald-Letnikov difference operator, but unlike Markovian systems, they couple estimation across the entire history, making both statistical analysis and practical identification more challenging.
AI.method: The proposed FO-GS is a two-stage estimator that exploits the diagonal structure of the fractional-difference operator to decouple the identification problem row-wise. Under the stability assumption, the method establishes high-probability, non-asymptotic error bounds for estimating both the fractional order and the system matrix in the heterogeneous setting.
AI.result: Both estimation errors scale as O(t^{-1/2}). Through experiments, FO-GS outperforms existing baselines in recovering both the fractional order and the underlying system dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The FO-GS method successfully addresses the challenging problem of identifying fractional-order systems with long-range dependence, providing theoretical guarantees with O(t^{-1/2}) convergence rates and demonstrating superior empirical performance over existing approaches.

title: Who Audits Whom, on What Substrate, with What Evidence? An Independence-Graded Audit Protocol for Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI systems plan, invoke tools and act with limited supervision; they are now both the subject of audits and, increasingly, the auditor. Independence, the foundation of assurance,is still applied to them as a binary. We argue that it must be graded along three orthogonal axes: principal independence (who controls the auditor), substrate independence (an auditor sharing the auditee's foundation-model family, toolchain or guardrails fails with it) and evidence independence (whether evidence is attestable rather than self-reported). Each axis has precedent; the contribution is to grade all three on a single audit, aggregate them by the weakest link, and apply the same rubric when the auditor is itself an agent. We give the model a formal basis by transplanting the beta-factor model of common-cause failure from reliability engineering, a seven-step protocol whose outputs a third party can verify, a structural detectability analysis of a procurement-controls agent audited at three grades, and a Monte Carlo study of the model in which a conventional internal audit of an agent-a real audit team, a second agent, provider logsp-surfaces 5.9% of the faults it could in principle see and none at all in half the fault classes. We map the triple to the EU AI Act as amended, ISO/IEC 42006, UK public-sector risk-management guidance and audit-regulator practice.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that AI auditor independence should be graded on three axes (principal, substrate, evidence) rather than treated as binary, and proposes a formal framework using the beta-factor model from reliability engineering to assess and aggregate independence levels.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that agentic AI systems are now both being audited and serving as auditors, but traditional independence concepts don't account for the unique risks of AI systems sharing common foundations, tools, or guardrails with their auditees.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal framework by: (1) transplanting the beta-factor model from reliability engineering; (2) proposing a seven-step verifiable protocol; (3) conducting structural detectability analysis on a procurement-controls agent at three grades; (4) running Monte Carlo simulations comparing conventional vs. AI auditing
AI.result: The Monte Carlo study reveals that conventional internal auditing of AI agents only surfaces 5.9% of detectable faults, and fails to detect any faults in half the fault classes—demonstrating significant gaps in current audit practices.
AI.conclusion: The triple-axis graded independence framework should be applied uniformly whether the auditor is human or AI, and the framework maps to existing regulatory regimes (EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42006, UK guidance).

title: Colla-Q: Toward Collaborative Experts in MoE Quantization via Minimax Precision Balancing
comment: Accepted by the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) 2026
summary: In this paper, we present a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) quantization method based on activation entropy. Although quantization reduces memory and computational costs, it can substantially degrade performance. In particular, performance decline is pronounced in quantized MoE models, where individual experts have a small number of parameters that are sensitive to low-bit representation. Considering that MoE operates as an ensemble model with collaborative contributions from routed experts, a significant performance decline of a particular expert due to quantization can harm model performance. Therefore, we propose Colla-Q, a bit-allocation framework to maintain balanced performance across experts through an activation-entropy-based bit-width allocation algorithm. This approach encourages each expert to operate collaboratively in the quantized model, thereby 1) improving the overall MoE performance and 2) reducing the dependence on the calibration dataset. Since uniformly adjusting each expert's performance facilitates robustness and stability of the MoE model, the proposed MoE quantization method can generalize more consistently across different calibration datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/mmai-laboratory/Colla_Q

AI.tldr: Colla-Q is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) quantization method that uses activation entropy-based bit-width allocation to maintain balanced performance across experts. It addresses the problem that quantization significantly degrades performance in MoE models due to individual experts being sensitive to low-bit representation.
AI.motivation: Quantization reduces memory and computational costs but degrades performance, especially in MoE models where individual experts have small parameter counts and are sensitive to low-bit representation. Since MoE operates as an ensemble with collaborative contributions from routed experts, significant performance decline in any single expert can harm overall model performance.
AI.method: Proposes Colla-Q, a bit-allocation framework based on activation entropy. The method allocates bit-width to each expert using an activation-entropy-based algorithm, encouraging collaborative operation across all experts in the quantized model. This approach reduces dependence on calibration datasets by uniformly adjusting each expert's performance.
AI.result: 1) Improves overall MoE performance, 2) Reduces dependence on calibration dataset, 3) Provides more robust and stable MoE model, 4) Generalizes more consistently across different calibration datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MoE quantization method can generalize more consistently across different calibration datasets due to balanced performance across experts, making the quantized MoE model more robust and stable.

title: Can MiniMax-H3 Reason About the Physical World? An Evaluation of Omni-Modal Generative Model
summary: Recent Omni-Modal Generative Models (Omni-Models) have advanced content generation toward unified modeling of text, images, video, and audio. MiniMax-H3 exemplifies this transition by combining multimodal context understanding with joint audio-visual generation in a shared latent framework. Its unified architecture raises a fundamental question: Can multimodal alignment improve the model's world reasoning, and what new evaluation paradigms do omni-modal inputs enable? To investigate this question, this work introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework organized around four complementary dimensions of physical world reasoning. Unlike existing evaluation frameworks for video generation and world models, which are often constrained by limited input modalities and evaluation settings where prompts closely match the target video content, our evaluation is specifically designed to exploit the multimodal inputs of Omni-Model. We construct a diverse set of novel tasks that require models to integrate complementary information across modalities. Specifically, we consider four scenarios, including implicit prompts paired with multiple frames, audio-image, prefix-videos, and audio-video inputs. Every single modality provides only partial evidence about the underlying event, requiring the model to jointly reason over the complementary semantic cues to infer latent event states and future dynamics. Across 517 evaluation instances, MiniMax-H3 achieves an overall success rate of 41.97%. Video-based Decision Reasoning yields the highest success rate at 56.00%, while Audio-based Disambiguation Reasoning is the weakest, reaching only 27.40%. These results indicate that effective multimodal integration remains key to fully exploiting the benefits of diverse input modalities. The project is available at https://github.com/gulucaptain/MiniMax-H3-Reason.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework for omni-modal generative models (like MiniMax-H3) that can process text, images, video, and audio. The framework evaluates physical world reasoning across four scenarios requiring joint reasoning over complementary multimodal inputs. The model achieved 41.97% overall success rate across 517 evaluation instances.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a fundamental question: whether multimodal alignment can improve a model's world reasoning capabilities, and what new evaluation paradigms omni-modal inputs enable. Existing evaluation frameworks are limited to single modalities and prompts closely matching target content, missing the opportunity to test joint reasoning across modalities.
AI.method: The authors constructed a diverse set of novel tasks across four complementary scenarios: (1) implicit prompts with multiple frames, (2) audio-image inputs, (3) prefix-videos, and (4) audio-video inputs. Each modality provides only partial evidence about underlying events, requiring models to integrate complementary semantic cues to infer latent event states and future dynamics.
AI.result: Across 517 evaluation instances, MiniMax-H3 achieved an overall success rate of 41.97%. Video-based Decision Reasoning performed best at 56.00%, while Audio-based Disambiguation Reasoning was weakest at 27.40%.
AI.conclusion: Effective multimodal integration remains the key challenge in fully exploiting the benefits of diverse input modalities. The gap between the best (56.00%) and worst (27.40%) reasoning types indicates significant room for improvement in multimodal reasoning capabilities.

title: Building Trust in Artificial Intelligence: A Necessity for Railway Applications
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is currently only applied to non-safety critical applications due to the strict standards and regulations for railway industries. We propose to review the three main fields necessary to increase trust in data science and AI algorithms and reach compliance: robustness, Operational Design Domain (ODD), and explainability. Robustness is the ability of an AI system to maintain its level of performance under any circumstances (ISO24029). ODDs allow the explicit definition of operating conditions under which a system is intended to operate, according to the recently published DIN DKE SPEC 99004. Explainability is the property of an AI system to express important factors influencing the AI system results in a way that humans can understand. Those 3 domains of research are already well investigated by nonrailway actors, with algorithms and methods ready to use for railway applications. A system view is necessary to ensure all trustworthy requirements interact continuously in a safe MLOps environment thereby fostering acceptance from regulators, operators and the public. Beyond safeguarding safety-critical applications, we aim to show that fostering deep trust in AI, as now required by regulatory frameworks worldwide, will unlock its full potential and transform the pace of adoption across mission-critical domains.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews three key domains (robustness, ODD, and explainability) needed to increase trust in AI algorithms for safety-critical railway applications, enabling compliance with strict industry standards. The authors argue these well-established research areas from non-railway sectors can be adapted for railway use through a system view in a safe MLOps environment.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to bridge the gap between AI's potential and its current limitation to non-safety critical applications in railways, driven by strict regulatory requirements. The authors aim to foster acceptance from regulators, operators, and the public by addressing trust concerns.
AI.method: The paper proposes a review approach, examining three research domains (robustness, ODD, explainability) that are already well-developed in non-railway contexts, and suggesting how they can be integrated into a system view with safe MLOps for railway applications.
AI.result: The paper identifies that algorithms and methods from these three domains are already ready for adaptation to railway applications. It emphasizes that a system view is necessary to ensure trustworthy requirements interact continuously in a safe MLOps environment.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion suggests that fostering deep trust in AI, as required by regulatory frameworks worldwide, will not only safeguard safety-critical applications but also unlock AI's full potential and transform adoption across mission-critical domains.

title: Rethinking How We Evaluate Methodological Progress in Health AI
summary: Methodological progress in artificial intelligence (AI) for electronic health records (EHRs) depends on our ability to determine which algorithms work better, and under which conditions. However, such progress is thought to be hindered by difficulties in reproducibility and in defining clinically meaningful evaluation tasks. We empirically study these barriers by re-implementing 12 historical and recent algorithms within a shared evaluation framework and evaluating them on two clinical datasets, MIMIC-IV and NWICU. We compare two complementary task families: expert-authored clinically meaningful tasks and generated tasks defined from randomly sampled event codes and prediction horizons. We ask whether relative algorithms comparisons transfer across task families and datasets, whether residual task heterogeneity contains useful methodological structure, and what a controlled comparison reveals about progress over the last decade. We find that aggregate pairwise comparisons transfer strongly across evaluation settings, including from randomly generated tasks to clinically meaningful tasks and across datasets. At the same time, clinically meaningful tasks exhibit greater task-method interaction, providing preliminary evidence that task properties can help explain when particular modeling choices are advantageous. Finally, newer algorithms do not consistently outperform earlier approaches: gradient-boosted trees remain highly competitive when paired with a modern, wide and sparse representation of the EHR. Together, these results suggest that useful methodological knowledge may require less task engineering than commonly assumed, while highlighting the importance of understanding the structured heterogeneity that remains across tasks and methods.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates 12 AI algorithms for electronic health records (EHRs) on MIMIC-IV and NWICU datasets, comparing expert-authored clinical tasks with randomly generated tasks. The study finds that algorithm rankings transfer across evaluation settings, though clinically meaningful tasks show more task-method interaction. Surprisingly, newer algorithms don't consistently outperform older approaches like gradient-boosted trees.
AI.motivation: The AI field for EHRs lacks clarity on which algorithms perform better under specific conditions. Progress is hindered by reproducibility issues and difficulties in defining clinically meaningful evaluation tasks. This study aims to understand these barriers empirically.
AI.method: The researchers re-implemented 12 historical and recent algorithms within a shared evaluation framework. They evaluated these on two clinical datasets (MIMIC-IV and NWICU) using two task families: expert-authored clinically meaningful tasks and randomly generated tasks (random event codes and prediction horizons). They analyzed whether algorithm comparisons transfer across task families and datasets, examined task heterogeneity structure, and assessed progress over the last decade.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Aggregate pairwise comparisons transfer strongly across evaluation settings, including from randomly generated tasks to clinically meaningful tasks and across datasets. (2) Clinically meaningful tasks exhibit greater task-method interaction, suggesting task properties can explain when particular modeling approaches are advantageous. (3) Newer algorithms do not consistently outperform earlier approaches—gradient-boosted trees remain highly competitive with modern wide and sparse EHR representations.
AI.conclusion: Useful methodological knowledge in EHR AI may require less task engineering than commonly assumed. However, understanding the structured heterogeneity across tasks and methods remains important. The study suggests that algorithm comparisons are relatively robust across different evaluation contexts, but task-specific factors still matter for method selection.

title: PDA++: Field-Aligned Planning and Scene-Adaptive Insertion in Remote Sensing
comment: Extended journal version of our ICML 2026 paper "Plan, Decouple, Assimilate: Physics-Aware Object Insertion in Remote Sensing Imagery"
summary: Remote sensing recognition is often constrained by scarce observations of rare targets and costly annotations, making realistic synthetic augmentation particularly valuable for few-shot and long-tailed scenarios. Object insertion provides an efficient way to increase target diversity while preserving authentic background scenes, but realistic insertion in overhead imagery requires the generated target to adapt coherently to its surrounding environment. To this end, we propose PDA++, a unified environment-aware object insertion framework organized as Plan, Decouple, and Assimilate. Planning determines scene-compatible poses through an affordance field that combines geometric clearance with structure- and scale-aware cues. Decoupling introduces a pose-conditioned background that provides precise spatial guidance together with target-scene context, allowing the reference object to preserve its identity while adapting to the target observation. This construction also naturally provides pixel-level masks for segmentation augmentation. Assimilation further improves local coherence by aligning multi-scale texture distributions through optimal transport. On the optical benchmark, PDA++ achieves a whole-image FID of 6.28 and improves average few-shot recognition mAP50 by 17.69 points, corresponding to a 28.8% relative gain over the real-data baseline. On SAR imagery, it improves ship detection by 4.10 mAP50 points and remains effective under cross-dataset transfer and amorphous-target insertion. Code is available at https://github.com/lisheyu972/PDA_PLUS.

AI.tldr: PDA++ is a unified environment-aware object insertion framework for synthetic augmentation in remote sensing. It addresses few-shot and long-tailed recognition challenges by inserting synthetic objects into overhead imagery with realistic adaptation to surrounding environments. The framework consists of three modules: Plan (scene-compatible pose determination), Decoupling (pose-conditioned background for spatial guidance), and Assimilation (texture distribution alignment via optimal transport).
AI.motivation: Remote sensing recognition is constrained by scarce observations of rare targets and costly annotations. Synthetic augmentation is particularly valuable for few-shot and long-tailed scenarios, but realistic object insertion in overhead imagery requires the generated target to adapt coherently to its surrounding environment.
AI.method: The proposed PDA++ framework has three components: (1) Planning - uses an affordance field combining geometric clearance with structure- and scale-aware cues to determine scene-compatible poses; (2) Decoupling - introduces a pose-conditioned background providing precise spatial guidance with target-scene context, allowing reference objects to preserve identity while adapting to target observation, also providing pixel-level masks for segmentation augmentation; (3) Assimilation - improves local coherence by aligning multi-scale texture distributions through optimal transport.
AI.result: On optical benchmark: whole-image FID of 6.28, improves average few-shot recognition mAP50 by 17.69 points (28.8% relative gain over real-data baseline). On SAR imagery: improves ship detection by 4.10 mAP50 points. Also effective under cross-dataset transfer and amorphous-target insertion.
AI.conclusion: PDA++ successfully enables realistic synthetic augmentation in remote sensing imagery. The environment-aware object insertion framework significantly improves few-shot recognition performance on both optical and SAR benchmarks, with good generalization capability across datasets and target types.

title: Where Should Agents Live? Energy-Memory Characterization of Agentic AI for the Edge-Cloud Continuum
summary: As telecommunication networks evolve toward autonomous 5G-Advanced and 6G operations, agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workflows, where large language models (LLMs) execute multi-step reasoning, invoke diagnostic tools, retrieve domain knowledge, and coordinate across agent teams, are increasingly embedded across the edge-cloud continuum. While the biological brain accomplishes complex cognition on an exceptionally modest metabolic power budget of approximately 20W contemporary LLMs are profoundly energy- and memory-intensive, making sustainable lifecycle orchestration a critical operational priority. However, existing AI lifecycle metrics evaluate only isolated, single-model inferences or overlook multi-agent execution graphs entirely. Consequently, network operators lack foundational models to determine whether distributed agent communication incurs meaningful energy costs and where across edge-cloud tiers agent teams should physically reside. To address this gap, we introduce agentic-eCAL, generalizing the Energy Cost of AI Lifecycle (eCAL) metric to directed multi-agent workflows by coupling a closed-form two-rate single-call energy model (compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode) with 7-layer OSI data transport. Grounded in hundreds of GPU benchmark configurations on NVIDIA A100 and H100, 16 open-weight models and 8 orchestration topologies, we validate components of the metric and study workflow placement implications. Our findings demonstrate that inter-agent text transport incurs 0.25% of workflow energy across 5G RAN, metro, and optical links. Therefore in edge-cloud agent placement the dominant energy cost of distribution is often not the transmission of inter-agent text itself, but the additional inference and context processing induced by that communication.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "agentic-eCAL," a metric for evaluating energy costs of distributed AI agent workflows across edge-cloud continuum in 5G-6G networks. The key finding is that inter-agent text transmission accounts for only 0.25% of total workflow energy, making inference and context processing the dominant energy costs.
AI.motivation: Existing AI lifecycle metrics evaluate only isolated single-model inferences or overlook multi-agent execution graphs entirely. Network operators lack models to determine energy costs of distributed agent communication and optimal physical placement across edge-cloud tiers. LLMs are energy- and memory-intensive while biological brains operate on ~20W, making sustainable lifecycle orchestration critical for autonomous 5G-Advanced and 6G operations.
AI.method: The authors generalize the Energy Cost of AI Lifecycle (eCAL) metric to directed multi-agent workflows by: (1) coupling a closed-form two-rate single-call energy model (compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode) with 7-layer OSI data transport; (2) validating with hundreds of GPU benchmark configurations on NVIDIA A100 and H100, 16 open-weight models, and 8 orchestration topologies.
AI.result: Inter-agent text transport incurs only 0.25% of workflow energy across 5G RAN, metro, and optical links. The dominant energy cost of distribution is not the transmission of inter-agent text itself, but the additional inference and context processing induced by that communication.
AI.conclusion: For edge-cloud agent placement, the primary energy consideration should focus on inference and context processing costs rather than network transmission bandwidth. This provides network operators with foundational models to determine where agent teams should physically reside across edge-cloud tiers.

title: Reaching Every Position Without Searching: Rotating Sparse Wiring on the Hypercube as a Substitute for Attention
summary: Attention pays, at every layer and for every input, the cost of searching for whom to connect. We ask how far one can get with wiring that is fixed, sparse, and simply rotated from layer to layer. Treating the $n$ positions of a sequence as the vertices of a $\log_2 n$-dimensional hypercube and connecting each position, at layer $\ell$, to its neighbour along dimension $\ell \bmod \log_2 n$, information from every position reaches every other in $\log_2 n$ layers with $2n$ links per layer instead of $n^2$. On a synthetic task that is unsolvable unless all positions are reached, this rotation matches all-to-all wiring at $1/32$ of the links, while the same sparse pattern held fixed across layers fails; what matters is that every dimension is touched, not the order. On character-level language modelling of a public corpus (the first $12$M characters of enwik8), a hybrid that keeps two attention layers among sixteen sparse ones reaches $0.06$ bits-per-character lower held-out loss than a fully attentive model of the same width at the same step budget (three seeds each, no overlap), with $1/7$ of the links, $42\%$ fewer parameters, and $2.4\times$ less wall-clock time; the purely rotated schedule is level with the hybrid. The same ordering holds on a second corpus of mixed Japanese, English and code, where the gap widens to $0.16$. The usable learning-rate window is four to eight times wider than attention's on both. We also report what did not work - learned coordinates, and a "dynamics" variant whose apparent gains turned out to be an artefact of a saturated kernel - and the measurement discipline (frozen corpus, full-coverage evaluation, seed spread as the bar for ranking) that we found necessary to say anything at all at this scale.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a "rotated" sparse attention mechanism where fixed sparse connections rotate across dimensions (based on hypercube topology) from layer to layer. This achieves comparable performance to full attention with 1/7 the links, 42% fewer parameters, and 2.4× speedup, while also providing a 4-8× wider learning rate window.
AI.motivation: Attention mechanisms incur heavy computational costs from dynamically determining connections at every layer and for every input. The authors investigate whether fixed, sparse, and systematically rotated wiring can replace learned attention while maintaining performance.
AI.method: The authors treat n sequence positions as vertices of a log₂n-dimensional hypercube. Each position at layer ℓ connects to its neighbor along dimension ℓ mod log₂n, creating a fixed sparse pattern that rotates across dimensions. They also test a hybrid approach with 2 attention layers among 16 sparse ones. Evaluation uses synthetic tasks (requiring all positions to communicate) and character-level language modeling on enwik8 (12M characters) and a mixed Japanese/English/code corpus.
AI.result: On the synthetic unsolvable task, rotated wiring matches all-to-all attention at 1/32 of the links, while fixed sparse patterns fail. On enwik8, the hybrid achieves 0.06 bits-per-character lower loss than full attention with 1/7 the links, 42% fewer parameters, and 2.4× faster wall-clock time. On the mixed corpus, the gap widens to 0.16 bits-per-character. The learning rate window is 4-8× wider than attention. What failed: learned coordinates and a "dynamics" variant whose gains stemmed from a saturated kernel artifact.
AI.conclusion: Fixed rotated sparse wiring can match or exceed full attention on language modeling tasks with dramatically reduced computational cost. The key is touching every dimension (not the specific order), and the wider learning rate window improves training robustness. The measurement discipline (frozen corpus, full-coverage evaluation, seed spread for ranking) was essential for valid comparisons at this scale.

title: Pose2Muscle: Structured Spatio-Temporal Decoding for Discrete Muscle Activity Estimation from Human Pose
summary: Muscle activity is fundamental to human movement, and understanding its patterns is critical for injury prevention and rehabilitation. Conventional muscle activity monitoring relies on specialized sensors such as surface electromyography, which limits its practicality for long-term real-world use. Existing studies suggest that muscle-related information can be inferred from human pose. However, the substantial gap between externally observable pose and internal muscle activation, limits the accuracy and generalization of current approaches. In this study, we propose Pose2Muscle, a pose-driven framework for discrete muscle activity estimation without requiring sEMG signals at inference time. Instead of directly regressing continuous sEMG signals, Pose2Muscle reformulates muscle estimation as a structured prediction problem over discrete muscle activity states, yielding a more stable and interpretable target space. The framework combines multi-scale spatio-temporal attention to capture motion patterns at complementary spatial and temporal scales with a directed acyclic graph-based decoder that maintains multiple candidate muscle-state hypotheses and performs structured trajectory inference over time. To support this task, we construct PoseEMG-43, a synchronized pose-sEMG dataset containing 2,992 movement instances from 43 daily-life actions performed by 14 participants. Experiments show that Pose2Muscle consistently outperforms representative retrieval- and pose-based baselines. It achieves an Adjacent-level Accuracy of 86.36% and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.8821 under the Random Split, and 63.97% and 0.6795, respectively, under the Subject-Level Split. These results demonstrate the feasibility of inferring structured muscle-state patterns from human pose and suggest the potential of Pose2Muscle for muscle-aware movement analysis when direct physiological sensing is impractical

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Pose2Muscle, a framework that infers discrete muscle activity states from human pose data without requiring sEMG sensors at inference time. It reformulates muscle estimation as a structured prediction problem and uses multi-scale spatio-temporal attention with a DAG-based decoder. The method is evaluated on a new dataset (PoseEMG-43) with 43 daily-life actions.
AI.motivation: Conventional muscle activity monitoring relies on sEMG sensors, which limits practicality for long-term real-world use. Although muscle-related information can be inferred from pose, the substantial gap between externally observable pose and internal muscle activation limits accuracy and generalization of current approaches.
AI.method: Pose2Muscle reformulates muscle estimation as a structured prediction problem over discrete muscle activity states (rather than continuous sEMG regression). It combines: 1) Multi-scale spatio-temporal attention to capture motion patterns at complementary spatial and temporal scales; 2) Directed acyclic graph-based decoder that maintains multiple candidate muscle-state hypotheses and performs structured trajectory inference over time. The PoseEMG-43 dataset was constructed with 2,992 movement instances from 43 daily-life actions performed by 14 participants.
AI.result: Pose2Muscle outperforms retrieval- and pose-based baselines. Under Random Split: 86.36% Adjacent-level Accuracy, 0.8821 Pearson correlation. Under Subject-Level Split: 63.97% Adjacent-level Accuracy, 0.6795 Pearson correlation.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of inferring structured muscle-state patterns from human pose, suggesting potential for muscle-aware movement analysis when direct physiological sensing is impractical. The performance drop under Subject-Level Split indicates some generalization challenges across subjects.

title: What Counts as Strategic Reasoning? A Systematic Mapping of Chess Research on Humans, Engines, and Language Models
comment: Under review; replication package available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695754
summary:
Chess has long served as a model domain for studying search, expertise, decision-making, and artificial intelligence. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has renewed the relevance of chess as a controlled environment for investigating strategic reasoning and comparing human and artificial decision-making. We present a systematic mapping study of recent research spanning human players, classical chess engines, neural and reinforcement-learning systems, LLMs, and hybrid approaches. The final map comprises 84 core study families, classified according to agent type, strategic-reasoning stages, and evaluation dimensions.
  The map reveals a literature strongly concentrated on situation assessment, evaluation, and action selection, while explicit planning, explanation, metacognition, and human--AI collaboration remain less explored. LLM research places particular emphasis on state representation and generalization, whereas grounded explanation appears more frequently in hybrid approaches combining language models with engines, expert knowledge, or other external structures. Two distinctions emerge that the map aggregates rather than resolves: hybrid systems differ in where and when heterogeneous capabilities combine, and evaluations that show improved human performance do not thereby establish human--AI synergy. We propose both as extensions of the mapping framework.
  We argue that chess provides a useful bridge between cognitive and computational perspectives on strategic reasoning, and identify explicit planning, grounded and faithful explanation, metacognitive calibration, and human--AI complementarity as directions for future research.

AI.tldr: A systematic mapping study of 84 research families examining chess as a domain for studying strategic reasoning across human players, classical engines, neural/RL systems, LLMs, and hybrid approaches. The study reveals gaps in explicit planning, explanation, metacognition, and human-AI collaboration, while identifying two key distinctions: where/how hybrid systems combine capabilities, and the difference between improved human performance and true human-AI synergy.
AI.motivation: Chess serves as a model domain for studying search, expertise, decision-making, and AI. The emergence of LLMs has renewed interest in chess as a controlled environment for investigating strategic reasoning and comparing human and artificial decision-making.
AI.method: Systematic mapping study classifying 84 core study families according to agent type (human players, classical engines, neural/RL systems, LLMs, hybrid approaches), strategic-reasoning stages, and evaluation dimensions.
AI.result: The literature concentrates heavily on situation assessment, evaluation, and action selection. Explicit planning, explanation, metacognition, and human-AI collaboration remain less explored. LLM research emphasizes state representation and generalization, while grounded explanation appears more in hybrid approaches. Two key distinctions emerge: (1) hybrid systems differ in where and when heterogeneous capabilities combine, and (2) improved human performance does not establish human-AI synergy.
AI.conclusion: Chess provides a useful bridge between cognitive and computational perspectives on strategic reasoning. Future research should focus on explicit planning, grounded and faithful explanation, metacognitive calibration, and human-AI complementarity.

title: LIGE-GR: A Smooth Leap from Ranking to Generative Recommendation in the LLM Era
summary:
The remarkable success of large language models (LLMs) has provided important inspiration for the next generation of recommender systems. Structurally, recommendation and language generation share a similarity: both aim to produce an ordered sequence that optimizes the user's experience. However, how to precisely absorb the essence of the LLM paradigm into mature industrial recommender systems remains an open problem.
  There are two challenges. First, it is unclear how to incorporate sequence-level generation and optimization from the LLM paradigm into recommendation. Second, real-world recommender systems are mature systems that have been iteratively customized for years around specific products, business constraints, serving infrastructure, and organizational ownership. Replacing such systems wholesale is often technically risky and organizationally disruptive.
  In this paper, we propose LIGE-GR, a listwise generation and evaluation recommendation framework that upgrades from a traditional ranking system based on itemwise recommendation toward a generative recommendation paradigm. Instead of rebuilding the entire recommendation stack from scratch, LIGE-GR generalizes the existing pointwise recommendation system into a listwise generation system. This allows mature recommender systems to benefit from listwise optimization while preserving compatibility with existing models, value functions, and serving infrastructure.
  We validate LIGE-GR in short-video recommendation on Instagram Reels and Facebook Video. On these recommendation surfaces, LIGE-GR improves time spent by 1.14 percent on Instagram Reels and 0.72 percent on Facebook Video, while requiring only modest additional inference resources.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LIGE-GR, a listwise generation and evaluation recommendation framework that upgrades traditional pointwise recommendation systems to a generative paradigm. The framework allows mature recommender systems to benefit from listwise optimization while preserving compatibility with existing infrastructure, validated on Instagram Reels and Facebook Video with modest improvements in time spent.
AI.motivation: The success of large language models (LLMs) provides inspiration for next-generation recommender systems, as both aim to produce ordered sequences optimizing user experience. However, integrating LLM paradigm into mature industrial recommender systems faces two challenges: incorporating sequence-level generation and optimization, and replacing existing systems without technical risk or organizational disruption.
AI.method: LIGE-GR generalizes existing pointwise recommendation systems into a listwise generation system rather than rebuilding the entire recommendation stack. It preserves compatibility with existing models, value functions, and serving infrastructure while enabling listwise optimization.
AI.result: Validated on short-video recommendation (Instagram Reels and Facebook Video), LIGE-GR improves time spent by 1.14% on Instagram Reels and 0.72% on Facebook Video, while requiring only modest additional inference resources.
AI.conclusion: LIGE-GR successfully bridges the gap between LLM paradigm and industrial recommender systems by enabling listwise optimization without wholesale system replacement, demonstrating practical improvements in real-world deployment with minimal resource overhead.

title: Visual Input and Its Framing Affect Attribute-based Descriptions Produced by Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are commonly used with only a single text prompt as the input, or plus an image. In this paper, we demonstrate that when the image exists, even if the text prompt is not about the specific instance (but only the concept it belongs to) in that image, the response would still be affected. For example, when the text prompt only asks for the attribute descriptions of a dog breed, an image depicting a specific dog from that breed would shift the response. Further, how the specific instance is framed in that image would determine towards which the response shifts. Detailed analyses also reveal that in the response, physical terms increase from 18% for text-only to 45% (40%) for subject-focused (subject-in-situation) framings. Overall, the unexpected effects of visual cues on LVLMs highlight the need to understand the presence of an image and its framing when evaluating the robustness of LVLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that images in LVLMs affect responses even when text prompts only ask about general concepts, not specific instances. The way the subject is framed in the image determines the direction of response shifts, with physical terms increasing significantly (18% → 45%/40%) compared to text-only inputs.
AI.motivation: The authors investigate an overlooked phenomenon: when LVLMs receive an image alongside a text prompt about a general concept, the specific instance in the image unexpectedly influences the response, even though the text doesn't mention that specific instance.
AI.method: The authors conducted experiments comparing responses across three conditions: (1) text-only prompts, (2) text prompts with subject-focused images, and (3) text prompts with subject-in-situation images. They analyzed the linguistic content of responses, particularly the proportion of physical terms used.
AI.result: The presence of an image shifts LVLM responses even when the text only asks about general concepts. The framing of the image (subject-focused vs. subject-in-situation) determines the direction of this shift. Physical terms increased from 18% in text-only conditions to 45% for subject-focused framings and 40% for subject-in-situation framings.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights the need to consider image presence and framing when evaluating LVLM robustness, as visual cues have unexpected and significant effects on model responses.

title: Visual Compliance via Executable Safety Rule Entailment
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 36 pages, 20 figures, 24 tables
summary: Recent advances in LLMs and VLMs have enabled safety systems to reason beyond simple risk patterns toward more contextual and semantic safety concerns. However, as risk patterns continue to evolve and safety rules become more complex, existing training-based end-to-end safeguards face persistent challenges in adaptability and explainable reasoning over complex safety rules. To address these challenges, we propose GuardEn (Guarding by Safety Rule Entailment), an executable safeguard framework that decomposes safety policies into atomic propositions through Safety-Rule Compilation, modeling their composition as executable code. At test time, Scene-Grounded Execution instantiates these atomic propositions with contextual visual information derived from scene graphs, enabling rule-grounded and interpretable safety reasoning. Experiments on SafetyVisionBench demonstrate the effectiveness of programmable safeguard for complex visual safety assessment, achieving an average improvement of 9.8 F1 points over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: GuardEn is a programmable safeguard framework for LLMs and VLMs that decomposes safety policies into atomic propositions, uses scene graphs for contextual reasoning, and achieves 9.8 F1 points improvement over baselines on SafetyVisionBench.
AI.motivation: Existing training-based end-to-end safeguards face challenges in adaptability and explainable reasoning as risk patterns evolve and safety rules become more complex. There's a need for systems that can reason over complex safety rules in a contextual and interpretable manner.
AI.method: The proposed GuardEn framework has two main components: (1) Safety-Rule Compilation - decomposes safety policies into atomic propositions modeled as executable code; (2) Scene-Grounded Execution - instantiates atomic propositions with contextual visual information from scene graphs at test time, enabling rule-grounded and interpretable safety reasoning.
AI.result: Experiments on SafetyVisionBench demonstrate that GuardEn achieves an average improvement of 9.8 F1 points over the strongest baseline for complex visual safety assessment.
AI.conclusion: The programmable safeguard approach (GuardEn) effectively addresses the challenges of adaptability and explainable reasoning in visual safety assessment for LLMs and VLMs, showing significant performance improvements over existing methods.

title: MoRE: Mixture of Reused Experts
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2026)
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures decouple model capacity from computational cost, yet incur high memory footprints as parameters grow linearly with the number of experts. Recurrent Transformers achieve parameter efficiency by reusing layer weights, but typically lack the capacity for competitive language modeling. We propose Mixture of Reused Experts (MoRE), a hybrid that shares expert pools across groups of adjacent layers. Each layer retains its own router but selects from a larger shared pool, expanding the diversity of routing combinations without additional parameters. To enable shared experts to distinguish between layers, we introduce lightweight learnable depth embeddings that condition each layer's input before routing. Experiments across three model scales (114M-1.15B parameters) show that MoRE consistently achieves lower perplexity and stronger downstream performance than standard MoEs and state-of-the-art weight-sharing architectures at matched compute and parameter budgets, with only minimal modifications to existing MoE implementations.

AI.tldr: MoRE proposes a hybrid Mixture-of-Experts architecture that shares expert pools across adjacent layers while maintaining per-layer routers, combined with lightweight depth embeddings to enable shared experts to distinguish between layers. This achieves parameter efficiency without sacrificing model capacity.
AI.motivation: MoE architectures decouple model capacity from computational cost but suffer from high memory footprints as parameters scale linearly with experts. Recurrent Transformers achieve parameter efficiency through weight reuse but lack competitive language modeling capacity. There is a need for architectures that combine parameter efficiency with strong modeling capacity.
AI.method: MoRE introduces: (1) Shared expert pools across groups of adjacent layers - each layer retains its own router but selects from a larger shared pool, expanding diversity of routing combinations without additional parameters; (2) Lightweight learnable depth embeddings that condition each layer's input before routing, enabling shared experts to distinguish between layers.
AI.result: Experiments across three model scales (114M-1.15B parameters) show MoRE consistently achieves lower perplexity and stronger downstream performance than standard MoEs and state-of-the-art weight-sharing architectures at matched compute and parameter budgets.
AI.conclusion: MoRE successfully combines parameter efficiency with competitive language modeling performance. It requires only minimal modifications to existing MoE implementations while outperforming both standard MoEs and weight-sharing approaches at matched compute and parameter budgets.

title: Online Multi-Camera 3D Tracking via ID Prediction over Recurrent Sparse Queries
summary: Online multi camera 3D tracking must maintain scene global identities across synchronized views, yet query-based trackers carry these identities only implicitly in the instance bank, where they fragment upon query interruption. We present an online architecture that recovers association accuracy by predicting IDs explicitly over recurrent sparse queries. An outside-in Sparse4D detector fuses calibrated views into world frame 3D detections while propagating a sparse query bank, and a causal MOTIP ID decoder associates detections against a finite trajectory memory. We adapt MOTIP's relative-ID prediction and recycled slot runtime to globally fused 3D observations, and introduce metric spatial gating and proximity based newborn recovery. On the official 2026 AI City Challenge Track 1 test set, our method raises HOTA from 29.63 with native instance bank identities to 38.01, primarily through an AssA increase from 20.83 to 31.10, and ranks third on the public leaderboard. Full-sequence validation over all 9,000 frames of each scene shows that decoupled ID training improves HOTA over native identities, whereas continuing detector training alongside the detached ID objective produces scene-dependent gains and losses.

AI.tldr: An online multi-camera 3D tracking architecture that recovers association accuracy by predicting IDs explicitly over recurrent sparse queries, rather than relying on implicit identities in instance banks. Uses Sparse4D detector for world frame 3D detection fused from calibrated views, combined with a causal MOTIP ID decoder for trajectory association. Achieved HOTA improvement from 29.63 to 38.01 on AI City Challenge Track 1 test set.
AI.motivation: Query-based multi-camera 3D trackers carry identities only implicitly in the instance bank, where they fragment upon query interruption. This limitation causes loss of global identity associations across synchronized views, reducing tracking accuracy.
AI.method: 1) Outside-in Sparse4D detector fuses calibrated views into world frame 3D detections while propagating a sparse query bank. 2) Causal MOTIP ID decoder associates detections against a finite trajectory memory. 3) Adapts MOTIP's relative-ID prediction and recycled slot runtime to globally fused 3D observations. 4) Introduces metric spatial gating and proximity-based newborn recovery. 5) Decoupled ID training from detector training.
AI.result: HOTA improved from 29.63 to 38.01 (28% relative gain), with AssA increase from 20.83 to 31.10 (49% relative gain). Ranked third on public leaderboard. Full-sequence validation over 9,000 frames per scene showed decoupled ID training improves HOTA over native identities, while joint detector training produces scene-dependent results.
AI.conclusion: Explicit ID prediction over recurrent sparse queries significantly improves multi-camera 3D tracking accuracy compared to implicit instance bank identities. Decoupled ID training is beneficial, but combining detector training with detached ID objective requires careful consideration as it produces scene-dependent gains and losses.

title: Faithful yet Collusive: Why Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Cannot Detect Collusion in LLM Pricing Agents under Oligopolistic Competition
comment: 20 pages, Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language models (LLM) deployed as autonomous pricing agents may sustain supracompetitive prices through tacit coordination. We develop a causal graph divergence framework that separately measures structural faithfulness and intent faithfulness of LLM pricing agents in Bertrand competition. Across nine LLMs under duopoly and triopoly conditions, collusive behavior and chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness dissociate along both dimensions: the most collusive model accurately reports cooperative intent yet reasons structurally unfaithfully, while the most structurally faithful model sustains supra-Nash pricing under both market structures. These findings establish that CoT monitoring alone cannot serve as a standalone safeguard against algorithmic collusion.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) deployed as autonomous pricing agents can sustain collusive pricing (supracompetitive prices) through tacit coordination, and whether chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring can detect such collusion.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of LLM-based autonomous agents in economic contexts raises concerns about algorithmic collusion—irms using AI agents may unknowingly engage in anti-competitive behavior. A key question is whether monitoring the reasoning process (CoT) of these agents can detect and prevent collusive outcomes.
AI.method: The authors develop a causal graph divergence framework to separately measure two dimensions of LLM behavior: (1) structural faithfulness—whether the model's reasoning aligns with the actual causal structure of the decision-making process, and (2) intent faithfulness—whether the model accurately reports its cooperative/coordinated intentions. They test this across nine LLMs under Bertrand competition settings with both duopoly (2 firms) and triopoly (3 firms) conditions.
AI.result: The study finds that collusive behavior and CoT faithfulness dissociate along both dimensions. The most collusive model accurately reports cooperative intent (high intent faithfulness) but reasons in a structurally unfaithful manner. Conversely, the most structurally faithful model still sustains supra-Nash pricing (above competitive levels) under both market structures. This means CoT monitoring alone fails to detect the collusion risk.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought monitoring alone cannot serve as a standalone safeguard against algorithmic collusion. The dissociation between structural faithfulness, intent faithfulness, and actual collusive outcomes suggests that regulators and firms need more comprehensive frameworks to detect and prevent AI-driven anti-competitive behavior.

title: Transformation Laws in Neural Representations: Structure, Realisability, and Construction
summary: How neural representations preserve the structure of input changes connects representation analysis with internal intervention. We study operable representational content through compatible actions of reference transformations on neural features. We characterise when a transformation descends through an encoder, and give a linear setting in which the defect is governed by the transformation's demand for discarded information, measured in the metric the representation induces. On a rectifier the failure to realise a transformation has two distinguishable sources --- what the source region has already made unrecoverable, and what it costs to satisfy every region the transformation visits with one operator --- and for a \textit{measured} harmonic carrier the same question has a closed answer: a linear realisation exists exactly when the retained harmonic blocks are invariant under the action. Using colour as the in-depth instance, we find that hue orbits in frozen visual features concentrate 84--88\% of their energy in the first two harmonics with rotation planes shared across shapes, that this organisation is substantially inherited from input and architecture and is reshaped by training and depth, and that the measured structure supports prediction, transport from new starting states, and composition --- with global and local realisations differing sharply in which they achieve. Guided by the measurements, we construct a compact interface whose rotation action is fixed by the structure and never fitted: it reads hue zero-shot at 3.4$^\circ$ median error on unseen shapes. Theory, structural measurement, and construction together establish transformation laws as a concrete object connecting the understanding of neural representations to their design.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how neural representations preserve the structure of input transformations, connecting representation analysis with internal intervention. The authors develop a theoretical framework for characterizing when transformations can be realized through neural encoders, apply it to color/hue representations in vision networks, and construct a zero-shot hue reader achieving 3.4° median error.
AI.motivation: Understanding how neural representations preserve the structure of input transformations is crucial for connecting representation analysis with internal intervention. The authors aim to establish "transformation laws" as concrete objects that bridge the understanding of neural representations to their design.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework characterizing when reference transformations descend through encoders, analyzing linear settings where transformation "defect" is governed by discarded information. They distinguish two failure sources in rectifier networks: unrecoverable information in source regions and costs of satisfying transformation requirements across regions. For harmonic carriers, they derive closed-form conditions for linear realizability. Empirically, they measure hue orbits in frozen visual features, analyze harmonic decomposition, and construct an interface based on measured structure.
AI.result: Theoretically, the authors characterize conditions for transformations to descend through encoders. Empirically, hue orbits concentrate 84-88% of energy in the first two harmonics with rotation planes shared across shapes. This organization is substantially inherited from input and architecture, reshaped by training and depth. The measured structure supports prediction, transport from new starting states, and composition, with global and local realizations differing sharply. The constructed interface achieves 3.4° median error on unseen shapes without any fitting.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes transformation laws as concrete objects connecting the understanding of neural representations to their design. The combination of theory, structural measurement, and practical construction provides a principled approach to understanding and manipulating neural representations, with color/hue serving as a detailed validation case.

title: JigSync: Gauge-Resolved Synchronization for Jigsaw Reassembly under Unknown Piece Orientation
summary: Square jigsaw reassembly requires recovering the spatial arrangement of shuffled fragments from their visual content and pairwise relationships. While recent studies have made substantial progress, existing benchmarks typically assume that all fragments are provided upright, reducing reassembly to a permutation problem. We study the generalized problem in which each fragment may also have gone through an unknown rotation. For this setting we establish a gauge-unobservability theorem: the minimum of the weighted least-squares objective is exactly invariant under a uniform global rotation of arbitrary magnitude, so no residual-based criterion can recover the global orientation. The theorem further identifies how the issue of global orientation can be resolved: an orientation anchor estimated from the content of a single fragment, lying outside its scope, suffices. To address the above, we propose JigSync, which attains 63.8% and 31.8% absolute accuracy (AA) on GAP-3 and GAP-5, respectively, the highest reported on both, while additionally recovering a rotation per piece that neither benchmark requires. We release JigSync, a degradation protocol that sweeps shape, erosion, photometry, grid size, and rotation independently.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the generalized square jigsaw reassembly problem where fragments can have unknown rotations, not just position. The authors establish a gauge-unobservability theorem showing that global rotation cannot be recovered from residual-based criteria, and propose JigSync which achieves state-of-the-art results by using an orientation anchor from fragment content.
AI.motivation: Existing jigsaw benchmarks assume fragments are upright, reducing the problem to permutation only. This paper aims to generalize the problem to include unknown rotations for each fragment, which is more realistic but introduces a fundamental identifiability issue.
AI.method: The authors prove a gauge-unobservability theorem: the weighted least-squares objective is invariant under uniform global rotation. They resolve this by using an orientation anchor estimated from a single fragment's content. Their method JigSync recovers both spatial arrangement and rotation per piece.
AI.result: JigSync achieves 63.8% absolute accuracy on GAP-3 and 31.8% on GAP-5, the highest reported on both benchmarks, while additionally recovering rotation per piece.
AI.conclusion: The gauge-unobservability theorem identifies the fundamental limitation of residual-based methods for global orientation recovery. By using content from a single fragment as an orientation anchor, the problem becomes solvable. JigSync sets new state-of-the-art results while providing additional rotation information not required by existing benchmarks.

title: Market Signal Injection: Adversarial Context Manipulation of LLM Pricing Agents
comment: 30 pages, Accepted to FinNLP 2026 Workshop @ EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language model (LLM) pricing agents may respond to how market data is presented, even when its numerical values remain unchanged. We introduce market signal injection (MSI), an attack that manipulates numerical formatting, competitor ordering, or qualitative market commentary without issuing explicit instructions. We evaluate nine open-weight models in simulated Bertrand duopoly and triopoly markets and three proprietary models in duopoly markets. Sentiment-based attacks produce the largest behavioral shifts, which propagate to other firms and alter profits and consumer surplus. Susceptibility varies across model families, and larger models are not consistently more robust. Matched neutral-text controls and a rule-based agent support a framing-based account of these shifts under the fixed demand parameters of our simulation. Episode-held-out probes distinguish baseline from attacked activations in all eleven re-evaluated model--condition pairs: linear AUC is 1.00 and MLP AUC ranges from 0.93 to 0.99. This separability does not by itself identify harmful pricing decisions. Input canonicalization removes the tested sentiment attacks, while decision boundary anchoring, which combines prompt constraints with output projection, provides partial mitigation under the tested adaptive attacks. These results identify data presentation as an attack surface for LLM pricing agents and motivate defenses that account for interactions among agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces market signal injection (MSI), an attack that manipulates LLM pricing agents by changing numerical formatting, competitor ordering, or qualitative commentary without explicit instructions. The attack exploits how market data is presented rather than its numerical values.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a novel attack surface for LLM-based pricing agents: how market data is presented (formatting, ordering, sentiment) rather than the data itself. This is motivated by the growing use of LLMs as autonomous agents in market contexts.
AI.method: The study evaluates nine open-weight models in simulated Bertrand duopoly and triopoly markets, plus three proprietary models in duopoly markets. They use matched neutral-text controls, rule-based agents, and episode-held-out probes to distinguish baseline from attacked activations.
AI.result: Sentiment-based attacks produce the largest behavioral shifts. These shifts propagate to other firms and alter profits and consumer surplus. Susceptibility varies across model families, and larger models are not consistently more robust. Linear probe AUC reaches 1.00, and MLP AUC ranges from 0.93 to 0.99 for distinguishing attacked from baseline activations.
AI.conclusion: Data presentation is a significant attack surface for LLM pricing agents. Input canonicalization can remove sentiment attacks, while decision boundary anchoring provides partial mitigation under adaptive attacks. Defenses must account for multi-agent interactions.

title: A Lightweight CNN Integrated Compact Convolutional Transformer for Multi-Scale Feature Learning and reducing computational complexity for breast cancer mammography image detection and classification
summary: Over the years, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated strong capability in cancer detection and classification using medical images. However, CNN-based models often struggle to capture long-range contextual dependencies. In such scenarios, integrating Compact Convolutional Transformer (CCT) architectures after the CCT layer allows CNN-extracted features to reshape into compact patch tokens using a CCT tokenizer, followed by the addition of positional embeddings to preserve spatial structure. Using 5-fold cross-validation, the model was tested on 3 sets of breast cancer mammography. With only 250,435 parameters, the model achieved 99%-100% accuracy across 3 datasets, indicating robust generalization. Explainable AI (XAI) was integrated into the model to explain the breast cancer classification process to enhance clinical trust. The results indicate that the proposed framework is suitable for computer-aided diagnosis systems, particularly in resource-constrained clinical environments. The novelty of the proposed CNN-integrated CCT overcomes the limitation of CNN's gradient degradation in the last layers by integrating convolutional tokenization with transformer-based learning. Lighter than ViT, which is effective in capturing long-range dependencies, the model has also proven efficient in breast cancer classification by capturing long-range dependencies among breast tissue regions.

AI.tldr: A lightweight CNN-integrated Compact Convolutional Transformer (CCT) model for breast cancer classification in mammography images, achieving 99-100% accuracy across 3 datasets with only 250,435 parameters while incorporating Explainable AI (XAI) for clinical trust.
AI.motivation: CNN-based models struggle to capture long-range contextual dependencies in medical image analysis, and existing Vision Transformers (ViT) are computationally heavy. The study aimed to overcome CNN's gradient degradation in last layers while maintaining efficiency for resource-constrained clinical environments.
AI.method: CNN-extracted features are reshaped into compact patch tokens using a CCT tokenizer, followed by positional embeddings to preserve spatial structure. The model was tested using 5-fold cross-validation on 3 breast cancer mammography datasets. XAI was integrated to explain the classification process.
AI.result: The model achieved 99%-100% accuracy across 3 datasets with only 250,435 parameters, demonstrating robust generalization. It effectively captures long-range dependencies among breast tissue regions while being lighter than ViT.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CNN-integrated CCT framework is suitable for computer-aided diagnosis systems, particularly in resource-constrained clinical environments. It successfully combines CNN's local feature extraction with transformer's long-range dependency modeling while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: MSR: Multiple Subject Reference for Video Generation
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures. Model weights and inference workflows are publicly available
summary: Conditioning a video generator on multiple images requires preserving appearance while associating each reference with its intended role. We present MSR (Multiple Subject Reference), a slot-aware conditioning scheme for LTX-based video generation. Each reference image is independently encoded as a static clip and represented by a separate latent-token group. A compact Fourier-feature multilayer perceptron adds a numeric slot embedding, while slot-dependent temporal offsets modify the group's rotary coordinates. The reference groups are prepended to noisy target tokens and serve as clean context during target-only flow-matching training.
