We implement this scheme through low-rank adaptation and release the resulting weights and inference workflows. Qualitative examples demonstrate compositions containing distinct characters and referenced environments in realistic and stylized scenes. Development observations suggest reduced reference confusion relative to an earlier continuous-reference baseline, while similar clothing, complex garments, and viewpoint changes remain challenging. We describe the conditioning mechanism, the retained training configuration, and the observed strengths and limitations of the released system. A supplementary audio-reference experiment adds voice conditioning while keeping the visual parameters frozen.

AI.tldr: MSR is a slot-aware conditioning scheme for LTX-based video generation that enables multiple reference images to be used while preserving appearance and associating each reference with its intended role. Each reference is encoded as a separate latent-token group with slot embeddings and temporal offsets.
AI.motivation: The core challenge is conditioning a video generator on multiple images while preserving individual appearance and correctly associating each reference image with its intended role in the generated video.
AI.method: Each reference image is independently encoded as a static clip and represented by a separate latent-token group. A compact Fourier-feature multilayer perceptron adds a numeric slot embedding, while slot-dependent temporal offsets modify the group's rotary coordinates. The reference groups are prepended to noisy target tokens and serve as clean context during target-only flow-matching training. Implementation uses low-rank adaptation.
AI.result: Qualitative examples demonstrate compositions containing distinct characters and referenced environments in realistic and stylized scenes. The system shows reduced reference confusion compared to an earlier continuous-reference baseline, though similar clothing, complex garments, and viewpoint changes remain challenging. A supplementary audio-reference experiment adds voice conditioning while keeping visual parameters frozen.
AI.conclusion: The released system successfully enables multi-subject reference conditioning in video generation with preserved appearance fidelity. Key limitations include challenges with similar clothing, complex garments, and viewpoint changes. The audio-reference experiment demonstrates the approach can be extended to voice conditioning while freezing visual parameters.

title: Bad Genius: Counterfactual-Guided Harness Evolution Beyond Task-Specific Shortcuts
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures; includes references and supplementary material
summary: Reliable agent evaluation is complicated by automatic harness optimization, which repeatedly uses a released benchmark $B_{\mathrm{rel}}$ to guide a Proposer that edits prompts, memory, retrieval, tools, and control code around a fixed target agent. Task holdout varies semantic tasks but leaves the benchmark protocol fixed, so a "bad genius" Proposer can produce a cheating harness whose released-benchmark gain depends on a benchmark-wide shortcut. We introduce Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE), which casts harness evolution as constraint generation over validity-preserving benchmark counterfactuals. After each Proposer update, a Challenger searches for an executable protocol transformation with large gain destruction. A validity firewall checks that task semantics are preserved, while a confirmation set determines whether the counterfactual enters a finite archive. We formalize an exact shortcut-neutralized benchmark $B_0$ and establish statistical guarantees linking finite counterfactual archives to $B_0$ and characterizing sequential Challenger search. We evaluate CHASE on a synthetic benchmark and on OfficeQA, where CHASE retains strong released-benchmark gains while substantially reducing gain destruction under valid protocol changes.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical flaw in agent evaluation where automatic harness optimization allows "cheating harnesses" to exploit benchmark shortcuts. The authors propose CHASE (Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution), which uses counterfactual analysis and a Challenger-Adversary framework to identify and neutralize such shortcuts while preserving valid task semantics.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that automatic harness optimization can manipulate evaluation benchmarks through a Proposer that edits prompts, memory, retrieval, tools, and control code around a fixed target agent. This creates "bad genius" harnesses whose gains depend on benchmark-wide shortcuts rather than genuine agent capability. Task holdout methods vary semantic tasks but leave the benchmark protocol fixed, failing to address this fundamental vulnerability.
AI.method: CHASE operates through three key components: (1) A Challenger that searches for executable protocol transformations capable of destroying harness gains after each Proposer update; (2) A validity firewall that ensures task semantics are preserved during transformations; (3) A confirmation set that determines whether counterfactuals enter a finite archive. The method formalizes an exact shortcut-neutralized benchmark B₀ and provides statistical guarantees linking finite counterfactual archives to B₀.
AI.result: Evaluated on a synthetic benchmark and OfficeQA, CHASE demonstrates the ability to retain strong released-benchmark gains while substantially reducing gain destruction under valid protocol changes. The approach successfully identifies and neutralizes shortcut-dependent gains while preserving legitimate evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a principled framework for robust agent evaluation that addresses the fundamental vulnerability of harness optimization. By casting the problem as constraint generation over validity-preserving counterfactuals and using adversarial search, CHASE offers a practical solution to detect and mitigate benchmarking shortcuts. The statistical guarantees and empirical validation on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks (OfficeQA) demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

title: APGEM: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation for Quantum Reinforcement Learning on a Real-World CVRP Case Study
comment: Accepted at The 6th International Multi-Conference on Artificial Intelligence Technology (MCAIT2026)
summary: Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) represents policies as variational quantum circuits (VQCs), making it attractive for combinatorial optimization such as the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP). On noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, however, decoherence degrades fidelity and destabilizes learning, and conventional error mitigation is applied statically without regard to the learning context. We introduce Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), a controller that selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE), Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC), Clifford Data Regression (CDR), and Readout Error Mitigation (REM) online, driven by a fidelity, entropy, and cost aware utility function and an epsilon-greedy rule over temporal-difference Q-scores. We evaluate on a realistic urban-logistics testbed, a Delhi-based CVRP over real landmarks with geodesic inter-node costs, exercised across five noise families and four severity levels. On this instance, the QRL agent outperforms constructive heuristics and approaches metaheuristics, while mitigation restores approximation ratios from 0.84-0.87 to 0.92-0.94 under high noise. The controller shifts from a CDR-dominated regime under short training horizons to a balanced deployment across all four techniques under longer horizons, indicating genuine regime-dependent selection. These preliminary results position adaptive, learning-aware mitigation as a practical route to noise-resilient QRL.

AI.tldr: APGEM is a novel controller that adaptively selects among four quantum error mitigation techniques (ZNE, PEC, CDR, REM) to enhance Quantum Reinforcement Learning for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem on noisy hardware, improving approximation ratios from 0.84-0.87 to 0.92-0.94.
AI.motivation: NISQ hardware suffers from decoherence that degrades fidelity and destabilizes learning in Quantum Reinforcement Learning; conventional error mitigation is applied statically without considering the learning context, making adaptive, learning-aware mitigation necessary.
AI.method: APGEM uses a fidelity, entropy, and cost-aware utility function with an epsilon-greedy rule over temporal-difference Q-scores to dynamically select among four error mitigation techniques (ZNE, PEC, CDR, REM). Evaluation was done on a Delhi-based CVRP with real landmarks and geodesic inter-node costs across five noise families and four severity levels.
AI.result: QRL agent outperforms constructive heuristics and approaches metaheuristics. Error mitigation restores approximation ratios from 0.84-0.87 to 0.92-0.94 under high noise. The controller shifts from CDR-dominated regime under short training horizons to balanced deployment across all techniques under longer horizons.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, learning-aware error mitigation represents a practical route to noise-resilient QRL, with regime-dependent selection providing genuine adaptability across different training conditions.

title: A Non-Linear Neuron Based Detection of Isolated Pixels in Binary and Grayscale Images using Contrast Sensitive Receptive Fields
summary: Identifying isolated points is important in image processing applications such as medical imaging, astronomy and quality control management. Other domains, such as cybersecurity, also present challenges that can be framed as image processing problems. One example of particular interest is the identification of anomalous single nodes in spatially organised networks where groups of nodes in different regions share similar feature values. This task can involve both binary and more complex grayscale images. However, existing methods face limitations: template matching is infeasible for grayscale images, while 2nd order derivative based methods are highly sensitive to noise and require user-specified thresholds. To overcome these issues, a novel method is proposed for detecting meaningful single-pixel deviations in images. This approach modifies and extends a neuron model, originally designed for anomaly detection, to operate on spatially diameter limited receptive fields that incorporate excitatory and inhibitory regions. The result is a method that is free from user-specified thresholds and parameters, and can be applied to both binary and grayscale images, providing an effective, robust and efficient solution.

AI.tldr: A novel threshold-free method for detecting isolated single-pixel anomalies in both binary and grayscale images, based on a modified neuron model with spatially limited receptive fields containing excitatory and inhibitory regions.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for identifying isolated points (anomalies) have significant limitations: template matching fails for grayscale images, while 2nd order derivative-based approaches suffer from noise sensitivity and require user-specified thresholds. This creates a need for a robust, parameter-free solution applicable across medical imaging, astronomy, quality control, and cybersecurity domains.
AI.method: The proposed method modifies and extends a neuron model originally designed for anomaly detection. It operates on spatially diameter-limited receptive fields that incorporate both excitatory and inhibitory regions, enabling detection of meaningful single-pixel deviations without any user-specified thresholds or parameters.
AI.result: The method successfully detects single-pixel anomalies in both binary and grayscale images, providing an effective, robust, and efficient solution that avoids the limitations of existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The novel approach offers a significant advancement in isolated point detection by eliminating the need for user-specified parameters while maintaining effectiveness across different image types. It provides a practical solution for various applications including medical imaging, astronomy, quality control, and cybersecurity anomaly detection in spatially organized networks.

title: Cultural Competence in Context: A Large Language Model Passes the Turing Test in Finland
summary: We report the results of a Turing Test conducted in Finland in the Finnish language. Because languages and cultural contexts are unevenly represented in LLM training data, we expected the model (ChatGPT 5.2) to perform worse in a Finnish-language Turing Test than in previously studied English-language US contexts. We also present model-generated role prompting as a replicable technique for conducting comparative LLM-based Turing Tests designed to improve construct validity. Contrary to our expectations, the LLM passed the Finnish Turing Test. A prominent source of error was participants' reliance on linguistic cues, particularly colloquial Finnish, as markers of human authorship. We reframe the Turing Test from a test of intelligence to a comparative method for examining whether an AI system can display credible membership in a particular social world. Because its outcome reflects model capabilities, prompted identity, insider competence among human participants, and their AI literacy, the method provides a useful probe of the human-machine boundary across domains.

AI.tldr: This study conducted a Finnish-language Turing Test using ChatGPT 5.2 in Finland, finding that the LLM passed despite expectations of poorer performance due to uneven language representation in training data. Participants incorrectly relied on linguistic cues like colloquial Finnish to detect AI authorship.
AI.motivation: The researchers sought to investigate whether LLMs perform differently in non-English languages and cultural contexts, given that training data is unevenly distributed. They also aimed to develop a replicable method (role prompting) for comparative LLM-based Turing Tests to improve construct validity.
AI.method: The study conducted a Turing Test in Finnish in Finland using ChatGPT 5.2. The researchers introduced model-generated role prompting as a technique for conducting comparative LLM-based Turing Tests. They examined participants' ability to distinguish AI-generated from human-generated text, particularly focusing on linguistic cues like colloquial Finnish.
AI.result: Contrary to expectations, ChatGPT 5.2 passed the Finnish Turing Test. A key finding was that participants incorrectly relied on linguistic cues, especially colloquial Finnish, as markers of human authorship, which led to errors in distinguishing AI from human writers.
AI.conclusion: The Turing Test should be reframed as a comparative method for examining whether AI can display credible membership in a particular social world, rather than as a test of intelligence. The method effectively probes the human-machine boundary by considering model capabilities, prompted identity, insider competence, and participants' AI literacy across different domains.

title: Anomaly Detection in General Ledger Data: Results from a Hybrid Approach
comment: Presented at the International Conference on Auditing and Artificial Intelligence 2024
summary: Journal Entry Tests (JETs) are a mandatory part of annual audits to evaluate and assess both highrisk audit areas and potential material misstatements. However, as JETs are designed to detect known patterns based on domain knowledge, the resulting lists are often very large and require substantial additional effort from the auditor. To ensure the economic efficiency of the audit, the number of false positives in JET result lists must be reduced. Especially machine learning (ML) methods represent a promising approach to improve anomaly detection in this field. In this research in progress paper, we investigate different approaches on how to combine JETs with ML-methods in a hybrid manner. We present specialized models to increase the detection performance and validity of anomaly detection results to improve audit efficiency. The experiments are based on synthetic data consisting of different normal and anomalous journal entries.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hybrid approaches combining mandatory Journal Entry Tests (JETs) with machine learning methods to improve anomaly detection in audit processes. The goal is to reduce false positives in JET result lists, thereby enhancing audit efficiency. Experiments are conducted using synthetic data containing normal and anomalous journal entries.
AI.motivation: JETs in annual audits generate large result lists with many false positives, requiring substantial additional auditor effort. The economic efficiency of audits needs improvement by reducing these false positives through more accurate anomaly detection.
AI.method: The research proposes hybrid models that combine traditional JETs (designed to detect known patterns based on domain knowledge) with machine learning methods. Specialized models are developed to increase detection performance and validity of anomaly detection results.
AI.result: The paper is characterized as "research in progress," so final results are not yet available. The experiments are based on synthetic data consisting of different normal and anomalous journal entries.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning methods represent a promising approach to improve anomaly detection in audit processes. The hybrid combination of JETs with ML has potential to enhance detection performance and reduce false positives, ultimately improving audit efficiency.

title: Prosthesis-Aware 3D Human Pose Estimation: A Dataset and Benchmark for RSP Users
summary: Recovering 3D human body motion from video is important for applications such as rehabilitation assessment and sports performance evaluation. For prosthesis users, this requires capturing both natural body joints and the geometry of the prosthetic device, a challenge that existing methods are not designed to address. Model-based estimators rely on body models trained on non-amputee individuals and cannot represent prosthesis geometry, while model-free methods lack body kinematic priors and are unreliable under occlusion. This challenge is particularly prominent for users of running-specific prostheses (RSPs), where the RSP has a complex curved geometry and moves dynamically during exercise. To fill this gap, we collect RSP3D, the first 3D dataset of RSP users, covering essential daily-life and exercise actions from participants with varied amputation conditions, using a multi-camera marker-based motion capture setup. We formally define the task of prosthesis-aware 3D pose estimation, evaluate representative methods in a zero-shot setting, and confirm their individual limitations. We further propose a hybrid baseline combining model-based body joint estimation with model-free RSP shape recovery, establishing a starting point for future research.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of 3D human body motion capture for prosthesis users, specifically those using running-specific prostheses (RSPs). Existing methods fail because they either rely on non-amputee body models or lack kinematic priors. The authors introduce RSP3D, the first 3D dataset of RSP users, and propose a hybrid baseline combining model-based and model-free approaches.
AI.motivation: Current 3D pose estimation methods are not designed for prosthesis users. Model-based estimators use body models trained on non-amputees and cannot represent prosthesis geometry, while model-free methods lack body kinematic priors and perform poorly under occlusion. This is particularly challenging for RSP users due to the complex curved geometry of the prosthetic device and dynamic movement during exercise.
AI.method: The authors collect RSP3D, the first 3D dataset of RSP users, covering daily-life and exercise actions from participants with varied amputation conditions, using a multi-camera marker-based motion capture setup. They formally define the task of prosthesis-aware 3D pose estimation and evaluate representative methods in a zero-shot setting. They propose a hybrid baseline combining model-based body joint estimation with model-free RSP shape recovery.
AI.result: The authors confirm the individual limitations of existing methods. The hybrid baseline establishes a starting point for future research in prosthesis-aware 3D pose estimation.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces the first 3D dataset of RSP users (RSP3D) and formally defines prosthesis-aware 3D pose estimation. The hybrid baseline combining model-based and model-free approaches provides a foundation for future research in this area.

title: HPOQuest: A Rare-Disease Diagnostic Agent Using Active Phenotype Acquisition
summary: More than 300 million people worldwide are affected by one of over 7,000 known rare diseases, yet diagnosis remains difficult because patients initially present with incomplete and heterogeneous phenotypes. We present HPOQuest, a training-free framework for sequential phenotype acquisition in rare-disease diagnosis. Starting from a small set of observed patient phenotypes, HPOQuest maintains a probabilistic disease ranking and iteratively selects informative follow-up questions to support clinicians during patient assessment. Confirmed phenotypes update the disease ranking, while all responses update the candidate question set. Across four benchmark cohorts, HPOQuest substantially improves diagnosis from sparse initial phenotypes, with gains of up to 30% points at Recall@1 and 45% points at Recall@5. These results demonstrate that sequential phenotype acquisition can substantially improve rare-disease diagnosis from limited initial clinical evidence.

AI.tldr: HPOQuest is a training-free framework for sequential phenotype acquisition in rare-disease diagnosis that iteratively selects informative follow-up questions to improve diagnostic accuracy from sparse initial clinical evidence.
AI.motivation: Over 300 million people are affected by rare diseases, but diagnosis remains challenging due to incomplete and heterogeneous patient phenotypes at initial presentation.
AI.method: HPOQuest maintains a probabilistic disease ranking and iteratively selects informative follow-up questions. Confirmed phenotypes update the disease ranking, while all responses update the candidate question set. The framework is training-free.
AI.result: Across four benchmark cohorts, HPOQuest achieved gains of up to 30% points at Recall@1 and 45% points at Recall@5, substantially improving diagnosis from sparse initial phenotypes.
AI.conclusion: Sequential phenotype acquisition can substantially improve rare-disease diagnosis from limited initial clinical evidence.

title: F-DACE: Fuzzy Disagreement-Aware Causal Evidence Fusion for Abstention-Safe Conversational Retail Decision Support
summary: Observational decision-support systems often expose one causal estimate as a recommendation even when plausible estimators disagree. The inherent engine of the proposed system is causal machine learning: a conditional-average-treatment-effect estimand identified by backdoor adjustment, estimated by an EconML DML causal forest and DoWhy linear regression, checked by two-way fixed effects, and converted into candidate levers by constrained optimisation. F-DACE is the decision layer on that engine. It represents precision, propensity overlap, placebo-refutation stability, interval overlap, and directional agreement as fuzzy memberships. Hard vetoes force abstention after estimand mismatch, failed diagnostics, informative sign conflict, or weak evidence. In 180 panel simulations spanning six identification conditions, F-DACE made a decision in 67.2% of runs and limited false recommendations to 17.2%; the corresponding rates were 33.3% for the causal forest and 35.6% for backdoor regression, matching deterministic unanimity rather than dominating it. Nearly all (30 of 31) false recommendations occurred under shared unmeasured confounding, which no fusion rule can diagnose when every component shares the omitted variable. The retail application aggregates a public Walmart panel to 6,435 store-weeks across 45 stores. F-DACE abstains for all five markdown indicators: some estimates are imprecise, one refutation fails, and MarkDown5 has a direct sign conflict. A LangGraph conversational agent exposes impact, what-if, and lever-optimization tools while a deterministic verifier preserves causal-layer status. On 24 live questions it achieved 100.0% tool-routing accuracy, 100.0% status fidelity, and 0.983 mean groundedness. On ten adversarial questions it resisted all injected instructions.

AI.tldr: F-DACE is a fuzzy logic-based decision-support system that integrates multiple causal estimation methods (causal forest, backdoor regression, two-way fixed effects) to make or abstain from recommendations in observational studies. It uses fuzzy membership functions to represent evidence quality and applies hard vetoes for failed diagnostics. In simulations, it made decisions 67.2% of the time with only 17.2% false recommendations, outperforming individual estimators. A LangGraph conversational agent was built on top, achieving high accuracy and robustness against adversarial prompts.
AI.motivation: Observational decision-support systems often expose a single causal estimate as recommendation even when plausible estimators disagree. This creates risk when different causal inference methods produce conflicting results. The authors propose a fusion framework that combines multiple causal estimators with fuzzy logic to either make a decision or abstain when evidence is insufficient or contradictory.
AI.method: The system uses a causal ML engine with: (1) CATE identified by backdoor adjustment; (2) estimated by EconML DML causal forest and DoWhy linear regression; (3) checked by two-way fixed effects; (4) converted to candidate levers via constrained optimization. F-DACE represents five quality dimensions (precision, propensity overlap, placebo-refutation stability, interval overlap, directional agreement) as fuzzy memberships. Hard vetoes force abstention after estimand mismatch, failed diagnostics, sign conflict, or weak evidence. Evaluated on 180 panel simulations across 6 identification conditions and real Walmart retail data (6,435 store-weeks, 45 stores).
AI.result: In 180 simulations: F-DACE made decisions in 67.2% of runs, limiting false recommendations to 17.2%, compared to 33.3% (causal forest) and 35.6% (backdoor regression). 30 of 31 false recommendations occurred under shared unmeasured confounding. In Walmart application, F-DACE abstained on all 5 markdown indicators due to imprecision, refutation failure, and sign conflicts. The LangGraph agent achieved 100.0% tool-routing accuracy, 100.0% status fidelity, 0.983 mean groundedness, and resisted all 10 adversarial instructions.
AI.conclusion: F-DACE provides a principled approach to decision-making under causal uncertainty by combining multiple estimators with fuzzy logic and abstention mechanisms. It outperforms individual estimators in balancing decision-making with false recommendation control. The method has a fundamental limitation: it cannot detect shared unmeasured confounding when all components share the omitted variable. The conversational agent layer demonstrates that causal reasoning can be embedded in user-facing tools while maintaining fidelity and robustness.

title: Vocabulary-Guided Gait Recognition
summary: What is a gait? Appearance-based gait networks consider a gait as the human shape and motion information from images. Model-based gait networks treat a gait as the human inherent structure from points. However, the considerations remain vague for humans to comprehend truly. In this work, we introduce a novel paradigm Vocabulary-Guided Gait Recognition, dubbed Gait-World, which attempts to explore gait concepts through human vocabularies with Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Although VLMs have achieved the remarkable progress in various vision tasks, the cognitive capability regarding gait modalities remains limited. The success element in Gait-World is the proper vocabulary prompt where this paradigm carefully selects gait cycle actions as Vocabulary Base, bridging the gait and vocabulary feature spaces and further promoting human understanding for the gait. How to extract gait features? Although previous gait networks have made significant progress, learning solely from gait modalities on limited gait databases makes it difficult to learn universal gait features for practicality. Therefore, we propose the first Gait-World model, dubbed α-Gait, which guides the gait network learning with vocabulary knowledge from VLMs. However, due to the heterogeneity of the modalities, directly integrating vocabulary and gait features is highly challenging as they reside in different embedding spaces. To address the issues, α-Gait designs Vocabulary Relation Mapper and Gait Fine grained Detector to map and establish vocabulary relations in the gait space for detecting corresponding gait features. Extensive experiments on CASIA-B, CCPG, SUSTech1K, Gait3D and GREW reveal the potential value and research directions of vocabulary information from VLMs in the gait field.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Vocabulary-Guided Gait Recognition (Gait-World), a novel paradigm that uses Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand gait through human vocabularies. The proposed α-Gait model bridges gait and vocabulary feature spaces using Vocabulary Relation Mapper and Gait Fine-grained Detector modules.
AI.motivation: Current gait recognition approaches consider gait as either appearance-based shapes or model-based structures, which remain vague for human comprehension. Additionally, learning universal gait features from limited databases is challenging. This work aims to leverage vocabulary knowledge from VLMs to enhance gait understanding and recognition.
AI.method: The proposed α-Gait model uses three key components: (1) Vocabulary Base - carefully selected gait cycle actions that bridge gait and vocabulary spaces; (2) Vocabulary Relation Mapper - maps vocabulary relations into gait space; (3) Gait Fine-grained Detector - detects corresponding gait features. The model integrates heterogeneous vocabulary and gait features from different embedding spaces.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on CASIA-B, CCPG, SUSTech1K, Gait3D, and GREW datasets demonstrate the potential value of vocabulary information from VLMs in gait recognition, opening new research directions in this field.
AI.conclusion: Vocabulary-guided gait recognition is a promising paradigm that bridges human vocabulary understanding with gait analysis. The integration of VLM knowledge through the α-Gait model shows potential for improving gait recognition, though further research is needed to fully explore this direction.

title: WetRobo: A Reproducible Robot Kit for Coding Agents in Biological Laboratories
comment: 9 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. Code and demonstrations: https://github.com/tsudalab/WetRobo
summary: Automating biological research requires general-purpose, reproducible robot systems that allow individual wet-lab researchers to delegate robot tasks without performing teleoperation or neural-network training. Vision-language-action policies have been proposed for general-purpose arms, but can lose performance when their operating environment changes. We therefore built WetRobo, a robot kit that can readily transfer between laboratories. It consists of one robot arm, laboratory equipment (an incubator, a reagent bottle with a cap, and a Petri dish), the existing code that moves the arm, teleoperation demonstrations of each task that we recorded, and a general AGENTS.md skill file. A biological experimentalist provides natural-language tasks without collecting local teleoperation training data or training a neural network. The coding agent observes the local laboratory and writes and executes programs, using external tools as needed for adaptation. We demonstrate use of WetRobo with OpenAI Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) on three successful tasks: lifting a Petri dish lid, removing a bottle cap, and opening the incubator door, all in real-world laboratories. The coding agent achieved the cap task in both laboratories, Lab X and Lab Y, whereas a VLA fine-tuned on Lab X demonstrations succeeded there but failed to transfer to Lab Y. These results point to a practical route for laboratory robotics: instead of training a policy for each laboratory, distribute a kit and let a coding agent adapt it in each laboratory. Code, demonstrations, and the evolved programs are available at https://github.com/tsudalab/WetRobo.

AI.tldr: WetRobo is a modular robot kit designed for automated biological research that can transfer between laboratories without requiring local training data or neural network fine-tuning. Instead of training vision-language-action policies for each lab, it uses a coding agent (OpenAI Codex) that observes the local environment and writes executable programs to adapt to different laboratories.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language-action (VLA) policies for general-purpose robot arms lose performance when their operating environment changes. This limits their ability to transfer between laboratories. The goal is to create a practical, reproducible robot system that individual wet-lab researchers can use without needing teleoperation or neural-network training.
AI.method: WetRobo consists of: (1) one robot arm, (2) laboratory equipment (incubator, reagent bottle with cap, Petri dish), (3) existing code for arm movement, (4) teleoperation demonstrations of each task, and (5) a general AGENTS.md skill file. A biological experimentalist provides natural-language tasks. A coding agent observes the local laboratory environment and writes/executes programs using external tools as needed for adaptation. The system was tested using OpenAI Codex (gpt-5.6-sol).
AI.result: Three tasks were demonstrated successfully in real-world laboratories: lifting a Petri dish lid, removing a bottle cap, and opening the incubator door. The coding agent achieved the cap task in both laboratories (Lab X and Lab Y). In contrast, a VLA model fine-tuned on Lab X demonstrations succeeded in Lab X but failed to transfer to Lab Y.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest a practical route for laboratory robotics: instead of training a policy for each laboratory, distribute a modular kit and let a coding agent adapt it in each laboratory. This approach avoids the need for local training data and enables cross-laboratory transfer.

title: Behavioral Fingerprinting and Navigation Prediction in Web Browsing
summary: Web browsing often appears ephemeral: users visit a few websites, complete a task, and move on. However, even short fragments of browsing activity can contain rich and structured behavioral signals. In this work, we conduct a comparative empirical study of two complementary behavioral inference tasks: session-level user identification and next-domain prediction. Both tasks are derived from the same cleaned event stream and evaluated on large-scale anonymous browsing traces, with sessionization and splitting adapted to the temporal requirements of each task. For user identification, we evaluate classical and neural models operating on session-level behavioral and domain features. For next-domain prediction, we combine graph-based modeling with Large Language Models (LLMs). Experimental results show that short browsing sessions are highly identifiable, while future navigation actions are highly predictable from long-term interaction structure combined with recent behavioral context. Furthermore, LLM-derived semantic features yield only marginal gains over purely structural and sequential models, indicating that repeated interaction patterns remain the dominant predictive signal in the evaluated web-browsing setup. These findings highlight the extent to which interaction history substantially contributes to both user identifiability and navigation predictability in browsing traces.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a comparative empirical study on two behavioral inference tasks using web browsing data: session-level user identification and next-domain prediction. Using large-scale anonymous browsing traces, the study evaluates classical/neural models for user identification and graph-based modeling combined with LLMs for next-domain prediction. Results show short browsing sessions are highly identifiable and future navigation is highly predictable from interaction history, while LLM-derived semantic features provide only marginal improvements over structural models.
AI.motivation: Web browsing generates rich behavioral signals even in short sessions, yet the extent of user identifiability and navigation predictability remains under-explored. The study aims to compare two complementary behavioral inference tasks derived from the same event stream to understand how interaction history contributes to both user identification and next-domain prediction.
AI.method: The study uses large-scale anonymous browsing traces with sessionization and splitting adapted to each task's temporal requirements. For user identification, classical and neural models operate on session-level behavioral and domain features. For next-domain prediction, graph-based modeling is combined with Large Language Models (LLMs). Both tasks are evaluated on the same cleaned event stream.
AI.result: Short browsing sessions are highly identifiable. Future navigation actions are highly predictable from long-term interaction structure combined with recent behavioral context. LLM-derived semantic features yield only marginal gains over purely structural and sequential models, indicating repeated interaction patterns remain the dominant predictive signal.
AI.conclusion: Interaction history substantially contributes to both user identifiability and navigation predictability in browsing traces. The dominant predictive signal comes from repeated interaction patterns rather than semantic content, highlighting the significance of structural and sequential behavioral features in web browsing analysis.

title: StrucPhysVideo: Learning Physical Dynamics from Structured Captions and Robot Actions
summary: Modeling physical dynamics, including how objects move, interact, and change state, is central to video world models for embodied AI. We present StrucPhysVideo, a family of video world models that bridges physics-focused data curation with language- and action-conditioned prediction of scene evolution. Our data pipeline combines motion-aware video segmentation, quality and content filtering, and physical relevance verification with structured annotations of objects, materials, and temporally localized interactions. By disentangling camera motion from object behavior and explicitly describing contact, deformation, and state transitions, the pipeline provides supervision grounded in observable physical events. Building on these data, we introduce StrucPhysVideo-TI2V, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) text-image-to-video model trained with a curriculum that progressively emphasizes physical dynamics while retaining general-domain video data. StrucPhysVideo-TI2V achieves state-of-the-art performance on Physics-IQ Verified, scoring 45.5% and outperforming Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video by 2.8 percentage points. Caption ablations across backbones further demonstrate the effectiveness of physics-focused supervision. We further extend StrucPhysVideo-TI2V to StrucPhysVideo-IA2V, an interactive image-action-to-video world model that predicts visual outcomes from robot end-effector commands. Action conditioning, causal autoregressive generation, and few-step distillation enable incremental robot rollouts with only four denoising steps. Together, StrucPhysVideo advances physical dynamics modeling from image- and language-conditioned video prediction toward action-driven interaction.

AI.tldr: StrucPhysVideo is a family of video world models that bridges physics-focused data curation with language- and action-conditioned prediction of scene evolution for embodied AI. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on Physics-IQ Verified (45.5%, +2.8% over Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video) and extends from text-image-to-video to interactive image-action-to-video prediction for robot interactions.
AI.motivation: Modeling physical dynamics (object movement, interaction, state changes) is central to video world models for embodied AI, but existing approaches lack sufficient focus on physical relevance and action-conditioned prediction.
AI.method: The approach involves: (1) A data pipeline combining motion-aware video segmentation, quality/content filtering, and physical relevance verification with structured annotations of objects, materials, and temporally localized interactions; (2) Disentangling camera motion from object behavior and explicitly describing contact, deformation, and state transitions; (3) StrucPhysVideo-TI2V, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts text-image-to-video model trained with a curriculum emphasizing physical dynamics; (4) StrucPhysVideo-IA2V, an interactive model using action conditioning, causal autoregressive generation, and few-step distillation for robot rollouts.
AI.result: StrucPhysVideo-TI2V achieves state-of-the-art performance on Physics-IQ Verified, scoring 45.5% and outperforming Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video by 2.8 percentage points. Caption ablations across backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of physics-focused supervision. StrucPhysVideo-IA2V enables incremental robot rollouts with only four denoising steps.
AI.conclusion: StrucPhysVideo advances physical dynamics modeling from image- and language-conditioned video prediction toward action-driven interaction, successfully bridging physics-focused data curation with language- and action-conditioned prediction for embodied AI applications.

title: Risk-Aware World Modeling with Flow-Guided Occupancy Evolution for Selective Trajectory Planning in Automated Driving
summary: Safe motion planning in automated driving requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise the current planned trajectory. We introduce RiskWorld, a risk-aware world modeling framework for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement. Spatial risk fields and temporal actor context are fused with visual bird's-eye-view features. Flow-guided evolution transports occupancy and scene features, while signed residuals correct occupancy after transport. One forecast is generated per planning step and reused across candidates. Each candidate is compared with a current-state persistence reference, yielding a nonnegative collision-score correction. The trajectory selected by current-world evaluation serves as the planning anchor and is replaced only when additional predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative satisfies component-wise constraints on predicted risk and trajectory error. Candidate geometries remain unchanged. We evaluate RiskWorld for open-loop planning on nuScenes using camera features, annotation-derived current and historical actor states, and dataset-provided map context. RiskWorld achieves the lowest collision rate at a long evaluation horizon of 3 s, and the second-best average L2 error among various state-of-the-art baselines, while running at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 90.81 M parameters. Within-setting ablations show that RiskWorld achieves lower collision rates than the current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates to be evaluated at low marginal computational cost.

AI.tldr: RiskWorld is a risk-aware world modeling framework for autonomous driving that fuses spatial risk fields and temporal actor context with visual bird's-eye-view features for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement. It achieves the lowest collision rate at 3s horizon while running at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090.
AI.motivation: Safe motion planning in automated driving requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise the current planned trajectory. Existing methods lack effective ways to predict future traffic risks and determine when trajectory replacement is necessary.
AI.method: RiskWorld uses flow-guided evolution to transport occupancy and scene features temporally, with signed residuals to correct occupancy after transport. It generates one forecast per planning step reused across candidates. Each candidate is compared with a current-state persistence reference, yielding a nonnegative collision-score correction. The trajectory is replaced only when predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative satisfies component-wise constraints on predicted risk and trajectory error.
AI.result: RiskWorld achieves the lowest collision rate at a 3s evaluation horizon, second-best average L2 error among state-of-the-art baselines, runs at 11.5 FPS on NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 90.81M parameters. Ablations show lower collision rates than current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates at low marginal cost.
AI.conclusion: RiskWorld demonstrates effective risk-aware planning by combining occupancy forecasting with selective trajectory replacement, balancing safety through collision avoidance and performance through efficient computation.

title: A GAN-Based Framework for Robust DDoS Attack Detection
summary: The availability and consistency of online services remain vulnerable due to Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. These attacks are evolving by adopting more complex strategies to evade traditional network security systems. Despite the effectiveness of machine learning models in detecting DDoS traffic, targeted adversarial attacks can degrade their classification accuracy. This work proposes a robust detection framework that integrates generative adversarial modelling with advanced machine learning models. We trained Random Forests, Deep Neural Ensembles, and Transformer-based models using the CICDDoS2019 dataset to establish the frameworks baseline performance. To enhance the models defensive capacity, we generated synthetic adversarial flows that simulate potential evasion attempts and adversarial traffic using a Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP). Then, we combined the generated traffic with benign and malicious traffic to construct hybrid datasets to train the models to learn more generalizable decision boundaries. The experimental results indicate that the proposed methodology significantly enhances detection accuracy and resilience, especially against unseen adversarial traffic. We also tested the designed framework using real-world generated traffic, which demonstrates its capability in practical settings. The scalable and efficient solution against adversarial DDoS attacks, introduced in this work, paves the way towards more resilient and adaptive network defense systems that combine generative adversarial augmentation with recent advances in learning models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a robust DDoS detection framework that uses WGAN-GP to generate synthetic adversarial flows for training machine learning models (Random Forests, Deep Neural Ensembles, Transformers), significantly improving detection accuracy and resilience against adversarial attacks.
AI.motivation: DDoS attacks are evolving to evade traditional security systems, and while machine learning can detect DDoS traffic, targeted adversarial attacks can degrade their classification accuracy, necessitating more robust detection mechanisms.
AI.method: The framework integrates WGAN-GP to generate synthetic adversarial flows simulating evasion attempts, combined with benign and malicious traffic to create hybrid datasets for training Random Forests, Deep Neural Ensembles, and Transformer-based models.
AI.result: The proposed methodology significantly enhances detection accuracy and resilience, especially against unseen adversarial traffic, and demonstrates practical effectiveness using real-world generated traffic.
AI.conclusion: The combination of generative adversarial augmentation with advanced learning models provides a scalable and efficient solution against adversarial DDoS attacks, paving the way for more resilient and adaptive network defense systems.

title: Occluded Gait Recognition with Mixture of Experts: An Action Detection Perspective
summary: Extensive occlusions in real-world scenarios pose challenges to gait recognition due to missing and noisy information, as well as body misalignment in position and scale. We argue that rich dynamic contextual information within a gait sequence inherently possesses occlusion-solving traits: 1) Adjacent frames with gait continuity allow holistic body regions to infer occluded body regions; 2) Gait cycles allow information integration between holistic actions and occluded actions. Therefore, we introduce an action detection perspective where a gait sequence is regarded as a composition of actions. To detect accurate actions under complex occlusion scenarios, we propose an Action Detection Based Mixture of Experts (GaitMoE), consisting of Mixture of Temporal Experts (MTE) and Mixture of Action Experts (MAE). MTE adaptively constructs action anchors by temporal experts and MAE adaptively constructs action proposals from action anchors by action experts. Especially, action detection as a proxy task with gait recognition is an end-to-end joint training only with ID labels. In addition, due to the lack of a unified occluded benchmark, we construct a pioneering Occluded Gait database (OccGait), containing rich occlusion scenarios and annotations of occlusion types. Extensive experiments on OccGait, OccCASIA-B,Gait3D and GREW demonstrate the superior performance of GaitMoE.OccGait is available at https://github.com/BNU-IVC/OccGait.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses occlusion challenges in gait recognition by proposing GaitMoE, which treats gait sequences as compositions of actions. The method uses Mixture of Temporal Experts (MTE) and Mixture of Action Experts (MAE) to adaptively handle occlusions by leveraging temporal continuity and gait cycles. A new benchmark dataset OccGait is also introduced.
AI.motivation: Extensive occlusions in real-world scenarios pose challenges to gait recognition due to missing/noisy information and body misalignment in position and scale. The key insight is that rich dynamic contextual information within gait sequences inherently possesses occlusion-solving traits: adjacent frames allow holistic body regions to infer occluded regions, and gait cycles enable information integration between holistic and occluded actions.
AI.method: The proposed GaitMoE framework adopts an action detection perspective where a gait sequence is viewed as a composition of actions. It consists of two components: (1) Mixture of Temporal Experts (MTE) - adaptively constructs action anchors by temporal experts; (2) Mixture of Action Experts (MAE) - adaptively constructs action proposals from action anchors by action experts. The method uses action detection as a proxy task with gait recognition in an end-to-end joint training framework, trained only with ID labels without requiring explicit action annotations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on OccGait, OccCASIA-B, Gait3D and GREW datasets demonstrate the superior performance of GaitMoE in handling occluded gait recognition scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The action detection perspective provides an effective solution for occlusion handling in gait recognition. The proposed GaitMoE framework, together with the new OccGait benchmark, advances the state-of-the-art in occluded gait recognition. The code and dataset are made publicly available.

title: The Mirage of Calibrated Confidence: Trajectory-Independence of Verbalized Confidence in Vision-Language Models
summary: A calibrated Vision-Language Model (VLM) can repeatedly self-correct, say "Wait, I should recheck," arrive at the wrong answer, and still report high confidence. We find that this occurs because verbalized confidence is largely trajectory-independent in the VLMs and calibration methods we evaluate. We examine this through three complementary lenses: content variation, token masking, and the model's own hesitation markers. We show that confidence is insufficiently sensitive to what the reasoning trajectory actually contains, and that calibration training can paradoxically worsen this disconnect. Since existing metrics like ECE and AUROC cannot detect this problem, we propose the Trajectory-Grounding Score (TGS) in two complementary forms: TGS-self, which compares confidence with and without access to the model's own trajectory, and TGS-pair, which tests whether the model assigns higher confidence to correct trajectories than to flawed ones along the vision, reasoning, and answer axes. We propose TGS-Bench, a model-agnostic suite spanning 10 benchmarks with controlled good/bad trajectory pairs, and show that conventional calibration rankings diverge from trajectory-grounding rankings, exposing a blind spot in current evaluation practice.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a critical blind spot in VLM confidence calibration: models can verbalize high confidence even after self-correction leads to wrong answers, because confidence is largely independent of the actual reasoning trajectory. Current metrics like ECE and AUROC fail to detect this issue.
AI.motivation: The authors observe that calibrated VLMs can exhibit a problematic behavior: they self-correct (saying "Wait, I should recheck"), arrive at wrong answers, yet still report high confidence. This reveals that verbalized confidence is trajectory-independent, potentially creating a false sense of reliability in AI systems.
AI.method: The authors examine this problem through three complementary lenses: content variation, token masking, and the model's own hesitation markers. They propose two new evaluation metrics: TGS-self (comparing confidence with/without access to the model's own trajectory) and TGS-pair (testing whether correct trajectories receive higher confidence than flawed ones). They also introduce TGS-Bench, a model-agnostic benchmark suite spanning 10 benchmarks with controlled good/bad trajectory pairs.
AI.result: The authors find that confidence is insufficiently sensitive to what the reasoning trajectory actually contains, and that calibration training can paradoxically worsen this disconnect. Conventional calibration rankings (based on ECE and AUROC) diverge from trajectory-grounding rankings, exposing a significant blind spot in current evaluation practice.
AI.conclusion: Current VLM calibration evaluation is flawed because it doesn't measure whether confidence is actually grounded in the reasoning process. The proposed TGS metrics and TGS-Bench provide a more meaningful evaluation framework that reveals how confidence relates to actual reasoning trajectories, highlighting the need for trajectory-aware calibration assessment.

title: Bias Amplification in Multi-Agent Network: How Biased Agents Shape Opinions and Rhetoric
comment: Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Bias and Fairness in AI (BIAS 2026), ECML PKDD 2026, Naples, Italy
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in applications involving interaction between agents, where their output plays a role in collective reasoning and decision-making processes. Despite significant research into the functioning of LLMs in such multi-agent systems, the processes of bias propagation in such systems are still a challenge. This work studies how biased opinions are propagated in the form of textual interaction in an environment of LLMs, in which a minority of agents maintain persistent extreme opinions, while the remaining agents iteratively update their beliefs through structured textual interactions. The findings show that even the presence of a small percentage of biased agents in such a system leads to significant shifts in the opinions of non-biased agents. It suggests that for the same percentage of biased agents, the shifts occur more quickly for the Llama~3.2 model when compared to a classical Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) model. Further semantic analysis demonstrates that rhetorical consistency in textual explanations increases systematically with biased exposure and, importantly, is partially decoupled from numerical convergenumericalutral agents adopt the vocabulary employed by the biased agents even in configurations where their numerical opinion shifts remain moderate. The research helps explain how bias and language develop together in multi-agent language model ecosystems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how biased opinions propagate through textual interactions in multi-agent systems composed of large language models, finding that even a small minority of biased agents can significantly shift the opinions of others, with semantic changes (vocabulary adoption) partially decoupled from numerical opinion shifts.
AI.motivation: Despite significant research into LLMs in multi-agent systems, the processes of bias propagation in such systems remain poorly understood. The researchers seek to understand how bias and language develop together in multi-agent LLM ecosystems.
AI.method: The study examines an environment where a minority of agents maintain persistent extreme opinions while remaining agents iteratively update beliefs through structured textual interactions. They compare Llama 3.2 model performance against the classical Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) model and conduct semantic analysis of rhetorical consistency.
AI.result: Even a small percentage of biased agents leads to significant opinion shifts among non-biased agents. The Llama 3.2 model shows faster shifts than the classical FJ model for the same percentage of biased agents. Rhetorical consistency in textual explanations increases systematically with biased exposure, and neutral agents adopt the vocabulary of biased agents even when numerical opinion shifts remain moderate.
AI.conclusion: The research demonstrates that bias and language develop together in multi-agent language model ecosystems, with semantic changes (vocabulary adoption) being partially decoupled from numerical opinion convergence, suggesting that linguistic influence can occur independently of explicit opinion changes.

title: DR.WILSS: Diffusion-Based Replay for Weakly Supervised Continual Semantic Segmentation
summary: Weakly supervised class-incremental semantic segmentation (WILSS) aims to train a segmentation model over multiple steps, each introducing new concepts to be learned with only image-level supervision. We introduce DR.WILSS, an innovative approach to address catastrophic forgetting in continual learning using diffusion-based generative replay. Our framework leverages language clues to guide the diffusion process, employing self-inpainting and regularization techniques to efficiently produce replay data, aiding the learning process. By generating high-quality replay data, the information from previously learned classes can be preserved during continual updates, a critical challenge in incremental learning scenarios. To further align the statistics of replay data with those of training samples, we apply LoRAs to the generative model. Experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks and generative architectures, while avoiding storage of training data and the use of additional resource-demanding tools during training. The proposed technique enables an optimal tradeoff between training complexity and inference-time accuracy, making DR.WILSS a promising solution for real-world applications.

AI.tldr: DR.WILSS is a diffusion-based generative replay method for weakly supervised class-incremental semantic segmentation that addresses catastrophic forgetting by using language-guided diffusion with self-inpainting, regularization, and LoRA adapters to generate high-quality replay data without storing training data.
AI.motivation: Weakly supervised class-incremental semantic segmentation (WILSS) faces catastrophic forgetting when learning new concepts with only image-level supervision. Existing methods either store training data (privacy/storage issues) or use computationally expensive generative models, requiring an efficient solution that preserves information from previously learned classes during continual updates.
AI.method: The proposed DR.WILSS framework leverages language clues to guide the diffusion process, employing self-inpainting and regularization techniques to efficiently produce replay data. LoRA adapters are applied to align the statistics of generated replay data with real training samples, enabling the model to preserve knowledge from previously learned classes during incremental learning.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks and generative architectures, while avoiding storage of training data and eliminating the need for additional resource-demanding tools during training. The method achieves an optimal tradeoff between training complexity and inference-time accuracy.
AI.conclusion: DR.WILSS presents a promising solution for real-world WILSS applications by effectively addressing catastrophic forgetting through diffusion-based generative replay, achieving superior performance without data storage privacy concerns or excessive computational overhead.

title: Collective Loss of Control in LLM Agent Systems: An Epidemic Account of Mutation, Contagion, and Recovery
summary: How does a multi-agent system evolve from a local deviation into collective loss of control? We propose an epidemic explanation organized around accidental mutation, contagion, and recovery. A spontaneous deviation creates a seed; communication enables other agents to adopt and retransmit its unsafe strategy; collective failure can emerge when propagation outpaces correction and containment. Thus, rare individual deviations can coexist with substantial collective risk. Motivated by reported OpenAI agent coordination incidents, we examine two ingredients of this mechanism. A deployment audit identifies implicit communication paths between nominally independent evaluation runs and verifies transport through a default Docker backend. RogueHandoff-20, a benchmark of 20 executable scenarios, tests recipient susceptibility by injecting unsafe trajectories generated by a modified Qwen-27B route. Across four native-pending routes, executed harm is 0-5% on normal tasks and 40-95% after injection, exceeding paired direct malicious requests by 5-45 percentage points. These results support low observed baseline harm alongside high conditional susceptibility; they do not establish natural rare-event rates or demonstrate an autonomous cascade. The account motivates complementary defenses: strengthen resistance and recovery alongside prevention of spontaneous deviations, and audit and restrict unintended communication paths that can turn local failures into collective loss of control.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how multi-agent AI systems can evolve from individual failures into collective loss of control through an epidemic-like mechanism involving accidental mutation, contagion, and recovery. The authors examine implicit communication paths between agent runs and test susceptibility using a benchmark (RogueHandoff-20) with modified Qwen-27B, finding high conditional harm (40-95%) despite low baseline harm (0-5%).
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from reported OpenAI agent coordination incidents, exploring how rare individual deviations can lead to substantial collective risk through unintended communication paths between nominally independent systems.
AI.method: The authors employ two methods: (1) A deployment audit identifying implicit communication paths between evaluation runs and verifying transport through Docker backend; (2) RogueHandoff-20 benchmark with 20 executable scenarios injecting unsafe trajectories from a modified Qwen-27B model to test recipient susceptibility.
AI.result: Results show 0-5% harm on normal tasks vs 40-95% harm after injection across four native-pending routes, exceeding direct malicious requests by 5-45 percentage points. This demonstrates low baseline harm but high conditional susceptibility.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that defenses should strengthen resistance and recovery alongside prevention of spontaneous deviations, and audit/restrict unintended communication paths to prevent local failures from cascading into collective loss of control.

title: Beyond Quadratic Loss: The Stability Phase Diagram of Adam
summary: Loss spikes are recurrent instabilities in neural-network training and can arise from multiple mechanisms. For Adam in particular, macroscopic loss spikes have been linked to optimizer dynamics, yet how its two momentum timescales govern them remains unclear. We investigate this dependence by mapping training dynamics across the $(β_1,β_2)$ plane. Across a range of model--task settings, an approximately linear boundary, $1-β_2=C(1-β_1)$, separates spiky from non-spiky dynamics, whereas a one-dimensional quadratic loss produces approximately cubic slope. A one-dimensional superquadratic loss $L(x)\propto|x|^n$ recovers the near-linear scaling and links the boundary coefficient to the effective loss exponent $n$. We further show that confident cross-entropy losses develop a core--wall landscape comprising a narrow quadratic core followed by a steep wall, which produces effective superquadratic behavior at the scale of an optimizer update. Together, these results connect Adam loss spikes to both the mismatch between momentum timescales and finite-scale superquadratic loss geometry beyond the Hessian.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the mechanism behind loss spikes in Adam optimizer training, focusing on how the two momentum timescales (β1, β2) govern these instabilities. The authors discover an approximately linear boundary 1-β2 = C(1-β1) that separates spiky from non-spiky dynamics across various model-task settings, and link this to superquadratic loss geometry beyond Hessian curvature.
AI.motivation: Loss spikes are common instabilities in neural network training, particularly with Adam optimizer. While macroscopic loss spikes have been linked to optimizer dynamics, the specific role of Adam's two momentum timescales (β1 for first-moment, β2 for second-moment) in causing these spikes remained unclear. This work aims to understand this dependence by mapping training dynamics across the (β1, β2) parameter plane.
AI.method: The authors map training dynamics across the (β1, β2) plane across multiple model-task settings. They analyze one-dimensional quadratic losses (producing ~cubic slope) and superquadratic losses L(x) ∝ |x|^n (recovering near-linear scaling). They also examine confident cross-entropy losses to characterize their core-wall landscape.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) An approximately linear boundary 1-β2 = C(1-β1) separates spiky from non-spiky dynamics; (2) Quadratic loss produces approximately cubic slope; (3) Superquadratic loss recovers near-linear scaling, linking the boundary coefficient C to effective loss exponent n; (4) Confident cross-entropy losses develop a core-wall landscape with narrow quadratic core + steep wall, producing effective superquadratic behavior at optimizer update scale.
AI.conclusion: Adam loss spikes arise from two interconnected mechanisms: (1) the mismatch between momentum timescales (β1 and β2), and (2) finite-scale superquadratic loss geometry beyond the Hessian. This provides a unified framework for understanding and potentially mitigating loss spikes in Adam-trained neural networks.

title: CSWAM: Better Causal Semantic Representations for Out-of-Distribution Generalization in World Action Models
summary: FastWAM-style world action models enable efficient action-only inference, but generalize poorly under visual distribution shifts. Their reconstruction-oriented representations emphasize appearance-specific details, limiting generalization to unseen scenes and objects. Without observation history, the model also lacks temporal evidence for robustly identifying task-relevant state changes and motion in unfamiliar visual conditions. To address these limitations, we present the Causal Semantic World Action Model (CSWAM), which augments FastWAM with a causal semantic expert built on V-JEPA 2.1. V-JEPA provides temporally grounded representations of semantic state changes and motion with less dependence on appearance-specific details. The expert learns their future evolution from a sparse history of current and past observations and shares the history-derived context with both the video and action streams through causal attention. At inference, CSWAM conditions action denoising on the current video state and observed semantic history, retaining efficient action-only inference. We conduct simulation and real-robot experiments to evaluate generalization under distribution shifts. With embodied pretraining, CSWAM raises Randomized success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Randomized transfer from 10.16% to 45.18%, a gain of 35.02 percentage points over FastWAM. Across two real-robot tasks and three OOD difficulty levels, CSWAM improves average success over FastWAM by 42.5 percentage points, from 27.5% to 70.0%.

AI.tldr: CSWAM augments FastWAM with a causal semantic expert built on V-JEPA 2.1 to improve generalization under visual distribution shifts. The model uses temporally grounded semantic representations that depend less on appearance-specific details, learns future evolution from sparse observation history, and shares context through causal attention. Experiments show significant improvements: 35.02 percentage point gain in Clean-to-Randomized transfer (10.16% to 45.18%) on RoboTwin 2.0, and 42.5 percentage point improvement (27.5% to 70.0%) across real-robot OOD tasks.
AI.motivation: FastWAM-style world action models enable efficient action-only inference but generalize poorly under visual distribution shifts. Their reconstruction-oriented representations emphasize appearance-specific details, limiting generalization to unseen scenes and objects. Without observation history, the model lacks temporal evidence for robustly identifying task-relevant state changes and motion in unfamiliar visual conditions.
AI.method: CSWAM augments FastWAM with a causal semantic expert built on V-JEPA 2.1. V-JEPA provides temporally grounded representations of semantic state changes and motion with less dependence on appearance-specific details. The expert learns future evolution from a sparse history of current and past observations and shares history-derived context with both video and action streams through causal attention. At inference, CSWAM conditions action denoising on current video state and observed semantic history, retaining efficient action-only inference.
AI.result: With embodied pretraining, CSWAM raises Randomized success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Randomized transfer from 10.16% to 45.18%, a gain of 35.02 percentage points over FastWAM. Across two real-robot tasks and three OOD difficulty levels, CSWAM improves average success over FastWAM by 42.5 percentage points, from 27.5% to 70.0%.
AI.conclusion: CSWAM successfully addresses the generalization limitations of FastWAM under visual distribution shifts by incorporating causal semantic representations from V-JEPA 2.1 and temporal history context. The approach maintains efficient action-only inference while significantly improving generalization to unseen scenes, objects, and visual conditions in both simulation and real-robot experiments.

title: Disentangling Long-Term Memory via Latent Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
summary: Personalized agents are required to reason over long-term history interactions to infer both explicit preferences and implicit behavioral evidence. While early flat retrieval methods score memory fragments independently and neglect the distributed information, current structured memory frameworks rely on query-agnostic static graphs that fail to capture the context-dependent relations. Crucially, raw textual memories are inherently entangled and noisy, making fine-grained personalization and cross-session reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present LGM, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term memory disentanglement into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of persisting fixed graphs, we design a tailored latent graph construction with a sparse autoencoder. Subject to each query, it maps historical interactions into latent memory nodes and disentangles the memory traces into sparse concept activations, dynamically synthesizing query-aware relational edge weights. (ii) A graph encoder then treats the query embedding as a conditioning preference to direct non-linear message passing across the task-specific latent subgraph. This yields a highly expressive memory representation for effective activations. Extensive experiments on long-term personalization benchmarks demonstrate that LGM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing both explicit and implicit preferences while enabling personalized responses.

AI.tldr: LGM is a neuro-symbolic framework for personalized agents that performs long-term memory disentanglement in a continuous latent space. It uses a sparse autoencoder to construct query-aware latent graphs from historical interactions, enabling effective capture of both explicit and implicit user preferences.
AI.motivation: Current personalized agents face limitations: flat retrieval methods score memory fragments independently, missing distributed information; static memory graphs fail to capture context-dependent relations; raw textual memories are entangled and noisy. These issues make fine-grained personalization and cross-session reasoning computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: LGM employs two key components: (1) A tailored latent graph construction with a sparse autoencoder that maps historical interactions into latent memory nodes, disentangles memory traces into sparse concept activations, and dynamically synthesizes query-aware relational edge weights. (2) A graph encoder that treats query embedding as a conditioning preference to direct non-linear message passing across task-specific latent subgraphs.
AI.result: LGM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on long-term personalization benchmarks in capturing both explicit and implicit preferences while enabling personalized responses.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic approach of LGM successfully shifts memory disentanglement into continuous latent space, providing a highly expressive memory representation that effectively handles personalization tasks.

title: Multi-Appliance Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring via Label-Preserving Aggregate Recomposition and Prediction Consistency
summary: Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) estimates appliance power sequences from aggregate power, but models trained on source households commonly lose accuracy in unseen households. Aggregate power also contains loads from other appliances and measurement error, so predictions may depend on the residual background that co-occurs with source-household targets. Time-aligned submetered measurements and the additive decomposition of aggregate power expose a relation unused by window-wise supervision: an aggregate window can be recomposed by replacing only its residual background while preserving all modeled target-appliance power sequences pointwise. We combine label-preserving aggregate recomposition with prediction consistency. Both windows receive complete power and operating-state supervision. For each appliance, disagreement between the two power predictions is penalized only when both satisfy a fixed reliability criterion and only to the extent that it exceeds a fixed margin. The proposed method is implemented using a multi-appliance architecture with two-stage shared-to-specific mixture-of-experts routing. On REDD, UK-DALE, and REFIT, the proposed method lowers appliance-averaged mean absolute error relative to single-window training from 14.75 to 13.14 W, from 8.88 to 8.51 W, and from 15.83 to 14.55 W. Label-preserving aggregate recomposition and prediction consistency are used only during training, and add no inference-time module or parameter.

AI.tldr: A novel NILM training method that uses label-preserving aggregate recomposition and prediction consistency to improve model generalization across unseen households, without adding inference-time complexity.
AI.motivation: NILM models trained on source households lose accuracy when applied to unseen households due to: 1) residual background (other appliances and measurement error) that co-occurs with target-appliance power, and 2) the lack of exploitation of the additive decomposition property of aggregate power.
AI.method: The method combines: 1) Label-preserving aggregate recomposition - replacing only the residual background in an aggregate window while preserving target-appliance power sequences pointwise, and 2) Prediction consistency - penalizing disagreement between two power predictions only when both satisfy a fixed reliability criterion and exceed a fixed margin. Implementation uses a multi-appliance architecture with two-stage shared-to-specific mixture-of-experts routing.
AI.result: On REDD, UK-DALE, and REFIT datasets, the method reduces appliance-averaged MAE from 14.75 to 13.14 W, 8.88 to 8.51 W, and 15.83 to 14.55 W respectively.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training method significantly improves NILM model generalization across unseen households without adding any inference-time module or parameter, by leveraging label-preserving aggregate recomposition and prediction consistency during training.

title: GeoCond: A Conditioning-Aware Reliability Adapter for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
summary: Feed-forward 3D foundation models such as VGGT predict cameras, depth, and point maps in a single pass, but can fail silently under low overlap, low parallax, and extreme relative rotation. Stratified analyses over these factors show that these failures are governed by geometric conditioning and are poorly captured by native aleatoric confidence. We introduce GeoCond, a lightweight reliability adapter for frozen feed-forward 3D backbones. GeoCond reads the backbone's predicted geometry and outputs pose-level uncertainty and a refinement gate. During training, it can be supervised by frame-permutation orbit variance, ground-truth pose error when labels are available, or cycle residuals from unlabelled independent pose graphs. At inference, the default head requires only one backbone pass and a small MLP. On VGGT, GeoCond improves out-of-distribution (OOD) AUSE (area under the sparsification-error curve; lower is better) from $0.32$ to $0.20$ over native confidence, transfers zero-shot to outdoor extreme-view scenes, and avoids the collapse caused by applying bundle adjustment uniformly. Across multiple backbones, cycle-distilled variants provide a ground-truth-free adaptation route, including cases where permutation variance vanishes on equivariant models. The same reliability signal supports gated refinement, pose-graph weighting, calibration, curation, and capture decisions. Reliable feed-forward 3D reconstruction requires not only predicting geometry, but also knowing when that geometry should be trusted.
