AI.tldr: GeoCond is a lightweight reliability adapter for frozen feed-forward 3D foundation models (e.g., VGGT) that predicts pose-level uncertainty and refinement gates. It addresses silent failures under low overlap, low parallax, and extreme rotation by leveraging geometric conditioning. The method can be trained via frame-permutation orbit variance, ground-truth pose error, or cycle residuals from unlabeled pose graphs. It improves OOD AUSE from 0.32 to 0.20 and enables applications like gated refinement, pose-graph weighting, and capture decisions.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward 3D foundation models like VGGT predict cameras, depth, and point maps in a single pass but can fail silently under challenging conditions (low overlap, low parallax, extreme relative rotation). These failures are governed by geometric conditioning and are poorly captured by native aleatoric confidence. There is a need to assess when predictions should be trusted.
AI.method: GeoCond is introduced as a lightweight reliability adapter that reads the backbone's predicted geometry and outputs pose-level uncertainty and a refinement gate. It can be trained using three supervision signals: (1) frame-permutation orbit variance, (2) ground-truth pose error (when labels available), or (3) cycle residuals from unlabeled independent pose graphs. At inference, it requires only one backbone pass and a small MLP.
AI.result: GeoCond improves out-of-distribution AUSE from 0.32 to 0.20 over native confidence on VGGT, transfers zero-shot to outdoor extreme-view scenes, and avoids collapse caused by uniform bundle adjustment. Cycle-distilled variants provide ground-truth-free adaptation, even when permutation variance vanishes on equivariant models. The reliability signal supports multiple applications: gated refinement, pose-graph weighting, calibration, curation, and capture decisions.
AI.conclusion: Reliable feed-forward 3D reconstruction requires not only predicting geometry but also knowing when that geometry should be trusted. GeoCond provides a practical solution for uncertainty estimation and reliable 3D reconstruction, with applications spanning multiple downstream tasks.

title: First Token Matters: Understanding Safety Collapse in Large Reasoning Models
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Includes appendices. Accepted at CICAI 2026
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit strong problem-solving abilities, yet their safety alignment often degrades when handling harmful queries. Existing approaches to improving safety largely rely on additional training or preference optimization, while offering limited understanding of the internal mechanisms behind safety failures. In this work, we investigate this failure through a token-level positional analysis of refusal dynamics and identify a localized vulnerability at the onset of reasoning, which we term Onset Refusal Collapse (ORC). We find that the refusal-related signal of LRMs drops sharply at the first generated token under harmful queries, which is associated with unsafe response generation. Motivated by this finding, we propose SafeToken, a lightweight inference-time intervention that injects a learned continuous safety anchor precisely at reasoning onset. Despite updating only a single token embedding, SafeToken effectively mitigates ORC, improves safety on harmful-query benchmarks, and largely preserves reasoning utility. These results suggest that safety failures in LRMs can arise from a transient breakdown at the critical transition from understanding to generation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates safety alignment failures in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) when handling harmful queries, identifying a phenomenon called "Onset Refusal Collapse (ORC)" where refusal signals drop sharply at the first generated token. The authors propose SafeToken, a lightweight inference-time intervention that injects a learned safety anchor at reasoning onset to mitigate this vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Existing safety alignment approaches for LRMs rely on additional training or preference optimization, but there is limited understanding of the internal mechanisms behind safety failures. The authors aim to investigate the token-level positional dynamics of refusal to understand why safety degrades when LRMs handle harmful queries.
AI.method: The authors conduct token-level positional analysis of refusal dynamics in LRMs. They identify a localized vulnerability at the onset of reasoning called Onset Refusal Collapse (ORC). Based on this finding, they propose SafeToken, a lightweight inference-time intervention that injects a learned continuous safety anchor precisely at reasoning onset by updating only a single token embedding.
AI.result: The refusal-related signal of LRMs drops sharply at the first generated token under harmful queries, which is associated with unsafe response generation. SafeToken effectively mitigates ORC, improves safety on harmful-query benchmarks, and largely preserves reasoning utility.
AI.conclusion: Safety failures in LRMs can arise from a transient breakdown at the critical transition from understanding to generation. A lightweight inference-time intervention (SafeToken) that targets this specific moment can effectively improve safety while preserving reasoning capabilities.

title: Trajectory Learnability for Offline On-Policy Distillation with Imperfect Teachers
summary: Offline on-policy distillation gains efficiency by collecting student trajectories and teacher supervision once and reusing them throughout optimization. The same reuse makes imperfect supervision persistent. Since even strong teachers can fail, we ask \emph{what remains learnable from imperfect teacher supervision?} Teacher failure is only a coarse problem-level signal and does not imply that all supervision along the associated student trajectory is unhelpful. A natural alternative is to estimate teacher recoverability along the trajectory, but repeated continuations largely erase the efficiency advantage of offline distillation. We instead use teacher-successful problems to define a cheap reference for what the student can learn. We train on teacher-successful problems and measure how the likelihood of each observed token in trajectories from teacher-failed problems changes. We use these signed likelihood changes as an operational \emph{learnability signal}: larger increases indicate behavior more strongly promoted by successful-only learning. We aggregate this signal into trajectory-level weights for the original distillation loss. Unlike continuation-based estimates, our learnability requires no additional generation and can be computed once from stored trajectories and model checkpoints. Across mathematical reasoning and code generation, our method improves an offline OPD baseline by up to 2.7 percentage points and matches or outperforms online OPD variants on multiple benchmarks. Despite the additional successful-only distillation stage, it uses 2 GPUs and about 22 GPU hours, compared with 3 GPUs and 36--48 GPU hours for representative online OPD methods.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses offline on-policy distillation (OPD) where imperfect teacher supervision persists due to trajectory reuse. The authors propose a "learnability signal" method that uses teacher-successful problems as a reference to identify which tokens in teacher-failed trajectories are actually learnable, without requiring additional generation.
AI.motivation: Offline OPD gains efficiency by collecting student trajectories and teacher supervision once and reusing them, but this makes imperfect supervision persistent. Teacher failure is only a coarse problem-level signal, not indicating which specific supervision is unhelpful. Continuation-based estimates to assess recoverability would erase the efficiency advantage of offline distillation.
AI.method: The method uses teacher-successful problems as a cheap reference. First, train on teacher-successful problems. Then measure how the likelihood of each token in teacher-failed trajectories changes. These signed likelihood changes serve as an operational learnability signal - larger increases indicate behavior more strongly promoted by successful-only learning. Aggregate this signal into trajectory-level weights for the original distillation loss.
AI.result: The method improves offline OPD baseline by up to 2.7 percentage points on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. It matches or outperforms online OPD variants on multiple benchmarks while using significantly fewer resources: 2 GPUs and ~22 GPU hours versus 3 GPUs and 36-48 GPU hours for representative online OPD methods.
AI.conclusion: The learnability signal approach effectively identifies learnable portions of teacher-failed trajectories without additional generation, achieving better performance than offline OPD baselines and matching online OPD methods with substantially lower computational cost.

title: Hyperbolic Graph Representation Learning for Differential Diagnosis on Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
summary: Biomedical knowledge graphs combine ontology-derived hierarchies with transversal associations among heterogeneous entities such as phenotypes, diseases, genes, proteins, and patients. This hybrid structure raises the question of whether hyperbolic embeddings, which naturally capture tree-like organization, remain useful beyond purely hierarchical graphs. We present a preliminary study of hyperbolic graph representation learning for Mendelian-disease differential diagnosis on a patient-integrated biomedical graph. Experiments on isolated ontology subgraphs show that hyperbolic models achieve strong performance in substantially lower dimensions than Euclidean baselines. We then evaluate the models on a link-prediction task that ranks candidate diseases for each patient. Results suggest that hyperbolic embeddings can exploit biomedical hierarchical structure while supporting diagnostic reasoning over heterogeneous patient-level graphs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether hyperbolic embeddings, which excel at capturing hierarchical structures, remain effective for hybrid biomedical knowledge graphs that combine ontological hierarchies with heterogeneous patient-level associations. The study applies hyperbolic graph representation learning to Mendelian-disease differential diagnosis.
AI.motivation: To determine if hyperbolic embeddings—typically used for tree-like hierarchical structures—can be effectively applied to biomedical knowledge graphs that combine ontology-derived hierarchies with transversal associations among heterogeneous entities (phenotypes, diseases, genes, proteins, patients).
AI.method: Two-stage experimental approach: (1) Evaluate hyperbolic models on isolated ontology subgraphs, comparing dimension requirements with Euclidean baselines; (2) Conduct link-prediction tasks to rank candidate diseases for patients using a patient-integrated biomedical graph.
AI.result: Hyperbolic models achieve strong performance in substantially lower dimensions than Euclidean baselines on ontology subgraphs. Link-prediction results suggest hyperbolic embeddings can exploit biomedical hierarchical structure while supporting diagnostic reasoning over heterogeneous patient-level graphs.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic embeddings are valuable beyond purely hierarchical graphs—they can effectively leverage biomedical hierarchical structure while supporting diagnostic reasoning across heterogeneous patient-level graphs, offering a promising approach for precision medicine applications.

title: Every Fixed Metric Has a Blind Spot: A Learned Atmospheric Critic for Scoring Forecast Realism
summary: Despite their high accuracy on point-wise metrics, machine learning weather forecasting models can exhibit different failure modes such as blurring, periodic irregularities, and other unphysical spatial artifacts. This has motivated a variety of metrics to detect known failure cases. Existing metrics fix a representation or transformation in advance, and that choice limits the artifacts they can detect. We propose to train a discriminator for separating reference data from the model's output, and using its output logit to obtain a divergence-like realism score. The discriminator learns whatever separates the model's fields from real weather, adapting to whichever failure mode that model exhibits. We compare our learned atmospheric critic to existing metrics using various synthetic corruptions applied to ERA5 reanalysis data. Our method successfully identifies the corruptions and ranks their severity, while existing metrics fail on at least one corruption. Additionally, we evaluate forecasts from real weather models, and find that the realism score degrades with longer lead times and the metric generally assigns higher realism to numerical models than to machine learning models.

AI.tldr: A learned "atmospheric critic" metric that trains a discriminator to distinguish real weather data from machine learning model outputs, providing a more flexible alternative to fixed metrics for detecting failure modes in weather forecasting models.
AI.motivation: Machine learning weather models, despite high point-wise accuracy, exhibit failure modes (blurring, periodic irregularities, unphysical artifacts) that existing fixed metrics cannot adequately detect due to their predetermined representations.
AI.method: Train a discriminator network to separate reference ERA5 reanalysis data from model outputs; use the discriminator's output logit as a divergence-like "realism score" that adapts to whatever failure modes the model exhibits.
AI.result: Method successfully identifies synthetic corruptions and ranks their severity, while existing metrics fail on at least one corruption type. On real forecasts, realism scores degrade with longer lead times and numerical models receive higher scores than ML models.
AI.conclusion: Learned discriminative metrics outperform fixed metrics for detecting weather model failure modes, offering a flexible approach that adapts to various artifacts without requiring predefined transformation functions.

title: Beyond Random Couplings: Contrastive Noise Alignment in Generative Flows
summary: Diffusion and flow-matching models are typically trained by corrupting data through independently sampled Gaussian noise. While simple and scalable, this forward process induces arbitrary data-noise couplings, forcing the network to learn high-curvature transports between unrelated endpoints. Existing optimal-transport methods reduce this burden by reassigning fixed noise samples to data, but the source noise distribution itself remains passive. To address this, we introduce Contrastive Noise Alignment (CNA), a training-time method that creates dynamic, contrastive couplings by optimizing the noise representations directly. By modeling the noise batch as an interacting particle system, CNA employs a cross-modal InfoNCE objective to align noise particles with their paired data targets. To prevent spatial collapse, this alignment is regularized using an angular entropy term and a radial norm penalty. We show theoretically that this equilibrium asymptotically preserves Gaussian structures, maintaining tractability during inference. Empirically, CNA improves the alignment between noise and data, reduces flow curvature, and provides better generation quality with fewer required sampling steps. For few-step, pixel-space generation (2-4 NFEs), CNA reduces FID by over 50\% compared to standard rectified flow, and by at least 24\% against Optimal Transport baselines.

AI.tldr: Contrastive Noise Alignment (CNA) is a training method for diffusion/flow-matching models that creates dynamic, contrastive couplings between noise and data by optimizing noise representations directly using a cross-modal InfoNCE objective, regularized by angular entropy and radial norm penalties.
AI.motivation: Standard diffusion models corrupt data with independently sampled Gaussian noise, which induces arbitrary data-noise couplings. This forces networks to learn high-curvature transports between unrelated endpoints. While optimal-transport methods reassign noise samples to data, the source noise distribution remains passive. CNA addresses this by making the noise distribution actively align with data.
AI.method: CNA models the noise batch as an interacting particle system and employs a cross-modal InfoNCE objective to align noise particles with their paired data targets. To prevent spatial collapse, alignment is regularized using an angular entropy term and a radial norm penalty. Theoretically, this equilibrium asymptotically preserves Gaussian structures.
AI.result: CNA improves alignment between noise and data, reduces flow curvature, and provides better generation quality with fewer sampling steps. For few-step pixel-space generation (2-4 NFEs), CNA reduces FID by over 50% compared to standard rectified flow, and by at least 24% against Optimal Transport baselines.
AI.conclusion: CNA successfully addresses the passive noise distribution problem in diffusion models through contrastive alignment, achieving substantial FID improvements in few-step generation scenarios while maintaining theoretical guarantees on Gaussian structure preservation.

title: Beyond Routine Compliance: Cunning Data Cultivates Safety Vigilance in Large Language Models
summary: Safety alignment teaches large language models (LLMs) to recognize harmful requests and reject risky instructions. Yet aligned models can fail when harmful intent is concealed within seemingly benign contexts. Robust safety therefore requires both knowledge of safety boundaries and \textbf{vigilance}: the ability to detect unusual premises, misleading reasoning, and latent risks beneath surface-level semantics. Vigilance requires models to scrutinize a request's underlying intent and assumptions before acting. To cultivate this capability, we introduce \textbf{cunning questions}, which are not necessarily safety-related but contain misleading premises, atypical reasoning, or subtle inconsistencies. We hypothesize that learning to look beyond such reasoning traps can transfer to safety-critical scenarios. Experiments show that Cunning training improves robustness to out-of-distribution jailbreak attacks and strengthens subsequent safety fine-tuning. Furthermore, augmenting an existing state-of-the-art safety alignment pipeline with Cunning establishes a new state of the art across our evaluated settings, reducing mean ASR across nine backbone--benchmark combinations from 17.40\% to 15.05\%. Trace analysis after matched safety fine-tuning suggests that safety judgments are more likely to govern responses before harmful planning begins. A conditional theoretical analysis further characterizes when invariance learned from cunning data can transfer to safety-related inputs. These findings suggest that cunning data can strengthen model vigilance and complement conventional safety alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "cunning questions" - queries containing misleading premises, atypical reasoning, or subtle inconsistencies - to train LLMs to look beyond surface-level semantics and detect hidden risks. This approach improves robustness against jailbreak attacks and enhances safety fine-tuning, reducing mean attack success rate from 17.40% to 15.05% across nine backbone-benchmark combinations.
AI.motivation: Current safety alignment teaches LLMs to recognize harmful requests, but aligned models fail when harmful intent is concealed within seemingly benign contexts. The authors argue that robust safety requires "vigilance" - the ability to detect unusual premises, misleading reasoning, and latent risks beneath surface-level semantics.
AI.method: The authors propose training with "cunning questions" - non-safety-related queries containing misleading premises, atypical reasoning, or subtle inconsistencies. They hypothesize that learning to identify reasoning traps transfers to safety-critical scenarios. They augment an existing state-of-the-art safety alignment pipeline with this "Cunning" training.
AI.result: Cunning training improves robustness to out-of-distribution jailbreak attacks and strengthens subsequent safety fine-tuning. When combined with existing safety alignment, it achieves new state-of-the-art results, reducing mean ASR from 17.40% to 15.05% across nine backbone-benchmark combinations. Trace analysis shows safety judgments are more likely to govern responses before harmful planning begins.
AI.conclusion: Cunning data can strengthen model vigilance and complement conventional safety alignment. A conditional theoretical analysis characterizes when invariance learned from cunning data can transfer to safety-related inputs, providing guidance for future applications.

title: Reliable Virtual Sensing: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Robustness Under Sensor Failures
summary: Virtual sensing, the estimation of hard-to-measure quantities from available sensor measurements, is a critical enabler for control and monitoring in cyber-physical systems. However, when sensors fail, learning-based predictors can produce physically implausible estimates that propagate to system-level failures. We argue that real-world deployment demands robustness and introduce MuViS-C, the first multi-domain benchmark of robustness against common sensor failures in learning-based virtual sensing. Building on an existing nominal-performance benchmark and established corruption taxonomies, it covers ten sensor failure modes, from subtle drifts to catastrophic signal dropouts, at multiple severities. These are paired with complementary robustness measures capturing average error under corruption, relative degradation, and worst-case fragility. Across nine datasets from six domains, we benchmark six architectures spanning gradient-boosted trees and the major inductive biases for sequence modeling: convolution, recurrence, attention, and MLP-mixing. On the attention-based architecture, we further probe three robustification strategies. We find that (i) every model degrades substantially under corruption, becoming worse than a naïve predictor on at least one corruption setting, (ii) gradient-boosted tree ensembles achieve strong robustness, and (iii) dedicated robustification closes the gap between the attention-based architecture and the most robust models, though each strategy hurts nominal performance. The benchmark's multi-domain design proves essential, as model rankings shift across datasets, and no single domain captures the full robustness picture. MuViS-C is open-source and extensible to new datasets, failure modes, measures, and models.

AI.tldr: MuViS-C is the first multi-domain benchmark for evaluating robustness of learning-based virtual sensing against common sensor failures. It covers 10 failure modes across 9 datasets from 6 domains, testing 6 architectures and 3 robustification strategies.
AI.motivation: Learning-based virtual sensors can produce physically implausible estimates when sensors fail, leading to system-level failures. Real-world deployment demands robustness, but no standardized benchmark exists for evaluating virtual sensing under sensor failures.
AI.method: Built on existing nominal-performance benchmarks and corruption taxonomies, the authors created MuViS-C covering ten sensor failure modes (from subtle drifts to catastrophic dropouts) at multiple severities. They benchmarked six architectures spanning gradient-boosted trees, convolution, recurrence, attention, and MLP-mixing across nine datasets from six domains, and tested three robustification strategies on attention-based models.
AI.result: Three key findings: (i) Every model degrades substantially under corruption, becoming worse than a naïve predictor in at least one setting; (ii) Gradient-boosted tree ensembles achieve strong robustness; (iii) Dedicated robustification closes the gap between attention-based architecture and most robust models, though each strategy hurts nominal performance. Model rankings shift across datasets, with no single domain capturing the full robustness picture.
AI.conclusion: MuViS-C provides the first standardized benchmark for evaluating virtual sensing robustness. The multi-domain design is essential as model performance varies across domains. The benchmark is open-source and extensible to new datasets, failure modes, measures, and models.

title: Learning A Unified Template for Gait Recognition
summary: "What I cannot create, I do not understand."Human wisdom reveals that creation is one of the highest forms of learning. For example, Diffusion Models have demonstrated remarkable semantic structure and memory in image generation, understanding, and restoration, which intuitively benefits representation learning. However, current gait networks rarely embrace this perspective, relying primarily on learning by contrasting gait samples under varying complex conditions, leading to semantic inconsistency and uniformity issues. To address these issues, we propose Origins with generative capabilities whose underlying philosophy is that different entities are generated from a unified template, inherently regularizing gait representations within a consistent and diverse semantic space to capture accurate gait differences. Admittedly, learning this unified template is exceedingly challenging, as it requires the comprehensiveness of the template to encompass gait representations with various conditions. Inspired by Diffusion Models, Origins diffuses the unified template into timestep templates for gait generative learning, and meanwhile transfers the unified template for gait representation learning. Especially, gait generative and representation learning serve as a unified framework for end-to-end joint training. Extensive experiments on CASIA-B, CCPG,SUSTech1K, Gait3D, GREW and CCGR-MINI demonstrate that Origins performs unified generative and representation learning, achieving superior performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Origins, a novel gait recognition framework that integrates generative capabilities with representation learning, inspired by the philosophy "What I cannot create, I do not understand." The key idea is that different gait entities are generated from a unified template, which regularizes gait representations within a consistent and diverse semantic space.
AI.motivation: Current gait networks primarily learn by contrasting gait samples under varying complex conditions, which leads to semantic inconsistency and uniformity issues. The authors advocate a creation-based learning approach, drawing inspiration from Diffusion Models' success in image generation, understanding, and restoration.
AI.method: Origins employs Diffusion Models to diffuse a unified template into timestep templates for gait generative learning, while simultaneously transferring this unified template for gait representation learning. These two learning paradigms (generative and representation) are unified in an end-to-end joint training framework.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets (CASIA-B, CCPG, SUSTech1K, Gait3D, GREW, and CCGR-MINI) demonstrate that Origins achieves superior performance in both unified generative and representation learning tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Origins framework successfully bridges generative and representation learning for gait recognition, providing a more comprehensive and semantically consistent approach that captures accurate gait differences across various conditions.

title: AeroWeaver: An Embodied-Agent Harness for Weaving Aerial Skills into Distributed, Adaptive Swarm Execution
summary: Collective intelligence is a collaborative autonomy paradigm in which multiple agents pursue shared objectives through local perception, information exchange, and coordinated action. UAV swarms embody this paradigm by coordinating multiple vehicles in tasks such as search, inspection, and tracking. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) agents have strengthened natural-language task understanding and high-level planning, providing a flexible semantic interface between mission descriptions and collective behavior. While these advances expand semantic reasoning, applying LLM agents to UAV swarms raises challenges in grounding model decisions in executable capabilities, reconciling global task reasoning with distributed execution, and using mission-specific experience for continual adaptation. To address these challenges, we introduce AeroWeaver, an embodied-agent harness that weaves individual UAV skills into coordinated mission-level behavior. AeroWeaver connects semantic decisions to governed skills, organizes role-conditioned local agents for distributed coordination, and uses role-indexed state-action-reward experience to refine skill selection online. Experiments and runtime validation show that AeroWeaver maintains valid skill execution under tested conditions and supports body-local multi-UAV operation without a central agent generating joint actions from global context, while reward-guided online updates provide a training-free path for adaptive learning swarm agents from accumulated execution experience. Code: https://github.com/Admire-ljb/AeroWeaver.

AI.tldr: AeroWeaver is an embodied-agent framework that enables large language model (LLM) agents to control UAV swarms by connecting semantic decisions to executable skills, organizing role-conditioned local agents for distributed coordination, and using role-indexed experience for online adaptation without training.
AI.motivation: Applying LLM agents to UAV swarms faces challenges in: (1) grounding model decisions in executable capabilities, (2) reconciling global task reasoning with distributed execution, and (3) using mission-specific experience for continual adaptation.
AI.method: AeroWeaver connects semantic decisions to governed skills, organizes role-conditioned local agents for distributed coordination, and uses role-indexed state-action-reward experience to refine skill selection online.
AI.result: AeroWeaver maintains valid skill execution under tested conditions and supports body-local multi-UAV operation without a central agent generating joint actions from global context, while reward-guided online updates provide a training-free path for adaptive learning.
AI.conclusion: AeroWeaver successfully enables LLM agents to control UAV swarms through a novel framework that combines semantic reasoning with distributed execution and training-free adaptive learning from accumulated execution experience.

title: TERN: A Delta-rule Memory with a Seasonal Reference and Online Adaptation for Epidemic Forecasting
summary: Weekly influenza surveillance counts guide vaccine distribution and public-health alerts, yet they are hard to forecast. Each region offers only a few seasons, waves shift in timing and height every year, and information that helps while a wave grows misleads after its peak, whereas last season's shape stays informative for a year. Existing epidemic graph models and general forecasters read a short fixed window and treat all past information alike, so they neither exploit earlier seasons nor discard stale associations when the epidemic phase changes. To address these limitations, we propose TERN, a forecaster built around a delta-rule fast-weight memory that decays channel-wise and erases along a learned address under gates driven by local epidemic-phase features, combined with an explicit seasonal reference and online adaptation. On three Cola-GNN influenza benchmarks, TERN outperformed epidemic graph models and general forecasters, matched or exceeded seasonal references, and a controlled comparison confirmed the contribution of the memory itself.

AI.tldr: TERN is a neural network forecaster for weekly influenza surveillance that uses a delta-rule fast-weight memory with channel-wise decay and learned address erasure under gates driven by local epidemic-phase features, combined with explicit seasonal reference and online adaptation, outperforming existing methods on three Cola-GNN influenza benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing epidemic forecasting methods have three key limitations: (1) each region offers only limited seasonal data, (2) information that helps during epidemic growth becomes misleading after peak (phase shift problem), and (3) current models use fixed short windows and treat all past information equally, neither exploiting earlier seasons nor discarding stale associations when epidemic phase changes.
AI.method: TERN employs a delta-rule fast-weight memory with two key mechanisms: (1) channel-wise decay that erases information along a learned address under gates driven by local epidemic-phase features, combined with an explicit seasonal reference and online adaptation.
AI.result: On three Cola-GNN influenza benchmarks, TERN outperformed epidemic graph models and general forecasters, matched or exceeded seasonal references, and controlled comparison confirmed the memory's contribution.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fast-weight memory architecture effectively addresses the phase-shift problem and limited data limitation in influenza forecasting, demonstrating superior performance over existing epidemic graph models and general forecasters while maintaining competitive performance with seasonal references.

title: Semantic-ITC: A Frame-wise Indoor Mobile Laser Scanning Dataset and Benchmark for Semantic Segmentation
summary: Semantic labels for indoor mobile laser scanning (MLS) frames remain largely absent from current point cloud semantic segmentation benchmarks, which mainly focus on reconstructed indoor scenes or outdoor LiDAR perception. This paper introduces Semantic-ITC, to the best of our knowledge the first public dataset and benchmark for frame-wise indoor MLS semantic segmentation. The dataset contains 52 indoor sequences, 79,108 MLS frames, and 1.23 billion labeled points collected in classrooms, corridors, meeting rooms, offices, and study areas. Labels are attached directly to measured LiDAR points in each frame using 16 semantic classes covering structural elements, furniture, room equipment, vegetation, and other indoor objects. Semantic-ITC preserves the sparse, non-uniform, and frame-wise sampling pattern of indoor MLS, making it distinct from scene-level reconstructed point clouds and mesh-based indoor datasets. The annotations are produced by a hybrid workflow that combines predictions from a visual foundation model applied to synchronized RGB images, structural information from BIM, and manual refinement, with the final labels assigned to the original LiDAR frames. A single-frame benchmark is provided, and the best baseline reaches 79.27\% mIoU. Remaining errors are concentrated around object boundaries and ambiguous indoor classes, indicating the challenges of indoor MLS segmentation under sparse frame geometry and long-tailed class distributions. The dataset provides a public benchmark for evaluating semantic segmentation directly on measured indoor MLS frames and supports future studies on frame-wise indoor MLS semantic segmentation.

AI.tldr: Semantic-ITC is the first public dataset and benchmark for frame-wise indoor mobile laser scanning (MLS) semantic segmentation, containing 52 sequences, 79,108 frames, and 1.23 billion labeled points across 16 semantic classes in indoor environments. The best baseline achieves 79.27% mIoU.
AI.motivation: Current point cloud semantic segmentation benchmarks lack semantic labels for indoor MLS frames, focusing mainly on reconstructed indoor scenes or outdoor LiDAR perception. This creates a gap in evaluating semantic segmentation directly on measured indoor MLS data.
AI.method: The dataset uses a hybrid annotation workflow combining: (1) predictions from a visual foundation model applied to synchronized RGB images, (2) structural information from BIM (Building Information Modeling), and (3) manual refinement. The annotations are attached directly to measured LiDAR points, preserving the sparse, non-uniform, frame-wise sampling pattern of indoor MLS.
AI.result: The best baseline model achieves 79.27% mIoU on the single-frame benchmark. Remaining errors are concentrated around object boundaries and ambiguous indoor classes, highlighting challenges from sparse frame geometry and long-tailed class distributions.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-ITC provides the first public benchmark for evaluating semantic segmentation directly on measured indoor MLS frames. It supports future research on frame-wise indoor MLS semantic segmentation and addresses the gap between scene-level reconstructed point clouds and actual MLS frame data.

title: TRIPROBE: Probing Task Separability Beyond Classification for XAI
summary: Modern evaluation of learning pipelines often reduces to downstream accuracy, leaving open the question of why tasks succeed or fail. TriProbe addresses this gap with a multi-level probing framework for explainable diagnosis of task separability. Rather than treating models as black boxes, TriProbe traces how separability evolves across inputs, learned features, and final classifiers. It decomposes multi-task problems into binary subtasks and applies three complementary probes: a Foundational Probe on input spaces, a Latent Probe on feature representations, and a Final Probe on classifier outputs. Using Maximum Fisher's Discriminant Ratio as a principled separability metric, TriProbe identifies bottlenecks and affected task pairs. Experiments on the Roshambo sEMG benchmark show how TriProbe reveals hidden breakdowns, guiding data collection, validation, and architecture design.

AI.tldr: TriProbe is a multi-level probing framework that diagnoses why learning tasks succeed or failure by tracing separability evolution across input spaces, learned features, and final classifiers using three complementary probes (Foundational, Latent, Final) with Maximum Fisher's Discriminant Ratio as the separability metric.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of learning pipelines only focuses on downstream accuracy, leaving the fundamental question of why tasks succeed or fail unanswered. There is a need to go beyond black-box evaluation to understand the underlying reasons for task performance.
AI.method: TriProbe decomposes multi-task problems into binary subtasks and applies three complementary probes: Foundational Probe on input spaces, Latent Probe on feature representations, and Final Probe on classifier outputs. It uses Maximum Fisher's Discriminant Ratio as a principled separability metric to identify bottlenecks and affected task pairs.
AI.result: Experiments on the Roshambo sEMG benchmark demonstrate that TriProbe reveals hidden breakdowns in learning pipelines, providing diagnostic insights that can guide data collection, validation, and architecture design decisions.
AI.conclusion: TriProbe provides a principled framework for explainable diagnosis of task separability, enabling practitioners to identify where separability breaks down in the pipeline and take targeted actions to improve model performance.

title: Spatially Adaptive Noise Injection
summary: Diffusion samplers reverse a learned noising process using either stochastic (DDPM) or deterministic (DDIM) updates, which represent endpoints of a single family controlled by a scalar noise-injection variance that is applied identically at every spatial location. This uniform approach neglects the geometry of natural images: high-curvature regions such as edges and textures, where the denoiser is uncertain, benefit from stochastic correction, whereas smooth regions, where the score is precise, are degraded by injected noise. This work investigates whether each pixel requires stochastic correction at a given timestep and introduces Spatially Adaptive Noise Injection (SANI), a novel sampling framework that dynamically adjusts noise application on a per-pixel basis. SANI integrates a probabilistic gating mechanism with a derived spatially adaptive variance, ensuring that noise is injected precisely where needed to refine complex features while preserving well-formed structures. Experimental results and decoupling ablations demonstrate that SANI consistently improves Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) over the vanilla DDPM and DDIM endpoint samplers across diverse sampling timesteps, while remaining competitive with variance-learning baselines, highlighting the importance of spatial adaptivity in diffusion sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Spatially Adaptive Noise Injection (SANI), a diffusion sampling framework that dynamically adjusts noise injection on a per-pixel basis rather than applying uniform noise across all spatial locations. The key insight is that high-curvature regions (edges, textures) benefit from stochastic correction while smooth regions are degraded by injected noise.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion samplers (DDPM and DDIM) apply noise uniformly across all spatial locations, ignoring the geometry of natural images. This uniform approach is suboptimal because different regions have different characteristics - complex regions need stochastic correction while smooth regions are precise and should not be perturbed.
AI.method: SANI integrates a probabilistic gating mechanism with a derived spatially adaptive variance. It determines on a per-pixel basis whether noise injection is needed at each timestep, injecting noise precisely where needed to refine complex features while preserving well-formed structures.
AI.result: SANI consistently improves Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) over vanilla DDPM and DDIM endpoint samplers across diverse sampling timesteps, while remaining competitive with variance-learning baselines.
AI.conclusion: The work highlights the importance of spatial adaptivity in diffusion sampling. By dynamically adjusting noise injection per-pixel, SANI achieves better image quality than uniform noise approaches, demonstrating that spatial adaptivity is a valuable dimension for improving diffusion models.

title: DiT-Garment: Garment Dynamics with Diffusion Transformers
summary: We present DiT-Garment to model dynamic 3D clothing over human body models in arbitrary motion. Unlike existing methods, DiT-Garment can animate garments with unseen designs and physical materials, while allowing for direct inference of deformations for any target pose. To achieve this, we leverage a 2D diffusion transformer architecture to learn 3D deformations in a 2D UV-space. As the result is non-deterministic, our generative model learns the distribution of possible outcomes. The template garment is represented as a 3D triangle mesh spatially aligned with a 3D human body model in a standardized pose. To work with different garment designs without the need of a common template or complex graph convolution operations, the diffusion transformer is conditioned on a 3D position map of the template, represented in UV-space, which allows to implicitly learn a deformation of the 3D space around the body in standard pose. Further conditioning on body motion and physical parameters allows to physically ground the model. We quantitatively and qualitatively evaluate DiT-Garment on both synthetic and real data. While only trained on synthetic simulations of automatically generated cloth designs, our method generalizes to captured and artist-made garment designs. Code and data are available for research purposes at https://dumoulina.github.io/dit-garment/.

AI.tldr: DiT-Garment uses a 2D diffusion transformer architecture to model dynamic 3D clothing deformations over human bodies in arbitrary poses. The method works in UV-space, allowing generalization to unseen garment designs without requiring common templates or graph convolution operations.
AI.motivation: Existing methods cannot animate garments with unseen designs and physical materials while allowing direct inference of deformations for any target pose. There was a need for a more flexible approach that could handle arbitrary garment designs without complex graph convolution operations.
AI.method: The method leverages a 2D diffusion transformer architecture to learn 3D deformations in 2D UV-space. The template garment is represented as a 3D triangle mesh aligned with a 3D human body in a standardized pose. The diffusion transformer is conditioned on a 3D position map of the template in UV-space, enabling implicit learning of deformation of the 3D space around the body. Further conditioning on body motion and physical parameters grounds the model physically.
AI.result: DiT-Garment was quantitatively and qualitatively evaluated on both synthetic and real data. Despite being trained only on synthetic simulations of automatically generated cloth designs, the method generalizes to captured and artist-made garment designs.
AI.conclusion: The diffusion transformer approach successfully enables dynamic 3D clothing modeling that can handle unseen garment designs and physical materials, with direct inference capability for any target pose. The UV-space representation eliminates the need for common templates or complex graph convolution operations.

title: Recursive Reasoning or Statistical Extrapolation? In-Context Learning in Multi-Agent Interdependent Decision-Making
summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve decisions using interaction history, yet it remains unclear whether such improvement reflects refined internal reasoning or mere extrapolation of statistical patterns. To disentangle these mechanisms, we study LLM agents in multi-agent incomplete-information games that require recursive belief reasoning. By constructing a public goods game and manipulating the statistical structure of historical feedback, we evaluate decision quality against a history-independent rational expectations equilibrium (REE) benchmark. Our experiments reveal that when historical statistical patterns are disrupted, the benefits of longer context largely vanish, degrading decision quality to the no-context baseline in a way sharply amplified by stronger strategic interdependence. These results suggest that, in such strategic environments, ICL behavior is more consistent with statistical extrapolation than with strategic reasoning. Our work extends the mechanistic study of ICL to strategic multi-agent settings, introduces REE as a diagnostic tool for distinguishing reasoning from extrapolation, and provides a reusable framework for probing the boundaries of LLM reasoning in recursive belief tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether in-context learning (ICL) in LLMs improves decision-making through genuine strategic reasoning or mere statistical pattern extrapolation. Using multi-agent incomplete-information games (public goods game) with recursive belief reasoning, the study finds that disrupting historical statistical patterns eliminates ICL benefits, suggesting ICL in strategic settings relies on extrapolation rather than true reasoning.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear whether ICL improvements in LLM agents reflect refined internal reasoning or statistical pattern extrapolation. This distinction is crucial for understanding LLM capabilities in strategic multi-agent environments.
AI.method: The authors construct a public goods game in multi-agent incomplete-information settings requiring recursive belief reasoning. They manipulate the statistical structure of historical feedback and evaluate decision quality against a history-independent rational expectations equilibrium (REE) benchmark.
AI.result: When historical statistical patterns are disrupted, the benefits of longer context largely vanish—decision quality degrades to the no-context baseline. This degradation is sharply amplified by stronger strategic interdependence.
AI.conclusion: ICL behavior in strategic environments is more consistent with statistical extrapolation than strategic reasoning. The paper introduces REE as a diagnostic tool and provides a reusable framework for probing LLM reasoning boundaries in recursive belief tasks.

title: Provable Guarantees for Spectral Structured Prediction
summary: Structured prediction is the simultaneous prediction of multiple labels, and is widely used in various fields, such as natural language processing and computer vision. In this paper, we study binary node label recovery on signed graphs with edge-flip noise, a model introduced by (Globerson et al., 2015), via a simple spectral method that decodes node labels from the signs of the principal eigenvector of the noisy signed adjacency matrix. We develop graph structure-agnostic theoretical guarantees for approximate inference of node labels as well as guarantees for maximum angle deviation with respect to the ground truth node labels. By leveraging tools from matrix concentration theory and eigenvector perturbation analysis, we derive new concentration inequalities that explicitly quantify the effect of the spectral gap of the adjacency matrix, number of nodes, degree distribution, and noise level. As a corollary, we relate our general results to the Cheeger constant and provide results for different classes of graphs. We perform several synthetic experiments to validate our theory. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to provide theoretical guarantees for the spectral-based approach. As a byproduct of our analysis, we derive technical results that might be of independent interest and useful for other machine learning problems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies binary node label recovery on signed graphs with edge-flip noise using a spectral method. The approach decodes node labels from the signs of the principal eigenvector of the noisy signed adjacency matrix. The authors provide theoretical guarantees including concentration inequalities that quantify the effects of spectral gap, number of nodes, degree distribution, and noise level.
AI.motivation: Structured prediction is widely used in NLP and computer vision. The authors aim to provide theoretical guarantees for a spectral-based approach to recover binary node labels on signed graphs with edge-flip noise, a model introduced by Globerson et al. (2015). This addresses the lack of theoretical analysis for such methods in the literature.
AI.method: The authors use a simple spectral method that decodes node labels from the signs of the principal eigenvector of the noisy signed adjacency matrix. They leverage tools from matrix concentration theory and eigenvector perturbation analysis to derive theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: The authors develop graph structure-agnostic theoretical guarantees for approximate inference of node labels, as well as guarantees for maximum angle deviation with respect to ground truth node labels. They derive new concentration inequalities that explicitly quantify the effect of spectral gap, number of nodes, degree distribution, and noise level. They relate results to the Cheeger constant and provide results for different classes of graphs. Synthetic experiments validate the theory.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first theoretical guarantees for the spectral-based approach to binary node label recovery on signed graphs with edge-flip noise. The analysis also yields technical results of independent interest for other machine learning problems.

title: Learning from Distributed Eyes: Leveraging Collaborative Perception for Automated Model Adaptation
summary: In autonomous driving, perception models often struggle to generalize to new environments due to domain shifts. While unsupervised model adaptation offers a feasible solution without labor-intensive manual labeling, existing methods that rely solely on the ego-vehicle's data often lead to inferior pseudo-labeling performance. To address this critical issue, we propose LDE, Learning from Distributed ``Eyes", a novel framework that transforms collaborative perception (CP) into a source of high-quality supervision for model adaptation. This pseudo-labeling approach is hyperparameter-insensitive and relatively reliable, assuming CP often outperforms single-agent's perception. However, naively implementing this approach encounters (1) the communication bottleneck of sharing rich features under time and bandwidth constraints, (2) the view discrepancy between the CP view and the learner's Field of View (FoV), and (3) the unreliability even in CP-generated labels. To address these issues, we design an adaptation-oriented feature sharing mechanism that selectively transmits the most critical information for adaptation, an FoV filtering method that meticulously eliminates mismatched labels, and a curriculum learning strategy to progressively exploit pseudo labels. Extensive experiments on 3D object detection tasks demonstrate that LDE consistently outperforms both the pre-trained models and state-of-the-art unsupervised adaptation methods.

AI.tldr: LDE proposes transforming collaborative perception into a source of high-quality supervision for unsupervised model adaptation in autonomous driving, addressing domain shift issues through a pseudo-labeling approach that leverages multiple "eyes" (agents) rather than single ego-vehicle data.
AI.motivation: Existing unsupervised model adaptation methods rely solely on the ego-vehicle's data, leading to inferior pseudo-labeling performance due to domain shifts. The key insight is that collaborative perception (CP) often outperforms single-agent perception, making it a promising source of supervision.
AI.method: The framework addresses three core challenges: (1) adaptation-oriented feature sharing mechanism to handle communication bottlenecks by selectively transmitting critical information; (2) FoV filtering method to eliminate mismatched labels caused by view discrepancy between CP view and learner's Field of View; (3) curriculum learning strategy to progressively exploit pseudo labels and handle unreliability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 3D object detection tasks demonstrate that LDE consistently outperforms both pre-trained models and state-of-the-art unsupervised adaptation methods.
AI.conclusion: LDE successfully leverages collaborative perception as supervision for model adaptation, providing a hyperparameter-insensitive and reliable pseudo-labeling approach that addresses key practical challenges in autonomous driving perception.

title: Reasoning through Evolution: Automatic Meta-path Discovery for LLM-based Fake News Detection
summary: Propagation structures provide crucial evidence for fake news detection, yet existing approaches primarily rely on supervised GNN-based models, which require substantial labeled data and exhibit limited generalization. Although large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, directly feeding them raw propagation graphs creates a significant modality mismatch and severe information overload, making structure-aware reasoning unreliable in zero-shot and few-shot settings. To bridge this gap, we propose MAGER, a multi-agent genetic evolution framework that automatically discovers meta-paths optimized for LLM reasoning. By compressing complex propagation graphs into informative subgraphs, the evolved meta-paths alleviate both information overload and modality mismatch, enabling frozen LLMs to perform structure-aware veracity reasoning. We further introduce a graph in-context learning strategy that retrieves semantically and structurally similar demonstrations to strengthen classification and reasoning. Extensive experiments show that MAGER substantially improves frozen LLMs as standalone fake news detectors in data-efficient settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/SenticNet/MAGER.

AI.tldr: MAGER is a multi-agent genetic evolution framework that discovers optimized meta-paths to compress complex propagation graphs into informative subgraphs, enabling frozen LLMs to perform structure-aware fake news detection in zero-shot and few-shot settings without requiring extensive labeled data.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based fake news detection approaches require substantial labeled data and have limited generalization. While LLMs have strong reasoning capabilities, directly feeding them raw propagation graphs creates modality mismatch and information overload, making structure-aware reasoning unreliable in data-efficient settings.
AI.method: The paper proposes MAGER, a multi-agent genetic evolution framework that automatically discovers meta-paths optimized for LLM reasoning. It compresses complex propagation graphs into informative subgraphs through evolved meta-paths, and introduces a graph in-context learning strategy that retrieves semantically and structurally similar demonstrations to strengthen classification and reasoning.
AI.result: MAGER substantially improves frozen LLMs as standalone fake news detectors in data-efficient settings (zero-shot and few-shot).
AI.conclusion: By addressing the modality mismatch and information overload problems through meta-path evolution and graph in-context learning, MAGER enables frozen LLMs to effectively perform structure-aware veracity reasoning, achieving significant improvements in data-efficient fake news detection scenarios.

title: Provable Guarantees and Efficient Learning of Structural Equation Models with Latent Confounders
summary: Causal discovery aims to recover causal relationships from observed data. In various fields, exploring causal relationships among variables remains an important topic, but this task becomes challenging due to the existence of latent confounders. Ignoring such confounders can lead to false associations and incorrect edge directions. In this paper, we study the linear structural equation model with latent confounders. We propose an algorithm that iteratively identifies terminal (observed) nodes and reconstructs the directed acyclic graph of the observed variables. To do this, we recover the precision matrix of the observed variables as a sparse plus low-rank matrix: a sparse matrix captures the conditional dependencies among observed variables, while a low-rank matrix captures the combined influence of a few latent confounders. We establish that for $p$ observed variables, $r$ latent confounders and $s$ edges, our procedure correctly identifies the directed causal relationship among observed variables, for $n \gtrsim \max\{s\log p,\ r p\}$ samples. Experimental results validate our theoretical contributions.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses causal discovery in linear structural equation models with latent confounders. The proposed method iteratively identifies terminal nodes and reconstructs the DAG of observed variables by decomposing the precision matrix into a sparse component (capturing direct causal relationships) and a low-rank component (capturing latent confounders).
AI.motivation: Causal discovery is important across various fields, but latent confounders pose significant challenges. Ignoring confounders leads to false associations and incorrect edge directions. Existing methods often fail to properly account for these unobserved variables.
AI.method: The algorithm works by recovering the precision matrix of observed variables as a sparse plus low-rank matrix decomposition. It iteratively identifies terminal (observed) nodes and reconstructs the directed acyclic graph. The sparse component captures conditional dependencies among observed variables, while the low-rank component captures the combined influence of latent confounders.
AI.result: For p observed variables, r latent confounders, and s edges, the procedure correctly identifies directed causal relationships among observed variables with sample complexity n ≳ max{s log p, r p}.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical analysis establishes sufficient sample complexity conditions for consistent causal structure recovery. Experimental results validate the theoretical contributions, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in handling latent confounders in causal discovery.

title: SVMemAgent: A Streaming Video Memory Agent for Query-Agnostic Online Frame Selection
summary: Most keyframe selection studies focus on offline settings, assuming access to the full video and query in advance. In contrast, real-world streaming scenarios require online frame selection under unknown video duration, without access to either the query or future frames during selection. To address this, we introduce Streaming Video Memory (SVMem), a compact and representative memory of previously observed content, updated continuously as the video stream unfolds. Building on this setting, we propose the Streaming Video Memory Agent (SVMemAgent), which dynamically maintains a memory by deciding at each timestep whether to replace an existing memory frame with the incoming frame or discard it. SVMemAgent is trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-driven rewards derived from diverse question-answer pairs, implicitly exposing the policy to a distribution of queries during training so that SVMem retains generally informative frames at inference, when queries are unavailable. Experiments on both online and offline video benchmarks show that SVMemAgent consistently outperforms online frame selection baselines and achieves competitive performance with offline methods that assume access to the full video and query. Through task-driven rewards, SVMemAgent learns an emergent keyframe selection policy that prefers frames containing textual information, which may benefit downstream VideoQA tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses online keyframe selection for streaming videos, where neither future frames nor queries are available during selection. It proposes SVMemAgent, which uses GRPO training with task-driven rewards to learn a memory management policy that retains generally informative frames.
AI.motivation: Traditional keyframe selection methods assume offline settings with full video and query access, but real-world streaming scenarios require online decisions under uncertainty about video duration and future content.
AI.method: The authors introduce Streaming Video Memory (SVMem) as a compact representative memory, and SVMemAgent which uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-driven rewards from diverse QA pairs to learn when to replace or discard incoming frames.
AI.result: SVMemAgent outperforms online frame selection baselines and achieves competitive performance with offline methods. The method learns an emergent policy that prefers frames containing textual information, beneficial for downstream VideoQA tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully bridges the gap between offline and online video keyframe selection, demonstrating that task-driven rewards can implicitly teach the policy to retain generally informative frames without query access at inference time.

title: The Uneven Impact of Generative AI on Student Learning: Examining the Roles of Reliance, Evaluation Literacy, and Course Policy in AI-related Courses
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is changing how students learn, yet the roles of course context, cognitive reliance, evaluation literacy, and early reliance remain underexplored. Using survey responses from 118 students across 12 AI-related courses at our institution, we examined differences in GenAI use and perceived learning experiences. We identified four user clusters: high-use students reporting many benefits, light users reporting less reliance and fewer benefits, and two moderate-use groups reporting different levels of benefit. We also found significant differences between free- and premium-version users, single- and multiple-tool users, and students experiencing different instructor policies. In multivariable regression models, academic benefit was associated with early reliance and academic task support; positive impact was associated with cognitive reliance, academic task support, confidence in GenAI reliability, and instructor policy; and negative impact was associated with early reliance and attitudinal change. The association between early reliance and negative impact became stronger as evaluation literacy increased. Finally, perceptions of GenAI-enhanced learning appear to reflect cognitive, performance, and self-efficacy benefits, while concerns about stress and diminished critical thinking are associated with lower perceived learning benefits. These findings suggest that institutions need better policies to address such inequities so that institutions can enable students to benefit from increasingly capable AI systems.

AI.tldr: This study examines how 118 students across 12 AI-related courses use generative AI (GenAI) and perceive its impact on learning. Four user clusters were identified: high-use (many benefits), light users (less reliance/fewer benefits), and two moderate-use groups with varying benefit levels. Key findings show significant differences based on tool type (free vs. premium, single vs. multiple), instructor policies, and various cognitive/behavioral factors. Early reliance was associated with both positive and negative outcomes, with evaluation literacy moderating this relationship.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a gap in understanding how GenAI affects student learning, particularly examining underexplored factors including course context, cognitive reliance, evaluation literacy, and early reliance patterns.
AI.method: Survey-based study with 118 students across 12 AI-related courses. Statistical analysis included cluster analysis to identify user groups and multivariable regression models to examine associations between variables.
AI.result: Four distinct user clusters identified with different usage patterns and perceived benefits. Significant differences found between free/premium users, single/multiple tool users, and across instructor policies. Academic benefit associated with early reliance and task support; positive impact with cognitive reliance, task support, confidence, and instructor policy; negative impact with early reliance and attitudinal change. Evaluation literacy strengthened the negative impact of early reliance.
AI.conclusion: Institutions need improved policies to address inequities in GenAI use, ensuring students can benefit from increasingly capable AI systems while mitigating concerns about stress and diminished critical thinking.

title: Revisiting the Objective of Echo Chamber Detection
summary: In this paper, we study the detection of an echo chamber in a social network, i.e., the identification of a set of nodes that agree on a topic, while disagreeing with the rest of nodes. We argue that this problem is different from other social network analysis problems such as community detection, and from other graph problems such as maximum graph cut and maximum clique. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to formalize the objective function of echo chamber detection, by using the theory of Fourier transforms of set functions (Stobbe and Krause, 2012). We propose scalable semidefinite relaxation, solved via an interior point method and sparse linear algebra. Experimentally, our algorithm recovers the ground truth echo chamber better than competing methods on small synthetic experiments. Our algorithm produces echo chambers with better network properties than competing methods on large real-world datasets. To independently validate our proposed objective function, we show that our algorithm finds echo chambers with more agreements with suspended users than competing methods on a small real-world dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper tackles echo chamber detection in social networks—identifying groups of nodes that share consensus on a topic while disagreeing with outsiders. The authors propose a novel objective function based on Fourier transforms of set functions and solve it using scalable semidefinite relaxation with interior point methods and sparse linear algebra.
AI.motivation: The authors argue that echo chamber detection is distinct from related problems like community detection, maximum graph cut, and maximum clique. Despite its importance in understanding polarization and information spread in social networks, no formal objective function existed for this problem prior to this work.
AI.method: The paper introduces a semidefinite relaxation approach to solve the echo chamber detection problem. The method leverages Fourier transforms of set functions (Stobbe and Krause, 2012) to formalize the objective function. The optimization is solved via interior point methods combined with sparse linear algebra techniques for scalability.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance: (1) better recovery of ground truth echo chambers on small synthetic experiments compared to competing methods, (2) produces echo chambers with better network properties on large real-world datasets, and (3) finds echo chambers with more agreements with suspended users on a small real-world dataset, validating the proposed objective function independently.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully formalizes echo chamber detection as an optimization problem and provides an effective algorithmic solution. The validation against suspended users provides independent confirmation that the proposed objective function captures meaningful echo chamber structure. The method scales well and outperforms existing approaches across multiple evaluation metrics.

title: Accuracy- and Real-Time-Aware 4D Radar Preprocessing for Autonomous Driving Perception Systems
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures, Transactions of the Korean Society of Automotive Engineers
summary: 4D radar has emerged as a promising next-generation sensor for improving the robustness of autonomous driving perception systems because of its stable sensing capability under adverse weather conditions. However, deploying 4D radar in embedded environments with limited hardware resources requires radar-representation preprocessing that jointly considers perception accuracy, real-time performance, and computational complexity. This paper proposes a preprocessing framework for 4D-radar-based 3D object detection. First, Percentile-based 3D Shape Preservation (P3DP) extracts point clouds from radar tensors while preserving object-shape information and suppressing noise and false alarms. Second, Multi-frame-based Noise Point Discrimination using Kernel Density Estimation (MF-KDE) improves the density and reliability of sparse radar point clouds. Finally, Embedded \& NetScore (ENS) evaluates suitability for embedded deployment by jointly considering accuracy, real-time performance, adverse-weather robustness, and model complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a preprocessing framework for 4D-radar-based 3D object detection in autonomous driving. The framework consists of three components: P3DP extracts point clouds while preserving object shapes and suppressing noise; MF-KDE uses kernel density estimation across multiple frames to improve point cloud density and reliability; and ENS evaluates embedded deployment suitability considering accuracy, real-time performance, weather robustness, and model complexity.
AI.motivation: 4D radar is promising for autonomous driving due to its robustness under adverse weather conditions, but deploying it in embedded environments with limited hardware resources requires balancing perception accuracy, real-time performance, and computational complexity.
AI.method: The proposed framework includes three key techniques: (1) P3DP uses percentile-based methods to extract point clouds from radar tensors while preserving 3D object shape information and suppressing noise and false alarms; (2) MF-KDE applies multi-frame kernel density estimation to discriminate noise points and improve density and reliability of sparse radar point clouds; (3) ENS provides a scoring mechanism to evaluate embedded deployment suitability by jointly considering accuracy, real-time performance, adverse-weather robustness, and model complexity.
AI.result: The paper presents a complete preprocessing framework that addresses the challenges of deploying 4D radar in embedded autonomous driving systems, balancing multiple performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed preprocessing framework enables 4D radar to be effectively deployed in resource-constrained embedded environments while maintaining perception accuracy and robustness under adverse weather conditions.

title: Beyond Truncation: Rethinking LLM Decoding as Ensemble Pruning
summary: We introduce Mahalanobis-Ensemble Decoding (ME-Decoding), a novel Large Language Model (LLM) decoding framework that frames candidate token selection as ensemble pruning. Existing selection strategies rely predominantly on scalar probabilities, ignoring geometric semantic relationships and causing candidate redundancy. Meanwhile, current geometry-aware methods often require complex optimization or directly reweighting the original token probabilities, leading to significant computational overhead or inference instability. To address this, we formulate decoding as a subset optimization problem using a Mahalanobis distance-driven objective to enhance semantic diversity while preserving high probabilities. Specifically, we dynamically discount redundant generation paths using a token similarity matrix, constructed via an adaptive-bandwidth kernel over token embeddings. We further devise an efficient greedy selection algorithm with near-linear complexity in the candidate size under early stopping, while establishing its theoretical approximation guarantees. This renders ME-Decoding a robust, plug-and-play module with negligible inference overhead. Extensive experiments across diverse reasoning and generation tasks demonstrate that our method consistently achieves strong performance.

AI.tldr: ME-Decoding is a novel LLM decoding framework that formulates token selection as ensemble pruning, using Mahalanobis distance to balance semantic diversity with probability preservation. It employs an adaptive-bandwidth kernel over token embeddings to construct a similarity matrix, with a greedy algorithm offering near-linear complexity and theoretical guarantees.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM decoding strategies rely mainly on scalar probabilities, ignoring geometric semantic relationships and causing candidate redundancy. Current geometry-aware methods either require complex optimization or directly reweight probabilities, leading to computational overhead or inference instability.
AI.method: 1) Formulate decoding as subset optimization using Mahalanobis distance-driven objective; 2) Construct token similarity matrix via adaptive-bandwidth kernel over token embeddings; 3) Develop greedy selection algorithm with near-linear complexity under early stopping; 4) Establish theoretical approximation guarantees.
AI.result: The method achieves strong performance across diverse reasoning and generation tasks while maintaining negligible inference overhead as a plug-and-play module.
AI.conclusion: ME-Decoding provides a robust, efficient solution for improving LLM decoding by balancing semantic diversity with probability preservation, offering theoretical guarantees and practical applicability.

title: Interpretable Patch-Based Deep Learning for Wildfire Spread Prediction from Ensemble Simulations
summary: Wildfire spread is traditionally predicted using physics-based simulators, which are physically interpretable but whose cost increases with each additional ensemble member. We ask how well deep learning surrogates can reproduce these simulations at a fraction of this cost, training them on 10,584 fire spread simulations at 2m resolution for the Rectoret region in Catalonia, Spain. Four architectures are compared: a patch-based U-Net, a transfer-learned ResNet-50, a physics-informed network constrained by the wind-driven advection equation and a Swin-Unet transformer. Among the terrain and vegetation variables, only surface fuel load predicts burn probability with any strength (r = 0.27) and including it lowers prediction error by 21%. The remaining variables correlate weakly and are highly duplicative. Next, an experiment with saliency, occlusion and rotation demonstrates the models' learning. Convolutional models rely primarily on distance from the current fire front, while Swin-Unet assigns more weight to fuel and terrain, a finding also noted in an unrelated wildfire dataset. When applied without retraining to the second region, Pedriza, all three convolutional models still predict fire spread, losing accuracy by a small but systematic margin.

AI.tldr: This paper trains four deep learning architectures (U-Net, ResNet-50, physics-informed network, Swin-Unet) on 10,584 wildfire spread simulations to predict fire propagation at 2m resolution, finding that only surface fuel load significantly predicts burn probability (r=0.27), and that convolutional models rely on distance from fire front while Swin-Unet emphasizes fuel and terrain features.
AI.motivation: Physics-based wildfire simulators are physically interpretable but computationally expensive, with costs increasing for each ensemble member. The authors investigate whether deep learning surrogates can reproduce these simulations at a fraction of the computational cost.
AI.method: Four deep learning architectures were trained on 10,584 fire spread simulations at 2m resolution for the Rectoret region in Catalonia, Spain: (1) patch-based U-Net, (2) transfer-learned ResNet-50, (3) physics-informed network constrained by wind-driven advection equation, and (4) Swin-Unet transformer. Saliency, occlusion, and rotation experiments were conducted to analyze model learning. Cross-region transferability was tested on the Pedriza region without retraining.
AI.result: Only surface fuel load predicts burn probability with meaningful strength (r = 0.27), reducing prediction error by 21% when included. Other terrain and vegetation variables correlate weakly and are highly duplicative. Convolutional models rely primarily on distance from the current fire front, while Swin-Unet assigns more weight to fuel and terrain features. When applied to Pedriza without retraining, all three convolutional models still predict fire spread but lose accuracy by a small systematic margin.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning surrogates can effectively approximate physics-based wildfire simulations at significantly lower computational cost. Surface fuel load is the most important predictor of burn probability. Model architecture significantly affects feature importance—transformers (Swin-Unet) capture fuel and terrain better than convolutional models. The models demonstrate reasonable cross-region transferability, though with some accuracy loss.

title: STUNet-Fusion: Spatiotemporal Needle-Tip Localization in Ultrasound Video via Multi-Channel Motion Fusion
summary: Needle-tip localization in ultrasound remains challenging because the needle may appear weak, discontinuous, or partially invisible, while imaging artifacts and anatomical structures can produce similar responses. To address this problem, we propose STUNet-Fusion, a spatiotemporal framework for needle-tip localization in ultrasound videos. The proposed method formulates the input as a tri-channel spatio-temporal fusion tensor, comprising grayscale appearance, grid-based motion feature, and raw frame difference. A shared ResNet-34 encoder extracts spatial features, ConvLSTM integrates temporal dependencies, and a U-Net decoder reconstructs a dense probability heatmap. The final coordinates are extracted via a soft-argmax operation to achieve sub-pixel localization accuracy.
