Experimental results demonstrate that this spatiotemporal fusion strategy significantly improves localization robustness compared to conventional baselines.

AI.tldr: STUNet-Fusion is a spatiotemporal deep learning framework for accurate needle-tip localization in ultrasound videos. It uses a tri-channel spatio-temporal fusion tensor (grayscale appearance, grid-based motion, frame difference) processed through a ResNet-34 encoder, ConvLSTM, and U-Net decoder to generate probability heatmaps, achieving sub-pixel accuracy via soft-argmax.
AI.motivation: Needle-tip localization in ultrasound is challenging because needles can appear weak, discontinuous, or partially invisible, while imaging artifacts and anatomical structures can produce similar responses, making accurate localization difficult.
AI.method: The method uses a tri-channel spatio-temporal fusion tensor as input combining grayscale appearance, grid-based motion features, and raw frame difference. A shared ResNet-34 encoder extracts spatial features, ConvLSTM integrates temporal dependencies, and a U-Net decoder reconstructs dense probability heatmaps. Final coordinates are extracted using soft-argmax operation for sub-pixel localization accuracy.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that the spatiotemporal fusion strategy significantly improves localization robustness compared to conventional baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed STUNet-Fusion successfully addresses the challenges of needle-tip localization in ultrasound videos by leveraging spatiotemporal information through a novel fusion approach, achieving improved robustness and sub-pixel accuracy.

title: Which LLM is Best for Translating Natural Language Goals to PDDL
summary: Bridging the gap between human intent and machine execution remains a challenge in automated planning, where expressing goals in formal languages like PDDL restricts accessibility to non-experts. This paper empirically evaluates whether current Large Language Models (LLMs) can reliably translate natural language testing goals, written in informal language by video game testers, into well-formed PDDL targets suitable for classical planning. We present a carefully designed prompt template, integrating insights from iterative experimentation, aimed at maximizing both accuracy and response coherence from multiple state-of-the-art LLMs. Six contemporary models are systematically assessed on correctness, speed, and error tendencies using real-world, domain-specific benchmarks. All models demonstrate high correctness, exceeding 92\%, with Gemini 2.5 Flash achieving the highest accuracy at 96\% and the lowest incidence of false positives, while GPT-4.1 leads in response speed. Despite these advances, critical distinctions exist in model performance, and occasional failures arise from language ambiguity and limitations in domain representation. Our analysis underscores both the significant progress and ongoing gaps in enabling LLMs to act as robust bridges between natural language objectives and automated planning pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether LLMs can reliably translate natural language goals from video game testers into PDDL for classical planning. Using a designed prompt template, six models were tested on real-world benchmarks. All models achieved >92% accuracy, with Gemini 2.5 Flash performing best (96%) and GPT-4.1 being fastest.
AI.motivation: The challenge: automated planning requires formal PDDL language, which is inaccessible to non-experts. The goal: determine if LLMs can bridge this gap by translating informal natural language goals into formal PDDL targets.
AI.method: Designed a prompt template through iterative experimentation; systematically assessed six state-of-the-art LLMs on correctness, speed, and error tendencies using real-world domain-specific benchmarks with natural language testing goals from video game testers.
AI.result: All models achieved >92% correctness. Gemini 2.5 Flash had highest accuracy (96%) and lowest false positives. GPT-4.1 led in response speed. Failures occurred due to language ambiguity and domain representation limitations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show significant potential as bridges between natural language objectives and automated planning, but critical performance differences exist and occasional failures from language ambiguity and domain representation limitations indicate ongoing gaps.

title: The evolution of sex for artificial intelligence: a population-genetic framework for multigenerational model populations
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Supplementary Information (26 pp) and a plain-language figure appendix for readers from biology (23 pp) are included as ancillary files. Code, configs and seeds: https://git.lab.gilest.ro/giorgio/MachineSex
summary:
Some aspects of AI development resemble a population process in which models are specialised, retrained on the output of peers, or combined by averaging weights. These practices lead to generations of models, in the biological sense studied by population genetics. Here, I develop this parallelism and interpret multigenerational model populations in terms of sexual and asexual reproduction, formally recombining the two fields. I test these analogies in an exact inheritance model, in trained networks (recurrent, feedforward and variational autoencoder generators) and in large language models, and show that they hold generally, with some measurable architecture-specific biases.
  Training recursively on model output is known to lead to model collapse, a process previously described as akin to genetic drift; I develop all that follows. A minimal model of a learner retrained on its parent's output reproduces the Wright-Fisher process exactly; verified real data added to each generation play the role of immigration, with the surprising finding that the absolute number of real data samples matters, not their share, exactly as in population genetics. Training a child on the average of its parents' outputs cancels the benefit of having several parents, matching blending inheritance (and reviving Jenkin's objection to Darwin), whereas combining parents so that each keeps its strongest contribution preserves it; merged language-model specialists exceeded every parent across seeds (the Fisher-Muller effect); and lineages become reproductively isolated, losing the ability to merge at all, when they have learned conflicting conventions and not when they have merely drifted apart.
  As AI societies become societies in time as well as in space, a mathematical framework for their inheritance acquires predictive power. Remarkably, that framework can be adapted almost wholesale from biology.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a formal parallelism between AI model development (training, retraining, weight averaging) and population genetics, treating successive generations of models as biological populations. The author shows that many concepts from population genetics (Wright-Fisher process, blending inheritance, Fisher-Muller effect, reproductive isolation) have direct analogues in AI development, with practical implications for model training strategies.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand the dynamics of multigenerational AI model populations by borrowing the well-established mathematical framework from population genetics, as AI systems increasingly train on outputs of other models.
AI.method: The author develops theoretical models and tests them on: (1) exact inheritance models, (2) trained neural networks (recurrent, feedforward, and variational autoencoder generators), and (3) large language models. The analysis involves formal recombination of concepts from population genetics with AI training practices.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) Recursive training on model output reproduces model collapse (like genetic drift). (2) A minimal learner model reproduces the Wright-Fisher process exactly. (3) Adding real data to each generation acts as "immigration" - absolute number matters, not proportion. (4) Training on parent averages equals blending inheritance (loses diversity benefit). (5) Preserving strongest parent contributions yields Fisher-Muller effect. (6) Lineages become reproductively isolated when learning conflicting conventions, not merely from drift.
AI.conclusion: The mathematical framework from population genetics can be adapted almost wholesale to understand and predict AI model population dynamics, providing predictive power as AI systems increasingly train on outputs of other models.

title: HAP: A Hand-Driven Active Perception Framework for Egocentric Head Motion Prediction
summary: Egocentric motion forecasting has primarily focused on hands and manipulated objects, leaving future human head motion comparatively underexplored. During manipulation, the head both redirects perception toward the target to acquire task-relevant evidence and coordinates with body and hand motion. We therefore formulate future six Degree of Freedom (6-DoF) head-motion prediction conditioned on observed hand motion and inferred target context, and propose HAP, a Hand-Driven Active Perception framework. HAP infers confidence for each target object from observed hand motion and object geometry. Then constructs a dynamic Predictive Target-Centric Amodal Occlusion Graph (P-TAOG) representing current and potential occlusion among candidate objects. Directed graph and causal temporal reasoning encode the evolving target conditioned perceptual state, which is fused with hand and head motion history. A horizon-wise gate then blends the learned trajectory with a constant velocity prior. We further introduce Bottle, an egocentric RGB-D dataset of object manipulation toward specified targets, with coordinated head and hand motion under changing target visibility. Experiments on the public dataset and Bottle show that HAP achieves lower head motion prediction errors than representative baselines, supporting the value of hand driven intention and dynamic occlusion reasoning for anticipating human head motion. Code will be released at https://HAP-ego.github.io/HAP.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes HAP (Hand-Driven Active Perception), a framework for predicting future 6-DoF head motion during egocentric object manipulation. The approach leverages observed hand motion and inferred target context to anticipate where users will look next, addressing the previously underexplored problem of head motion forecasting.
AI.motivation: Egocentric motion forecasting has primarily focused on hands and manipulated objects, while human head motion remains underexplored. During manipulation, the head serves dual purposes: redirecting perception toward task-relevant targets and coordinating with body/hand motion. Understanding head motion is crucial for predicting user attention and intention in AR/VR, human-robot interaction, and activity recognition.
AI.method: HAP framework consists of three main components: (1) Target inference module that estimates confidence scores for candidate objects based on observed hand motion and object geometry; (2) Predictive Target-Centric Amodal Occlusion Graph (P-TAOG) that models current and potential occlusions among objects using directed graph and causal temporal reasoning; (3) Horizon-wise gating mechanism that blends learned trajectory predictions with constant velocity priors. The framework fuses hand motion history, head motion history, and dynamic occlusion-aware perceptual states for prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on a public dataset and the newly introduced Bottle dataset (egocentric RGB-D with coordinated head/hand motion under changing target visibility) demonstrate that HAP achieves lower head motion prediction errors compared to representative baselines, validating the effectiveness of hand-driven intention modeling and dynamic occlusion reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HAP framework successfully demonstrates that incorporating hand-driven intention signals and dynamic occlusion reasoning significantly improves 6-DoF head motion prediction. The introduction of the Bottle dataset provides a valuable benchmark for future research in egocentric perception and motion forecasting.

title: Clueing up LLMs with Tool-Augmented Deductive Reasoning
summary: Despite recent advances in large language models (LLMs), performing logically consistent deductive reasoning over extended interactions remains challenging. Tasks that require integrating evidence across multiple reasoning steps, maintaining consistency with prior inferences, and updating beliefs under new constraints can surface limitations in current models while providing a useful testbed for evaluating reasoning enhancements. In this paper, we implement a text-based, multi-agent version of the classic board game Clue as an environment to evaluate multi-step, agentic deductive reasoning. In this setting, agents must infer hidden information from a sequence of observations, maintain consistency across turns, and reason over an evolving set of logical constraints. We instantiate six LLM-based agents (GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash) as players that engage in turn-based gameplay; using three agents per model family, we establish baseline performance across repeated games. We then introduce a tool-augmented approach in which a structured possibility matrix converts implicit game state from generated reasoning logs into an explicit representation of remaining possibilities. The possibility matrix encodes extended-turn memory and deductive constraints, offloading these tasks from the agent. We compare this approach against the baseline to evaluate how tool augmentation supports reasoning quality and task success for autonomous agents in a strategic reasoning environment.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates multi-step deductive reasoning in LLMs using a text-based Clue game environment. Authors test GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash agents (3 per model) in turn-based gameplay, then introduce a tool-augmented approach using a structured possibility matrix to maintain explicit game state and logical constraints. The study compares tool-augmented reasoning against baseline performance to assess reasoning quality improvements.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs struggle with logically consistent deductive reasoning over extended interactions. Tasks requiring evidence integration across multiple reasoning steps, consistency maintenance, and belief updating under new constraints expose limitations in existing models. A strategic game environment like Clue provides a useful testbed for evaluating these reasoning enhancements.
AI.method: The authors implement a text-based, multi-agent version of Clue as the evaluation environment. Six LLM-based agents (GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, three agents per model family) engage in turn-based gameplay. A tool-augmented approach is introduced using a structured possibility matrix that converts implicit game state from generated reasoning logs into an explicit representation of remaining possibilities. This matrix encodes extended-turn memory and deductive constraints, offloading these cognitive tasks from the agents.
AI.result: The abstract does not provide specific quantitative results or findings.
AI.conclusion: The abstract suggests the study compares tool-augmented reasoning against baseline to evaluate how external memory and constraint representation tools support reasoning quality and task success for autonomous agents in strategic reasoning environments. Specific conclusions are not provided in the abstract.

title: Accurate Trace Estimation with Fewer Random Bits via Recursive TensorSketch
summary: We consider the problem of estimating the trace of an implicit matrix $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{d^p\times d^p}$ that can only be accessed through matrix-vector products queries. The \textit{Hutchinson trace estimator}% ~\cite{Girard1987algorithme, article-hutchinson} is a classical sketching method for this problem. Their estimator, $H_{m}(\mathbf{A}) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} {\mathbf{z}^{(i)}}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{z}^{(i)}, \quad \text{where } \ {\mathbf{z}^{(i)}}\in \mathbb{R}^{d^p}$, and $z^{(i)}_j \in {N}(0, 1), j\in [d^p]$, satisfies the following guarantees: (i) $\mathbb{E}[H_{m}(\mathbf{A})]=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A})$, and (ii) $\mathrm{Var}[H_{m}(\mathbf{A})]=\frac{2}{m}||\mathbf{A}||_F^2$. Generating one query vector $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}$ requires $O(d^p)$ random bits; thus, $m$ queries require $O(md^p)$ random bits, which can be prohibitive in large-scale applications. Recent work by Meyer et al.~\cite{meyer2025hutchinsonsestimatorbadkroneckertraceestimation} proposes a variant of the Hutchinson trace estimator in which each query vector in $\mathbb{R}^{d^p}$ is constructed as the Kronecker product of $p$ random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, requiring $O(mpd)$ random bits for $m$ query vectors. The estimator of~\cite{meyer2025hutchinsonsestimatorbadkroneckertraceestimation} is unbiased; however, its variance grows exponentially with $p$. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing a sketching-based estimator that requires $O\!\big(p (d + m)\log m\big)$ random bits, yields an unbiased estimate of the trace, and simultaneously achieves a variance bound that grows polynomially with $p$.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the trace estimation problem for large implicit matrices (d^p × d^p) that can only be accessed via matrix-vector products. The authors propose a sketching-based estimator that reduces random bit complexity from O(md^p) to O(p(d + m)log m) while maintaining unbiasedness and achieving polynomial (instead of exponential) variance growth with respect to p.
AI.motivation: The Hutchinson trace estimator is a classical method for trace estimation but requires O(d^p) random bits per query, which is prohibitive for large-scale applications. While Meyer et al. (2025) proposed a Kronecker product variant reducing bits to O(mpd), it suffers from exponentially growing variance with p. This work aims to overcome this limitation.
AI.method: The paper proposes a sketching-based estimator that uses a structured random vector approach. By constructing query vectors as Kronecker products of p random vectors in R^d (similar to prior work) but with a different sketching mechanism, the method achieves O(p(d + m)log m) random bits while maintaining an unbiased estimate with polynomially growing variance.
AI.result: The proposed estimator: (1) requires O(p(d + m)log m) random bits, (2) yields an unbiased estimate of the trace, and (3) achieves a variance bound that grows polynomially with p (compared to exponential growth in prior work).
AI.conclusion: The authors successfully address the variance explosion issue of prior Kronecker-based trace estimators. Their method provides a practical solution for trace estimation in high-dimensional Kronecker-structured problems, with significantly reduced random bit requirements and favorable variance properties.

title: Version- and Scope-Aware Question Answering over Normative Documents: A Deployed System and an End-to-End Evaluation at Production Scale
summary: Correctly answering a question grounded in normative documents often depends on information outside any single passage: whether the retrieved document is the version currently in force; whether it applies to the jurisdiction, subject (such as an institution or applicant), and date at issue; and whether each normative claim can be traced to its supporting source text. Hosted retrieval services have substantially lowered the engineering cost of building an initial system over such corpora, making "upload the documents and ask" a common default. We evaluate this default on approximately 73,000 candidate normative documents supplied to a production deployment. The evaluation uses a stratified sample of 200 questions from our published benchmark, with a gold source document for every question; the released sampling rule reads no system outputs or scores. We compare the hosted service with a governed system that resolves version and scope through explicit rules before generation. The governed system scored 97.7 overall, while the hosted service scored 88.1, a gap of 9.6 points computed from unrounded means. The question set, the answer text evaluated for both systems, the scores, and the scripts used to reproduce the reported benchmark statistics are public. The governed configuration has operated as a commercial product since January 2026 and serves 1,126 registered users; named customer organizations include Zhipu AI and Lecheng Health. By mid-April 2026, it had reached roughly 100,000 calls per workday.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates two approaches for building QA systems over normative documents: a simple hosted retrieval service ("upload and ask") versus a governed system with explicit rules for version/scope resolution. The governed system significantly outperforms the hosted service (97.7 vs 88.1, a 9.6-point gap) on a benchmark of 200 questions from ~73,000 documents.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of hosted retrieval services has made "upload documents and ask" a default approach, but this may fail for normative documents where correctness depends on external factors: whether the document is the current version, whether it applies to the relevant jurisdiction/subject/date, and whether claims can be traced to source text.
AI.method: Evaluation on ~73,000 candidate normative documents using a stratified sample of 200 questions from a published benchmark, with gold source documents for every question. The sampling rule was designed to be independent of system outputs or scores. Compared a hosted retrieval service against a governed system that resolves version and scope through explicit rules before generation.
AI.result: The governed system scored 97.7 overall while the hosted service scored 88.1, representing a 9.6-point gap. The governed system has operated as a commercial product since January 2026 with 1,126 registered users (including Zhipu AI and Lecheng Health) and reached ~100,000 calls per workday by mid-April 2026.
AI.conclusion: The "upload documents and ask" default is insufficient for normative document QA. A governed system with explicit rules for version and scope resolution significantly outperforms simple hosted retrieval, demonstrating the importance of structured governance in production legal/policy QA systems.

title: Label-free steering: Compressing test-time reinforcement learning into bias-only subspaces
summary: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) enables models to improve their reasoning without relying on labeled training data, but existing approaches typically optimize a large fraction of the model parameters. This raises a natural question: can effective test-time adaptation emerge when both the reward signal and the optimization space are severely restricted? We answer this question with label-free bias-only TTRL, which uses majority-vote pseudo-labels as rewards and optimizes only approximately 100K bias parameters while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. On MATH-500, our approach reaches 76.67% accuracy, slightly exceeding our own labeled bias-steering reproduction while optimizing 76,000x fewer parameters than full-parameter TTRL. The same training procedure improves performance across vision-language and audio reasoning tasks, including MathVista, AI2D, LogicVista, and MMAU. We further show that the learned steering vectors transfer to 4,500 held-out MATH problems, indicating that the adaptation is not limited to the problems used during test-time optimization. Finally, we analyze why this highly restricted adaptation can work, showing that majority-vote reliability improves with rollout consensus and that bias subspaces with greater accessible gradient energy exhibit stronger downstream trainability. These results demonstrate that substantial test-time adaptation can emerge from optimizing a tiny bias-only subspace using entirely label-free rewards.

AI.tldr: This paper explores whether effective test-time adaptation can emerge when both the reward signal and optimization space are severely restricted. The answer is yes: label-free bias-only TTRL using majority-vote pseudo-labels as rewards and optimizing only ~100K bias parameters (while freezing the backbone) achieves 76.67% accuracy on MATH-500, slightly exceeding full-parameter TTRL while using 76,000x fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to answer a fundamental question: can effective test-time adaptation emerge when both the reward signal and the optimization space are severely restricted? Existing TTRL approaches typically optimize a large fraction of model parameters, and this work investigates the limits of adaptation under extreme constraints.
AI.method: The proposed approach, "label-free bias-only TTRL," uses majority-vote pseudo-labels as rewards and optimizes only approximately 100K bias parameters while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. This is in contrast to full-parameter TTRL which optimizes the entire model.
AI.result: On MATH-500, the approach reaches 76.67% accuracy, slightly exceeding the authors' own labeled bias-steering reproduction while optimizing 76,000x fewer parameters than full-parameter TTRL. The same training procedure improves performance across vision-language and audio reasoning tasks including MathVista, AI2D, LogicVista, and MMAU. Learned steering vectors transfer to 4,500 held-out MATH problems, showing the adaptation is not limited to problems used during test-time optimization.
AI.conclusion: Substantial test-time adaptation can emerge from optimizing a tiny bias-only subspace using entirely label-free rewards. The analysis shows that majority-vote reliability improves with rollout consensus and that bias subspaces with greater accessible gradient energy exhibit stronger downstream trainability.

title: Sim-to-Real Traffic Scene Understanding by Decoupling Semantics from Caption Generation with V-JEPA
comment: Winner of Track 2 at the AI City Challenge 2026, with the paper published at the ECCV conference 2026 (ECCV-W)
summary: Track 2 of the AI City Challenge 2026 requires both visual question answering (VQA) and traffic event description generation under a challenging synthetic-to real domain shift. Existing vision-language approaches often entangle semantic understanding with language generation, making them susceptible to hallucination and inconsistent reasoning across event phases. In this work, we propose a decoupled semantic understanding framework that first resolves predefined traffic questions into structured semantic facts and subsequently uses these facts to guide caption generation. A frozen V-JEPA encoder extracts predictive scene representations, while a lightweight Llama-based predictor produces answers for VQA queries. To improve reliability, we introduce a training-free structured refinement mechanism that exploits statistical priors, inter-question relationships, and temporal event consistency to correct prediction errors. The refined semantic facts are then provided to Qwen3-VL-8B to generate pedestrian and vehicle descriptions for each traffic event. Experimental results on the official 2026 AI City Challenge Track 2 benchmark show that the proposed method achieves 87.09% VQA accuracy and an overall S2 score of 60.0853, ranking first among all participating teams. These results demonstrate that predictive world representations combined with structured semantic refinement enable more accurate and reliable traffic understanding, leading to higher-quality lan guage generation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a decoupled semantic understanding framework for the AI City Challenge 2026 Track 2, which addresses visual question answering (VQA) and traffic event description generation under synthetic-to-real domain shift. The method separates semantic understanding from language generation, using a V-JEPA encoder for scene representations, a Llama-based predictor for VQA, and a training-free refinement mechanism to correct errors. The approach achieves 87.09% VQA accuracy and 60.0853 S2 score, ranking first.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language approaches entangle semantic understanding with language generation, making them susceptible to hallucination and inconsistent reasoning across event phases under synthetic-to-real domain shift conditions.
AI.method: The proposed method includes: (1) A decoupled semantic understanding framework that resolves traffic questions into structured semantic facts first, then uses these facts to guide caption generation; (2) A frozen V-JEPA encoder for extracting predictive scene representations; (3) A lightweight Llama-based predictor for answering VQA queries; (4) A training-free structured refinement mechanism using statistical priors, inter-question relationships, and temporal event consistency to correct prediction errors; (5) Qwen3-VL-8B for generating pedestrian and vehicle descriptions for each traffic event.
AI.result: The method achieves 87.09% VQA accuracy and an overall S2 score of 60.0853 on the official 2026 AI City Challenge Track 2 benchmark, ranking first among all participating teams.
AI.conclusion: Predictive world representations combined with structured semantic refinement enable more accurate and reliable traffic understanding, leading to higher-quality language generation. The decoupled approach effectively addresses the challenges of synthetic-to-real domain shift in VQA and event description tasks.

title: CERA-MoA: Co-Evolving Routing Mechanisms with Continually Learning LLM Agents
summary: Current Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) paradigms generally treat query routing and agent fine-tuning as separate processes, limiting their ability to respond to evolving agent capabilities. This disconnect prevents routing strategies from adapting to evolving agent capabilities during post-training and prevents agents from achieving synergistic data-driven specialization. To resolve this, we introduce CERA-MoA (Co-Evolving Router with continually learning Agents for Mixture-of-Agents), an iterative reinforcement learning framework where the dynamic router and independent agent policies co-evolve. We design a predictive familiarity estimator that leverages mid-layer hidden states to evaluate semantic competence among agents, avoiding the overhead of full rollouts. Based on these familiarity scores, a cumulative-threshold adaptive routing mechanism dynamically activates a tailored minimal agent subset, achieving a trade-off between task performance and efficiency. By proactively allocating targeted training samples to agents based on their evolving competence, CERA-MoA promotes capability differentiation. Extensive experiments across various domains demonstrate that CERA-MoA outperforms state-of-the-art static-agent routing and fix-workflow fine-tuning baselines.

AI.tldr: CERA-MoA introduces an iterative reinforcement learning framework where the dynamic router and agent policies co-evolve, using mid-layer hidden states for familiarity estimation and adaptive routing to achieve better task performance and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current Mixture-of-Agents paradigms treat query routing and agent fine-tuning as separate processes, preventing routing strategies from adapting to evolving agent capabilities during post-training and preventing agents from achieving synergistic data-driven specialization.
AI.method: 1) Predictive familiarity estimator leveraging mid-layer hidden states to evaluate semantic competence among agents (avoiding full rollouts); 2) Cumulative-threshold adaptive routing mechanism that dynamically activates a tailored minimal agent subset; 3) Proactive allocation of targeted training samples to agents based on evolving competence.
AI.result: CERA-MoA outperforms state-of-the-art static-agent routing and fix-workflow fine-tuning baselines across various domains.
AI.conclusion: The co-evolutionary framework successfully enables dynamic router adaptation and capability differentiation among agents, achieving better trade-off between task performance and efficiency.

title: Peak-Aware Short-Term Load Forecasting Across Distribution Grid Aggregation Levels
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables, Accepted at IEEE PES ISGT Europe 2026
summary: For distribution system operators, short-term load forecasting (STLF) supports congestion management, voltage control, and asset protection. Most existing approaches focus on overall accuracy across all time steps and neglect performance during high-demand (HD) periods, where larger forecast errors can increase the risk of congestion and voltage violations. In this paper, we study peak-aware STLF across three operator-relevant distribution grid aggregation levels, area codes (AC), secondary substations (SUB), and low-voltage (LV) feeders, using open datasets from the United Kingdom and Switzerland. We compare statistical baselines, machine learning models (LightGBM and XGBoost), and recent time-series foundation models (Chronos Bolt and Chronos-2) under a peak-aware evaluation framework that reports both overall and HD forecasting performance using NMAE and MAPE. The results show that Chronos-2 achieves the best HD performance across all aggregation levels, with HD-NMAE and HD-MAPE of 0.039 and 4.53% at AC, 0.080 and 9.45% at SUB, and 0.138 and 16.14% at LV, while Chronos-Bolt consistently ranks second best. Compared with the gradient boosted ML models, Chronos-2 reduces mean HD-NMAE by about 20-51% across levels while remaining best or near-best on the overall metrics. A quantile analysis of the probabilistic Chronos outputs further identifies aggregation-specific operating points, and runtime measurements indicate that foundation model inference is fast enough for practical deployment. Overall, the findings highlight peak-aware evaluation and aggregation specific quantile selection as a practical pathway toward more operationally relevant STLF in distribution networks.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses short-term load forecasting (STLF) for distribution system operators, emphasizing the need for accurate predictions during high-demand (HD) periods. The study compares statistical baselines, gradient boosting models (LightGBM, XGBoost), and time-series foundation models (Chronos Bolt, Chronos-2) across three aggregation levels (area codes, secondary substations, low-voltage feeders) using UK and Switzerland datasets. A peak-aware evaluation framework is proposed to assess both overall and HD forecasting performance.
AI.motivation: Existing STLF approaches focus on overall accuracy across all time steps but neglect performance during high-demand periods, where larger forecast errors can lead to congestion and voltage violations. Distribution system operators need better forecasting during peak periods to manage congestion, voltage control, and protect assets.
AI.method: The study compares statistical baselines, machine learning models (LightGBM and XGBoost), and time-series foundation models (Chronos Bolt and Chronos-2) under a peak-aware evaluation framework. They use open datasets from the UK and Switzerland across three operator-relevant aggregation levels: area codes (AC), secondary substations (SUB), and low-voltage (LV) feeders. Performance is evaluated using NMAE and MAPE metrics for both overall and HD forecasting. Quantile analysis of probabilistic Chronos outputs is also performed.
AI.result: Chronos-2 achieves the best HD performance across all aggregation levels with HD-NMAE and HD-MAPE of 0.039 and 4.53% at AC, 0.080 and 9.45% at SUB, and 0.138 and 16.14% at LV. Chronos-Bolt consistently ranks second best. Compared with gradient boosted ML models, Chronos-2 reduces mean HD-NMAE by about 20-51% across levels while remaining best or near-best on overall metrics. Foundation model inference is fast enough for practical deployment.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight peak-aware evaluation and aggregation-specific quantile selection as a practical pathway toward more operationally relevant STLF in distribution networks. Chronos-2 and Chronos-Bolt foundation models outperform traditional ML approaches, especially during high-demand periods, making them suitable for practical deployment in distribution grid operations.

title: Learning Where to Focus: Self-Supervised Multi-Scale ViTs for Histopathology
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, plus supplementary material. Accepted at DAGM GCPR 2026
summary: Pathologists diagnose diseases by first locating suspicious tissue and then examining it at higher magnification, whereas self-supervised vision transformers (ViTs) allocate the same spatial resolution to every image region despite diagnostic evidence being sparse and spanning multiple biological scales. Recent pathology foundation models have substantially improved representation quality by scaling training data and model capacity, but largely retain uniform tokenization. We instead investigate whether pathology representations can be improved by learning where to allocate spatial resolution during self-supervised learning. To this end, we propose CRAFT (Coarse-to-fine Region-Adaptive Feature Tokenization), a DINO-based framework that learns image-dependent mixed-scale representations by using self-supervised attention to selectively refine informative regions while preserving coarse context, together with a symmetric cross-scale regularization objective that encourages complementary coarse and fine representations. Across CAMELYON16, TCGA-Lung subtype classification, and TCGA-LUAD survival prediction, CRAFT consistently outperforms comparable-scale self-supervised methods while requiring lower inference computation. Despite using only a compact 22M parameter backbone trained on comparatively small pathology datasets, CRAFT remains competitive with, and often surpasses, substantially larger pathology foundation models.

AI.tldr: CRAFT is a self-supervised vision transformer framework for pathology image analysis that learns to adaptively allocate spatial resolution to different image regions, rather than using uniform tokenization. It uses attention-based selective refinement for informative regions while preserving coarse context, with a cross-scale regularization objective. The method outperforms comparable-scale methods while remaining competitive with larger foundation models despite using only 22M parameters.
AI.motivation: Current pathology foundation models use uniform spatial resolution across all image regions, despite diagnostic evidence being sparse and spanning multiple biological scales. This inefficiency limits representation quality and wastes computation on uninformative regions.
AI.method: CRAFT is a DINO-based framework that learns image-dependent mixed-scale representations through: 1) Self-supervised attention to selectively refine informative regions while preserving coarse context, and 2) A symmetric cross-scale regularization objective that encourages complementary coarse and fine representations.
AI.result: CRAFT consistently outperforms comparable-scale self-supervised methods across CAMELYON16 (breast cancer metastasis detection), TCGA-Lung subtype classification, and TCGA-LUAD survival prediction tasks, while requiring lower inference computation. Despite using only a compact 22M parameter backbone trained on comparatively small pathology datasets, it remains competitive with or surpasses substantially larger pathology foundation models.
AI.conclusion: Learning where to allocate spatial resolution during self-supervised learning significantly improves pathology representations. The approach achieves better performance with smaller model size and lower computational cost, suggesting that adaptive resolution allocation is more effective than uniform tokenization for histopathology image analysis.

title: Compositional Policy Violations: When Step-Level Compliance Fails In Agentic AI Workflows
summary: Agentic workflows now make consequential decisions in regulated settings, and the governance placed around them is almost entirely step-scoped: input-output classifiers, per turn rails, and span-level evaluators. The policies organizations actually hold, such as referral thresholds, authority limits, and review requirements, are properties of the whole execution rather than of any one step. This mismatch admits a failure mode we call a Compositional Policy Violation (CPV): every individual step passes its own check while the composed execution violates the governing policy. A predicate over a single step cannot evaluate a property that step does not determine, so no improvement in the accuracy of the step-scoped monitors detects this class. We define CPVs as the failure of step-level compliance to compose, and present a taxonomy of four types: Authority Creep, Threshold Laundering, Cumulative Sum Violation, and Context Collapse. We show that the correct repair for each class is dictated by where the guarded quantity mutates. We then introduce a provenance-aware runtime architecture that evaluates policies over complete execution traces, recomputing guarded quantities from raw provenance rather than the pipeline's derived representation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Compositional Policy Violations (CPVs), a failure mode in agentic workflows where individual step-level compliance checks pass but the overall execution violates organizational policies. The authors identify this as a fundamental mismatch between step-scoped governance and policy properties that are inherently holistic (e.g., referral thresholds, authority limits). They propose a provenance-aware runtime architecture that evaluates policies over complete execution traces rather than individual steps.
AI.motivation: Current governance of agentic workflows in regulated settings is almost entirely step-scoped (input-output classifiers, per-turn rails, span-level evaluators). However, organizational policies such as referral thresholds, authority limits, and review requirements are properties of whole executions, not individual steps. This mismatch creates a gap where every individual step passes checks while the composed execution violates the governing policy—a problem that cannot be solved by improving step-scoped monitor accuracy alone.
AI.method: The authors define CPVs as the failure of step-level compliance to compose, and present a taxonomy of four types: Authority Creep, Threshold Laundering, Cumulative Sum Violation, and Context Collapse. They analyze that the correct repair for each class is dictated by where the guarded quantity mutates. They then introduce a provenance-aware runtime architecture that evaluates policies over complete execution traces, recomputing guarded quantities from raw provenance rather than the pipeline's derived representation.
AI.result: The paper identifies four distinct types of CPVs, each with different failure characteristics. The authors demonstrate that the appropriate repair strategy depends on the mutation location of the guarded quantity. The proposed provenance-aware runtime architecture addresses this by evaluating policies over complete execution traces rather than individual steps, using raw provenance data to recompute guarded quantities instead of relying on derived representations.
AI.conclusion: Step-scoped governance is fundamentally insufficient for ensuring policy compliance in agentic workflows operating in regulated settings. A provenance-aware runtime architecture that evaluates policies over complete execution traces is necessary to detect and prevent Compositional Policy Violations. This approach recomputes guarded quantities from raw provenance to ensure accurate policy evaluation across the entire execution.

title: ReDIL-GNN: Resynthesis Domain Incremental Learning for Circuit Graph Neural Networks
summary: Logic resynthesis preserves circuit functionality while changing gate vocabulary, topology, and structural statistics, creating domain shift for circuit graph neural networks (GNNs) without changing task labels. To study this setting, we introduce ReDIL-GNN, a resynthesis domain-incremental learning framework that adapts a fixed prediction or representation head as new synthesis styles arrive and evaluates retention on all previously observed domains. Because not every shift should be adapted blindly, ReDIL-GNN further introduces the Resynthesis Adaptability Index (RAI), a pre-adaptation score that combines adaptation need, source-equivalence recoverability, structural coverage, and update compatibility. We evaluate supervised hardware-security tasks and representation-learning models using task-native metrics for classifiers and source-equivalence retrieval metrics for embedding models, comparing naive fine-tuning with LwF, Online EWC, MAS, ER, A-GEM, DER++, ER+LwF, and equivalence-guided replay. Across the studied pipelines, RAI separates unsupported shifts from promising updates, ranging from 0.001 for a structurally uncovered GNN-RE ABC-rewrite shift to 0.824 for the best original-only GNN-RE adaptation case. In practice, ReDIL-GNN turns resynthesis-aware circuit learning into a deployment control loop: RAI screens each new synthesis flow before update, guiding whether to reuse the current model, apply retention-aware adaptation, or defer adaptation until the shift is better supported.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses domain shift in circuit Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) caused by logic resynthesis, which changes gate vocabulary, topology, and structural statistics while preserving functionality. It introduces ReDIL-GNN, a resynthesis domain-incremental learning framework with a novel Resynthesis Adaptability Index (RAI) that pre-assesses whether adaptation is beneficial before applying retention-aware learning methods.
AI.motivation: Logic resynthesis preserves circuit functionality but creates domain shift for circuit GNNs without changing task labels. This domain shift can degrade model performance, but not every shift should be adapted blindly. The need exists for a framework that can determine when adaptation is worthwhile and guide deployment decisions accordingly.
AI.method: ReDIL-GNN framework adapts fixed prediction/representation heads as new synthesis styles arrive while evaluating retention on all previously observed domains. The key innovation is the Resynthesis Adaptability Index (RAI), which combines four factors: adaptation need, source-equivalence recoverability, structural coverage, and update compatibility to score each new synthesis flow before update.
AI.result: RAI effectively separates unsupported shifts from promising updates, ranging from 0.001 (structurally uncovered GNN-RE ABC-rewrite shift) to 0.824 (best original-only GNN-RE adaptation case). The framework enables a deployment control loop where RAI screens each new synthesis flow to guide decisions: reuse current model, apply retention-aware adaptation, or defer adaptation.
AI.conclusion: ReDIL-GNN successfully turns resynthesis-aware circuit learning into a practical deployment control loop. RAI serves as an effective pre-adaptation screening mechanism that prevents blind adaptation to unsuitable shifts while identifying promising adaptation cases, offering a principled approach to managing domain-incremental learning in hardware security and circuit representation learning tasks.

title: On-the-Fly Homographies Calibration for Multi-Camera Tracking
summary: Precise multi-camera tracking traditionally relies on rigorous 3D site calibration, yet this requirement is often operationally impossible in large-scale deployments. Privacy regulations frequently prohibit recording video for offline calibration; limited bandwidth precludes synchronizing high-resolution streams from hundreds of cameras; and covering immense physical sites with calibration targets is logistically infeasible. We present a multi-camera homography calibration system designed to overcome these barriers through "on-the-fly" geometric refinement. Starting from coarse manual homographies, we introduce a centroid-based projection optimization (PO) that continuously aligns the ground-plane geometry using live detection streams. Because PO operates asynchronously on already-transmitted, lightweight metadata, it adds zero computational latency to the real-time tracker. This allows the system to adapt automatically to camera movements or environmental changes without human intervention. This optimized geometry feeds a multi-camera bird's-eye-view (BEV) tracker that fuses detections and unifies trajectories across zones. Crucially, by operating strictly on live anonymous metadata, our solution ensures a privacy-safe, zero-overhead, and resilient tracking pipeline that maintains global consistency in dynamic environments where static, recorded-video calibration is impossible.

AI.tldr: A multi-camera homography calibration system that enables "on-the-fly" geometric refinement for large-scale tracking deployments where traditional 3D site calibration is impossible due to privacy, bandwidth, or logistical constraints. It uses centroid-based projection optimization on live metadata with zero latency overhead.
AI.motivation: Address the operational impossibility of rigorous 3D site calibration in large-scale multi-camera deployments, where privacy regulations prohibit video recording, limited bandwidth prevents high-resolution stream synchronization, and covering vast physical sites with calibration targets is logistically infeasible.
AI.method: Centroid-based projection optimization (PO) that continuously aligns ground-plane geometry using live detection streams. Starts from coarse manual homographies and operates asynchronously on already-transmitted lightweight metadata, adding zero computational latency to the real-time tracker.
AI.result: A privacy-safe, zero-overhead, resilient tracking pipeline that automatically adapts to camera movements or environmental changes without human intervention, maintaining global consistency in dynamic environments where static, recorded-video calibration is impossible.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system enables multi-camera BEV tracking in scenarios where traditional calibration methods fail, by leveraging live anonymous metadata for continuous geometric refinement while preserving privacy and adding no computational overhead.

title: Infinite-Parameter LLMs: Generating and Adapting Weights from Live Data
summary: The scaling laws hold that a language model grows more capable with more parameters and more training data, and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have ridden these laws to remarkable results, activating only a fraction of an enormous stored parameter bank for each token. That success is built on static pretraining data. A deployed model faces a different world, where much of the data that would make it more useful is not in its training set but in the live interaction it is currently handling, such as the facts a user supplies or the corrections they give. A conventional model cannot learn from this data, because its weights are frozen after training. Instead, the knowledge and behaviour supplied at run time are placed in the prompt, by retrieval or instruction, and re-read on every request only to be discarded once the request ends. We ask how an architecture could learn from live interaction by writing it into its weights. Taking inspiration from MoE, we propose the \textbf{Infinite-Parameter LLM}. A compact hypernetwork turns the data given at run time into a low-rank modulation of a shared base network, so the feed-forward weights are generated from live data rather than stored in a fixed bank. Where prior weight generators read the context once and freeze, we carry a Bayesian belief over the generator's latent code and update it online, so the effective weight is re-derived from that evolving belief as the session proceeds rather than fixed after one read. The stored footprint stays fixed, yet the weights the model can compile are effectively infinite. For the knowledge and behaviour supplied at run time, carrying them in the weights rather than the prompt is amortized in compute, frees the context window, persists across turns, and can generalise better than in-context use. We specify an evaluation protocol that tests exactly this against in-context learning and retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the "Infinite-Parameter LLM" - an architecture that enables language models to learn from live interaction data by using a hypernetwork to generate weights from run-time data rather than relying on frozen post-training weights. The key innovation is carrying a Bayesian belief over the generator's latent code and updating it online as the session proceeds.
AI.motivation: Conventional LLMs cannot learn from live interaction data after training - their weights are frozen. All knowledge and behavior must be placed in the prompt on every request, only to be discarded after the request ends. This wastes compute, fills the context window, doesn't persist across turns, and may not generalize as well as weight-based learning.
AI.method: The approach uses a compact hypernetwork that transforms run-time data (user facts, corrections, etc.) into low-rank modulation of a shared base network. Unlike prior weight generators that read context once and freeze, this method carries a Bayesian belief over the generator's latent code and updates it online throughout the session, so the effective weight is continuously re-derived from the evolving belief.
AI.result: The stored footprint remains fixed while the weights the model can compile are effectively infinite. Benefits include: amortized compute cost (weights generated once vs. re-reading prompt every request), freed context window, persistence across conversation turns, and better generalization than in-context learning.
AI.conclusion: The paper specifies an evaluation protocol that tests this approach against in-context learning and retrieval baselines, specifically evaluating the model's ability to learn and generalize from live interaction data.

title: Online Robust Reinforcement Learning Through Monte-Carlo Planning
summary: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a powerful framework for solving complex decision-making problems, yet it often relies on the assumption that the simulator and the real-world dynamics are identical. Although this assumption helps achieve the success of MCTS in games like Chess, Go, and Shogi, the real-world scenarios incur ambiguity due to their modeling mismatches in low-fidelity simulators. In this work, we present a new robust variant of MCTS that mitigates dynamical model ambiguities. Our algorithm addresses transition dynamics and reward distribution ambiguities to bridge the gap between simulation-based planning and real-world deployment. We incorporate a robust power mean backup operator and carefully designed exploration bonuses to ensure finite-sample convergence at every node in the search tree. We show that our algorithm achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/2})$ for the value estimation at the root node, comparable to that of standard MCTS. Finally, we provide empirical evidence that our method achieves robust performance in planning problems even under significant ambiguity in the underlying reward distribution and transition dynamics.

AI.tldr: A robust variant of Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) that handles model ambiguities between simulators and real-world dynamics, incorporating a robust power mean backup operator and exploration bonuses for finite-sample convergence.
AI.motivation: Standard MCTS assumes identical simulator and real-world dynamics, which fails in real-world scenarios with low-fidelity simulators due to modeling mismatches in transition dynamics and reward distributions.
AI.method: The algorithm addresses transition dynamics and reward distribution ambiguities by: (1) incorporating a robust power mean backup operator, and (2) using carefully designed exploration bonuses to ensure finite-sample convergence at every node in the search tree.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves a convergence rate of O(n^{-1/2}) for value estimation at the root node, comparable to standard MCTS. Empirical evidence shows robust performance under significant ambiguity in reward distribution and transition dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robust MCTS variant successfully bridges the gap between simulation-based planning and real-world deployment while maintaining theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical robustness.

title: PULSE: Unlocking Practical Image Compression on Single-Thread CPU
summary: Despite recent progress in learned image compression, existing methods remain computationally expensive on resource-constrained hardware, particularly CPUs. We introduce PULSE, a practical codec that enables (1) low-latency decoding on diverse hardware platforms with an ultra-low-complexity 5.2 kMAC/pixel neural receiver, and (2) efficient bit-exact entropy coding with an integer linear CDF predictor and a meta prior. To recover compression performance under this tight budget, we introduce an agentic evolution process guided by heuristic probes that iteratively improves the architecture through human-LLM collaboration. PULSE decodes a 1080p image in 126 ms on a single CPU thread while achieving compression performance comparable to HM. After perceptual optimization, PULSE competes with larger perceptual codecs like MS-ILLM. Codes are at https://github.com/microsoft/GenCodec/tree/main/PULSE

AI.tldr: PULSE is a practical learned image compression codec designed for resource-constrained hardware, featuring an ultra-low-complexity 5.2 kMAC/pixel neural receiver and efficient entropy coding. It uses an agentic evolution process with human-LLM collaboration to achieve HM-comparable compression at 126ms decoding time for 1080p images on a single CPU thread.
AI.motivation: Existing learned image compression methods are computationally expensive and impractical for resource-constrained hardware, particularly CPUs, necessitating a codec that balances compression efficiency with low computational complexity.
AI.method: PULSE employs: (1) an ultra-low-complexity 5.2 kMAC/pixel neural receiver for low-latency decoding, (2) an integer linear CDF predictor with meta prior for efficient bit-exact entropy coding, and (3) an agentic evolution process guided by heuristic probes that iteratively improves the architecture through human-LLM collaboration.
AI.result: PULSE decodes a 1080p image in 126 ms on a single CPU thread while achieving compression performance comparable to HM. After perceptual optimization, PULSE competes with larger perceptual codecs like MS-ILLM.
AI.conclusion: PULSE demonstrates that practical neural image compression with ultra-low complexity is achievable, enabling high-quality image compression on diverse hardware platforms with minimal computational resources while maintaining performance competitive with established and larger perceptual codecs.

title: Suppressed, Not Erased: A Representational Trace of Edited Facts Survives Even Weight-Free Knowledge Editing
summary: Knowledge-editing benchmarks certify local correctness, whether an edited model produces the new fact on near-edit prompts but not how much of the original fact remains decodable inside the model. We study residual knowledge directly with a linear trace probe: after editing a fact, we ask whether the original object is still recoverable from the model's hidden states. On GPT-2-XL, across three mechanistically distinct editors applied to 50 CounterFact edits, the original object remains linearly decodable well above chance after a successful edit (probe accuracy 0.96 for ROME, 0.86 for constrained fine-tuning, and 0.79 for the memory-based editor GRACE, against a chance level of 0.50; all edits reach 100% generation-based success). The GRACE result is the most informative: GRACE changes zero base-model weights, overriding the fact through an external memory, yet the original object is still decodable from the underlying network, so the residual trace cannot be attributed to an incomplete weight update. We read this as evidence that editing, even when behaviorally successful, suppresses rather than erases the original association in representational space. We also report a relearning-savings instrument that did not behave reliably in our setting and discuss why; we treat it as a negative methodological result rather than evidence. Code and data are released.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers that knowledge editing methods (ROME, constrained fine-tuning, GRACE) suppress but don't erase original facts - residual knowledge remains linearly decodable from model hidden states even after behaviorally successful edits. Notably, GRACE, which doesn't modify model weights at all, still leaves traces of the original knowledge.
AI.motivation: Current knowledge-editing benchmarks only verify local correctness (whether edited models produce new facts on near-edit prompts) but fail to measure how much original knowledge remains decodable in the model's hidden states. The authors investigate this "residual knowledge" directly.
AI.method: Linear trace probe: after editing facts in GPT-2-XL using three different editors (ROME, constrained fine-tuning, GRACE) on 50 CounterFact edits, the authors test whether the original object remains recoverable from the model's hidden states using a linear probe.
AI.result: Original objects remain linearly decodable well above chance after successful edits: ROME achieves 0.96 probe accuracy, constrained fine-tuning 0.86, and GRACE 0.79 (chance level 0.50). All edits achieve 100% generation-based success. The GRACE result is particularly significant - it changes zero base-model weights but original knowledge is still decodable, proving residual traces cannot be attributed to incomplete weight updates.
AI.conclusion: Editing, even when behaviorally successful, suppresses rather than erases the original association in representational space. The authors also report a relearning-savings instrument that didn't behave reliably as a negative methodological result.

title: A Geometric Theory of Decision Boundaries in Structured Markov Decision Processes
summary: Classical dynamic programming represents optimal sequential decisions through value functions and policies. While this functional representation is natural for computing optimal decisions, it does not directly identify the mathematical object governing policy reconstruction, representation complexity, or oracle-query complexity once an optimal policy is fixed. This paper addresses this question by developing a geometric theory of structured optimal policies in which the decision-boundary geometry induced by the policy becomes the primary object of analysis. We show that, under suitable structural regularity conditions, this geometry provides the minimal representation required for policy reconstruction and determines the statistical and computational complexity of the reconstruction problem. Building upon this representation, we establish structural properties of policy-induced decision geometry, introduce intrinsic notions of boundary and decision complexity, derive information-theoretic measures of decision compression, and obtain statistical guarantees for boundary estimation and policy reconstruction from black-box policy queries. Collectively, these results demonstrate that, for the structured decision problems considered here, the complexity of policy reconstruction is governed by the geometry of the decision boundary rather than by the cardinality of the ambient state space. Controlled numerical experiments examine the principal theoretical predictions and provide empirical evidence consistent with the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a geometric theory of structured optimal policies in dynamic programming, where decision-boundary geometry becomes the primary object of analysis. The key insight is that, under structural regularity conditions, the geometry of the decision boundary determines the minimal representation needed for policy reconstruction and governs its statistical/computational complexity—rather than the cardinality of the ambient state space.
AI.motivation: Classical dynamic programming represents optimal decisions through value functions and policies, but this representation doesn't directly identify the mathematical object governing policy reconstruction, representation complexity, or oracle-query complexity. The authors aim to address this fundamental question.
AI.method: The paper develops a geometric theory of structured optimal policies by analyzing the decision-boundary geometry induced by policies. Under suitable structural regularity conditions, they establish structural properties of policy-induced decision geometry, introduce intrinsic notions of boundary and decision complexity, derive information-theoretic measures of decision compression, and obtain statistical guarantees for boundary estimation and policy reconstruction from black-box policy queries.
AI.result: The geometry of the decision boundary provides the minimal representation required for policy reconstruction and determines the statistical and computational complexity of the reconstruction problem. The complexity of policy reconstruction is governed by the geometry of the decision boundary rather than by the cardinality of the ambient state space.
AI.conclusion: For structured decision problems, the complexity of policy reconstruction is governed by the geometry of the decision boundary rather than by the cardinality of the ambient state space. Controlled numerical experiments examine the principal theoretical predictions and provide empirical evidence consistent with the proposed framework.

title: FIVE-VLA: Fast and EffectIVE Autonomous Driving with Recurrent Action Memory
summary: State-of-the-art vision-language-action models (VLA) for autonomous driving face critical limitations: excessive parameter counts, inefficient high-resolution image processing, and lack of temporal memory. We introduce Fast and EffectIVE VLA (FIVE-VLA) to address these through two key contributions. First, we employ an efficient vision encoder that processes high-resolution ($448 \times 896$) images while generating only 98 tokens, over $5\times$ fewer than existing approaches, and bypass text generation entirely for single-pass trajectory prediction. Second, we propose Recurrent Action Memory (RAM), a lightweight module that conditions action prediction on previous action tokens, providing temporal context critical for manoeuvres such as overtaking and emergency braking. With only 641M parameters, FIVE-VLA completes $\sim$10% more routes without traffic rule infractions than the previous state-of-the-art VLA on the challenging Bench2Drive closed-loop driving benchmark. Non-reactive open-loop simulation on the large-scale real-world NVIDIA Physical AI AV dataset shows 10.2% and 7.7% lower collision-violation rates than SimLingo in single- and four-view settings, respectively. Additionally, FIVE-VLA runs at $\sim$30 fps on an A100 and $\sim$4 fps on a T4 GPU (proxy to an edge device), representing an 8-30$\times$ speedup over previous methods.

AI.tldr: FIVE-VLA is a novel vision-language-action model for autonomous driving that addresses three critical limitations of existing VLAs: excessive parameters, inefficient high-resolution image processing, and lack of temporal memory. It uses an efficient vision encoder processing 448×896 images with only 98 tokens and introduces Recurrent Action Memory (RAM) for temporal context.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art VLAs for autonomous driving face critical limitations: (1) excessive parameter counts, (2) inefficient high-resolution image processing, and (3) lack of temporal memory. These limitations hinder real-world deployment and performance in complex maneuvers like overtaking and emergency braking.
AI.method: Two key contributions: (1) Efficient vision encoder that processes 448×896 images generating only 98 tokens (5x fewer than existing approaches) and bypasses text generation for single-pass trajectory prediction; (2) Recurrent Action Memory (RAM), a lightweight module that conditions action prediction on previous action tokens to provide temporal context.
AI.result: With only 641M parameters, FIVE-VLA completes ~10% more routes without traffic rule infractions than previous state-of-the-art on Bench2Drive. On NVIDIA Physical AI AV dataset, it shows 10.2% and 7.7% lower collision-violation rates than SimLingo in single- and four-view settings. It runs at ~30 fps on A100 and ~4 fps on T4 GPU, representing an 8-30x speedup over previous methods.
AI.conclusion: FIVE-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters (641M), faster inference (8-30x speedup), and better safety metrics across closed-loop driving benchmarks and open-loop simulation, demonstrating the effectiveness of the efficient vision encoder and Recurrent Action Memory for autonomous driving applications.

title: Function Lives Where Variance Doesn't: Task-Weighted Charts of a Language Model's Computation
summary: How many dimensions does a language model's computation actually use? The question is ill-posed until one names a functional. Task-weighted charts make it well-posed: low-dimensional coordinate systems fit against a chosen functional of the representation, under the functional's own metric, turning distillation into plain least squares. Across six models from three families, spanning 70m to 7B parameters, next-token prediction needs 70--90% of the residual stream's width to stay within 5% of intact perplexity, a width consumed by the rare tail of language, and the variance profile predicts none of it: two directions carry 90% of GPT-2's activation variance and almost none of its function. Dimension is per-functional: the model's own uncertainty reads from six coordinates where the full predictive distribution needs hundreds; and it grows with depth. The dissociation is exploitable: when only a few dimensions can be kept, charts trained under the functional's metric preserve the model's predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "task-weighted charts" to measure the effective dimensionality of language model computations against specific functionals (like next-token prediction). Across 6 models (70M-7B parameters), the authors find that next-token prediction requires 70-90% of the residual stream width, and variance-based metrics poorly predict functional importance.
AI.motivation: The question "how many dimensions does a language model use?" is ill-posed without specifying a functional. The authors aim to make this question well-posed by using task-weighted charts that fit low-dimensional coordinate systems against a chosen functional under its own metric.
AI.method: The authors use task-weighted charts: low-dimensional coordinate systems fit against a chosen functional of the representation, under the functional's own metric. They tested across six models from three families (70M to 7B parameters), examining next-token prediction and analyzing variance profiles.
AI.result: Next-token prediction needs 70-90% of the residual stream width to stay within 5% of intact perplexity. The rare tail of language consumes this width. Variance profile predicts none of it: two directions carry 90% of GPT-2's activation variance but almost none of its function. The model's own uncertainty reads from six coordinates while the full predictive distribution needs hundreds. Dimension grows with depth. Charts trained under the functional's metric preserve predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression.
AI.conclusion: Dimension is per-functional, not a fixed property. Variance-based metrics are poor proxies for functional importance. The dissociation between variance and function is exploitable: task-weighted charts outperform variance-based compression when only a few dimensions can be kept.

title: Weakening Neurons: An Input-Output Functionality in Transformers with Outsize Influence
summary: We analyze the learned input-output behavior of GLU-based neurons in large language models (LLMs). We propose a simple analysis method: For each neuron, we compute the cosine similarities between its input (reading) and output (writing) weight vectors. In this scheme, a strong negative cosine similarity indicates the neuron weakens the direction it detects in the residual stream, so we call this a weakening neuron. This allows us to gain a number of novel insights. First, we show that nine different LLMs have similar patterns: weakening neurons appear mostly in late layers whereas their counterparts, (conditional) strengthening neurons, are frequent in early-middle layers. Second, we find that weakening neurons display surprising behavior: even though there are few, they activate often and have a large influence on model behavior. Third, weakening neurons have a strong effect on model output when gate values are negative -- which is surprising since negative gate values are not expected to encode functionality.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes GLU-based neurons in LLMs by computing cosine similarities between input and output weight vectors. The study reveals that weakening neurons (negative cosine similarity) are concentrated in late layers while strengthening neurons appear in early-middle layers, and that despite being few, weakening neurons activate frequently and have significant influence, especially when gate values are negative.
AI.motivation: Understand the learned input-output behavior of GLU-based neurons in large language models, as these neurons play a critical role in transformer architectures but their functional mechanisms remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Compute cosine similarities between each neuron's input (reading) and output (writing) weight vectors. Neurons with strong negative cosine similarity are classified as "weakening neurons" (they weaken the direction they detect), while those with positive cosine similarity are "strengthening neurons."
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Nine different LLMs show similar patterns - weakening neurons appear mostly in late layers while strengthening neurons are frequent in early-middle layers; (2) Weakening neurons, despite being few in number, activate often and have large influence on model behavior; (3) Weakening neurons strongly affect model output when gate values are negative, which is surprising since negative gate values are not expected to encode functionality.
AI.conclusion: Weakening neurons represent a functionally important but previously overlooked class of neurons in LLMs. Their concentration in late layers, frequent activation, and strong influence—particularly with negative gate values—suggests they play a critical role in model computation that differs fundamentally from the expected function of GLU gates.

title: VibeAvatar: Aligning Phonetic Kinematics and Human Aesthetics for High-Fidelity Talking Avatar Synthesis
summary: Multi-modal talking avatar synthesis aims to generate realistic talking videos from a reference portrait and speech. Despite rapid progress in diffusion-based methods, existing approaches still struggle to jointly achieve accurate lip articulation, human-preferred motion aesthetics, and efficient inference. We observe that phonetic accuracy and motion aesthetics arise from fundamentally different sources and should be addressed at complementary stages rather than learned implicitly by a single generator. Based on this insight, we propose VibeAvatar, which disentangles these two objectives through a Phonetic Kinematics Adapter (PKA) that converts recognition-oriented speech features into phonetic-kinematic conditions at the conditioning stage, and an Aesthetic Motion Policy (AMP) that optimizes a flow-consistent stochastic sampling policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the post-training stage. With a lightweight flow-based motion generator operating in a compact 1D warp-based latent motion space, VibeAvatar achieves state-of-the-art results in articulation, aesthetics, and efficiency on both objective metrics and user studies, while generating a 10-second 512px video in under 10 seconds with only $\sim$3GB VRAM.

AI.tldr: VibeAvatar is a multi-modal talking avatar synthesis method that disentangles phonetic accuracy and motion aesthetics into separate components: a Phonetic Kinematics Adapter (PKA) for conditioning and an Aesthetic Motion Policy (AMP) optimized via GRPO. Using a lightweight flow-based generator in a compact 1D warp latent space, it achieves state-of-the-art results in lip articulation, motion aesthetics, and inference efficiency, generating 10-second 512px videos in under 10 seconds with ~3GB VRAM.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based methods for talking avatar synthesis struggle to jointly achieve accurate lip articulation, human-preferred motion aesthetics, and efficient inference. The key insight is that phonetic accuracy and motion aesthetics arise from fundamentally different sources and should be addressed at complementary stages rather than learned implicitly by a single generator.
AI.method: VibeAvatar proposes two key components: (1) Phonetic Kinematics Adapter (PKA) that converts recognition-oriented speech features into phonetic-kinematic conditions at the conditioning stage; (2) Aesthetic Motion Policy (AMP) that optimizes a flow-consistent stochastic sampling policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the post-training stage. The system uses a lightweight flow-based motion generator operating in a compact 1D warp-based latent motion space.
AI.result: VibeAvatar achieves state-of-the-art results in articulation, aesthetics, and efficiency on both objective metrics and user studies. It can generate a 10-second 512px video in under 10 seconds with only ~3GB VRAM.
AI.conclusion: By disentangling phonetic accuracy and motion aesthetics into complementary stages, VibeAvatar successfully addresses the trade-off between lip articulation quality, human-preferred motion aesthetics, and computational efficiency, establishing a new benchmark for multi-modal talking avatar synthesis.

title: Lost in Perception: Isolating Perceptual and Reasoning Failures in Multimodal Physics and Geometry Reasoning
summary: Multimodal LLMs report strong performance on scientific reasoning benchmarks, yet most treat perception and reasoning as a single measurable process. We introduce a five-task diagnostic experiment across physics and geometry benchmarks that isolates failures to perception, reasoning, or both. Incorrect diagram interpretation degrades performance even on problems models solve correctly from text alone, and accuracy generally rises from raw images to human-authored captions. Recovery under corrected captions is high for some models, separating perception-blocked failures from genuine reasoning bottlenecks. Which reasoning error follows a perception failure depends on domain: physics failures resolve into calculation errors, geometry into conceptual misapplication. As a discussion beyond our core experiments, InternS1-mini, despite heavy scientific pretraining and thinking capabilities, falls below the weakest model from experiments on every task, with reasoning traces frequently truncating before completion.
