title: When Edit Flows are Edit Jumps: replicating Edit Flows and EvoFlows
summary: Antibody lead optimization calls for a small, bounded set of edits to an existing candidate: substitutions, but also insertions and deletions. Edit-based generative models are the only ones that allocate such an edit budget without fixing the edit positions, the edit count, or the output length in advance. However, the existing approaches Edit Flows and EvoFlows did not release code or complete training specifications. Here, we show that both methods follow the same underlying process -- edits firing one at a time, at learned rates, in continuous time -- the pure-jump case of generator matching over finite sequences. With EditJumps we introduce the first open implementation of this framework, with a single generalist antibody editor trained on 1.66M Observed Antibody Space homolog pairs to propose homolog-like variants of a seed sequence, editing unseen leads zero-shot, without the per-family retraining original approaches require. Replicating this system from scratch exposes why open code is essential for generative biology: reconciling published edit distributions required reverse-engineering an undocumented rate-scaling hyperparameter that dictates realized mutation counts. Moreover, we show that published evaluation metrics are highly sensitive to reference sample size, frequently flipping method rankings. We release our full codebase, automated test suite, and configurations at: https://github.com/VisiumCH/editjumps

AI.tldr: EditJumps is the first open-source implementation of edit-based generative models for antibody lead optimization. It trains a single generalist antibody editor on 1.66M homolog pairs to propose variants through learned edit rates in continuous time, enabling zero-shot editing without per-family retraining. The work reveals critical reproducibility issues in prior methods, including undocumented hyperparameters and evaluation metric sensitivity to sample size.
AI.motivation: Antibody lead optimization requires bounded edits (substitutions, insertions, deletions) to existing candidates without pre-specifying edit positions, count, or output length. While edit-based generative models like Edit Flows and EvoFlows exist, their closed-source nature prevented reproducibility and wide adoption. The authors aimed to create an open implementation and expose hidden complexities in prior approaches.
AI.method: The authors reverse-engineered the underlying process shared by Edit Flows and EvoFlows -- edits firing one at a time at learned rates in continuous time (pure-jump case of generator matching). They trained EditJumps on 1.66M Observed Antibody Space homolog pairs as a single generalist antibody editor, enabling zero-shot editing of unseen leads without per-family retraining.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Reconciling published edit distributions required reverse-engineering an undocumented rate-scaling hyperparameter that controls realized mutation counts; (2) Published evaluation metrics are highly sensitive to reference sample size, frequently causing method rankings to flip.
AI.conclusion: Open code is essential for generative biology. The authors provide the first open implementation of edit-based antibody optimization, demonstrate the importance of reproducibility in computational biology, and reveal that evaluation metrics require careful consideration of sample size effects. Full codebase, test suite, and configurations are released.

title: Geometry beneath the Waves: Dense Priors for Sparse-View Underwater 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Underwater 3D reconstruction supports applications ranging from marine ecosystem monitoring and subsea inspection to underwater archaeology, education, and immersive visualisation. 3D Gaussian Splatting has made real-time photorealistic novel-view rendering practical, while underwater variants incorporate physically based image-formation models to separate medium effects from scene radiance. Their reconstruction quality, however, remains fundamentally limited by the geometry used for initialisation.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses underwater 3D reconstruction using 3D Gaussian Splatting, which is limited by the quality of initial geometry. The work targets applications in marine monitoring, subsea inspection, and underwater archaeology.
AI.motivation: Underwater 3D reconstruction has important applications (marine ecosystem monitoring, subsea inspection, underwater archaeology, education, immersive visualization), but current methods using 3D Gaussian Splatting are limited by the quality of geometry used for initialization.
AI.method: The paper incorporates physically based image-formation models to separate medium effects from scene radiance in underwater variants of 3D Gaussian Splatting.
AI.result: The reconstruction quality remains fundamentally limited by the geometry used for initialization.
AI.conclusion: Improving the initial geometry is key to enhancing underwater 3D reconstruction quality using 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques.

title: A Convergence Framework for Deep $V$-Learning: Error Propagation and Sharp Action-Gap Bounds
summary: We establish convergence bounds for deep $V$-learning with horizon $H$. The algorithm fits a scalar value function to targets from executed transitions and selects actions using a predictive model and the value function. For current observed-successor targets with fresh true-kernel outcomes, the conditional mean is $\mathcal{T}^βV$, which averages over behavior-policy actions. The Bellman optimality update is $\mathcal{T} V$. We decompose the update error into six residuals: fitting, transition reuse, target construction, replay, action selection, and exploration. Under $L^s$ concentrability, their $L^p$ norms ($p=s/(s-1)$) control expected $L^1$ policy loss. The bound explicitly weights residuals from only the last $H-1$ update blocks, plus an initialization term for shorter runs. We quantify the cost of a shared sampling distribution across horizon levels. For statistical error bounds of order $n^{-ν}$, we derive optimal continuous allocations and an integer allocation whose objective is within a factor $2^ν$ of the constrained optimum. A margin condition with exponent $α$ gives action error of order $Λ^{1+α/p}$, where $Λ$ combines network drift and score error; a one-step construction proves the exponent sharp. Bounds on the distance between frozen and optimal scores transfer an optimal-gap condition to frozen-iterate gap bounds while retaining the mass of optimal ties. Survival probabilities and coverage conditions at deployment yield bounds for policies selected with approximate scores. Separate spatial ReLU networks per horizon level give a conditional neural regression rate, and the finite-state case gives a log-free expected fit rate. These results give expected policy-loss consistency for the fixed-horizon generative-reset approximate-ERM procedure with exact action scores and provide an explicit residual-decay criterion for FIFO/interleaved SGD.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes convergence bounds for deep V-learning with horizon H, analyzing error decomposition into six residuals and deriving optimal sample allocations under L^s concentrability conditions. The work provides expected policy-loss consistency for fixed-horizon generative-reset approximate-ERM procedures with explicit residual-decay criteria.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to establish theoretical convergence guarantees for deep V-learning algorithms, which are important in reinforcement learning but often lack rigorous finite-sample analysis. The authors seek to understand how various error sources (fitting, transition reuse, target construction, replay, action selection, exploration) contribute to policy loss and to derive optimal resource allocation strategies.
AI.method:
The methodology involves:
1. Decomposing update errors into six residuals
2. Using L^s concentrability to control expected L^1 policy loss via L^p norms (p = s/(s-1))
3. Deriving optimal continuous and integer sample allocations for statistical error bounds of order n^(-ν)
4. Applying margin conditions with exponent α to obtain action error bounds
5. Using separate spatial ReLU networks per horizon level for conditional neural regression
6. Analyzing the gap between frozen and optimal scores
AI.result:
Key results include:
- Bound explicitly weights residuals from only last H-1 update blocks plus initialization term
- Quantified cost of shared sampling distribution across horizon levels
- Optimal continuous allocations derived with integer allocation within factor 2^ν of constrained optimum
- Margin condition yields action error of order Λ^(1+α/p), with exponent proven sharp via one-step construction
- Gap bounds transfer optimal-gap condition to frozen-iterate gap bounds
- Conditional neural regression rates for spatial ReLU networks
- Log-free expected fit rate for finite-state case
AI.conclusion: The paper provides expected policy-loss consistency for fixed-horizon generative-reset approximate-ERM procedure with exact action scores. It establishes an explicit residual-decay criterion for FIFO/interleaved SGD. The theoretical bounds connect algorithmic parameters to statistical rates, offering guidance for practical implementation while preserving the mass of optimal ties through survival probabilities and coverage conditions.

title: Toward Markerless Video-based Tremor Analysis: Objective Quantification of Pathological Tremor in Mouse Preclinical Models
summary: Tremor is a movement disorder characterized by involuntary, rhythmic oscillations of body parts and is a hallmark of several neurological conditions, including Parkinson's disease and essential tremor. Elucidating its underlying mechanisms relies heavily on mouse models, which offer genetic manipulability and translational relevance to human neural circuitry. Accordingly, these models are indispensable for studying tremor pathophysiology. So far, electromyography and accelerometers have been used as methods to quantitatively observe tremors in mice. However, these methods have several drawbacks, such as high costs and complex setups. In particular, the invasive surgical implantation of devices causes significant stress to the animals. Although RGB-based methods offer non-invasive and cost-effective alternatives, they often lack the sensitivity required to detect subtle tremors. Therefore, this paper addresses these challenges by achieving mouse tremor severity estimation using conventional RGB cameras only. To address the challenging task of isolating tremor-related vibrations while the mouse itself is also in motion, our pipeline incorporates segmentation-based pre-processing to extract the mouse region and a Tremor Score Estimation Module that captures subtle tremors with high sensitivity. In the experiments, we assessed tremors in unrestrained mice using a non-invasive method with two standard cameras. The results demonstrated a strong correlation with accelerometer measurements and confirmed that the method accurately captured the intensity-dependent characteristics of tremors. The project page is available at https://isogawalab.github.io/Video-based-Tremor-Analysis-Project/.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a non-invasive, RGB camera-based method for estimating mouse tremor severity. The approach uses segmentation-based pre-processing to isolate the mouse region and a Tremor Score Estimation Module to capture subtle vibrations. The method correlates strongly with accelerometer measurements while avoiding the invasiveness and cost of traditional approaches.
AI.motivation: Current methods for quantifying mouse tremors (electromyography and accelerometers) have significant drawbacks: high costs, complex setups, and require invasive surgical implantation causing animal stress. While RGB-based methods offer non-invasive alternatives, they lack sensitivity for detecting subtle tremors. There was a need for a cost-effective, non-invasive method that can accurately capture tremor intensity in unrestrained mice.
AI.method: The proposed pipeline incorporates: (1) Segmentation-based pre-processing to extract the mouse region from video frames, isolating the mouse from background motion; (2) A Tremor Score Estimation Module designed to capture subtle tremors with high sensitivity. The method uses two standard RGB cameras to assess tremors in unrestrained mice without any surgical implantation.
AI.result: The experiments demonstrated a strong correlation with accelerometer measurements, confirming the method accurately captures intensity-dependent characteristics of tremors. The approach achieves non-invasive tremor detection while maintaining accuracy comparable to invasive gold-standard methods.
AI.conclusion: RGB camera-based tremor analysis is a viable alternative to accelerometer/EMG methods, offering non-invasive, cost-effective tremor severity estimation with high sensitivity. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional methods while providing reliable quantitative measurements suitable for studying tremor pathophysiology in mouse models of neurological conditions like Parkinson's disease and essential tremor.

title: WaveTLM: Reliable Time-Series Language Modeling through Task Compilation
summary: Time-series language models provide a shared natural-language interface across temporal tasks, but plausible text does not guarantee reliable task outputs. Responses may appear reasonable while hallucinating the required object: numerical sequences can violate shape, scale, channel order, or temporal alignment, and textual decisions can fall outside the legal label space. We formulate reliable time-series language modeling, separating task-object reliability from predictive quality. We introduce ExecTS-QA, a contract-grounded benchmark spanning forecasting, imputation, classification, anomaly detection, and waveform analysis. We further propose WaveTLM, a unified compiler-executor model whose task compiler transforms user requests, visible arguments, and wave-grounded evidence into typed task states, while task-native executors construct numerical tensors, legal decisions, or structured records. On ExecTS-QA, a single WaveTLM checkpoint achieves 99.40% contract-valid coverage, compared with 37.83% for the strongest evaluated string-first baseline, while retaining balanced predictive performance across all five task families. Evaluations on SciTS, TSQA, IRTS-ToolBench, and ARFBench provide additional evidence of transfer. The code, construction scripts, and ExecTS-QA dataset will be publicly released upon publication. These results show that task compilation can convert plausible language generation into reliable time-series outputs.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the critical problem of hallucination in time-series language models, where plausible text outputs can contain numerically invalid or legally impossible results. The authors propose a compiler-executor architecture (WaveTLM) and a contract-grounded benchmark (ExecTS-QA) to ensure task-object reliability while maintaining predictive quality.
AI.motivation: Time-series language models can generate seemingly reasonable text that actually contains invalid numerical outputs (e.g., wrong shapes, scales, or temporal alignment) or impossible classification decisions (outside legal label space). Current evaluation metrics focus on predictive quality but overlook whether outputs satisfy task constraints - a fundamental reliability gap.
AI.method: The authors introduce: (1) ExecTS-QA benchmark - a contract-grounded dataset spanning 5 task families (forecasting, imputation, classification, anomaly detection, waveform analysis) with explicit validity constraints; (2) WaveTLM - a unified compiler-executor model where the task compiler transforms user requests, visible arguments, and wave-grounded evidence into typed task states, and task-native executors construct numerical tensors, legal decisions, or structured records that satisfy contractual constraints.
AI.result: A single WaveTLM checkpoint achieves 99.40% contract-valid coverage, dramatically outperforming the strongest string-first baseline (37.83%). The model retains balanced predictive performance across all five task families. Transfer evaluations on SciTS, TSQA, IRTS-ToolBench, and ARFBench provide additional evidence of generalization.
AI.conclusion: Task compilation - separating task-object reliability from predictive quality - can effectively convert plausible language generation into reliable time-series outputs. This architectural approach provides a promising direction for building trustworthy time-series language models that satisfy both predictive accuracy and structural validity constraints.

title: DISTA-Net++: Rethinking Infrared Small Target Unmixing Beyond Sub-Pixel Separation
summary: Long-range infrared imaging frequently confronts dense target clusters whose diffraction-limited signatures merge into a single indistinguishable blob, concealing the number, sub-pixel positions, and radiant intensities of the underlying sources. While deep learning has advanced general object detection, resolving such Closely-Spaced Infrared Small Targets (CSIST) remains largely unexplored, owing to a systemic infrastructure void and a fundamental paradigm mismatch. The dominant formulation, which reduces unmixing to a blind, discrete sub-pixel separation, is inherently insufficient: without semantic guidance, the ill-posed inverse problem admits ambiguous solutions plagued by false and missed detections, while grid-based discretization locks predictions onto fixed lattice centers, chaining precision to prohibitively expensive grid refinement. We argue that CSIST unmixing should instead be informed and continuous. To ground this paradigm shift, we establish the first comprehensive open-source ecosystem for the field, comprising the large-scale CSIST-100K benchmark, a tailored metric suite, and the GrokCSO toolkit. Upon this foundation, we propose DISTA-Net++, which anchors a dynamic deep unfolding backbone with two synergistic mechanisms: a Count-Guided Prior that injects the global target count as an explicit semantic constraint to regularize the solution space, and a Continuous Coordinate Rectification that regresses off-grid offsets to decouple localization accuracy from grid resolution. Extensive experiments validate our paradigm: even under the most economical 3x division, DISTA-Net++ surpasses 7x-division state-of-the-art methods by 16.15% in CSO-mAP and 62.96% in count accuracy at merely one-sixth of their computation, demonstrating that unmixing precision need not be purchased with finer discretization. The complete ecosystem is available at https://github.com/GrokCV/GrokDet.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of detecting Closely-Spaced Infrared Small Targets (CSIST) in long-range infrared imaging, where dense target clusters merge into indistinguishable blobs. The authors propose DISTA-Net++, which uses a dynamic deep unfolding backbone with Count-Guided Prior (semantic constraint using target count) and Continuous Coordinate Rectification (off-grid offset regression). They also establish the first open-source ecosystem including CSIST-100K benchmark and GrokCSO toolkit.
AI.motivation: Long-range infrared imaging frequently encounters dense target clusters whose diffraction-limited signatures merge into single indistinguishable blobs, concealing the number, sub-pixel positions, and radiant intensities of underlying sources. Existing deep learning approaches for general object detection fail to resolve CSIST due to: (1) systemic infrastructure void - lack of dedicated benchmarks and tools, and (2) fundamental paradigm mismatch - the dominant blind discrete sub-pixel separation approach is inherently insufficient: without semantic guidance, the ill-posed inverse problem admits ambiguous solutions with false/missed detections, while grid-based discretization chains precision to expensive grid refinement.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) Establish first comprehensive open-source ecosystem comprising CSIST-100K benchmark, tailored metric suite, and GrokCSO toolkit. (2) Propose DISTA-Net++ with dynamic deep unfolding backbone incorporating two synergistic mechanisms: (a) Count-Guided Prior that injects global target count as explicit semantic constraint to regularize solution space, and (b) Continuous Coordinate Rectification that regresses off-grid offsets to decouple localization accuracy from grid resolution.
AI.result: Even under the most economical 3x division, DISTA-Net++ surpasses 7x-division state-of-the-art methods by 16.15% in CSO-mAP and 62.96% in count accuracy at merely one-sixth of their computation. This demonstrates that unmixing precision need not be purchased with finer discretization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed paradigm of informed and continuous CSIST unmixing is validated. The Count-Guided Prior effectively leverages semantic count information to constrain the solution space, while Continuous Coordinate Rectification achieves sub-pixel localization accuracy without requiring fine grid discretization. The established ecosystem (CSIST-100K, metrics, GrokCSO toolkit) provides foundation for future research in this underexplored domain.

title: Interpretable Multi-Instance Learning Enables Early Prediction of Key Molecular Alterations from Routine Flow Cytometry in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
summary: Background: Molecular testing for NPM1 and FLT3-ITD mutations guides critical early treatment decisions in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but results can take weeks, long after these decisions must be made. Flow cytometry, already performed within hours of admission as part of routine care, may carry enough signal to predict these mutations directly, without added cost or delay. Methods: We developed an interpretable multi-instance learning classifier based on a decision tree, in which each patient sample is modeled as a collection of individual cells and mutation status is inferred from cell-level predictions. The model was benchmarked against a random forest trained on clinical variables and a deep convolutional neural network adapted for multitube flow cytometry data. Performance was assessed by cross-validation on a discovery cohort of 197 patients and tested on an independent cohort of 161 patients, using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and positive predictive value. Results: In cross-validation on the discovery cohort, the MIL model achieved mean AUROCs of 0.96 (SD=0.05) for NPM1 and 0.86 (SD=0.10) for FLT3-ITD, outperforming the clinical baseline and matching deep learning approaches. The model then successfully generalized to the independent test cohort of 161 patients, reaching AUROCs of 0.90 (NPM1) and 0.82 (FLT3-ITD), with positive predictive values of 0.87 and 0.68, respectively. Cell-level interpretation recovered established immunophenotypic signatures (CD33${}^{+}$ /CD34___ for NPM1-mutated cases, CD33${}^{+}$ /low side-scatter for FLT3-ITD), directly linking model predictions to known biology.  Conclusions: These results show that an interpretable model applied to data already collected in routine care can predict AML molecular status within hours, offering a practical route to earlier, biology-informed treatment decisions.

AI.tldr: This study developed an interpretable multi-instance learning (MIL) classifier using flow cytometry data to predict NPM1 and FLT3-ITD mutations in AML patients within hours, bypassing the weeks-long wait for molecular testing.
AI.motivation: Molecular testing for NPM1 and FLT3-ITD mutations takes weeks, but treatment decisions in AML must be made much earlier. Flow cytometry is already performed within hours of admission as routine care, so the researchers hypothesized it could predict these mutations without added cost or delay.
AI.method: A multi-instance learning classifier based on a decision tree was developed, modeling each patient sample as a collection of individual cells. Mutation status was inferred from cell-level predictions. The model was compared against a random forest (clinical variables) and a deep convolutional neural network (multitube flow cytometry). Performance was assessed via cross-validation on a discovery cohort (n=197) and tested on an independent cohort (n=161), using AUROC and positive predictive value.
AI.result: In cross-validation, the MIL model achieved mean AUROCs of 0.96 (SD=0.05) for NPM1 and 0.86 (SD=0.10) for FLT3-ITD, outperforming the clinical baseline and matching deep learning approaches. On the independent test cohort, AUROCs were 0.90 (NPM1) and 0.82 (FLT3-ITD), with PPVs of 0.87 and 0.68 respectively. Cell-level interpretation recovered established immunophenotypic signatures: CD33+/CD34+ for NPM1-mutated cases and CD33+/low side-scatter for FLT3-ITD.
AI.conclusion: An interpretable model applied to routine flow cytometry data can predict AML molecular status within hours, offering a practical route to earlier, biology-informed treatment decisions. The model successfully links predictions to known biological markers, providing clinical interpretability.

title: Using OCR Heads to Verbalize Image Semantics
summary: How do VLMs map from pixels to semantics? To understand this general question, we focus on a narrow one: studying how VLMs perform optical character recognition (OCR). Across four models, we identify attention heads causally necessary for OCR, and discover that these are in fact general-purpose heads that output interpretable semantic features across all image tokens. For example, pointing these heads at an image token containing the word "bike" causes Qwen3-VL-8B to output "bike," but pointing them at a bird wing causes the model to output the token "feathers." We collapse these heads' attention weights into a single verbalization lens transformation that reveals interpretable semantic features in hidden states across all layers. When combined with projection to vocabulary space, we can obtain interpretable labels starting from layer 0, showing that image representations are in fact aligned with language in early layers. We find that we can also use the inverse of this transformation to edit non-word concepts, e.g., replacing a tractor with a revolver in a naturalistic image, providing causal evidence that this subspace is useful for more than just OCR. Our results are an example of how the study of specific mechanisms can shed light on broader interpretability problems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how Vision-Language Models (VLMs) map visual inputs to semantic understanding, focusing on optical character recognition (OCR) as a lens. The study identifies specific attention heads that serve as general-purpose semantic feature extractors across all image tokens, and introduces a "verbalization lens" transformation that reveals interpretable semantic features in hidden states from early layers.
AI.motivation: To understand how VLMs map from pixels to semantics, the authors narrow the question to studying OCR performance. They aim to identify specific mechanisms that enable semantic understanding in VLMs, using OCR as a concrete test case.
AI.method: The authors studied four VLM models, identifying attention heads causally necessary for OCR through intervention experiments. They collapsed these heads' attention weights into a "verbalization lens transformation" and combined it with projection to vocabulary space to obtain interpretable labels. They also tested the inverse transformation for editing non-word concepts in naturalistic images.
AI.result: The identified attention heads are general-purpose semantic feature extractors. When pointed at an image token containing "bike," the model outputs "bike"; when pointed at a bird wing, it outputs "feathers." The verbalization lens reveals interpretable semantic features starting from layer 0, showing early alignment between image representations and language. The inverse transformation successfully edited non-word concepts (e.g., replacing a tractor with a revolver), providing causal evidence that this subspace is useful beyond OCR.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that specific mechanisms (particular attention heads) can shed light on broader interpretability problems in VLMs. The discovered semantic subspace is not limited to OCR but can be leveraged for visual concept editing, providing causal evidence of its general-purpose nature. This work illustrates how studying narrow, specific questions can reveal broader insights into VLM interpretability.

title: Physics-based prediction, uncertainty quantification and decision-making for IN718 crystallographic texture intensity across LPBF defocus regimes
comment: 69 pages, 9 figures, 9 tables. Includes supplementary material (S1-S7)
summary: Reliable prediction of crystallographic texture in laser powder bed fusion is critical for linking process conditions with anisotropic response and for qualification. However, black-box models may fail under shift and cannot distinguish weak data support from loss of physical validity. This study develops a two-stage physics-based model for <001> || BD (build direction) texture in Inconel 718. Stage 1 maps process variables to melting mode and melt pool geometry. Stage 2 predicts texture by combining an empirical physics model with a random-forest residual model. A k-nearest-neighbor weight attenuates residual corrections for poorly supported queries, while a study-specific areal beam-power-density criterion withholds predictions outside the adopted conduction envelope. Conformal intervals are evaluated on the retained physics-valid set, and SHAP and Sobol analyses assess residual sensitivity. Under a controlled leave-one-defocus-out evaluation, the physics anchor achieved R^2 = 0.778, against -0.001 for the black-box model and 0.750 for the gated hybrid. Under leave-one-group-out cross-validation, the gated hybrid reached R^2 = 0.592 against 0.538 for the black-box model. Retained-set coverage was 92.9% at a mean full width of 3.65 multiples of a uniform distribution (MUD) under grouped cross-validation and 100% at a width of 3.21 MUD under transfer to a withheld +80 mm defocus regime. An illustrative mapping produced a retained BD elastic-modulus span of 127-187 GPa. On nine conditions from a separately built sample set, the framework withheld three, attenuated three, and matched the measured ordering for the rest. Separating data applicability, physics validity, and predictive uncertainty into distinct decisions lets the framework transfer where an unconstrained model does not, and withhold predictions where no model class performs adequately.

AI.tldr: A two-stage physics-based framework predicts <001> || BD texture in LPBF Inconel 718, combining empirical physics with ML residuals while filtering physically invalid predictions through melt pool geometry criteria.
AI.motivation: Black-box models fail under distribution shift and cannot distinguish weak data support from physical invalidity. Reliable texture prediction is critical for linking process conditions to anisotropic material response in laser powder bed fusion.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: Stage 1 maps process variables to melting mode and melt pool geometry; Stage 2 combines empirical physics model with random-forest residual model, using k-nearest-neighbor weighting to attenuate corrections for poorly supported queries. An areal beam-power-density criterion withholds predictions outside the conduction envelope. Conformal intervals evaluated on retained physics-valid set; SHAP and Sobol analyses assess residual sensitivity.
AI.result: Under leave-one-defocus-out: physics anchor R²=0.778 vs black-box -0.001 vs gated hybrid 0.750. Under leave-one-group-out: gated hybrid R²=0.592 vs black-box 0.538. Retained-set coverage 92.9% at 3.65 MUD (grouped CV), 100% at 3.21 MUD (transfer to +80mm defocus). BD elastic-modulus span 127-187 GPa. On nine test conditions: withheld 3, attenuated 3, matched ordering for rest.
AI.conclusion: Separating data applicability, physics validity, and predictive uncertainty into distinct decisions enables transfer learning where unconstrained models fail, and withholds predictions where no model class performs adequately. The framework achieves R²=0.778 with physics anchor and successfully transfers across defocus regimes while maintaining physical validity.

title: Copy What Is Seen, Generate What Is Not: Training-Free Anomaly-Aware Video Restoration
summary: A surveillance system that detects an anomaly often has to repair the footage as well, yet the two tasks are studied in isolation: training-free anomaly detectors stop at a score or a label, while training-free video editing answers to a user prompt rather than to a detector. This paper proposes AVR (Anomaly-aware Video Restoration), which closes that gap with frozen pretrained models alone and generates content only where the clip offers no evidence to copy. Motion evidence first gates open-vocabulary proposals into spatio-temporal masks. A background prior computed from the clip then fills every pixel the anomaly ever uncovers, leaving diffusion to synthesize only what no frame showed, and a frozen verifier decides per clip whether to trust a classical, a prior-anchored, or a background-conditioned restorer. Extensive experiments on three surveillance datasets, under both full-reference anomaly injection and real anomalies, show that AVR leads full-frame fidelity under oracle masks, matches three trained video inpainters inside the edited region, and outperforms a detect-then-generate pipeline on the masks it produces itself, while suppressing both the residual anomaly and the flicker of free diffusion.

AI.tldr: AVR (Anomaly-aware Video Restoration) is a novel framework that bridges anomaly detection and video restoration using frozen pretrained models. It uses motion evidence to create spatio-temporal masks, fills uncovered pixels with a background prior, and employs diffusion to synthesize only unobserved content, with a verifier selecting the best restoration approach.
AI.motivation: The gap between anomaly detection and video restoration tasks - existing methods study them in isolation: training-free anomaly detectors only output scores/labels, while training-free video editing responds to user prompts rather than detector outputs. This paper aims to close this gap.
AI.method: 1) Motion evidence gates open-vocabulary proposals into spatio-temporal masks. 2) Background prior computed from clip fills every pixel the anomaly uncovers. 3) Diffusion synthesizes only what no frame showed. 4) Frozen verifier decides per clip whether to use classical, prior-anchored, or background-conditioned restorer.
AI.result: AVR leads full-frame fidelity under oracle masks, matches three trained video inpainters inside the edited region, and outperforms a detect-then-generate pipeline on self-produced masks, while suppressing both residual anomaly and flicker of free diffusion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AVR framework successfully bridges anomaly detection and video restoration for surveillance systems, achieving superior performance through the innovative use of frozen pretrained models, background priors, and an adaptive verifier mechanism.

title: Preventing Model Collapse: A Fisher-Rao Perspective on the Dynamics of Training with Synthetic Data
comment: 8 pages. Extended version of the paper accepted for presentation at the 2026 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC). This version contains the full proofs of the auxiliary lemmas, omitted from the conference version for space
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now routinely trained using synthetic data, since high-quality human data has been exhausted by the ever increasing needs of larger and larger models. However, recursive training on synthetic data frequently induces model collapse, a degenerative feedback loop where models progressively forget the true underlying data distribution. Training on a mixture of synthetic and fresh human data is a logical countermeasure and can prevent model collapse. However, it is an open question as to what is the exact minimum required ratio of human-to-synthetic data to maintain training stability. In this paper, we establish rigorous theoretical guarantees on the minimum rate of human data required to prevent model collapse. Although previous work established a formal lower bound for this ratio, such bound can be vacuous for very high dimensions, as the analysis relies on the usual Euclidean metric in R^n and is not adapted to the space of categorical probability distributions. Instead, in this paper we explicitly leverage the information-geometric structure of the probability simplex by analyzing the dynamics of the process under the Fisher-Rao metric. We derive quantitative contraction and invariance bounds that are stable and do not become trivial as the dimensions increase. Thus, we show that the effective required data ratio to prevent model collapse is different than previously implied.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses model collapse in LLMs trained on synthetic data by deriving the minimum human-to-synthetic data ratio needed to prevent this degeneration. The key innovation is using Fisher-Rao metric instead of Euclidean metric to get non-trivial bounds in high dimensions.
AI.motivation: Recursive training on synthetic data causes model collapse (progressive forgetting of true data distribution). While mixing human data with synthetic data prevents collapse, the minimum required ratio of human-to-synthetic data was unknown. Previous theoretical bounds became vacuous in high dimensions due to using Euclidean metric.
AI.method: The paper uses information-geometric analysis by employing the Fisher-Rao metric on the probability simplex, rather than the usual Euclidean metric in R^n. This allows for deriving quantitative contraction and invariance bounds that remain stable across dimensions.
AI.result: The paper establishes rigorous theoretical guarantees on the minimum rate of human data required to prevent model collapse. The derived bounds are non-trivial and stable even for very high dimensions, showing the effective required data ratio differs from previous implications.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly leveraging the information-geometric structure of the probability simplex, the paper provides practical guidance on human-to-synthetic data ratios that can prevent model collapse in LLM training, with bounds that scale properly with dimensionality.

title: Decodable but Misrouted: Sparse Features Uncover a Readout Gap in Vision-Language Models for Harmful Meme Detection
summary: When a large vision-language model misclassifies a harmful meme, the failure may reflect missing internal evidence or an inability to route represented evidence to its output. We distinguish these cases in Gemma-3 and Qwen3.5 using sparse autoencoders, role-conditioned probes, causal interventions, and recovery experiments across six harmful content benchmarks, with additional Spanish and Hindi-English code-mixed evaluations. Sparse readouts outperform native prediction on all six primary binary tasks: Qwen averages $0.740$ versus $0.432$ native macro-F1, while residual reconstruction reaches $0.486$, whereas Gemma improves from $0.532$ to $0.714$. These differences reflect supervised accessibility rather than a pre-existing, native decision rule, and the most influential token role depends on the task. Under the evaluated score scales, Qwen silent-feature ablation is $24-63$ times more probe-sensitive, whereas routed-feature patching on literal yes/no tasks is $16-140$ times more output-sensitive. Calibration-only routing recovers $93.3$% of the mean gap, and probe-distilled LoRA improves native predictions, although shared multi-task adaptation causes negative transfer. A case study of Gemma-3-12B on Facebook Hateful Memes finds a distributed rank-32 image-prompt interaction, reaching $0.756$ versus $0.685$ native macro-F1. Robustness controls show that the signal extends beyond English, is not explained solely by accompanying OCR, and depends on paired visual evidence. Thus, routing, rather than representation alone, is a recurring bottleneck in harmful meme classification.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why large vision-language models fail to classify harmful memes, distinguishing between two failure modes: missing internal evidence vs. inability to route represented evidence to output. Using sparse autoencoders, causal interventions, and probe-based methods on Gemma-3 and Qwen3.5 across six harmful content benchmarks, the authors find that routing (not representation) is the primary bottleneck, with sparse readouts significantly outperforming native predictions.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand the mechanistic reasons behind vision-language model failures in harmful meme classification. The key insight is that models may contain relevant internal representations but fail to properly route this evidence to their outputs - a distinction with important implications for model improvement.
AI.method: The study employs multiple mechanistic analysis methods: (1) sparse autoencoders to decompose internal representations, (2) role-conditioned probes to assess feature accessibility at different token positions, (3) causal interventions including silent-feature ablation and routed-feature patching, and (4) recovery experiments using calibration-only routing and probe-distilled LoRA. Evaluations span six harmful content benchmarks with additional multilingual (Spanish, Hindi-English code-mixed) robustness controls.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Sparse readouts outperform native prediction on all six tasks - Qwen achieves 0.740 vs 0.432 native macro-F1, while Gemma improves from 0.532 to 0.714; (2) Residual reconstruction reaches 0.486 macro-F1; (3) Qwen's silent-feature ablation is 24-63 times more probe-sensitive; (4) Routed-feature patching on literal yes/no tasks is 16-140 times more output-sensitive; (5) Calibration-only routing recovers 93.3% of the mean gap; (6) A case study on Facebook Hateful Memes finds distributed rank-32 image-prompt interaction reaching 0.756 vs 0.685 native macro-F1; (7) Signal extends beyond English and beyond OCR-based explanations.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that routing, rather than representation alone, is the recurring bottleneck in harmful meme classification for vision-language models. The most influential token role depends on the specific task. Additionally, shared multi-task adaptation causes negative transfer, while probe-distilled LoRA improves native predictions. These findings suggest future work should focus on improving evidence routing mechanisms rather than solely on representation learning.

title: NeuroECG: ECGFounder-Based Deep ECG Representation for EEG-Free Neurological Prognostication After Cardiac Arrest
summary: Neurological prognostication after cardiac arrest commonly relies on electroencephalography (EEG). However, EEG demands high clinical resources. Bedside electrocardiography (ECG) is standard and low-cost. Yet, its value for predicting neurological outcomes remains underexplored. In this study, we propose NeuroECG, an ECGFounder-based deep representation framework for EEG-free auxiliary prognostication. NeuroECG adapts a pretrained ECG foundation model via task-specific fine-tuning. We implement a gradual unfreezing strategy on single-channel bedside monitoring ECG. Multiple ECG segments per patient are encoded into segment-level deep features. These embeddings are aggregated via quantile pooling ($q = 0.24$) and compressed using principal component analysis (PCA). Experiments on 412 ECG-available patients from the multicenter I-CARE database show that the adapted ECGFounder backbone achieves the best performance among ECG-only backbone baselines, with a test AUROC of 0.7333. We further combine the learned deep ECG representation with static clinical covariates. The proposed NeuroECG model achieves a test AUROC of 0.8077 and an AUPRC of 0.8970. These results support deep bedside ECG representations as a useful source of auxiliary prognostic information. Their integration with static clinical covariates improves prediction in an EEG-free setting. The source code is available at https://github.com/goddream66/NeuroECG_

AI.tldr: NeuroECG is a deep learning framework that uses bedside ECG data to predict neurological outcomes after cardiac arrest, bypassing the need for EEG. It adapts a pretrained ECG foundation model (ECGFounder) through fine-tuning, achieving AUROC of 0.8077 when combined with clinical covariates.
AI.motivation: Current neurological prognostication after cardiac arrest relies on EEG, which requires high clinical resources. Bedside ECG is standard and low-cost but underutilized for this purpose. This study aims to develop an EEG-free auxiliary prognostic tool using ECG data.
AI.method: NeuroECG adapts a pretrained ECG foundation model (ECGFounder) via task-specific fine-tuning with gradual unfreezing on single-channel bedside monitoring ECG. Multiple ECG segments per patient are encoded into segment-level deep features, aggregated using quantile pooling (q=0.24), and compressed via PCA. The learned deep ECG representation is combined with static clinical covariates.
AI.result: On 412 patients from the multicenter I-CARE database, the adapted ECGFounder backbone achieved test AUROC of 0.7333 (best among ECG-only baselines). When combined with clinical covariates, NeuroECG achieved test AUROC of 0.8077 and AUPRC of 0.8970.
AI.conclusion: Deep bedside ECG representations can serve as a useful source of auxiliary prognostic information for neurological outcomes after cardiac arrest. Integration with static clinical covariates significantly improves prediction in an EEG-free setting, offering a low-cost alternative to EEG-based prognostication.

title: NormLift: From Lifted Features To Semantic Reliability In 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Training-free weighted aggregation is widely used to lift 2D semantic features onto 3D Gaussians for open-vocabulary scene understanding, yet its theoretical role remains insufficiently understood. Existing analyses typically justify this operation from the rendering side, treating Gaussian features as linearly composable Euclidean variables for reconstructing 2D feature maps. However, this view does not match downstream 3D usage, where each Gaussian is often queried independently in a cosine-based embedding space. We revisit feature lifting from the 3D side and formulate per-Gaussian assignment as a cosine alignment problem on the CLIP unit sphere. Under this objective, the L2-normalized semantic back-projected feature emerges as the closed-form solution, providing a complementary interpretation of the standard lifting rule from the perspective of per-Gaussian semantic assignment. The same formulation further yields a norm decomposition into intra-view and inter-view consistency, suggesting that feature magnitude itself can serve as a semantic reliability signal. Calibrated by effective multi-view support, this reliability score guides a mode-voting refinement that preserves CLIP feature validity by avoiding linear averaging. Experiments on open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation show that NormLift is an efficient, training-free framework that achieves strong performance across evaluation protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NormLift, a training-free framework for lifting 2D semantic features onto 3D Gaussians for open-vocabulary scene understanding. It reinterprets the standard lifting operation as a cosine alignment problem on the CLIP unit sphere, where L2-normalized semantic features emerge as the closed-form solution. The method uses feature magnitude as a semantic reliability signal and applies mode-voting refinement to preserve CLIP feature validity.
AI.motivation: Existing analyses justify feature lifting from the rendering side (treating Gaussian features as linearly composable for 2D reconstruction), but this doesn't match downstream 3D usage where each Gaussian is queried independently in a cosine-based embedding space. The theoretical role of training-free weighted aggregation remains insufficiently understood.
AI.method: The authors formulate per-Gaussian assignment as a cosine alignment problem on the CLIP unit sphere. Under this objective, the L2-normalized semantic back-projected feature emerges as the closed-form solution. This formulation yields a norm decomposition into intra-view and inter-view consistency, where feature magnitude serves as a semantic reliability signal. This reliability score is calibrated by effective multi-view support and guides a mode-voting refinement that preserves CLIP feature validity by avoiding linear averaging.
AI.result: NormLift achieves strong performance across evaluation protocols for open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation, while being an efficient training-free framework.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complementary interpretation of standard feature lifting from the perspective of per-Gaussian semantic assignment, demonstrating that feature magnitude itself can serve as a semantic reliability signal. The proposed NormLift framework offers an efficient, training-free solution that preserves CLIP feature validity through mode-voting refinement.

title: Higher-order pruning of experts in mixture-of-experts language models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models suffer from large parameter counts, which create a significant memory bottleneck. Expert pruning is the most direct approach for reducing this parameter count, yet existing methods make pruning decisions for each expert independently, and assume experts' contributions are purely additive. In reality, expert usage in MoEs is inherently cooperative. We derive HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order pruning objective which provably minimizes an upper bound on the error resulting from pruning. We show that REAP (a state-of-the-art first-order pruning method) is a special case of HOPE where interaction terms are ignored. Across three frontier MoE models (up to 122B parameters), two distinct calibration sets, and multiple benchmarks (including math, instruction following, coding, and an agentic suite), we demonstrate that HOPE produces better pruning decisions than existing methods, and its advantage is most pronounced at high pruning rates and on challenging agentic workloads. At 50% pruning, HOPE outperforms all baselines and achieves an average rank of 1.58 out of 5 methods (versus 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP), with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding. Over all conditions, HOPE again achieves the best average rank and surpasses every other method in the majority of head-to-head comparisons. By preserving cooperative expert structure that first-order methods ignore, HOPE enables aggressive compression with minimal degradation, particularly on complex tasks where diverse expert combinations are invoked over long sequences.

AI.tldr: HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts) is a second-order pruning method for MoE language models that preserves cooperative expert interactions, outperforming first-order methods like REAP, especially at high pruning rates (50%) and on agentic workloads with up to +6.1% gains.
AI.motivation: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models suffer from large parameter counts creating memory bottlenecks. Existing expert pruning methods make decisions for each expert independently and assume contributions are purely additive, ignoring the inherently cooperative nature of expert usage in MoEs.
AI.method: HOPE derives a second-order pruning objective that provably minimizes an upper bound on the error from pruning, capturing expert interaction terms. REAP (state-of-the-art first-order method) is shown to be a special case of HOPE when interaction terms are ignored.
AI.result: At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves average rank 1.58 vs 2.42 for REAP (next-best), with gains up to +6.1% on agentic coding. HOPE outperforms all baselines across 3 frontier MoE models (up to 122B parameters), two calibration sets, and multiple benchmarks (math, instruction following, coding, agentic suite). Advantages are most pronounced at high pruning rates and on challenging agentic workloads.
AI.conclusion: By preserving cooperative expert structure that first-order methods ignore, HOPE enables aggressive compression with minimal degradation, particularly on complex tasks where diverse expert combinations are invoked over long sequences.

title: PhysVGGT: Feed-Forward Dense Physical Property Estimation from A Single Image
summary: Physical properties, such as friction, hardness, stiffness, and density, govern how robots should grasp, manipulate and interact with objects, yet estimating these properties from RGB images remains challenging. Existing methods typically employ per-object reconstruction augmented with physical properties or directly query vision-language models at test time, which results in substantial computational overhead that limits their applicability. In this work, we present PhysVGGT, a feed-forward model that predicts dense maps of friction coefficient, Shore hardness, Young's modulus, and density, together with object-level mass, from a single RGB image in one forward pass. The key idea of PhysVGGT is to formulate physical property estimation as a dense per-pixel prediction problem and employ a visual geometry transformer to extract geometry-aware tokens from the input image followed by a dense prediction branch for estimating local physical properties and a global prediction branch for estimating object-level mass. In addition, we introduce a scalable pseudo-label generation pipeline that enables large-scale weakly supervised training for dense physical property prediction, substantially reducing the need for expensive direct physical measurements. Extensive experiments show that PhysVGGT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ABO-500 dataset and generalizes effectively to the out-of-distribution NeRF2Physics dataset. Moreover, PhysVGGT eliminates the need for per-object reconstruction and test-time optimization, achieving an inference latency of only 0.13s per image, making it $27\times$ faster than the previous state of the art.

AI.tldr: PhysVGGT is a feed-forward model that predicts dense physical property maps (friction, hardness, Young's modulus, density) and object-level mass from a single RGB image in one forward pass, using a visual geometry transformer architecture with dense and global prediction branches, achieving 27x speedup over prior work.
AI.motivation: Physical properties (friction, hardness, stiffness, density) are essential for robot grasping and manipulation, but estimating these properties from RGB images remains challenging. Existing methods require per-object reconstruction or test-time vision-language model queries, creating substantial computational overhead that limits practical applicability.
AI.method: The method proposes formulating physical property estimation as a dense per-pixel prediction problem. It uses a visual geometry transformer (VGT) to extract geometry-aware tokens from the input image, followed by two prediction branches: (1) a dense prediction branch for estimating local physical properties per pixel, and (2) a global prediction branch for estimating object-level mass. A scalable pseudo-label generation pipeline enables large-scale weakly supervised training, reducing the need for expensive direct physical measurements.
AI.result: PhysVGGT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ABO-500 dataset and generalizes effectively to the out-of-distribution NeRF2Physics dataset. It eliminates the need for per-object reconstruction and test-time optimization, achieving an inference latency of only 0.13s per image, making it 27× faster than the previous state of the art.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PhysVGGT successfully demonstrates that physical properties can be predicted efficiently from a single RGB image using a feed-forward architecture. The dense prediction formulation combined with the visual geometry transformer enables accurate and fast inference, potentially enabling real-time robotic manipulation tasks that require physical property estimation.

title: StableEval Arena: A Cost-Aware Agentic Benchmark for Stablecoin Price Stability Prediction
summary: We introduce StableEval Arena, a cost-aware benchmark framework for evaluating agentic AI systems on stablecoin peg-risk prediction. StableEval Arena evaluates LLM-backed agentic systems on diagnosing peg stress and forecasting deviations from the one-dollar peg over a hidden seven-day horizon, using leakage-safe historical replay with exchange price-volume data and market-context features. We report two complementary experiment blocks: a 120-case stress-enriched validation block and a 507-case natural-distribution full-arena evaluation block. Across six LLM-backed agent configurations and baselines, StableEval Arena measures prediction quality, calibrated-label behavior, structured-output reliability, latency, token consumption, and estimated inference cost. Rather than ranking agents by accuracy alone, the framework treats trustworthiness as a joint property of forecast quality, operational reliability, and computational cost. The results show a gap between protocol-following reliability and financial-risk reliability: agents reliably produce valid structured outputs at modest measured cost, but still miss most rare severe-stress and sustained-depeg cases. To support auditing and replication, we release the benchmark dataset on Hugging Face and the source code on GitHub.

AI.tldr: StableEval Arena is a cost-aware benchmark framework for evaluating LLM-backed agentic AI systems on stablecoin peg-risk prediction. It evaluates systems on diagnosing peg stress and forecasting 7-day deviations from the $1 peg using leakage-safe historical replay. The framework was tested on 120 stress-enriched and 507 natural-distribution cases across six agent configurations, measuring prediction quality, output reliability, latency, token consumption, and cost.
AI.motivation: There is a need to evaluate agentic AI systems on stablecoin peg-risk prediction - specifically diagnosing peg stress and forecasting deviations from the one-dollar peg over a hidden seven-day horizon. Existing evaluations likely lack cost-awareness and don't properly assess the trustworthiness of such systems in financial risk contexts.
AI.method: StableEval Arena uses leakage-safe historical replay with exchange price-volume data and market-context features. It evaluates six LLM-backed agent configurations and baselines across two experiment blocks: a 120-case stress-enriched validation block and a 507-case natural-distribution full-arena evaluation block. The framework measures prediction quality, calibrated-label behavior, structured-output reliability, latency, token consumption, and estimated inference cost.
AI.result: Results reveal a gap between protocol-following reliability and financial-risk reliability: agents reliably produce valid structured outputs at modest cost, but still miss most rare severe-stress and sustained-depeg cases. The framework treats trustworthiness as a joint property of forecast quality, operational reliability, and computational cost.
AI.conclusion: StableEval Arena provides a comprehensive cost-aware evaluation framework for stablecoin peg-risk prediction. While agents demonstrate reliable structured output generation at reasonable cost, they struggle to detect rare but critical severe-stress and sustained-depeg events, highlighting a significant limitation in financial-risk reliability that needs addressing.

title: Dose-Aware Cold Diffusion with Physics Consistency for Generalizable Low-Dose CT Reconstruction
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN 2026)
summary: Reducing radiation dose in computed tomography significantly degrades image quality and poses challenges for accurate and clinically reliable reconstruction. While recent approaches have shown promise for low-dose CT, they often struggle to generalize across continuous and previously unseen dose levels, leading to artifacts and loss of anatomical detail. To address these limitations, we propose Dose-Aware Cold Diffusion (DACD), a physics-consistent reconstruction framework that explicitly models radiation dose as a continuous latent factor within a cold diffusion process. The proposed DACD framework integrates image-based dose-aware perception, multi-scale structural prior extraction, and dose-calibrated step allocation to adaptively guide the denoising trajectory. In addition, an iterative forward-backprojection correction is incorporated into the reverse refinement process to enforce projection-domain data consistency. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks, including Mayo-2020, Mayo-2016, and LoDoPaB-CT, demonstrate that DACD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion-based and physics-guided methods in both quantitative accuracy and visual fidelity, particularly under ultra-low-dose conditions. The results show that DACD achieves robust generalization across a continuous range of dose levels, including those unseen during training.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Dose-Aware Cold Diffusion (DACD), a physics-consistent CT reconstruction framework that models radiation dose as a continuous latent factor within a cold diffusion process to handle ultra-low-dose CT imaging across continuous and unseen dose levels.
AI.motivation: Reducing radiation dose in CT significantly degrades image quality, and existing low-dose CT methods struggle to generalize across continuous and previously unseen dose levels, leading to artifacts and loss of anatomical detail.
AI.method: DACD integrates three key components: (1) image-based dose-aware perception for dose modeling, (2) multi-scale structural prior extraction, and (3) dose-calibrated step allocation for adaptive denoising guidance. Additionally, iterative forward-backprojection correction is incorporated into the reverse refinement process to enforce projection-domain data consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks (Mayo-2020, Mayo-2016, LoDoPaB-CT) demonstrate that DACD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion-based and physics-guided methods in both quantitative accuracy and visual fidelity, particularly under ultra-low-dose conditions.
AI.conclusion: DACD achieves robust generalization across a continuous range of dose levels, including those unseen during training, representing a promising advance for clinical low-dose CT reconstruction.

title: Changepoint-Aware World Models: Detecting Dynamics Shifts and Recovering by Forgetting Stale Replay in Model-Based RL
comment: Accepted to the RSS 2026 Workshop on Robot World Models (R-WM)
summary: A robot's learned model of its own dynamics is only valid until those dynamics change: actuators wear, payloads shift, and joints stiffen. A model-based agent that keeps training as if nothing happened adapts slowly, dragged back by a replay buffer full of stale experience. We present Changepoint-Aware World Models (CAWM), a DreamerV3 agent that detects an abrupt dynamics shift from its own internal prediction error, using an online CUSUM test against a rolling baseline that fires only on abrupt change rather than on slow learning drift. It then forgets stale replay, keeping the learned representation while flushing obsolete data. On simulated locomotion under two robot-relevant shifts, doubled gravity and halved actuator gain, CAWM recovers substantially faster than passive retraining. It also beats a strong baseline that respawns a fresh dynamics model on detection, the deep-world-model analogue of model-bank methods. With the response triggered at the shift, CAWM gains +95 to +153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds, while matching that respawn at asymptote. Running the detector in closed loop reproduces this gain on the gravity shift. The benefit holds across both shift types, and is largest when the shift is severe enough that old data is genuinely obsolete.
