title: Automated Dental Caries Segmentation in Panoramic Radiographs Using Dual-Stage Deep Learning
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the Workshop on Machine Learning in Medical Imaging, MLMI 2025, held in conjunction with MICCAI 2025
summary: Early detection of dental caries remains challenging due to limitations in traditional diagnostic methods, particularly for proximal lesions in posterior teeth. Deep learning models show promise for automated caries detection but face scalability constraints due to requirements for large volumes of expertly annotated training data. This study presents a dual-stage deep learning framework combining Faster R-CNN for tooth localization with U-Net for pixel-wise caries segmentation in panoramic radiographs. We developed a systematic transformation pipeline to convert large-scale polygon-annotated datasets into high-resolution binary segmentation masks, enabling pixel-wise supervised learning. The framework was trained using both expert-verified datasets and algorithmically processed labels from 3,000 panoramic images. Our approach achieved robust performance with an IoU of 0.9013, Dice coefficient of 0.9482, Recall of 0.9433, and Precision of 0.9774, demonstrating superior accuracy compared to existing methods while significantly reducing false-positive rates. The dual-stage framework effectively addresses data annotation bottlenecks in dental AI applications and demonstrates potential for scalable, automated caries detection systems that can improve diagnostic consistency and support clinical decision-making.

AI.tldr: This study proposes a dual-stage deep learning framework for automated dental caries detection in panoramic radiographs, combining Faster R-CNN for tooth localization with U-Net for pixel-wise segmentation. The method addresses the challenge of requiring large annotated datasets by using a systematic transformation pipeline and achieves high performance metrics (IoU: 0.9013, Dice: 0.9482).
AI.motivation: Early detection of dental caries is challenging due to limitations in traditional diagnostic methods, particularly for proximal lesions in posterior teeth. Deep learning models show promise but face scalability constraints due to the need for large volumes of expertly annotated training data.
AI.method: Dual-stage deep learning framework: (1) Faster R-CNN for tooth localization, (2) U-Net for pixel-wise caries segmentation. A systematic transformation pipeline converts large-scale polygon-annotated datasets into high-resolution binary segmentation masks. Training used 3,000 panoramic images with both expert-verified and algorithmically processed labels.
AI.result: Achieved robust performance: IoU of 0.9013, Dice coefficient of 0.9482, Recall of 0.9433, and Precision of 0.9774. Demonstrated superior accuracy compared to existing methods with significantly reduced false-positive rates.
AI.conclusion: The dual-stage framework effectively addresses data annotation bottlenecks in dental AI applications and demonstrates potential for scalable, automated caries detection systems that can improve diagnostic consistency and support clinical decision-making.

title: FedGuide: Diffusion Prior Alignment and Value Baseline Guidance for Heterogeneous Federated Reinforcement Learning
summary: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) enables collaborative policy learning across distributed agents with heterogeneous environments. While recent methods based on variance reduction, divergence penalization, and momentum optimization improve FRL under heterogeneous settings, they still primarily synchronize policy or value-network parameters and do not explicitly address distributional mismatch among heterogeneous clients. Therefore, we propose \textbf{FedGuide}, a FRL framework that uses diffusion priors as behavior models to provide personalized data supported distributions for heterogeneous local policy learning. Instead of directly averaging local policies, FedGuide aggregates those diffusion priors through Optimal-Transport Mixture-of-Experts (OT-MoE), preserving heterogeneous behavior modes in distribution space. It further develops a Distribution Correction Estimation (DICE) value baseline to provide low-variance, return-aware guidance for local policy improvement. Experiments across heterogeneous environments show that FedGuide outperforms representative FRL methods in client-average returns, final-round performance, and worst-round robustness, while maintaining stable learning under stronger heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: FedGuide is a Federated Reinforcement Learning framework that uses diffusion priors as behavior models to handle heterogeneous environments. It aggregates these priors via Optimal-Transport Mixture-of-Experts (OT-MoE) and uses a Distribution Correction Estimation (DICE) value baseline for low-variance, return-aware guidance.
AI.motivation: Current FRL methods primarily synchronize policy or value-network parameters but do not explicitly address distributional mismatch among heterogeneous clients. This limits collaborative learning when agents operate in different environments.
AI.method: 1) Use diffusion priors as behavior models to provide personalized data-supported distributions for heterogeneous local policy learning. 2) Aggregate diffusion priors through Optimal-Transport Mixture-of-Experts (OT-MoE) to preserve heterogeneous behavior modes in distribution space. 3) Develop a Distribution Correction Estimation (DICE) value baseline to provide low-variance, return-aware guidance for local policy improvement.
AI.result: FedGuide outperforms representative FRL methods in client-average returns, final-round performance, and worst-round robustness, while maintaining stable learning under stronger heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: FedGuide effectively addresses distributional mismatch in heterogeneous FRL settings by leveraging diffusion-based behavior models and optimal-transport aggregation, achieving superior performance across multiple metrics while maintaining stability under high heterogeneity.

title: KDTwin: Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation for Lightweight Multi-Task Driving Scene Segmentation
summary: Efficient perception models are essential for real-time autonomous driving, where accuracy and computational cost must be carefully balanced. However, applying knowledge distillation to multi-task driving scene segmentation is challenging because drivable-area and lane segmentation exhibit different spatial characteristics and class imbalance. We propose KDTwin, a task-aware distillation framework for lightweight multi-task segmentation networks. The proposed method performs distillation at both the shared encoder and task-specific decoders. Encoder-level pairwise distillation transfers spatial relational knowledge to enhance the student's shared representation. For the decoders, we use a weighted loss for drivable-area segmentation and a boundary-aware loss for lane segmentation, enabling task-adaptive knowledge transfer without increasing inference complexity. Experiments on BDD100K show consistent improvements across the evaluated CNN-based and Transformer-based student models without increasing inference-time parameters or FLOPs. The results show that designing distillation objectives according to task-specific characteristics can effectively enhance multi-task segmentation performance for autonomous driving. The source code is available at https://github.com/chequanghuy/KDTwin.

AI.tldr: KDTwin is a task-aware knowledge distillation framework for lightweight multi-task segmentation networks in autonomous driving. It performs distillation at both the shared encoder and task-specific decoders, using pairwise spatial relational knowledge transfer and task-adaptive losses (weighted loss for drivable-area and boundary-aware loss for lane segmentation). Experiments on BDD100K show consistent improvements across CNN-based and Transformer-based student models without increasing inference complexity.
AI.motivation: Efficient perception models are essential for real-time autonomous driving, but applying knowledge distillation to multi-task driving scene segmentation is challenging due to different spatial characteristics and class imbalance between tasks like drivable-area and lane segmentation.
AI.method: The proposed KDTwin framework performs distillation at two levels: (1) Encoder-level pairwise distillation that transfers spatial relational knowledge to enhance the student's shared representation; (2) Task-specific decoder distillation using a weighted loss for drivable-area segmentation and a boundary-aware loss for lane segmentation, enabling task-adaptive knowledge transfer without increasing inference complexity.
AI.result: Experiments on BDD100K show consistent improvements across evaluated CNN-based and Transformer-based student models without increasing inference-time parameters or FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Designing distillation objectives according to task-specific characteristics can effectively enhance multi-task segmentation performance for autonomous driving. The source code is available at https://github.com/chequanghuy/KDTwin.

title: The Automaton Underneath: The Additive Input Pathway Is a Parasitic Attractor for State Tracking in Householder Linear RNN
summary: Linear RNNs with input-dependent Householder-product transitions (DeltaNet/DeltaProduct-class) can provably represent hard state-tracking automata, yet trained models fail to length-generalize -- a gap recent work attributes to optimization, without a causal account. We give one, in a pre-registered, within-architecture causal ablation: the same model with one term deleted -- the additive input injection $b_t = W_b e_t$. With $b_t$, models fit length 32 and collapse out-of-distribution on parity, $S_4$, $A_5$, and non-solvable $S_5$ word problems (0.20 at position 512 on $S_5$). Without it -- input acting only through the orthogonal transitions -- the same architecture learns the exact automaton: median accuracy 1.00 at 16x the training length, at every width admitted by a representation law we state and test: the minimal number of Householder factors per token equals the maximal reflection length of the task's generators in the format-pinned representation (parity 1, $S_4$ 3, $A_5$ and $S_5$ 4); below it, nothing fits. The contrast with DeltaProduct's $S_4$/$A_5$ at $n_h{=}2$ (group-element classification, $SO(3)$ realization) shows the law is representation-relative: task format is a hidden variable in state-tracking benchmarks. Two pre-registered arms locate the mechanism. (i) Initialized at a verified-exact solution with $W_b{=}0$, Adam grows the additive path and pulls the model off the exact solution; $-b$ controls stay at 1.00. (ii) Our registered prediction that the fit routes through $b_t$ fired its kill criterion: all 49 fitting seeds retain in-domain fit under $W_b{:=}0$ -- and at law-minimal width, zeroing $W_b$ at inference restores exact generalization (parity 5/5, $S_5$ 5/5, $S_4$ 4/5, $A_5$ 4/5). The additive pathway is parasitic: it destabilizes, then conceals, a correctly learned automaton. All 202 runs pre-registered; all numbers regenerate from artifacts.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and solves the length generalization gap in linear RNNs (DeltaNet/DeltaProduct-class). The authors discover that an "additive input injection" term (b_t = W_b e_t) causes models to fail on out-of-distribution tasks. By removing this term (letting input act only through orthogonal transitions), the same architecture achieves exact generalization across multiple group-theoretic benchmarks (parity, S4, A5, S5). They also establish a "representation law" linking the minimal number of Householder factors to the maximal reflection length of task generators.
AI.motivation: The gap between theoretical capability and empirical length generalization in linear RNNs was previously attributed to optimization issues without a causal explanation. This work provides a causal account through a pre-registered ablation study, identifying the additive input injection term as the root cause of failure.
AI.method: The authors conducted a pre-registered, within-architecture causal ablation study. They compared model performance with and without the additive input injection term (b_t). They tested on multiple formal language tasks (parity, S4, A5, S5 word problems) across varying sequence lengths. They also formulated and verified a "representation law" relating the minimal number of Householder factors to the task's maximal reflection length. Two experimental arms were conducted: (i) starting from a verified-exact solution with W_b=0 and observing Adam's optimization behavior, and (ii) testing predictions about the mechanism by zeroing W_b at inference time.
AI.result: With b_t: models fit length 32 but collapse out-of-distribution (0.20 accuracy at position 512 on S5). Without b_t: models achieve median accuracy 1.00 at 16x training length across all tested widths. The representation law holds: parity requires 1 Householder factor, S4 requires 3, A5 and S5 require 4. When initialized at an exact solution with W_b=0, Adam's optimization grows the additive path and pulls the model off the exact solution, while controls with -b stay at 1.00. Zeroing W_b at inference restores exact generalization (parity 5/5, S5 5/5, S4 4/5, A5 4/5). All 202 runs were pre-registered.
AI.conclusion: The additive input injection pathway is "parasitic" - it destabilizes and conceals a correctly learned automaton. Length generalization failure is not fundamentally an optimization issue but is caused by this specific architectural component. The representation law provides a theoretical foundation for understanding what width is needed for different state-tracking tasks. The paper demonstrates that the exact automaton can be learned and generalizes when the problematic pathway is removed, even after training with it.

title: LaSeD: Label-Semantic Self-Distillation for Visual-Only Surgical Phase Recognition
summary: Surgical phase recognition maps each video frame to a clinically meaningful workflow phase, supporting context-aware assistance, documentation, and postoperative analysis. Most methods treat phase annotations only as class IDs, whereas recent surgical vision-language models often require additional video--text data, captions, or instruction tuning. We propose \emph{LaSeD}, a label-semantic self-distillation framework that uses phase names as privileged training-time context while retaining visual-only deployment without a ground-truth phase-name hint. LaSeD initializes a frozen teacher and a student from the same pretrained VLM checkpoint. The teacher receives the frame, a fixed task prompt, and the ground-truth phase-name hint; the student receives the same frame and prompt without the hint, and only its visual encoder is optimized. Training combines hard phase-token supervision with feature-level distillation from cached teacher representations. At inference, the teacher and hint are removed, and the student predicts one of the seven Cholec80 phases through constrained digit-token logits without an additional classifier head. On the Cholec80 evaluation split, LaSeD achieves 86.20\% accuracy, 77.75\% macro recall, 78.13\% macro precision, and 64.15\% macro Jaccard. Under the identical protocol, it improves a visual-only Qwen3-VL-4B baseline by 9.45, 9.42, 11.93, and 12.22 percentage points, respectively. Visual-only means that the image is the only sample-specific inference input, while all frames share the same fixed task prompt. These results suggest that phase names provide a useful low-cost signal for adapting VLMs to surgical workflow analysis. (The code will be published soon.)

AI.tldr: LaSeD is a label-semantic self-distillation framework for surgical phase recognition that uses phase names as privileged training-time context while enabling visual-only deployment. It achieves 86.20% accuracy on Cholec80, improving a Qwen3-VL-4B baseline by 9.45 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Current methods treat phase annotations only as class IDs, while vision-language models require additional text data or captions. The paper aims to leverage phase names as low-cost training signals while maintaining visual-only inference for practical deployment.
AI.method: LaSeD initializes a frozen teacher and student from the same pretrained VLM checkpoint. The teacher receives frame + task prompt + ground-truth phase-name hint, while the student receives frame + prompt without hint. Training combines hard phase-token supervision with feature-level distillation from cached teacher representations. Inference uses constrained digit-token logits without an additional classifier head.
AI.result: On Cholec80 evaluation split: 86.20% accuracy, 77.75% macro recall, 78.13% macro precision, 64.15% macro Jaccard. This improves the visual-only Qwen3-VL-4B baseline by 9.45, 9.42, 11.93, and 12.22 percentage points respectively.
AI.conclusion: Phase names provide a useful low-cost signal for adapting VLMs to surgical workflow analysis. The self-distillation approach effectively transfers semantic knowledge from the teacher (with phase-name hints) to the student (visual-only), achieving strong performance without requiring additional text data at inference time.

title: One Axis, No Brake: Self-Knowledge Limits the Filtering of Harmful Peer Conformity in LLMs
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are expected to be more reliable because agents can catch each other's mistakes. But peer pressure cuts both ways: the same correction that fixes a wrong answer can overturn a right one. The tempting safeguard is a brake that keeps the beneficial revisions and blocks the harmful ones. We show this brake is hard to build, for a simple reason: a revision is harmful exactly when the original answer was right, so deciding whether to block it is the same as knowing whether the model was already correct. This turns the open-ended hunt for a brake into one measurable quantity, the model's self-knowledge: any brake built from a deploy-time signal is a correctness probe in disguise, and self-knowledge is far from perfect (AUROC $\approx 0.64$--$0.89$ across six model families). We call this ceiling the wall. Even white-box steering of the model's own correctness direction does not breach it: it changes how often the model revises, but harmful and beneficial revisions move together. At population scale the wall becomes the cliff: when most agents start wrong, debate amplifies the shared mistake into a confident, wrong consensus. In our multiple-choice societies, more agents, more model diversity, and a stronger member do not fix it. What helps is adding information before the revision, not filtering after it. Local agreement is not global correctness.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems face a fundamental limitation called "the wall": while agents can catch each other's mistakes, they can also overturn correct answers. Building a "brake" to filter harmful revisions is impossible because harmful revisions occur precisely when the original answer was right, making the filtering problem equivalent to already knowing the correct answer. Self-knowledge as a correctness probe achieves only AUROC 0.64-0.89, and even white-box steering cannot breach this ceiling. At scale, this becomes "the cliff" where wrong consensus amplifies. The solution is adding information before revision, not filtering after.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems are expected to be more reliable through peer correction, but this mechanism can both fix wrong answers and overturn correct ones. The authors investigate whether a "brake" can be built to allow beneficial revisions while blocking harmful ones.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation across six model families, measuring self-knowledge as a correctness probe (AUROC), testing white-box steering, and simulating population-scale behavior with multiple-choice societies.
AI.result: The wall: any brake built from deploy-time signals is a correctness probe in disguise, and self-knowledge is far from perfect (AUROC ≈ 0.64–0.89). White-box steering changes revision rates but beneficial and harmful revisions move together. At population scale, more agents, diversity, or stronger members amplify wrong consensus into confident, wrong answers (the cliff).
AI.conclusion: Local agreement does not equal global correctness. Adding information before revision (not filtering after) is the only solution that works. The fundamental limitation is that distinguishing harmful from beneficial revisions requires knowing the ground truth, which is precisely what the system lacks.

title: Capability Emergence Can Be Forecast: Per-Seed, In Advance, With Calibrated Intervals, Certified False Alarms, and a Blind Pre-Registered Gate
summary: Emergent capabilities are widely treated as unpredictable: loss improves smoothly while abilities appear abruptly. Prior work offers early-warning indicators but never scores them as forecasts: no lead time at controlled false-alarm rate, no calibration, no negatives, no blind tests. We supply that discipline and show that, in grokking model systems and small language models, emergence timing is forecastable per run, in advance, with calibrated uncertainty. Across 30 transformers at identical configuration, the formation time of the previous-token head forecasts each seed's induction-head emergence at Spearman rho=0.977 with median lead 975 steps (~15% of training); a best-case loss rule ties the ranking with 50-step lead (a nowcast). Conformal intervals covered 15/15 held-out seeds, and the frozen rule passed blind pre-registered gates on TWO never-seen configurations (10/10 and 9/10 coverage). A trap-language rung then attacked our own rule as pre-registered: where previous-token context pays for the task itself, the bare precursor false-alarms on 10/10 capability-blocked runs, while the mechanism-composed conjunction is certified in both language classes (0 false alarms) and times emergence at rho=1.000. Finally, a gap-origin study broke the fixed offset (both lr and batch move the gap ~2.3x; no external clock owns it) and revealed the law beneath: across 80 valid-anchor runs the anchor fires at 0.843 of time-to-emergence -- t_event ~= 1.19 x t_anchor -- and this multiplicative rule passed its own blind gate (5/5) at a third unseen configuration. False alarms are certified against 33 manufactured negatives. The precursor leads across 3 public model families (Pythia, OLMo, OLMo-2; 7 suites), with OLMo-2 at 1B tokens showing precursor formed, capability absent. Four pre-registered kill criteria fired and are reported. Every freeze precedes its data in a public commit chain.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that previously considered "unpredictable" emergent capabilities in AI models can be forecasted with calibrated uncertainty. The authors show that formation of a "previous-token head" reliably predicts emergence of "induction-head" capabilities across multiple model families, with Spearman correlation of 0.977 and median lead of 975 training steps. They validate this through blind tests, conformal prediction intervals, and a "trap-language" experiment designed to false-alarm their own predictor.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a fundamental limitation in understanding AI emergence: emergent capabilities have been treated as inherently unpredictable, appearing abruptly without warning. Prior work identified early-warning indicators but never rigorously scored them as forecasts with lead time, calibration, or blind testing. The authors seek to establish a disciplined forecasting framework for capability emergence.
AI.method: The authors employed multiple rigorous methodologies: (1) Correlational analysis across 30 transformers at identical configuration using Spearman rho; (2) Conformal prediction intervals for calibrated uncertainty; (3) Blind pre-registered tests on two unseen configurations; (4) A "trap-language" experiment to test false-alarm rates; (5) Gap-origin study varying learning rate and batch size; (6) Cross-model validation across three public model families (Pythia, OLMo, OLMo-2) with 7 suites; (7) Manufacturing 33 negative examples to certify false-alarm rates. All experiments were pre-registered with public commit chains.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Previous-token head formation predicts induction-head emergence with rho=0.977 and median 975-step lead (~15% of training); (2) Best-case loss rule achieves 50-step lead (nowcast); (3) Conformal intervals covered 15/15 held-out seeds; (4) Frozen rule passed blind tests (10/10 and 9/10 coverage); (5) Trap-language revealed bare precursor false-alarms on 10/10 capability-blocked runs while mechanism-composed conjunction achieves 0 false alarms with rho=1.000; (6) Gap-origin study found anchor fires at 0.843 of time-to-emergence (t_event ≈ 1.19 × t_anchor), passing blind gate (5/5); (7) OLMo-2 at 1B tokens showed precursor formed but capability absent; (8) Four pre-registered kill criteria were reported.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides strong evidence that emergent capabilities in AI models are forecastable with calibrated uncertainty, not truly unpredictable. The previous-token head serves as a reliable precursor indicator, and a multiplicative law (t_event ≈ 1.19 × t_anchor) governs emergence timing. The rigorous methodology—including blind tests, negative examples, and pre-registration—suggests these findings are robust. The authors note that "every freeze precedes its data in a public commit chain," enabling reproducibility. This work challenges the notion of emergence as fundamentally unpredictable and opens avenues for forecasting and potentially controlling capability emergence in AI systems.

title: Track, Articulate, Act: Generating Articulation from Casual Human Videos
summary: Human videos contain rich causal evidence for robot manipulation: they reveal how hand motion induces object motion and produces task-relevant changes in object state. In this work, we study articulated objects such as doors, drawers, cabinets, laptops, ovens, and hinged containers that are ubiquitous in daily life and present unique challenges for embodied interaction. These objects cannot be represented by a single pose; their motion depends on the underlying parts and joints. We introduce a real-to-sim framework that reconstructs a simulation-ready articulated object and hand-object interaction from a casual monocular RGB video, without RGB-D or multi-view input, prior scans, manually specified joints, or robot demonstrations. Our key insight is that dense 3D point tracks provide an embodiment-agnostic articulation cue: points on the fixed link remain approximately stationary, while points on the moving link follow coherent revolute or prismatic motion. Our method segments the links, estimates the joint and its state trajectory, reconstructs an articulated asset, and aligns the recovered 3D hand motion with the object. Central to our approach is a modular recipe that repurposes powerful pretrained models for single-image 3D reconstruction, mesh segmentation, and 3D scene flow, connecting their predictions through explicit geometric reasoning to infer articulation. We use the reconstructed articulated object and the human hand trajectory to replay interactions through contact in MuJoCo. The framework shows how pretrained vision models and explicit motion reasoning can turn casual human videos into articulated object models suitable for downstream embodied interactions. https://track-articulate-act.github.io/

AI.tldr: A framework that reconstructs simulation-ready articulated objects and hand-object interactions from casual monocular RGB videos, using dense 3D point tracks as articulation cues and pretrained vision models with explicit geometric reasoning.
AI.motivation: Articulated objects (doors, drawers, cabinets, etc.) are ubiquitous in daily life but present unique challenges for embodied interaction because their motion depends on underlying parts and joints, not a single pose. Current methods require RGB-D, multi-view input, prior scans, or robot demonstrations, which limits scalability. The authors aim to extract causal evidence from human videos showing how hand motion induces object motion.
AI.method: The key insight is that dense 3D point tracks provide embodiment-agnostic articulation cues: points on fixed links remain stationary while points on moving links follow coherent revolute or prismatic motion. The method uses a modular recipe repurposing pretrained models for single-image 3D reconstruction, mesh segmentation, and 3D scene flow, connecting predictions through explicit geometric reasoning to: (1) segment links, (2) estimate joint and state trajectory, (3) reconstruct articulated asset, and (4) align recovered 3D hand motion with the object. Interactions are replayed through contact in MuJoCo.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates that pretrained vision models and explicit motion reasoning can turn casual human videos into articulated object models suitable for downstream embodied interactions.
AI.conclusion: This work enables real-to-sim reconstruction of articulated objects from casual monocular RGB videos without specialized sensors, prior scans, or robot demonstrations, opening possibilities for large-scale training data collection from human videos.

title: CompileRover: Revolutionizing Virtual Machine Compiler Optimization with a Tri-Role LLM-Driven Framework
summary: Code optimization plays a crucial role in the development of virtual machine compilers, with optimization frameworks significantly enhancing the performance of generated assembly code. However, existing virtual machine compiler outputs frequently exhibit redundant computations, inefficient loop structures, and suboptimal function implementations, which collectively impair execution efficiency. To address these shortcomings, we propose CompileRover, an advanced optimization framework specifically designed for virtual machine compilers. CompileRover employs a sophisticated three-role collaboration mechanism, comprising a referee, an advisor, and an operator, effectively overcoming performance bottlenecks by leveraging comprehensive optimization algorithms and novel methodologies, including control flow analysis, code structure transformations, and dynamic execution pattern recognition. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that CompileRover consistently surpasses state-of-the-art virtual machine compilers, achieving significant improvements in execution performance across various benchmarks. Furthermore, performance analyses validate that the introduced optimizations notably reduce execution overhead, improve dataflow consistency, and robustly enhance compiler performance, showcasing CompileRover as an effective and reliable approach to optimizing virtual machine compilers.

AI.tldr: CompileRover is an optimization framework for virtual machine compilers that uses a three-role collaboration mechanism (referee, advisor, operator) to overcome performance bottlenecks through control flow analysis, code structure transformations, and dynamic execution pattern recognition.
AI.motivation: Existing virtual machine compiler outputs exhibit redundant computations, inefficient loop structures, and suboptimal function implementations, impairing execution efficiency.
AI.method: The proposed framework employs a three-role collaboration mechanism comprising a referee, an advisor, and an operator, leveraging comprehensive optimization algorithms including control flow analysis, code structure transformations, and dynamic execution pattern recognition.
AI.result: CompileRover consistently surpasses state-of-the-art virtual machine compilers, achieving significant improvements in execution performance across various benchmarks. The optimizations notably reduce execution overhead and improve dataflow consistency.
AI.conclusion: CompileRover represents an effective and reliable approach to optimizing virtual machine compilers, demonstrating robust performance enhancement capabilities.

title: Adaptive Convolutional Sparse Coding via Information Bottleneck for Robust Visual Signal Representation
summary: Visual signals require compact yet sufficient representations for robust downstream prediction. Convolutional sparse coding (CSC) provides an explicit mechanism for suppressing redundant components while preserving signal content, but its sparsity coefficient is typically fixed and manually selected. We propose an adaptive convolutional sparse coding framework for robust visual signal representation. Specifically, we unfold the CSC optimization with the Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA) and treat the sparsity coefficient as a differentiable variable jointly learned with the network parameters. From the information bottleneck perspective, this coefficient controls the trade-off between information retention and compression: the sparsity term promotes compact representations, while the reconstruction term together with task loss preserves task-relevant signal content. We further introduce a label-free post-training strategy that adjusts the compression strength for corrupted inputs with the main network parameters fixed. Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate competitive clean-data recognition and greatly improved robustness under different input perturbations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive convolutional sparse coding (CSC) framework that treats sparsity coefficients as differentiable variables learned jointly with network parameters, inspired by the information bottleneck principle. A label-free post-training strategy is also introduced to adjust compression for corrupted inputs.
AI.motivation: Traditional convolutional sparse coding uses fixed, manually-selected sparsity coefficients, which may not be optimal for different data or corruptions. The authors aim to learn adaptive sparsity coefficients automatically and improve robustness to input perturbations.
AI.method: The method unfolds CSC optimization using FISTA (Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm) and treats the sparsity coefficient as a differentiable variable jointly learned with network parameters. They also introduce a label-free post-training strategy to adjust compression for corrupted inputs while keeping main network parameters fixed.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet show competitive clean-data recognition accuracy and significantly improved robustness under various input perturbations.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive CSC framework, with its learnable sparsity coefficients and post-training strategy, effectively balances information retention and compression for robust visual signal representation.

title: Tabular Deep Learning vs Classical Machine Learning for Urban Land Cover Classification
comment: Published in NeurIPS 2025 The 5th Muslims In ML (MusIML) Workshop
summary: Urban Land Cover (ULC) classification plays a crucial role in urban planning, environmental monitoring, and sustainable development. We study this task using the ULC dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, which includes tabular features derived from high-resolution aerial imagery across nine classes (e.g., roads, trees, grass, water). The dataset presents typical remote sensing challenges, including high dimensionality, heterogeneous features, and class imbalance. In a unified, reproducible pipeline, we benchmark classical machine learning models (e.g., Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost) against Tabular Deep Learning (TDL) models (TabNet, FT-Transformer, TabTransformer, TabSeq, and 1D CNNs). To address class imbalance, we employ weighted cross-entropy loss for TDL models and evaluate performance using accuracy, macro-precision, macro-recall, macro-F1, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices. Our results show that while tree ensembles remain strong general baselines, TDL models can match or exceed their performance when non-linear interactions are significant and imbalance handling is effective, providing complementary advantages for urban land cover mapping. See code: https://github.com/mtesha/tdl-vs-ml-urbanlandcover

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks classical machine learning models (Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost) against Tabular Deep Learning models (TabNet, FT-Transformer, TabTransformer, TabSeq, 1D CNNs) for Urban Land Cover classification using the UCI dataset with 9 classes. Tree ensembles remain strong baselines, but TDL models can match or exceed their performance when non-linear interactions are significant and imbalance handling is effective.
AI.motivation: Urban Land Cover classification is crucial for urban planning, environmental monitoring, and sustainable development. The task faces challenges including high dimensionality, heterogeneous features, and class imbalance. There is a need to systematically compare classical ML approaches with modern Tabular Deep Learning (TDL) models.
AI.method: A unified, reproducible pipeline is developed to benchmark classical ML models against TDL models. Weighted cross-entropy loss is employed for TDL models to address class imbalance. Performance is evaluated using accuracy, macro-precision, macro-recall, macro-F1, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices.
AI.result: Tree ensembles (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost) remain strong general baselines. TDL models (TabNet, FT-Transformer, TabTransformer, TabSeq, 1D CNNs) can match or exceed their performance when non-linear interactions are significant and imbalance handling is effective, providing complementary advantages for urban land cover mapping.
AI.conclusion: TDL models offer competitive performance to classical ML methods, especially in scenarios with significant non-linear interactions and effective class imbalance handling. The choice between classical and deep learning approaches should consider the specific characteristics of the dataset.

title: In-Context Robot Learning with VLM Agents
comment: Project Page: https://cheng-haha.github.io/GPT-Policy GitHub Code: https://github.com/cheng-haha/GPT-Policy
summary: Enabling robots to adapt to unfamiliar environments as readily as humans remains a moonshot goal of embodied AI. No finite collection of demonstrations can cover every task and situation a robot will encounter, making the ability to learn from context at deployment essential for generalization. Such in-context learning (ICL), however, remains largely beyond the reach of existing robotic policies. The broad agentic capabilities of commercial vision-language models (VLMs), such as GPT-6 Astra, raise a compelling question: can these models learn from demonstrations, examples, and interaction feedback, then translate that information into executable and verifiable robot behavior from a new initial state without gradient updates or persistent changes to task-specific parameters? We introduce GPT-Policy, a general-agent framework for in-context robot learning. GPT-Policy integrates a context compiler that preserves task-relevant visual transitions, a VLM that proposes robot-tool actions, and a constrained controller that verifies and executes each action and reports its outcome. We evaluate its reliability and limitations through task success and efficiency metrics, matched comparisons across models, and controlled context ablations. In real-robot trials, human video demonstrations improve task completion even without robot action labels, while aligned action references yield further gains on contact-sensitive tasks. These findings position GPT-Policy as a step toward robot adaptation through in-context learning, providing an empirical foundation for translating the general-purpose capabilities of VLMs into physical behavior and clarifying the challenges that must be overcome for reliable deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GPT-Policy, a framework enabling robots to learn from context (demonstrations, examples, feedback) at deployment using vision-language models like GPT-6 Astra, without gradient updates. It integrates a context compiler, VLM for action proposal, and constrained controller for execution verification.
AI.motivation: The goal is to enable robots to adapt to unfamiliar environments as readily as humans through in-context learning (ICL). Current robotic policies cannot learn from context at deployment without gradient updates, limiting generalization to new tasks and situations.
AI.method: GPT-Policy integrates three components: (1) context compiler preserving task-relevant visual transitions, (2) VLM (GPT-6 Astra) proposing robot-tool actions, and (3) constrained controller verifying and executing each action while reporting outcomes. Evaluation includes task success/efficiency metrics, model comparisons, and controlled context ablations on real robots.
AI.result: In real-robot trials, human video demonstrations improve task completion even without robot action labels. Aligned action references yield further gains on contact-sensitive tasks.
AI.conclusion: GPT-Position represents a step toward robot adaptation through in-context learning, providing empirical foundation for translating general-purpose VLM capabilities into physical behavior. It clarifies challenges for reliable deployment.

title: TwinMark: A Unified Watermark for Provable Survival Under Feature and Logit Distillation
summary: We propose TwinMark, a watermarking scheme that reads a single SHAKE128 secret through two complementary linear functionals of model-output summaries: a covariance projector against the carrier-set covariance (cov-Feat) and a class-conditional Fisher-aligned linear carrier decoded from class-mean logits (cc-FALC). The two readouts share one bit vector and cover the two extraction surfaces of a deployed vision model: a classifier API attacked by KL knowledge distillation (KD) (Std. KL-KD), and a representation-only host attacked by feature-matching KD (FM-KD). Each readout admits a teacher-measurable a posteriori certificate that lower-bounds post-distillation detection power, and the two channels combine under a regime-restricted OR rule whose test statistic (calibrated null or bit vote) is selected by the exposed surface. cov-Feat admits a rank-blind operator-norm certificate, cc-FALC admits a centered-logit-gap certificate that decouples bit capacity from class count: at K=1024 in m=100 classes (a 10.24x over-encoding), the bit-vote attains z=23.0 sigma at a teacher-accuracy cost of +0.9+-0.2%p. Across 13 attacks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Mini-ImageNet, TwinMark verifies on every cell whose post-attack model retains task utility, survives cross-architecture distillation onto ResNet-18/50, VGG-16, and MobileNet-V3, and ports to GNSS few-shot, VOC detection, ISIC segmentation, and STL-10 SimCLR.

AI.tldr: TwinMark is a dual-channel watermarking scheme that protects machine learning models from knowledge distillation attacks by using two complementary readouts (cov-Feat and cc-FALC) from a single SHAKE128 secret, with certificates that guarantee detection power post-distillation.
AI.motivation: Protect deployed ML models from knowledge distillation attacks where attackers use model outputs to train unauthorized copies. Existing watermarking schemes fail against modern distillation techniques (KL-KD and FM-KD) that target different model components.
AI.method: TwinMark uses two complementary linear functionals: (1) cov-Feat - a covariance projector against carrier-set covariance, and (2) cc-FALC - class-conditional Fisher-aligned linear carrier from class-mean logits. Both read from the same secret key and combine under a regime-restricted OR rule. Each readout provides a certificate: rank-blind operator-norm for cov-Feat, centered-logit-gap for cc-FALC.
AI.result: At K=1024 bits with m=100 classes (10.24x over-encoding), achieves z=23.0 sigma detection with only +0.9±0.2% teacher accuracy cost. Verified across 13 attacks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Mini-ImageNet. Survives cross-architecture distillation onto ResNet-18/50, VGG-16, and MobileNet-V3. Successfully ports to GNSS few-shot, VOC detection, ISIC segmentation, and STL-10 SimCLR.
AI.conclusion: TwinMark provides robust watermarking that survives both standard KL-KD and feature-matching KD attacks across multiple datasets, architectures, and tasks. The dual-channel design with certificates ensures detection even when one extraction surface is compromised.

title: PointZero: 3D Point Track Completion for Learning Transferable 3D Dynamics
summary: World models endow perceptual systems with the ability to predict how scenes evolve under interaction. They are most beneficial when trained on diverse volumes of data, to instill a rich prior into downstream applications. Existing methods typically require robot action labels to learn action-conditioned 3D dynamics, which excludes web video data from the training pool. We study 3D point track completion as a pre-training objective for learning transferable 3D dynamics without robot data. Given a single RGB-D observation and sparse partial 3D trajectories (tracks), we predict future 3D tracks of all observed points. We show this objective produces a rich 3D dynamics prior, without requiring robot action labels. We contribute a diverse dataset of 2.9 million synthetic frames spanning deformable, articulated, and rigid objects, and use it to train PointZero. We show that a flexible and expressive transformer, PointZero, outperforms prior methods on the same data. We demonstrate the utility of our pre-training objective by post-training PointZero for two downstream applications: (1) action-conditioned 3D dynamics prediction and (2) imitation learning. When fine-tuned to condition on end-effector pose, PointZero outperforms the baselines on the recent PGND 3D dynamics benchmark. When fine-tuned to predict robot actions and 3D tracks, PointZero outperforms or matches the baselines on 6/7 simulated and real-world robot manipulation tasks. We furthermore evaluate training PointZero from scratch to isolate the benefits of our proposed architecture from those of our proposed pre-training objective and dataset. We release the dataset, checkpoints, and full training recipe.

AI.tldr: PointZero is a transformer-based model that learns 3D dynamics prior through point track completion (predicting future 3D trajectories from sparse partial tracks), trained on 2.9M synthetic frames without requiring robot action labels, and can be fine-tuned for downstream tasks like action-conditioned dynamics prediction and imitation learning.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for learning action-conditioned 3D dynamics require robot action labels, excluding web video data from training. The authors aim to learn transferable 3D dynamics without robot data by using a pre-training objective that doesn't require action labels.
AI.method: The authors propose 3D point track completion as a pre-training objective: given a single RGB-D observation and sparse partial 3D trajectories, predict future 3D tracks of all observed points. They contribute a diverse dataset of 2.9 million synthetic frames spanning deformable, articulated, and rigid objects, and train PointZero (a transformer-based model) on this data.
AI.result: PointZero outperforms prior methods on the same data. When fine-tuned for action-conditioned 3D dynamics prediction on the PGND benchmark, it outperforms baselines. When fine-tuned for imitation learning (predicting robot actions and 3D tracks), it outperforms or matches baselines on 6/7 simulated and real-world robot manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pre-training objective (3D point track completion) produces a rich 3D dynamics prior without requiring robot action labels. The approach demonstrates that learning from diverse synthetic data with this objective can effectively transfer to downstream robotics tasks like dynamics prediction and imitation learning.

title: Integrated Optimization of Automated Warehouse Operations and Last-Mile Transport for Differentiated On-Demand Delivery
summary: In the context of differentiated on-demand goods delivery services, this study proposes an integrated optimization method for automated guided vehicles (AGVs) based smart warehouse operations and the last-mile multi-modal transport. A deep reinforcement learning algorithm for multi-objective joint scheduling is designed to establish a dynamic connection between two systems, solving key challenges such as achieving high-throughput continuous order scheduling, meeting competing requirements, and improving the overall system sensitivity and adaptability. For warehouse optimization within this framework, we propose an improved algorithm based on multi-objective, Multi-Reward Machines-A* Guided Deep Q-Network (MORM-AGDQN), which combines service level, system cost, and external transportation demand. For external optimization, we propose an improved algorithm based on a Multi-Reward, Multi Head attention-Heterogeneous Capacity Vehicle Routing Problem (MRMH-HCVRP) framework, which incorporates the optimized scheduling order sequence and grouping, combined with customer location, demand, and priority, vehicle capacity, speed, and service range. The results show that the proposed framework significantly outperforms traditional methods, achieving 100% on-time delivery rate for warehousing operations. After joint optimization, the average delivery time for the last mile was reduced by 29.3% to 53.2%, the total transportation distance was reduced by 46.4%, the high-priority service rate was increased to over 92%, and a balance was maintained between operating costs and customer satisfaction.

AI.tldr: This study proposes an integrated optimization framework combining automated guided vehicles (AGVs) for smart warehouse operations with last-mile multi-modal transport using deep reinforcement learning. The framework uses MORM-AGDQN for warehouse optimization and MRMH-HCVRP for external transport optimization, achieving 100% on-time delivery rate, 29.3-53.2% reduction in delivery time, 46.4% reduction in transportation distance, and over 92% high-priority service rate.
AI.motivation: The research addresses key challenges in integrating warehouse operations with last-mile delivery: achieving high-throughput continuous order scheduling, meeting competing requirements (service level vs. cost), and improving system sensitivity and adaptability in differentiated on-demand goods delivery services.
AI.method: Two improved algorithms are proposed: (1) MORM-AGDQN (Multi-Reward Machines-A* Guided Deep Q-Network) for warehouse optimization combining service level, system cost, and external transportation demand; (2) MRMH-HCVRP (Multi-Reward, Multi Head attention-Heterogeneous Capacity Vehicle Routing Problem) for external optimization incorporating scheduling order sequence, grouping, customer location, demand, priority, vehicle capacity, speed, and service range.
AI.result: The proposed framework significantly outperforms traditional methods: 100% on-time delivery rate for warehousing operations; average delivery time reduced by 29.3% to 53.2%; total transportation distance reduced by 46.4%; high-priority service rate increased to over 92%; balance maintained between operating costs and customer satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: The integrated deep reinforcement learning approach successfully bridges warehouse and last-mile transport systems, achieving substantial improvements in efficiency, delivery speed, and service quality while balancing operational costs and customer satisfaction.

title: PANORAMA: Panoptic Grounded Captioning via Mask Proposal Selection
summary: Intelligent systems that act in the world require image understanding that is both comprehensive and spatially grounded. Current vision-language models (VLMs) can generate fluent and detailed image captions, but reliably associating them with image pixels remains challenging. Existing methods that combine dense captioning with pixel-level grounding often produce either incomplete descriptions or inaccurate segmentation masks. We study this problem through panoptic grounded captioning, a task that requires a VLM to describe both foreground objects and background regions while grounding each referring phrase with pixel-level masks. We make three contributions. First, we introduce PanoCaps, a human-annotated benchmark constructed from panoptic segmentation datasets. It provides dense captions with near-complete pixel coverage and image-text alignments at the entity level, supporting both training and evaluation. We further propose a phrase-mask matching protocol and a generalized Panoptic Quality (gPQ) metric that jointly evaluates textual and mask agreement. Second, we formulate phrase grounding as selection from a phrase-conditioned pool of mask proposals and introduce PANORAMA, a VLM that conditions a pretrained segmenter on contextualized phrase representations to obtain candidate masks and learns to select those corresponding to each phrase. Training this interface jointly with caption generation enables PANORAMA to produce high-quality masks while allowing each phrase to refer to a single region or multiple instances. Third, PANORAMA achieves the best overall grounding on PanoCaps and matches or exceeds specialized models across several pixel-level grounding tasks. Experiments show that our method produces precise entity-level segmentations while maintaining detailed, mask-consistent captions. Code, data and models are available at https://www.di.ens.fr/willow/research/panorama/.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of combining detailed image captioning with precise pixel-level grounding in vision-language models. The authors introduce PanoCaps (a benchmark for panoptic grounded captioning) and PANORAMA (a VLM that selects phrase-conditioned masks from a proposal pool). The method achieves state-of-the-art grounding performance while maintaining detailed, mask-consistent captions.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs can generate fluent image captions but struggle to reliably associate them with specific image pixels. Existing methods combining dense captioning with pixel-level grounding often produce incomplete descriptions or inaccurate segmentation masks. There is a need for a unified task (panoptic grounded captioning) that requires describing both foreground objects and background regions with pixel-level mask grounding for each phrase.
AI.method: The authors make three contributions: (1) PanoCaps - a human-annotated benchmark providing dense captions with near-complete pixel coverage and entity-level image-text alignments; (2) A phrase-mask matching protocol and generalized Panoptic Quality (gPQ) metric for evaluation; (3) PANORAMA - a VLM that formulates phrase grounding as selection from a phrase-conditioned pool of mask proposals. The method conditions a pretrained segmenter on contextualized phrase representations to generate candidate masks, then learns to select masks corresponding to each phrase. Training is done jointly with caption generation.
AI.result: PANORAMA achieves the best overall grounding performance on PanoCaps and matches or exceeds specialized models across several pixel-level grounding tasks. The method produces precise entity-level segmentations while maintaining detailed, mask-consistent captions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed panoptic grounded captioning task and PANORAMA model successfully bridge the gap between detailed image captioning and precise pixel-level grounding. The PanoCaps benchmark and gPQ metric provide valuable resources for future research in spatially-grounded image understanding.

title: LightSleepX: A Lightweight, Inception-Based Dual-Modal Network for Sleep Staging
summary: Automatic sleep staging is fundamental to personal health monitoring, yet many existing approaches are ill-suited for real-world applications. Traditional pipelines often rely on hand-crafted features or shallow machine learning models that struggle to generalize, while state-of-the-art deep learning methods, though accurate, are computationally heavy and impractical for resource-constrained environments. This paper introduces LightSleepX, a lightweight framework designed to deliver robust sleep analysis in resource-constrained environments. LightSleepX combines an Inception-style architecture with depthwise separable convolutions and Multi-scale Enhanced Attention for efficient multi-modal EEG/EOG feature extraction, and a Mamba encoder for rule-free long-range temporal modeling. On public benchmark datasets, LightSleepX achieves 85.9% accuracy and a 0.803 macro-F1 score on Sleep-EDF-20, and 81.8% accuracy and a 0.796 macro-F1 score on the cross-subject ISRUC-S3 dataset. With 0.049M parameters and 195.9 MFLOPs, the framework targets practical local deployment where computational cost and privacy are central constraints.

AI.tldr: LightSleepX is a lightweight automatic sleep staging framework combining Inception-style architecture, depthwise separable convolutions, Multi-scale Enhanced Attention, and a Mamba encoder for efficient multi-modal EEG/EOG feature extraction and long-range temporal modeling. It achieves 85.9%/81.8% accuracy on Sleep-EDF-20 and ISRUC-S3 datasets with only 0.049M parameters and 195.9 MFLOPs.
AI.motivation: Traditional sleep staging approaches either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow models that struggle to generalize, or use computationally heavy deep learning methods impractical for resource-constrained environments. There is a need for accurate yet lightweight frameworks for practical local deployment where computational cost and privacy are central constraints.
AI.method: LightSleepX combines: (1) Inception-style architecture with depthwise separable convolutions for efficient multi-modal EEG/EOG feature extraction; (2) Multi-scale Enhanced Attention for enhanced feature representation; (3) Mamba encoder for rule-free long-range temporal modeling. The framework is evaluated on Sleep-EDF-20 and ISRUC-S3 datasets.
AI.result: On Sleep-EDF-20: 85.9% accuracy, 0.803 macro-F1. On ISRUC-S3 (cross-subject): 81.8% accuracy, 0.796 macro-F1. Model size: 0.049M parameters, 195.9 MFLOPs.
AI.conclusion: LightSleepX successfully delivers robust sleep analysis in resource-constrained environments with state-of-the-art accuracy while maintaining extremely low computational cost (0.049M params, 195.9 MFLOPs), making it suitable for practical local deployment where computational cost and privacy are key constraints.

title: RLLBC-Lib: An Educational Code Library for Reinforcement Learning and Learning-Based Control
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an exciting concept as well as a remarkable success story worth sharing. However, RL builds on rather complex interactions between different objects that play out over several cycles. Such dynamics are often best explained with an easily accessible implementation. We present RLLBC-Lib, a carefully crafted code library with the goal of lowering the entry barrier for students and other learners of RL in the context of learning-based control. At its heart, RLLBC-Lib comprises a comprehensive library of tabular RL approaches to enforce a clear understanding of the theoretical foundations. A deep RL library follows the same design principles, underscoring the parallels between simple tabular and state-of-the-art deep RL approaches. Additionally, RLLBC-Lib provides a collection of implementations illustrating core RL principles and contrasting RL to other learning-based control approaches. Finally, RLLBC-Lib provides an ideal basis for creating programming assignments with automated grading.

AI.tldr: RLLBC-Lib is a code library designed to lower the entry barrier for learning reinforcement learning (RL) in the context of learning-based control, featuring tabular RL approaches, deep RL implementations, and tools for automated grading.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning involves complex interactions between different objects that occur over multiple cycles, making it difficult for students and learners to grasp. The motivation is to provide an easily accessible implementation to explain these dynamics.
AI.method: The paper presents RLLBC-Lib, which includes: (1) a comprehensive library of tabular RL approaches to teach theoretical foundations, (2) a deep RL library following the same design principles to show parallels between tabular and deep RL, (3) implementations illustrating core RL principles and contrasting RL with other learning-based control approaches, and (4) tools for creating programming assignments with automated grading.
AI.result: RLLBC-Lib provides a carefully crafted code library that serves as an educational tool for teaching RL concepts, bridging the gap between simple tabular methods and state-of-the-art deep RL approaches.
AI.conclusion: RLLLBC-Lib is an effective educational resource that lowers the entry barrier for RL learners and provides an ideal basis for creating programming assignments with automated grading.
